• Kerala is known for its rich wetland ecosystems, including the famous **Vembanad Lake**, India's longest freshwater lake.
 
• The state has taken initiatives to conserve its wetlands under various schemes, including the **Ramsar Convention**, but it has not notified all wetlands under the Wetlands Rules, 2017.
 
• Kerala’s wetlands play a vital role in tourism, fisheries, and flood control, making their conservation crucial.

• The rules prohibit activities such as encroachment, dumping of solid waste, and discharge of untreated sewage within wetlands.
 
• They emphasize the importance of **wetland authorities** at the state level for sustainable management.
 
• Wetlands are vital for biodiversity, water purification, flood control, and climate change mitigation.

question:
Consider the following statements regarding India's Ramsar Sites:

1. India has the highest number of Ramsar sites in South Asia.

2. Keibul Lamjao is the only floating National Park in the world and is also a Ramsar site.

3. All Ramsar sites in India are located in coastal regions.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 and 2 are correct**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__
 

__ 
 
• **India has the highest number of Ramsar sites in South Asia:** 
 
• As of **2023**, India has **75 Ramsar sites**, the highest in South Asia. 
 
• The Ramsar Convention is an international treaty aimed at the conservation and sustainable use of wetlands. 
 
• The designation of these sites highlights India’s commitment to wetland conservation. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.* 
 
 

 
• **Keibul Lamjao National Park:** 
 
• Located in **Manipur**, it is the **only floating National Park** in the world. 
 
• It is situated on the **Loktak Lake**, a Ramsar site, and is known for its unique floating vegetation called **phumdis**. 
 
• It is also the habitat of the endangered **Sangai deer** (Manipur's state animal). *Hence, statement 2 is correct.* 
 
 

 
• **All Ramsar sites in India are not located in coastal regions:** 
 
• Ramsar sites in India are spread across both **coastal** and **inland regions**. 
 
• For example, **Sambhar Lake (Rajasthan)** and **Wular Lake (Jammu & Kashmir)** are inland Ramsar sites. 
 
• This makes the statement that all Ramsar sites are located in coastal regions incorrect. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.* 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Ramsar Convention:** 
 
• It was adopted on **2 February 1971** in the city of Ramsar, Iran. 
 
• The aim is the **conservation and wise use of wetlands** through local, regional, and national actions and international cooperation. 
 
• India became a signatory to the Ramsar Convention in **1982**. 
 
 

 
• **Importance of Ramsar Sites:** 
 
• They are recognized for their **ecological, economic, cultural, and recreational value**. 
 
• Wetlands act as **natural water purifiers**, mitigate floods, and provide habitats for biodiversity. 
 
• Examples of Ramsar sites in India include **Chilika Lake (Odisha)**, **Sundarbans Wetland (West Bengal)**, and **Ashtamudi Wetland (Kerala)**. 
 
 

 
• **State-wise distribution of Ramsar Sites:** 
 
• India’s Ramsar sites are distributed across several states, including **Uttar Pradesh (10 sites)**, **Punjab (6 sites)**, and **Tamil Nadu (14 sites)**. 
 
• The diverse locations demonstrate the country’s varied geography and wetland ecosystems. 
 
 

 
• **Recent Additions:** 
 
• In **2022**, India added several Ramsar sites, including **Pallikaranai Marsh Reserve Forest** and **Sakhya Sagar Lake**. 
 
• These additions reflect India's proactive approach to wetland conservation. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Wetland Conservation in India:** 
 
• The **Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017** were introduced to regulate wetlands' use and ensure their conservation. 
 
• Wetlands International, an NGO, also works on wetland preservation in India. 
 
 

 
• **Global Ramsar Sites:** 
 
• As of 2023, there are over **2,500 Ramsar sites globally**, covering an area of more than **256 million hectares**. 
 
• Countries like the **United Kingdom** and **Mexico** also have a significant number of Ramsar sites. 
 
 
 
a1:T

question:
Consider the following statements on the International Big Cat Alliance:

1. India is the initiator and lead coordinator of the alliance.

2. It focuses on the conservation of 6 species of big cats.

3. The alliance promotes scientific data sharing among member nations.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Statement 1:** India is the initiator and lead coordinator of the International Big Cat Alliance. *This statement is correct as India has spearheaded the establishment of the alliance to enhance conservation efforts for big cats globally.* 
• **Statement 2:** The alliance focuses on the conservation of 6 species of big cats. *This statement is incorrect as the alliance focuses on the conservation of 7 species of big cats: namely, tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar, and puma.* 
• **Statement 3:** The alliance promotes scientific data sharing among member nations. *This statement is correct as the alliance aims to foster collaboration and exchange of scientific data, best practices, and resources for big cat conservation.* 
• *Based on the analysis, only statements 1 and 3 are correct, making **Option 2** the correct answer.* 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **International Big Cat Alliance (IBCA):** 
• Launched in **2023** during the G20 presidency held by India. 
• Focuses on the conservation of big cats across the globe, including fostering cooperation among member nations. 
• Member nations include countries that are home to big cats as well as those interested in their conservation. 
• **Big Cats:** 
• The term "big cats" refers to 7 species: **tiger, lion, leopard, snow leopard, cheetah, jaguar, and puma.** 
• They are apex predators and play a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance. 
• India hosts populations of **tigers, lions, leopards, and snow leopards**, and recently reintroduced cheetahs from Namibia. 
• **Scientific Collaboration in Conservation:** 
• IBCA emphasizes sharing **scientific data** to enhance knowledge about big cat populations, habitats, and threats. 
• Promotes the use of advanced technologies like **camera traps, satellite tracking, and genetic studies** for conservation efforts. 
• **India’s Role in Conservation:** 
• India has been a global leader in big cat conservation with initiatives like **Project Tiger (1973)** and **Project Snow Leopard (2009)**. 
• India also successfully reintroduced **cheetahs** in Madhya Pradesh under its conservation efforts. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Global Big Cat Threats:** 
• Big cats face threats like **habitat loss, poaching, human-wildlife conflict, and climate change**. 
• Conservation efforts are essential to prevent their extinction. 
• **Conservation Funding:** 
• IBCA aims to mobilize resources and funding for conservation projects globally. 
• Promotes partnerships with **NGOs, governments, and private stakeholders**.

question: The UN Sustainable Development Report 2024 primarily tracks progress towards which global goals?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Sustainable Development Goals**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** were adopted by the **United Nations Member States** in **2015** as a universal call to action to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure peace and prosperity for all by **2030**.
 
• The **SDGs** consist of **17 goals** and **169 targets**, aimed at addressing a wide range of global challenges, including poverty, inequality, climate change, environmental degradation, and justice.
 
• The **UN Sustainable Development Report 2024** primarily tracks progress made towards achieving these goals by analyzing data from countries and presenting an annual assessment of efforts and outcomes.
 
• Each goal under the **SDGs** is interconnected, emphasizing the need for coordinated actions across sectors such as health, education, energy, and environmental sustainability.
 
• The report utilizes tools like the **Sustainable Development Goals Index** to rank countries based on their performance towards achieving the SDGs, encouraging international collaboration and accountability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Millennium Development Goals (MDGs):**

 
 
• The **MDGs** were a precursor to the SDGs and focused on eight goals to combat poverty, hunger, disease, illiteracy, environmental degradation, and discrimination by **2015**.
 
• While significant progress was made under the MDGs, they were criticized for their limited scope, which led to the broader and more inclusive framework of the SDGs.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Protection Goals:**
 
 
• These goals are often part of larger frameworks like the SDGs, focusing on issues such as **climate action, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable resource management**.
 
• While they are critical, they are not the primary focus of the **UN Sustainable Development Report 2024**, which tracks the SDGs comprehensively.
 
 
 
• **Human Rights Goals:**
 
 
• The SDGs incorporate elements of human rights, such as **gender equality, reduced inequality, and justice**, making them a universal framework that aligns closely with human rights principles.
 
• However, human rights goals as a standalone category are not directly tracked by the **UN Sustainable Development Report**.
 
 
 
• **Sustainable Development Goals Index:**
 
 
• The **SDG Index** ranks countries annually based on their progress toward achieving the 17 SDGs.
 
• It uses metrics such as **healthcare access, education quality, renewable energy use, and environmental conservation** to evaluate performance.
 
• This index is a central feature of the **UN Sustainable Development Report**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Features of the SDGs:**

 
 
• The SDGs apply to all countries, emphasizing **universal goals** rather than being limited to developing nations.
 
• They integrate **social, economic, and environmental dimensions** of sustainable development.
 
• Each goal has specific **indicators and targets** to measure progress.
 
 
 
• **Global Partnerships:**
 
 
• The SDGs highlight the importance of **collaborative efforts** across governments, NGOs, private sector, and academia.
 
• Goal 17 specifically emphasizes **Partnerships for the Goals** to mobilize resources for achieving the targets.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Implementation:**
 
 
• Challenges include **data availability, financing gaps, political will, and global inequalities**.
 
• The **UN Sustainable Development Report** provides insights and recommendations to address these challenges.

question: A saturated geological unit which can yield water to the wells at a sufficient rate to support a well is called ______.
solution:
The correct answer is an __**aquifer**__.

__
 
• A saturated** geological unit** that can **yield water **to the **wells** at a sufficient rate to support a well is called an **aquifer**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

__
 
• An **aquifer** is a body of porous **rock or sediment **saturated with **groundwater**. Groundwater enters an** aquifer** as precipitation seeps through the **soil**. It can move through the **aquifer** and **resurface through springs and wells.**
 
• There are **two general types** of **aquifers**: **confined **and** unconfined**.
 
 
• **Confined aquifers** have a layer of impenetrable** rock or clay above them**, while **unconfined aquifers** lie below a **permeable layer of soil.**
 
 
 
• Many different types of sediments and rocks can form **aquifers**, including **gravel, sandstone, conglomerates**, and **fractured limestone.**
 
• A common misconception about aquifers is that they are **underground rivers or lakes. **While groundwater can seep into or out of aquifers due to their porous nature, it cannot move fast enough to **flow like a river.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

__
 
• **Karst:**__

 __
 
• ​Karst is a type of landscape where the dissolving of the bedrock has created sinkholes, sinking streams, caves, springs, and other characteristic features.
 
• Karst is associated with soluble rock types such as limestone, marble, and gypsum.
 
 
 
• **Estuary:**__
 __
 
• ​An estuary is a partially enclosed coastal body of brackish water with one or more rivers or streams flowing into it, and with a free connection to the open sea.
 
 
 
• **Reservoir:**__
 
 
• ​A reservoir is most commonly an enlarged natural or artificial lake created using a dam to store freshwater.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

• They are designed to divert water from streams and rivers to agricultural fields.
 
• These channels help in the efficient distribution of water across terraced fields.
 
 
 
• **Johads**
 
 
• Johads are small earthen check dams found in the state of Rajasthan.
 
• They are constructed to capture and store rainwater for recharging groundwater and providing water for agriculture and drinking.
 
• Johads play a vital role in improving the water table in arid and semi-arid regions.

• Kuls are water channels found in the mountainous regions of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.

question: Which of the following is the best definition of ecological efficiency?

options.text: The amount of energy utilised at different trophic levels in a food chain
The amount of energy stored at different trophic levels in a food chain
The ratio between the mass and the energy flow at different trophic levels in a food chain
The ratio between energy flows at different points in a food chain

solution:
The correct answer is __**The ratio between energy flows at different points in a food chain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Ecological efficiency refers to the efficiency with which energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next in a food chain.
 
• Typically, only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is passed on to the next level; this is known as the 10% law.
 
• This concept helps in understanding the energy dynamics and the structure of ecosystems.
 
• Higher trophic levels receive less energy, which explains why there are typically fewer organisms at higher levels in a food chain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trophic Levels**

 
 
• In ecology, a trophic level is the position that an organism occupies in a food chain.
 
• Primary producers (plants) are at the first trophic level, primary consumers (herbivores) at the second, secondary consumers (carnivores that eat herbivores) at the third, and so on.
 
 
 
• **Energy Flow**
 
 
• Energy flow in an ecosystem is one-way: from the sun to producers, then to consumers, and finally to decomposers.
 
• Energy is lost at each trophic level, primarily as heat resulting from metabolism.
 
 
 
• **10% Law**
 
 
• The 10% law states that only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level.
 
• This rule was first introduced by Raymond Lindeman in 1942.
 
 
 
• **Food Chain**
 
 
• A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms through which nutrients and energy pass as one organism eats another.
 
• In a food chain, each organism occupies a different trophic level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mist**

 
 
• Mist consists of small droplets of water suspended in the air.
 
• It is typically created when warm, moist air meets sudden cooling.
 
• Mist is less dense than fog and visibility is generally clearer than in fog conditions.
 
 
 
• **Blizzard**
 
 
• A blizzard is a severe snowstorm characterized by strong sustained winds of at least 35 mph (56 km/h).
 
• It typically lasts for a prolonged period—typically three hours or more.
 
• Blizzards can cause whiteout conditions and significant snow accumulation.
 
 
 
• **Frost**
 
 
• Frost refers to a thin layer of ice that forms on solid surfaces when the temperature drops below freezing.
 
• It typically occurs in clear, calm conditions where there is a loss of radiative heat.
 
• Frost can damage crops and other plants.

question: Under India's updated State Action Plan on Climate Change (SAPCC) for 2025, which sector received the highest budgetary allocation for climate adaptation?

__

• This step aligns with India's National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), which emphasizes resource efficiency, climate resilience, and sustainable development in agriculture and water management.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

question: Who founded the value of ‘G’?
solution:
The correct answer is **'__Henry Cavendish__'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __**Key points**__

 
• The **gravitational constant** (also known as the **universal gravitational constant**, the **Newtonian constant of gravitation**, or the **Cavendish gravitational constant**), denoted by the capital letter *G*, is an empirical physical constant involved in the calculation of gravitational effects in Sir Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation and in Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity.
 
• In Newton's law, it is the** proportionality constant** connecting the** gravitational force between two bodies with the product of their masses and the inverse square of their distance**.
 
• The Einstein field equations, it quantifies the relation between the** geometry of spacetime and the energy–momentum tensor** (also referred to as the stress–energy tensor).
 
• The measured value of the constant is known with some certainty t**o four significant digits.**
 
• In SI units, its value is approximately **6.674×10−¹¹ m³⋅kg−¹⋅s−²**
 
• The modern notation of Newton's law involving *G* was introduced in the 1890s by C. V. Boys.
 
• The first implicit measurement with an **accuracy within about 1%** is attributed to** Henry Cavendish in a 1798 experiment.**

question: Which famous experiment was done by Michael Faraday in 1831?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Discovery of electromagnetic induction**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Michael Faraday, an English scientist, conducted the famous experiment in 1831 which led to the discovery of electromagnetic induction.
 
• Electromagnetic induction is the process of generating an electromotive force (EMF) through the relative motion between a conductor and a magnetic field.
 
• This discovery paved the way for numerous technological advancements, including the development of electric generators and transformers.
 
• Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF in any closed circuit is equal to the rate of change of the magnetic flux through the circuit.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Electromagnetic Induction**

 
 
• Electromagnetic induction refers to the generation of an electric current by changing the magnetic field. This phenomenon is fundamental to many types of electrical devices, including generators and transformers.
 
• Faraday's Experiment: In 1831, Faraday discovered that when a magnet is moved in and out of a coil of wire, an electric current is induced in the wire. This is known as Faraday's law of induction.
 
• Lenz's Law: This law states that the direction of the induced current is such that it opposes the change in magnetic flux that caused it. This is a consequence of the law of conservation of energy.
 
• Applications: The principles of electromagnetic induction are applied in many devices, such as inductors, transformers, and many types of electrical generators.
 
 
 
• **Quantum Magnetometers**
 
 
• Quantum magnetometers are devices that measure magnetic fields using quantum effects. These are used in various applications, including medical imaging and geological surveys.
 
 
 
• **Law of Elasticity**
 
 
• The law of elasticity, also known as Hooke's Law, states that the deformation of a material is directly proportional to the force applied to it, provided the material's elastic limit is not exceeded.
 
 
 
• **Natural Radioactivity**
 
 
• Natural radioactivity refers to the spontaneous decay of unstable atomic nuclei, resulting in the emission of radiation. This phenomenon was discovered by Henri Becquerel in 1896.

question: Which of the following best reflects the fundamental objective of applying generative design in aerospace systems engineering?

options.text: Facilitating seamless integration of multi-payload platforms in shared bus structures
Optimizing mechanical configurations for minimum mass and maximum structural resilience
Enhancing life-support redundancies to meet crew safety protocols in deep-space missions
Designing adaptive thrust mechanisms to dynamically control orbital corrections

solution:
The correct answer is __**Optimizing mechanical configurations for minimum mass and maximum structural resilience**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Generative design** in aerospace engineering focuses on creating optimized mechanical configurations that minimize mass while maximizing structural resilience. This ensures the systems are lightweight yet durable enough to withstand extreme conditions.
 
• It leverages advanced **algorithmic design tools** and **AI-driven simulations** to explore multiple design options and choose the most efficient structure.
 
• Reducing mass is critical in aerospace systems as it directly impacts fuel efficiency, payload capacity, and overall mission success. Structural resilience ensures that components endure high stress and varying environmental conditions.
 
• The process integrates **finite element analysis (FEA)** and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) to test designs for their ability to handle pressure, temperature, and aerodynamic forces effectively.
 
• **Generative design** enables engineers to develop lightweight components such as fuselage structures, wing designs, and spacecraft bodies without compromising safety or performance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

While generative design can aid in achieving this, its focus is more on structural optimization. Hence, this statement is **incorrect**.
 
• **Enhancing life-support redundancies:** This pertains to ensuring crew safety in deep-space missions, which involves systems engineering but does not directly relate to the purpose of generative design. Hence, this statement is **incorrect**.
 
• **Designing adaptive thrust mechanisms:** Adaptive thrust mechanisms are crucial for orbital corrections but are more related to propulsion engineering rather than generative design's core objective. Hence, this statement is **incorrect**.
 
• **Applications of generative design:** Generative design is widely used in aerospace for creating lightweight and optimized components such as engine mounts, brackets, and spacecraft structures. It supports innovations in material science, such as using **carbon composites** and **additive manufacturing** techniques.
 
• **Advantages:** Generative design reduces design time, improves component efficiency, and supports sustainability by minimizing material usage.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Generative Design in Aerospace:** The aerospace industry extensively uses generative design to create structures that balance **lightweight design** and **structural durability**.
 
• **Historical Examples:** NASA and SpaceX utilize generative design for optimizing spacecraft components like **lander legs** and **fuselages**. For instance, SpaceX's Falcon series employs lightweight designs to maximize payload efficiency.
 
• **Material Science Integration:** Generative design often incorporates advanced materials like **titanium alloys** and **carbon fiber composites**, which are lightweight and strong.
 
• **Future Prospects:** With advancements in AI and machine learning, generative design will continue to play a crucial role in developing next-generation aerospace systems.

• The orbit's altitude is approximately **747 kilometers** above Earth, ensuring optimal radar imaging capabilities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO):**

 
 
• A GTO is an elliptical orbit used to transfer satellites from low Earth orbit to geostationary orbit.
 
• This orbit is commonly used for communication satellites that need to maintain a fixed position relative to Earth.
 
• However, NISAR does not use this orbit because it requires global coverage, which a geostationary satellite cannot provide.
 
 
 
• **Geostationary Earth Orbit (GEO):**
 
 
• Satellites in GEO orbit at an altitude of approximately 35,786 km and match Earth's rotation to stay over a fixed point.
 
• GEO is ideal for communication, weather monitoring, and broadcasting satellites.
 
• NISAR, designed for Earth observation, requires frequent revisits to different regions, making GEO unsuitable.
 
 
 
• **Low Earth Equatorial Orbit (LEEO):**
 
 
• LEEO is a type of low Earth orbit where satellites travel close to the equator.
 
• It is commonly used for regional observation and communication satellites.
 
• NISAR needs to monitor global phenomena, making polar sun-synchronous orbit a better choice.
 
 
 
• **Polar Sun-Synchronous Orbit:**
 
 
• This orbit combines polar coverage with consistent lighting conditions, making it suitable for imaging and remote sensing satellites like NISAR.
 
• It enables monitoring of the entire Earth’s surface, including polar regions, over time.
 
• Such orbits are used extensively in environmental studies, disaster monitoring, and climate research.

question: Aditya-L1 is placed in a halo orbit around which type of gravitationally balanced point in space?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lagrangian**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Aditya-L1 is India's first solar observatory mission, launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) to study the Sun.
 
• The spacecraft is placed in a halo orbit around the Lagrange Point 1 (L1), a specific location in space approximately 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
 
• Lagrange Points are positions where the gravitational forces of two large celestial bodies (such as the Earth and the Sun) and the centrifugal force balance each other.
 
• Placing Aditya-L1 at the L1 point allows continuous observation of the Sun without any occultation (eclipses) or interference from Earth's shadow.
 
• From this vantage point, Aditya-L1 can provide real-time data on solar activities such as solar wind, coronal mass ejections (CMEs), and solar flares, which are critical for understanding space weather.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Polar Orbit**

 
 
• A polar orbit is one in which a satellite passes over the Earth's poles during each revolution.
 
• Satellites in polar orbits have an inclination of close to 90 degrees and can provide complete coverage of the Earth's surface over time.
 
• This type of orbit is typically used for Earth observation, weather satellites, and reconnaissance missions.
 
• However, this orbit is not suitable for solar observations as it does not provide a constant view of the Sun.
 
 
 
• **Sun-synchronous Orbit**
 
 
• A Sun-synchronous orbit is a near-polar orbit that allows a satellite to pass over the same region of the Earth at the same local solar time.
 
• This orbit is often used for remote sensing and Earth observation satellites to ensure consistent lighting conditions for imaging.
 
• Sun-synchronous orbits are not designed for studying the Sun, as they are limited to Earth-centered applications.
 
 
 
• **Geostationary Orbit**
 
 
• A geostationary orbit is a circular orbit around the Earth with an altitude of approximately 35,786 kilometers, where a satellite appears stationary relative to a point on the Earth's surface.
 
• Satellites in geostationary orbits are primarily used for communication, weather monitoring, and broadcasting services.
 
• This orbit is not suitable for solar missions because it is Earth-centered and does not provide a stable vantage point for continuous Sun observation.
 
 
 
• **Lagrange Points and Aditya-L1**
 
 
• There are five Lagrange Points (L1 to L5) in a two-body system where gravitational and centrifugal forces balance out.
 
• The L1 point is located between the Earth and the Sun, providing a stable position for continuous solar observation.
 
• The halo orbit around L1 ensures that Aditya-L1 has an unobstructed view of the Sun and can carry out its mission objectives effectively.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Chandrayaan-1**, launched by the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) in October 2008, was India’s first lunar mission.
 
• The mission made a significant breakthrough by discovering **lunar hydration (water molecules)** on the Moon’s surface using NASA’s Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) instrument onboard.
 
• This discovery confirmed the presence of **hydroxyl (OH) and water (H2O) molecules** in the polar regions of the Moon.
 
• Chandrayaan-1 provided evidence of water ice in permanently shadowed craters near the Moon's poles, revolutionizing our understanding of lunar resources.
 
• The mission successfully functioned for **312 days** and significantly contributed to lunar science, including creating a detailed 3D atlas of the Moon's surface.

• It consisted of an orbiter, a lander named Vikram, and a rover named Pragyan.
 
• While the lander lost communication during its descent, the orbiter continues to function, sending valuable data about the Moon’s surface and exosphere.
 
• Chandrayaan-2 further refined the findings of Chandrayaan-1 regarding the presence of water molecules.
 
 
 
• **Chandrayaan-3**
 
 
• As of October 2023, Chandrayaan-3 is ISRO’s latest lunar mission and focuses on demonstrating safe landing and roving capabilities.
 
• It is a follow-up mission to Chandrayaan-2, consisting of a lander and rover but no orbiter.
 
• The primary goal is to ensure a successful soft landing on the Moon and study its surface composition and seismic activity.
 
 
 
• **Chandrayaan-4**
 
 
• Chandrayaan-4 is not an officially announced mission by ISRO as of now. It is speculated to be a potential future lunar mission.
 
• ISRO is currently focusing on Chandrayaan-3 and other interplanetary missions like Gaganyaan and Aditya-L1.
 
 
 
• **Lunar Hydration Discovery**
 
 
• The discovery of water on the Moon is crucial for future human exploration, as it can support life, act as a resource for producing oxygen, and be used as rocket fuel.
 
• This finding has reshaped strategies for lunar exploration, making the Moon a potential hub for space missions.

question: What happens if a satellite orbits Earth with 24-hour period?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Appears stationary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A satellite with a 24-hour orbital period is in a geostationary orbit if it orbits above the Earth's equator and follows the direction of Earth's rotation.
 
• Such satellites are positioned at an altitude of approximately 35,786 km (22,236 miles) from Earth's surface, ensuring that the satellite's orbital speed matches Earth's rotational speed.
 
• From an observer on Earth's surface, the satellite appears stationary in the sky because it maintains a fixed position relative to a specific point on Earth. ***Hence, the satellite appears stationary.***
 
• This phenomenon is essential for communication satellites and weather satellites, as it allows continuous coverage of a specific area on Earth without the need for tracking moving satellites.
 
• The concept of geostationary orbit was first proposed by Arthur C. Clarke in 1945, and it has since become a cornerstone in satellite technology.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geostationary Orbit (GEO):**

 
 
• A geostationary orbit is a circular orbit in the Earth's equatorial plane at an altitude where the orbital period is exactly 24 hours.
 
• It is also known as a Clarke Orbit, named after Arthur C. Clarke, who first proposed its use for communication satellites.
 
• This orbit is particularly useful for satellites that provide television broadcasting, weather monitoring, and communication services.
 
 
 
• **Orbital Mechanics:**
 
 
• The satellite must satisfy the condition of orbital resonance, meaning the satellite's orbital period matches Earth's rotational period.
 
• The force of gravity and the satellite's centrifugal force are balanced at this altitude, ensuring a stable orbit.
 
• A satellite in this orbit travels at a speed of approximately 3.07 km/s (11,068 km/h).
 
 
 
• **Applications of Geostationary Satellites:**
 
 
• Communication Satellites: Examples include INSAT series in India, which provide telecommunication, television, and meteorological services.
 
• Weather Satellites: These monitor weather patterns and provide real-time data for forecasts, such as NOAA's GOES satellites.
 
• Navigation Satellites: Some navigation systems use satellites in geostationary orbits to provide accurate positional data.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Geostationary Orbits:**
 
 
• The orbit lies directly above the Earth's equator (zero-degree latitude).
 
• The satellite's orbit is circular, not elliptical.
 
• These satellites always appear stationary relative to a fixed location on Earth's surface, which simplifies ground-based antenna design.
 
• Geostationary satellites provide coverage to approximately one-third of the Earth's surface.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 __

• **India’s Space Achievements:**

• The payload capacity of PSLV varies depending on the configuration, with a maximum capacity of around **1,750 kg to sun-synchronous orbit**.

• **Other Indian Launch Vehicles:** 
• ISRO operates other launch vehicles such as the **Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV)** and **GSLV Mk III**, which are designed for heavier payloads and higher orbits. 
• **Small Satellite Launch Vehicle (SSLV)** is ISRO's newest development, aimed at launching small payloads at lower costs.

• **Global Recognition:** PSLV's reliability and cost-effectiveness have attracted several countries to use its services for satellite launches. 
• **Historical Achievements:** PSLV contributed to India's first interplanetary mission, **Mangalyaan**, which successfully reached Mars in **2014**.

__
 
• **Space Situational Awareness (SSA)** is essential for tracking and monitoring **space debris**, which poses a threat to operational satellites and other space assets.
 
• SSA helps in **collision avoidance** by predicting potential impacts between operational satellites and debris, ensuring safe operations.
 
• It plays a critical role in protecting **India's space assets**, including satellites used for communication, navigation, weather forecasting, and defense purposes.

• Space debris includes defunct satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments from collisions or explosions in orbit.
 
• As of **2023**, there are over **34,000 pieces of debris larger than 10 cm** and millions of smaller fragments orbiting Earth.
 
• Debris travels at high speeds, making even small fragments capable of causing significant damage.
 
 
 
• **ISRO's SSA Program:**
 
 
• Launched as part of ISRO's **Directorate of Space Situational Awareness and Management (DSSAM)**.
 
• Includes initiatives like **Netra (Network for Space Object Tracking and Analysis)**, which monitors objects in low-Earth orbit and geostationary orbit.
 
• Netra uses **ground-based radar and optical telescopes** to track space objects and debris.
 
 
 
• **Global Context:**
 
 
• SSA programs are part of international efforts to ensure **space sustainability**.
 
• Organizations like **NASA**, **ESA (European Space Agency)**, and **JAXA (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency)** also have active SSA programs.
 
• The **United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA)** promotes guidelines to reduce space debris.
 
 
 
• **Challenges in Space Debris Management:**
 
 
• Identifying and tracking millions of debris fragments is technically challenging.
 
• Developing cost-effective methods for **debris removal** remains a major hurdle.
 
• International collaboration is required to ensure debris mitigation standards are followed universally.

• Protecting these assets is crucial for **national security**, economic development, and scientific progress.
 
 
 
• **Collision Avoidance Strategies:**
 
 
• Satellites can be maneuvered to avoid collisions using **propulsion systems**.
 
• Real-time tracking and prediction are critical for timely decision-making.
 
 
 
• **International Agreements:**

• Global cooperation is key to addressing space debris and ensuring sustainable exploration.

question: What distinguishes ISRO's Aditya-L1 mission from other solar observatories?

options.text: It uses radar waves to study the Sun
It will study the solar corona from Lagrange Point 1
It is placed in a lunar orbit

solution:
The correct answer is __**It will study the solar corona from Lagrange Point 1**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Aditya-L1 Mission:** The **Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO)** launched the Aditya-L1 mission as India's first dedicated solar observatory. It is designed to study the **Sun's atmosphere, including its corona, chromosphere, and photosphere.** 
• **Lagrange Point 1 (L1):** The spacecraft is positioned at **Lagrange Point 1**, which is located approximately **1.5 million kilometers from Earth**. This unique location provides an uninterrupted view of the Sun without being affected by Earth's shadow. 
• **Study of Solar Corona:** The Aditya-L1 mission focuses on studying the **solar corona**, the outermost layer of the Sun. The corona plays a critical role in understanding solar activities such as **solar flares and coronal mass ejections**, which can impact Earth's climate and satellite communications. 
• **Scientific Instruments:** The mission carries a suite of **seven payloads** designed to observe various layers of the Sun and analyze its magnetic field, solar wind, and particle behavior. These instruments aim to provide comprehensive data for solar physics research. 
• **Significance of L1 Point:** Lagrange Point 1 is strategically chosen for its ability to provide a stable vantage point to continuously monitor the Sun, making Aditya-L1 unique compared to other solar observatories that either orbit Earth or study the Sun from different perspectives. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Lagrange Points:** 
• Lagrange Points are positions in space where the gravitational forces of two large celestial bodies, such as the Earth and the Sun, balance the centripetal force felt by a smaller object. 
• There are **five Lagrange points (L1, L2, L3, L4, L5)**. Aditya-L1 is placed at L1, offering a stable location for continuous solar observations. 
• Spacecraft positioned at L1 can maintain their position with minimal fuel consumption, making it ideal for long-term missions. 
• **Solar Corona:** 
• The solar corona is the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere, extending millions of kilometers into space. 
• It is characterized by extremely high temperatures, reaching up to **1-3 million Kelvin**, much hotter than the surface of the Sun. 
• Studying the corona is crucial for understanding **space weather phenomena** that affect satellites, power grids, and communication systems on Earth. 
• **Payloads on Aditya-L1:** 
• The mission includes instruments such as **Visible Emission Line Coronagraph (VELC)**, Solar Ultraviolet Imaging Telescope (SUIT), and Plasma Analyser Package for Aditya (PAPA). 
• These payloads are designed to measure the Sun's magnetic fields, study solar winds, and capture high-resolution images of the solar atmosphere. 
• **Impact of Solar Studies:** 
• Understanding solar activities helps scientists predict **geomagnetic storms** and their effects on Earth's environment. 
• Solar research contributes to advancements in space exploration, satellite technology, and the protection of communication networks. 
• **Global Solar Observatories:** 
• Aditya-L1 joins the ranks of other solar observatories like NASA's **Parker Solar Probe** and the European Space Agency's **Solar Orbiter**. 
• While Parker Solar Probe approaches closer to the Sun, Aditya-L1's focus on the corona from L1 adds a unique dimension to global solar research. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **India's First Solar Mission:** Aditya-L1 marks India's entry into solar exploration, showcasing ISRO's capabilities in space science. 
• **Launch Details:** The mission was launched aboard the **PSLV-C57 rocket** from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. 
• **Collaborations:** The mission benefits from collaborations with scientific institutions like the **Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA)** and the **Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA)**. 
• **Long-Term Goals:** Data from Aditya-L1 will aid in developing predictive models for solar activities and their impact on space weather, benefiting both scientific research and practical applications. </ul

• Data collected by Aditya-L1 will help in understanding the **origin, propagation, and impact** of solar storms on Earth's magnetosphere. 
• **Lagrange Points:** 
• Lagrange Points are positions in space where the gravitational forces of two large celestial bodies (e.g., Earth and Sun) and the centrifugal force balance out. 
• The **L1 point** allows uninterrupted observations of the Sun because it remains fixed relative to the Earth-Sun system. 
• Other missions, like the **Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO)**, have also utilized L1 for solar studies. 
• **ISRO's Solar Mission Achievements:** 
• Aditya-L1 is a landmark mission for ISRO as it marks India's entry into advanced **heliophysics research**. 
• This mission follows other successful space missions by ISRO, including **Chandrayaan** and **Mangalyaan.** 
• ISRO collaborated with several national research institutions for payload development, such as the **Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA)** and **Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics (IUCAA).** 
• **Space Weather and Its Impact:** 
• Space weather primarily refers to the conditions on the Sun and the solar wind that can affect Earth's atmosphere and technology. 
• Solar storms can disrupt satellite communication, GPS systems, and power grids on Earth. 
• Aditya-L1 aims to provide insights into mitigating the impact of such events by understanding the **Sun's behavior**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Facts about Aditya-L1:** 
• The spacecraft weighs approximately **1,500 kg** and is powered by **solar panels.** 
• The mission cost is estimated at around **₹378 crore**, highlighting India's cost-effective space programs. 
• It is expected to operate for over **5 years** at L1, continuously collecting data. 
• **International Context:** 
• Aditya-L1 joins other solar observation missions like NASA's **Parker Solar Probe** and ESA's **Solar Orbiter.** 
• These missions collectively contribute to global solar research and space weather prediction capabilities.

• The **Chandrayaan-3 lander, Vikram**, utilized advanced technology known as the **Lander Hazard Detection and Avoidance Camera and Processing Algorithm** for identifying and avoiding potential hazards during its landing process.

• This technology is crucial for ensuring a **safe and precise landing** on the uneven lunar surface, which is scattered with craters, rocks, and slopes.

• The hazard detection system works by employing **high-resolution cameras** and **computational algorithms** to scan the landing site in real-time, identifying safe zones and avoiding risky areas.

• It plays a pivotal role in the **autonomous decision-making** of the lander, enabling it to adjust its trajectory and orientation without human intervention.

• Such technology significantly enhances the **mission’s success rate**, as it ensures the lander avoids areas that could potentially damage the spacecraft or jeopardize the mission.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The mission's primary objective is to demonstrate **safe landing and rover operations** on the lunar surface.

• It builds upon the learnings from **Chandrayaan-2**, which faced landing challenges in 2019.

• **Key Features of Lander Hazard Detection Technology:** 

• The system uses **optical cameras** and **sensor arrays** to analyze the terrain during descent.

• It integrates with **navigation systems** to provide real-time data for trajectory correction.

• The onboard algorithms are capable of recognizing features like **craters, slopes, and boulders** and selecting a safe landing spot.

• **Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR):** Used for detailed mapping of the lunar surface prior to landing.

• **Global Context:**

• Such missions contribute to the global understanding of lunar geology and open avenues for future **human exploration**.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bee has five eyes**__
 
• **Eyes**-Incredible as it may seem, the honey bee has FIVE eyes,** two large compound eyes and three smaller ocelli eyes in the centre of its head.**
 
• Bees need eyes not only to pick up colours and** UV markings in flowers, as well as shapes but also to navigate. Thus the two sets of eyes are adapted to perform different tasks simultaneously.**
 
• The two large eyes at the side of the head (**known as 'compound eyes'**) are used for picking up shapes and colours in the immediate environment, whilst the three small eyes on the top of the head (**known as the 'ocelli'**) are important for navigation and orientation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/64078d158dd71116afa90974a63b238712ee87e212c16783d16217c3cb1597bb.png]

• **Legs **– The honey bee has three pairs of legs, **six legs in** total.
 
• However, the rear pair is specially designed with stiff hairs to store pollen when flying from flower to flower.
 
• This is why a heavily laden worker bee is seen to have two golden pouches in a full season.
 
• The front pair of legs have special slots to enable the bee to** clean its antenna**.
 
• **Wings **– The honey bee has **four wings** in total.
 
• The front and rear wings hook together to form one big pair of wings and unhook for easy folding when not flying.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• ** The correct answer is option 3, i - d, ii - c, iii - b, iv - a.**__
 
• **DNA ligase joins the 3'** end of the new DNA fragment to the 5' end of the previous one, thus it plays a role in the joining of Okazaki fragments.
 
• ** RNA primase synthesizes** a short RNA primer that provides a 3'-OH group for DNA polymerase to extend the new strand.
 
• **DNA polymerase** is responsible for nucleotide polymerization, which means it adds nucleotides to the 3'-OH end of the growing strand during DNA replication.
 
• ** Helicase is an enzyme that unwinds the double-stranded DNA** during DNA replication, thus it plays a role in the initiation of replication.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• ** ****Helicase is an enzyme** that unwinds the double-stranded DNA during DNA replication, thus it plays a role in the initiation of replication. It separates the two strands of DNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the complementary base pairs. This opens up the DNA double helix and allows DNA replication to proceed.
 
• **RNA **primase synthesizes a short RNA primer that provides a 3'-OH group for DNA polymerase to extend the new strand. The RNA primer is later removed by an exonuclease and replaced with DNA nucleotides by DNA polymerase.
 
• **DNA polymerase is responsible for nucleotide polymerization,** which means it adds nucleotides to the 3'-OH end of the growing strand during DNA replication. It also has proofreading activity, which helps to correct errors that may occur during replication.
 
• ** DNA ligase joins the 3' end of the new DNA fragment to the 5' end of the previous one**, thus it plays a role in the joining of Okazaki fragments. Okazaki fragments are short, discontinuous pieces of DNA that are synthesized on the lagging strand during DNA replication. DNA ligase seals the gaps between the fragments to form a continuous strand.

question: In the context of cell division, which chromosomal behaviour takes place at the leptotene stage?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Chromosomes begin to condense**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• During the leptotene stage, chromosomes start to condense and become visible under a microscope.
 
• This stage is the initial phase of prophase I in meiosis, where chromosomes appear as long, thread-like structures.
 
• The condensation of chromosomes helps in their subsequent alignment and pairing during meiosis.
 
• Chromosomal condensation is crucial for the accurate segregation of chromosomes into daughter cells.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Leptotene Stage**

 
 
• The leptotene stage is the first stage of prophase I in meiosis.
 
• During this stage, chromosomes start to condense and become visible as thin threads.
 
• It is followed by the zygotene stage, where homologous chromosomes begin to pair and synapse.
 
 
 
• **Meiosis**
 
 
• Meiosis is a type of cell division that reduces the chromosome number by half, resulting in four genetically distinct daughter cells.
 
• It consists of two consecutive divisions: meiosis I and meiosis II.
 
• Meiosis is essential for sexual reproduction and contributes to genetic diversity.
 
 
 
• **Chromosomal Synapsis**
 
 
• Synapsis is the pairing of homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis.
 
• It occurs during the zygotene stage, following the leptotene stage.
 
• Synapsis is crucial for the exchange of genetic material between homologous chromosomes through crossing over.

subject: GK
question: What is the primary function of telomerase enzyme?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Telomere lengthening**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Telomerase** is an enzyme responsible for maintaining the length of telomeres, which are repetitive nucleotide sequences at the ends of chromosomes.
 
• Telomeres protect chromosomes from degradation, fusion with neighboring chromosomes, and incomplete replication during cell division.
 
• The enzyme adds DNA sequence repeats to the telomere regions, compensating for the shortening that occurs during DNA replication.
 
• Telomerase activity is particularly high in germ cells, stem cells, and certain cancer cells, ensuring their proliferative capacity.
 
• In most somatic cells, telomerase activity is low or absent, leading to progressive telomere shortening and cellular aging.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **DNA replication**

 
 
• DNA replication is the process by which a cell duplicates its DNA, resulting in two identical DNA molecules.
 
• This process involves enzymes like DNA polymerase, helicase, and ligase, but telomerase is not directly involved in the core replication process.
 
• While telomerase addresses the replication of telomeres, it is not responsible for the replication of the entire DNA strand.
 
 
 
• **DNA repair**
 
 
• DNA repair refers to the mechanisms by which cells identify and correct damage to the DNA molecules that encode their genome.
 
• It involves processes like base excision repair, nucleotide excision repair, and mismatch repair.
 
• Telomerase does not play a role in DNA repair but focuses on preventing the loss of genetic information at chromosome ends.
 
 
 
• **RNA transcription**
 
 
• RNA transcription is the process of synthesizing RNA from a DNA template, carried out by RNA polymerase enzymes.
 
• It is a critical step in gene expression but is unrelated to telomere lengthening or the activity of telomerase.

subject: GK
question: The term "pleiotropy" refers to:
solution:
The correct answer is __**One gene affects multiple traits**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Pleiotropy** refers to a situation where a single gene affects multiple phenotypic traits.
 
• This occurs because the gene encodes a product (such as a protein) that is involved in multiple biological processes.
 
• Examples of pleiotropy include the gene responsible for sickle-cell anemia, which affects red blood cell shape and provides resistance to malaria.
 
• Pleiotropic effects can be observed in both normal physiological processes and genetic disorders.
 
• Pleiotropy is a fundamental concept in genetics and demonstrates how genes can have far-reaching effects on an organism's phenotype.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: Multiple genes affect one trait**

 
 
• This describes a phenomenon known as **polygenic inheritance**, where a trait is governed by two or more genes.
 
• Examples include human height, skin color, and eye color, which result from the combined effect of several genes.
 
• Polygenic traits often show continuous variation, unlike pleiotropic traits, which are influenced by a single gene.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: Gene mutation in one allele**
 
 
• This refers to a mutation in one copy of a gene (allele) that can affect its function.
 
• Such mutations can lead to genetic disorders if the mutated allele is dominant or if the condition is recessive and both alleles are affected.
 
• While this is a distinct genetic concept, it does not describe pleiotropy.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Gene duplication**
 
 
• Gene duplication is an evolutionary process where a segment of DNA containing a gene is copied, resulting in multiple copies of that gene in the genome.
 
• This can lead to the evolution of new gene functions or increased gene dosage but is unrelated to pleiotropy.
 
 
 
• **Explanation of Pleiotropy:**
 
 
• Pleiotropy is critical for understanding the complexity of genetic interactions and how single genes can have multiple impacts on an organism's physiology and development.
 
• It is also significant in studying diseases with pleiotropic effects, such as Marfan syndrome, where a single gene mutation affects the connective tissue throughout the body.

question: Which of the following sequences correctly represents flow of genetic info?
solution:
The correct answer is __**DNA → RNA → Protein**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The correct sequence of the flow of genetic information is **DNA → RNA → Protein**, commonly referred to as the **Central Dogma of Molecular Biology**.
 
• **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)** acts as the genetic material, storing all the information necessary for the synthesis of proteins.
 
• **RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)** is synthesized from DNA in a process called **transcription**. This RNA (typically mRNA) acts as a template for protein synthesis.
 
• **Protein synthesis**, also known as **translation**, occurs at the ribosome where mRNA is decoded to assemble amino acids into a polypeptide chain.
 
• This process is essential for cellular functions, as proteins serve as enzymes, structural components, and signaling molecules in all living organisms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Central Dogma of Molecular Biology**

 
 
• The concept was first proposed by Francis Crick in 1958.
 
• It explains the flow of genetic information within a biological system, stating that DNA is transcribed into RNA, and RNA is translated into protein.
 
• This principle is fundamental to molecular biology and underlies the mechanism of gene expression.

• **Examples **of pluripotent cells are** stem cells** in animals and meristematic cells in higher plants.

question: Which of the following plant hormones regulates growth, particularly by stimulating cell elongation in stems?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Auxin.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Stem Elongation**__

 __
 
• Stem elongation refers to the rapid growth in the length of the internodes of the upper stem before the reproductive phase starts for the plant.
 
• Stem elongation causes many problems for the plant, such as skinny stems that are too weak to support large flowers, as well as plants that grow too high vertically and appear spindly, so it should be prevented.
 
 
 
• **Auxin**__
 __
 
• Auxin is a group of plant hormones that regulate growth, particularly by stimulating cell elongation in stems.
 
• Auxins also play a role in cell division and differentiation, in fruit development, in the formation of roots from cuttings, in the inhibition of lateral branching and in leaf fall.
 
• The most important naturally occurring auxin is **ß- indolyl acetic acid (IAA).**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Ethylene**__

 __
 
• Ethylene is the first-identified plant hormone known to regulate numerous processes in plant growth, development, and response to biotic and abiotic stresses.
 
• Ethylene is best known for its effect on fruit ripening and thus has great commercial importance in agriculture.
 
 
 
• **Gibberellin**__
 __
 
• Gibberellin is a group of plant hormones that occur in seeds, young leaves, and roots.
 
• It stimulates the growth of main stems, especially when applied to the whole plant.
 
• It is commercially obtained from fungi.
 
 
 
• **Cytokinin**__
 
 
• Cytokinins are plant hormones that influence not only numerous aspects of plant growth, development and physiology, including cell division.
 
• Cytokinins are also produced by other prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms such as bacteria, fungi, microalgae and insects.

question: Which of the following is the middle layer in the root apical meristem that gives rise to the cortex?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Periblem.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Periblem is the middle layer in the root apical meristem that gives rise to the cortex.**
 
• The lateral root initiation involves a series of rapid divisions in pericycle cells located on the xylem of the root.
 
• It grows out through the cortex and epidermis.
 
• A part of the vascular cambium is formed by a **pericycle.**
 
• The pericycle is a unique layer of cells in plants, located between the endodermis and phloem.
 
• It has two different types of cells **parenchyma and sclerenchyma cells.**
 
• The endodermis is the central, innermost layer of any land plant root cell, consisting of closely packed cells.
 
• It is the boundary between the cortex and stele.
 
• The plant endodermis plays an important role in selecting what gets into the plant from the soil, like Water intake, Hormone, and ion movement in and out of the roots 'vascular system.
 
• The epidermis is located in a plant root, which is the first single layer.
 
• The major role of the epidermis is the protective tissue of plants which forms the outer covering of the entire plant surface and protects the underlying tissues.
 
• The plants have waxy, water-resistant layers on the outer surface of epidermal cells which in turn reduces water loss and provides protection against mechanical or environmental injury and invasion of parasitic fungi.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The root cap/calyptra:**

 
 
• It is a section of tissue at the tip of a plant root.
 
• It is also called calyptra.
 
• Root caps contain statocytes which are involved in gravity perception in plants.
 
• If the cap is carefully removed the root will grow randomly.
 
• The root cap protects the growing tip in plants.

question: What is the outermost layer found in the cell envelope of the bacterial cell called?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Glycocalyx**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Glycocalyx:

 
 
• It is a **surface layer that covers the cell membrane of many bacteria, epithelial cells or other cells.**
 
• It is made up of** proteoglycans, glycoproteins and glycolipids.**
 
• Glycocalyx is a** viscous polysaccharide or polypeptide slime that covers microbes.**
 
• It enhances adherence to surfaces. resists phagocytic engulfment by the white blood cells.
 
• It prevents antibiotics from contacting the microbe.
 
 
 
• Functions:
 
 
• ​It protects the cell from dehydration **(capsule).**
 
• It protects the bacterial cell from engulfment and destruction by the immune system's white blood cells (capsule).
 
• Glycocalyx gives the bacterial cell a sticky character which enables it to attach to surfaces.
 
• Glycocalyx also helps the bacterial cells to adhere to each other. This forms a bacterial aggregate that can't be engulfed by the immune cells.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The bacterial cell wall is made up of peptidoglycans (also known as murein), diaminopimelic acid, and teichoic acid.
 
• All three molecules are unique to prokaryotes and not found in eukaryotes.

question: In cells, proteins are synthesised in _______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ribosome.**__ 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ribosomes:-**

 
 
• They are complex molecular machines composed of RNA and protein molecules.
 
• They exist in all living cells, from bacteria to eukaryotes, and are essential for protein synthesis.
 
• **The primary function of ribosomes is to synthesize proteins through a process called translation. **
 
• They read the genetic information encoded in mRNA (messenger RNA) and use it to assemble amino acids in the correct order to form a protein chain.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mitochondria:-**

 
 
• Mitochondria are double-membraned organelles found in the cells of eukaryotic organisms.
 
• They have an outer membrane and an inner membrane that encloses the mitochondrial matrix.
 
• The inner membrane is highly folded into structures called cristae, which increase its surface area for energy production.
 
• One of the primary functions of mitochondria is to generate energy through aerobic respiration.
 
• This process involves the conversion of nutrients, particularly glucose, into adenosine triphosphate (ATP), which is the cell's primary energy currency.
 
• This process occurs in the mitochondria's inner membrane, specifically in the cristae.
 
 
 
• **Golgi apparatus:-**
 
 
• It is also known as the Golgi complex or Golgi body
 
• It is a membranous organelle found in eukaryotic cells.
 
• It consists of a series of flattened membrane-bound sacs or cisternae arranged in stacks, along with associated vesicles.
 
 
 
• **Nucleus:-**
 
 
• It is a membrane-bound organelle found in eukaryotic cells.
 
• It contains the cell's genetic material, including DNA, and serves as the control center of the cell. 
 
• The nucleus is typically spherical and surrounded by a double-layered membrane known as the nuclear envelope.

• **Anton Van Leeuwenhoek:-**

 
 
• Microbiologist and microscopist Antonie Philips van Leeuwenhoek was from the Netherlands.
 
• He is frequently referred to as "the Father of Microbiology."
 
• **Single-celled life forms were discovered by Anton Van Leeuwenhoek in 1674.**
 
• Anton van Leeuwenhoek in Holland made more crucial discoveries using a microscope after Robert Hooke discovered cells in cork. He said that cells are the building blocks of life.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Single-celled life:-**

 
 
• **It refers to organisms that consist of only one cell, as opposed to multicellular organisms which are composed of multiple cells. **
 
• These single-celled organisms are known as unicellular organisms.
 
• They are some of the simplest forms of life on Earth and have been present for the majority of the planet's history.
 
• Single-celled organisms can be found in various environments, including water, soil, and even inside other organisms.

question: Which of the following options indicates the size of PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms)?
solution:
The correct answer is __**About 0.1 µm**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• PPLOs (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms) are the smallest free-living organisms known.
 
• They are characterized by their extremely small size, about 0.1 µm in diameter.
 
• PPLOs lack a cell wall, which contributes to their small size and flexible shape.
 
• These organisms are responsible for causing respiratory diseases, particularly in livestock.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms):**

 
 
• PPLOs are a group of bacteria that belong to the class Mollicutes.
 
• These organisms are known for their lack of a rigid cell wall, making them resistant to antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis.
 
• They are often referred to as mycoplasmas, with Mycoplasma pneumoniae being a well-known species causing atypical pneumonia in humans.
 
• PPLOs thrive in osmotically balanced environments due to their lack of a cell wall, which makes them susceptible to osmotic lysis in hypotonic conditions.
 
 
 
• **Importance in Research:**
 
 
• The small size and simple genetic structure of PPLOs make them important models for studying the minimal requirements for cellular life.
 
• Research on PPLOs has provided insights into the evolution of bacteria and the mechanisms of pathogenesis in respiratory infections.
 
 
 
• **Clinical Relevance:**
 
 
• PPLOs are significant pathogens in veterinary medicine, causing respiratory diseases such as contagious bovine pleuropneumonia.
 
• In humans, mycoplasmas can lead to a range of respiratory and urogenital infections, requiring specific diagnostic and treatment approaches.
 
• Due to their lack of a cell wall, infections caused by PPLOs are treated with antibiotics that inhibit protein synthesis, such as tetracyclines or macrolides.

question: In the year 1925, who extracted lipids from an erythrocyte sample and found that lipid monolayers are good for measuring molecular surface area versus lateral pressure?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gorter and Grendel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In 1925, Dutch scientists **Evert Gorter and François Grendel** conducted a groundbreaking experiment involving erythrocyte (red blood cell) lipid extraction.
 
• They found that the lipids extracted from erythrocytes could form a monolayer, which was pivotal in understanding the molecular surface area versus lateral pressure.
 
• Their work was fundamental in the development of the **fluid mosaic model of cell membranes**.
 
• Gorter and Grendel's experiment was one of the first to suggest that cell membranes are composed of a lipid bilayer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lipid Monolayers and Bilayers:**

 
 
• A **lipid monolayer** is a single layer of lipid molecules arranged on the surface of the water, with their hydrophobic tails in the air and hydrophilic heads in the water.
 
• A **lipid bilayer** is a double layer of lipids that form the fundamental structure of cell membranes, with hydrophobic tails facing inward and hydrophilic heads facing outward.
 
• These structures are crucial for maintaining the integrity and functionality of cell membranes.
 
 
 
• **Erythrocytes (Red Blood Cells):**
 
 
• Erythrocytes are the most common type of blood cell and are responsible for transporting oxygen from the lungs to the body's tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues back to the lungs.
 
• Their membrane composition and properties are essential for their deformability and functionality.
 
 
 
• **Surface Area vs. Lateral Pressure:**
 
 
• This concept involves measuring the surface area occupied by lipid molecules as a function of the lateral pressure applied to the monolayer.
 
• It is used to study the physical properties of lipid layers and understand cell membrane mechanics.
 
 
 
• **Fluid Mosaic Model:**
 
 
• Proposed by Singer and Nicolson in 1972, this model describes the cell membrane as a fluid combination of lipids and proteins.
 
• The lipids provide a flexible matrix, while proteins float in or on this lipid bilayer, contributing to various cellular functions.

question: Which of the following is an example of prokaryotic cells?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bacteria**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Bacteria** are single-celled organisms that lack a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles, making them prokaryotic.
 
• Bacteria are among the most ancient and diverse forms of life on Earth, thriving in various environments.
 
• Bacteria can be classified into various shapes such as cocci (spherical), bacilli (rod-shaped), and spirilla (spiral-shaped).
 
• Bacteria play crucial roles in processes like nutrient cycling, fermentation, and as part of the microbiome in various organisms.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Prokaryotic Cells**

 
 
• Prokaryotic cells are primitive cells that lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
 
• They have a simple cell structure with genetic material (DNA) present in a nucleoid region.
 
• Examples include Bacteria and Archaea.
 
 
 
• **Eukaryotic Cells**
 
 
• Eukaryotic cells have a well-defined nucleus and various membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, and Golgi apparatus.
 
• These cells are more complex and are found in organisms such as animals, plants, fungi, and protists.
 
• Examples include Plasmodium (a protist), Leishmania (a protist), and Yeast (a fungus).
 
 
 
• **Plasmodium**
 
 
• Plasmodium is a genus of parasitic protozoa that causes malaria in humans and other animals.
 
• It is a eukaryotic organism with a complex life cycle involving both an insect vector (mosquito) and a vertebrate host.
 
 
 
• **Leishmania**
 
 
• Leishmania is a genus of protozoan parasites, transmitted by the bite of infected sandflies.
 
• It causes diseases known as leishmaniasis in humans.
 
 
 
• **Yeast**
 
 
• Yeast is a type of fungus that is used in baking, brewing, and scientific research.
 
• It is a eukaryotic microorganism with a well-defined nucleus and other organelles.

question:
Which of the following researchers observed densely stained reticular structures surrounding the nucleus (Hint: Figure)?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3a1aa91b59a94a3c3197478a51d1e0369ff85eb45f707f028637b4d842535fec.png]
solution:
The correct answer is __**Camillo Golgi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Camillo Golgi was an Italian physician, pathologist, and scientist.
 
• He is renowned for discovering the Golgi apparatus, a complex of vesicles and folded membranes within the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells.
 
• The Golgi apparatus plays a critical role in sorting and packaging proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery to other organelles.
 
• Golgi's discovery was a pivotal moment in cell biology, and he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1906 for his contributions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Golgi Apparatus**

 
 
• The Golgi apparatus, also known as the Golgi complex, is an organelle found in most eukaryotic cells.
 
• It is involved in the modification, sorting, and packaging of proteins and lipids for secretion or use within the cell.
 
• The Golgi apparatus is composed of a series of flattened, stacked pouches called cisternae.
 
• The cis face of the Golgi apparatus is the receiving side, while the trans face is the shipping side.
 
 
 
• **Camillo Golgi's Contributions**
 
 
• Camillo Golgi developed a staining technique called the "black reaction" or "Golgi stain," which allowed him to visualize the Golgi apparatus and other cellular structures.
 
• This staining method involves using silver nitrate to selectively stain the nervous system tissue, enabling the detailed study of neurons and their connections.
 
• Golgi's work laid the foundation for our understanding of the organization and function of the nervous system.
 
• His discoveries have had a lasting impact on the field of cell biology and neuroscience.
 
 
 
• **Other Notable Researchers**
 
 
• **William Harvey:** An English physician who made significant contributions to the understanding of the circulatory system, particularly the function of the heart and blood vessels.
 
• **Francis Crick:** A British molecular biologist, biophysicist, and neuroscientist who co-discovered the structure of DNA with James Watson.
 
• **Louis Pasteur:** A French biologist, microbiologist, and chemist renowned for his discoveries of the principles of vaccination, microbial fermentation, and pasteurization.
