question: Which government initiative focuses on improving the road infrastructure in rural areas of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 

• **Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY)** was launched by the Government of India in **December 2000** to improve **rural road connectivity**. The scheme aims to provide **all-weather roads** to unconnected villages. 

• The focus of PMGSY is on **rural areas**, ensuring that villages with a population of **500 or more** (250 or more in hilly, tribal, or desert areas) are connected with all-weather roads. 

• It is a **centrally sponsored scheme**, with funding shared between the **Central and State Governments**. The ratio is typically **60:40** for most states and **90:10** for North-Eastern and Himalayan states. 

• The program also emphasizes the use of **innovative technologies**, such as cold mix, waste plastic, and fly ash, to ensure sustainable construction. 

• PMGSY has significantly contributed to **improving rural connectivity**, enhancing access to markets, healthcare, and education, thereby boosting the rural economy and reducing poverty. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 

• **Bharatmala Pariyojana:** 
 

• The **Bharatmala Pariyojana** is a flagship highway development program launched in **2017** to enhance the road network across India. 

• It focuses on **developing economic corridors, border roads, coastal roads, and expressways** to strengthen India’s national highway infrastructure. 

• This program is aimed at improving **freight movement** and reducing logistics costs. 
 
 

• **National Highways Development Project (NHDP):** 
 

• NHDP was launched by the Government of India in **1998** to develop and maintain **national highways**. 

• The project focused on initiatives like the **Golden Quadrilateral**, which connects India’s four major metros: Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, and Kolkata. 

• It primarily targets the development of **major arterial roads** rather than rural roads. 
 
 

• **Setu Bharatam Programme:** 
 

• Launched in **2016**, the Setu Bharatam Programme focuses on building **railway overbridges (ROBs)** and underbridges (RUBs) to eliminate level crossings on national highways, enhancing road safety. 

• It does not specifically address rural connectivity but instead emphasizes **safety and modernization** of existing road infrastructure. 
 
 

• **Impact of PMGSY:** 
 

• Improved rural connectivity has led to better **economic integration** of villages with nearby towns and cities. 

• Studies show that PMGSY has reduced travel time, improved **access to healthcare**, and increased school attendance rates in rural areas. 

• The scheme has contributed to **poverty alleviation** by facilitating rural employment and enhancing agricultural productivity. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 

• **PMGSY Phase I:** Focused on connecting habitations with a population of 500 or more in plain areas and 250 or more in hilly/tribal/desert areas. 

• **PMGSY Phase II:** Initiated in **2013** to consolidate the existing rural road network by upgrading roads that connected villages to rural growth centers. 

• **PMGSY Phase III:** Launched in **2019**, this phase focuses on **consolidation and upgrading** of the rural road network, targeting **125,000 km** of roads. 

• The Ministry of Rural Development oversees the implementation of the scheme, with technical support from agencies like **NIRDPR** and **NRIDA**.

 __

• AMRUT focuses on providing basic services such as **water supply, sewerage, urban transport, and development of green spaces** to improve the quality of life in urban areas. 
• This mission covers **500 cities** with a population of over 1 lakh and is designed to ensure that every household has access to a water tap and a sewer connection.

• The mission is funded through a combination of **central assistance**, state government contributions, and user charges, ensuring financial sustainability.

• It aims to promote cities that are sustainable and inclusive, using technology and data-driven approaches. 
• 100 cities have been selected under this mission, and it includes projects like integrated transport systems, digital governance, and smart water management. 
• **Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban):** 
• Launched on **2nd October 2014**, this mission aims to achieve sanitation and eliminate open defecation in India by constructing toilets and promoting behavioral change. 
• It focuses on solid waste management and urban cleanliness, ensuring hygiene in cities and towns.

• Also known as the **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY)**, it was launched in **2015** to provide affordable housing to urban poor by 2022.

• **Components:** The mission includes projects related to **water supply augmentation**, sewerage treatment, non-motorized urban transport, and creating green spaces in urban areas. 
• **Monitoring and Evaluation:** The implementation of AMRUT is closely monitored by the central government to ensure adherence to its objectives.

question: What was the primary aim of import substitution policy in India's early planning era?

options.text: Replace foreign imports with domestic production

solution:
The correct answer is __**Replace foreign imports with domestic production**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• **Import substitution policy** was a strategy adopted by India during its early planning era, particularly under the **Second Five-Year Plan (1956-1961)**, to promote self-reliance by reducing dependence on foreign imports. 

• The primary objective was to **develop domestic industries** to produce goods that were previously imported, thereby fostering **economic self-sufficiency**. 

• This policy involved the use of **high tariffs and quotas** on imports to protect nascent domestic industries from foreign competition. 

• It was part of a larger strategy aimed at achieving **industrialization** and reducing India's reliance on foreign products, particularly in the wake of its colonial history. 

• Import substitution was also aligned with the idea of creating a **planned economy** where the state played a central role in directing industrial and economic growth. 

• Examples include the development of industries such as **steel, chemicals, textiles, and heavy machinery**, which were prioritized to replace imports. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Key Features of Import Substitution Policy:** 
 

• The policy aimed at creating a **self-reliant economy** by reducing dependence on foreign goods and focusing on domestic production. 

• It involved the use of **protectionist measures** such as import tariffs, quotas, and bans to restrict imports. 

• Encouraged the growth of **public sector enterprises** in key industries like steel, heavy machinery, and energy production. 

• Promoted the development of indigenous industries, particularly in the areas of **manufacturing and capital goods**. 

• Focused on reducing the outflow of foreign exchange by minimizing imports of consumer goods. 
 
 

• **Outcomes of Import Substitution:** 
 

• India successfully developed a strong base in **heavy industries** and infrastructure during the early planning years. 

• However, the policy led to reduced competition, resulting in **low-quality goods and inefficiency** in production. 

• It created a **license raj** system, which involved complex bureaucratic controls and regulations, often stifling private sector growth. 

• The policy contributed to **technological stagnation** and limited innovation in the industrial sector due to a lack of competition from foreign firms. 
 
 

• **Transition from Import Substitution:** 
 

• By the early **1990s**, India shifted its focus from import substitution to **export-oriented industrialization** as part of economic liberalization and globalization policies. 

• The **1991 economic reforms** marked a significant shift in trade policy, reducing tariffs, removing import quotas, and promoting foreign direct investment (FDI). 

• This transition was aimed at integrating India into the **global economy**, increasing competitiveness, and fostering economic growth. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Historical Context:** 
 

• India’s focus on import substitution was influenced by its colonial experience, during which the country was highly dependent on foreign goods and lacked a strong industrial base. 

• The strategy was inspired by the **Soviet model of planned economic development**, emphasizing state control and self-reliance. 
 
 

• **Examples of Import Substitution in India:** 
 

• The establishment of **Bhilai Steel Plant** in collaboration with the Soviet Union in 1955 was a key milestone in building India’s industrial base. 

• The indigenous production of goods like **fertilizers, cement, and pharmaceuticals** reduced dependency on imports significantly during the planned economy era. 

• The **Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL)** was set up to manufacture aircraft domestically, reducing reliance on foreign technology. 
 
 

• **Criticism of Import Substitution:** 
 

• Critics argue that the policy led to inefficiency, lack of innovation, and limited competitiveness in the global market. 

• The restrictive trade policies also resulted in a **lack of foreign exchange reserves** and foreign investment.

1. Exclusively Wattal men plant a banner before dancing.

2. It celebrates apple harvests in southern Kashmir.

Which is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Dumhal** is a traditional folk dance performed by the **Wattal tribe of Kashmir**.

• The dance is **exclusively performed by the men of the Wattal tribe**, who plant a ceremonial banner or flag into the ground before starting the dance. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• The dance does not have any specific connection with the celebration of the **apple harvest in southern Kashmir**. It is a ritualistic dance performed on certain occasions and does not commemorate specific agricultural events. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• The performers wear colorful costumes and move in a circular motion around the planted flag while singing and dancing to rhythmic music.

• The Dumhal is regarded as one of the most unique and vibrant dance forms of Jammu and Kashmir, showcasing the rich cultural heritage of the region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The Wattal tribe is a small community in Jammu and Kashmir known for its unique cultural traditions and practices.

• The tribe is primarily involved in performing arts and holds a significant place in Kashmiri folklore.

• **Costumes and Musical Instruments:**

• The performers of Dumhal wear long, flowing, and colorful robes, often adorned with beads and ornaments.

• Musical instruments such as drums and traditional Kashmiri flutes are used to accompany the dance.

• **Purpose of Dumhal:**

• Dumhal is performed on special occasions, including religious ceremonies and cultural celebrations.

• It is considered a sacred dance and is often associated with invoking blessings and honoring traditions.

• **Other Folk Dances of Jammu and Kashmir:**

• **Rouf:** A popular dance performed by Kashmiri women during festivals and celebrations.

• **Bacha Nagma:** Performed by young boys dressed as women, this dance is a significant part of Kashmiri weddings.

• **Hikat:** A traditional dance where performers hold hands and move in a circular motion.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Geographical Context:**

• Kashmir is known for its rich and diverse cultural heritage, with dance and music playing a crucial role in its traditions.

• The region’s unique topography and climate have influenced its cultural practices, including the attire and themes of folk dances.

• **Significance of Folk Dances:**

• Folk dances like Dumhal serve as a medium for storytelling and preserving the community's history and heritage.

• They also play a role in fostering social cohesion and identity within the tribal and rural communities of Kashmir.

• **Preservation Efforts:**

• Various cultural organizations and government initiatives are working to preserve traditional art forms like Dumhal.

• Efforts include organizing cultural festivals and providing platforms for tribal communities to showcase their heritage.

question: ______ is defined as the temperature to which the air would have to cool (at constant pressure and constant water vapour content) in order to reach saturation.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dew point temperature.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Dew point temperature (DPT):

 
 
• It is a temperature at which moisture present in the atmosphere starts condensing or it is the temperature at which the first droplet of moisture is formed.
 
• As we know that for each pressure, the air has a specific saturation temperature, therefore for fully saturated air DBT, WBT and DPT are equal.
 
• When the relative humidity of the air is 100%, i.e the air is saturated, the dew point temperature (DPT) equals the wet-bulb temperature (WBT), which is also equal to the dry-bulb temperature.
 
• So DBT = WBT = DPT
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Relative humidity:

 
 
• It is defined as the ratio of the mass of vapour to the mass of vapour under saturation conditions.
 
• Relative humidity represents vapour absorption capacity.

question: Unique Transaction Reference number is a ______ character code used to uniquely identify a transaction in the RTGS system.
solution:
The correct answer is __**22.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• RTGS stands for **Real-Time Gross Settlements.**
 
• RTGS is a system where there is a continuous and real-time settlement of fund transfers, individually on a transaction-by-transaction basis.
 
• Unique Transaction Reference (UTR) number is a **22 character **code used to uniquely identify a transaction in the RTGS system.
 
• **The unique Transaction Reference number** is used to identify a specific bank transaction in India.
 
• All banks in India use UTR numbers for all types of money transfers.
 
• UTR numbers can recognize and keep an eye on financial transactions.
 
• NEFT transactions UTR numbers are **16 characters** long.
 
• Example of a UTR number: **XXXXRCYYYYMMDD########**
 
 
• **XXXX** indicates IFSC (this is the first 4 characters) and is the bank code of the sender.
 
• **R** indicates the RTGS system.
 
• **C **indicates the transaction channel.
 
• **YYYYMMDD** indicates the date of the transaction in this order: year, month, and day.
 
• **########** indicates the sequence number.

question: Which of the following is one of the three 'Domestic Systemically Important Banks' in India?
solution:
The correct answer is the __**State Bank of India (SBI)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Some banks**, due to their **size**, **cross-jurisdictional activities**, **complexity**, lack of **substitutability **and **interconnectedness**, **become systemically important**.

 
 
• SIBs are perceived as banks that are ‘**Too Big To Fail (TBTF)**’.
 
• This perception of** TBTF creates an expectation of government support** for these banks at the time of distress.
 
• **SIBs** are subjected to **additional policy measures **to deal with the systemic risks and moral hazard issues posed by them.
 
• The **Financial Stability Board** (FSB), in consultation with the **Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS)** and** national authorities**, has identified **Global Systemically Important Banks (G-SIBs)** since 2011.
 
 
• Financial Stability Board (FSB) is an international body that monitors and makes recommendations about the global financial system. It was established in 2009. India is a member.
 
 
 
• The** BCBS** finalized its **framework **for dealing with '**Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D-SIBs)** in October 2012.
 
 
• The** D-SIB framework** focuses on the impact that the **distress or failure of banks **will have on the **domestic economy**.
 
• As opposed to the G-SIB framework, the **D-SIB framework is based on the assessment conducted** by the **national authorities**, who are best placed to evaluate the impact of failure on the local financial system and the local economy.
 
• The **RBI had issued the framework** for dealing with D-SIB in 2014.
 
• The** D-SIB framework** requires the **Reserve Bank **to **disclose **the **names **of **banks designated **as **D-SIBs** starting from 2015 and place these banks in appropriate buckets depending upon their Systemic Importance Scores (SISs).
 
• **SBI, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank** continue to be identified as **Domestic Systemically Important Banks** (D-SIBs), under the same bucketing structure as in the **2018 list of D-SIBs**.

• **The central bank **is referred to as **‘The lender of last resort'.**

• The lender of last resort serves to protect depositors and to prevent panicked clients from withdrawing funds from banks with temporary low liquidity.
 
• Commercial banks often avoid borrowing from lenders of last resort since doing so shows that the bank is in financial distress.

question: Money multiplier can be expressed as ______.

options.text: Statutory liquidity ratio / Cash Reserve Ratio
Cash reserve ratio – Statutory liquidity ratio

solution:
The correct answer is __**1/ Cash Reserve Ratio.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The money multiplier can be expressed as **1/ Cash Reserve Ratio.**
 
• The money multiplier is the amount of **money created by commercial banks **for a given fixed amount of base money and reserve ratio.
 
• An increase in a **cash reserve ratio prevents the banks from lending more money and reduces the money multiplier.**
 
 
• An increase in the banking habit of the population will increase lending, thereby will lead to more deposits in the banking system, hence increasing the money multiplier.
 
• Even if there is an increase in the population of the country, the money multiplier in an economy does not necessarily increase. 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• 
 **The statutory liquidity ratio **means ensuring that commercial banks are solvent and that they invest in government securities.

 
 
• 
 By sapping market liquidity, an increase in the SLR limits the bank's ability to lend while also aiding in the management of inflation.
 
 
• 
 The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) utilizes the statutory liquidity ratio as a tool for its monetary policy to evaluate the liquidity available to banks.

question: The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India provides overnight liquidity to banks is called ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Marginal standing facility rate**__.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Marginal standing facility rate**
 
• The penal rate at which banks can borrow, on an overnight basis, from the Reserve Bank by dipping into their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (**SLR**) portfolio up to a predefined limit (**2 per cent**).
 
• This provides a safety valve against unanticipated liquidity shocks to the banking system. The MSF rate is placed at **25** basis points above the policy repo rate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reverse repo rate**

 
 
• ​The rate at which a nation's central bank borrows money from its own **domestic commercial banks** is known as the **Reverse Repo Rate**. It is a tool for the **RBI's** **monetary policy** that can be used to manage a nation's money supply. Assuming all other factors stay constant, the **money supply **decreases when the **reverse repo rate **increases** **and vice versa.
 
• The amount of money accessible in the market will decrease if the** Reverse Repo rate** rises because commercial banks will be more enticed to deposit their funds with the **RBI**.
 
 
 
• **Repo rate**
 
 
• The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank provides liquidity under the liquidity adjustment facility (**LAF**) to all LAF participants against the collateral of government and other approved securities.
 
 
 
• **Leverage rate**
 
 
• **​A leverage ratio **is any of a number of financial metrics that examine the amount of capital that comes from debt (loans) or evaluates a company's capacity to satisfy its financial obligations. Companies employ a combination of stock and debt to finance their operations, therefore the** leverage ratio **category is crucial.
 
• By understanding how much debt a firm has, you can assess its ability to pay off its loans when they become due.

question: Which of the following is one of the Open Market Operations by the Reserve Bank of India?

options.text: Buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market
Buying and selling of bonds issued by commercial banks in the open market
Only buying of bonds issued by the Government in the open market
Only selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market

solution:
The correct answer is __**Buying and selling of bonds issued by the Government in the open market**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Open Market Operations (OMO) is conducted by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for the sale or purchase of government securities (g-secs), financial assets or bonds issued by the government to the banks in order to adjust the money supply.

 
 
• The RBI does this to regulate the liquidity from the system and to infuse liquidity into the system.
 
 
 
• There are two types of Open Market Operations: Outright Purchase and Repurchase Agreement. Hence option 1 is correct.
 
 
• Outright Purchase or PEMO is a permanent transaction which involves the RBI selling or purchasing securities in the open market to regulate the money supply.
 
• A Repurchase Agreement is a short-term agreement that involves the RBI buying and purchasing government securities after a specified date.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Open Market Operations are flexible and easily reversible thereby reducing the lags of monetary policy.
 
• In 1948, the RBI mentioned the OMO purchase for the first time in its Annual Report.
 
• Government securities or G-Secs are tradable instruments issued by central governments and state governments.
 
• They are risk-free instruments and can be short-term like Treasury bills (T-bills) with a maturity of less than a year or long-term like government bonds with a maturity of a year or more than a year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points:__**Money - 

 
• In a modern economy, money consists mainly of currency notes and coins issued by the monetary authority of the country.
 
• In India currency notes are issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), which is the monetary authority in India.
 
• However, coins are issued by the Government of India.
 
• Apart from currency notes and coins, the balance in savings, or current account deposits, held by the public in commercial banks is also considered money since cheques drawn on these accounts are used to settle transactions.
 
• Such deposits are called demand deposits as they are payable by the bank on demand from the account holder.
 
• Other deposits, e.g. fixed deposits, have a fixed period to maturity and are referred to as time deposits. 

Money supply - 

 
• The total stock of money in circulation among the public at a particular point in time is called money supply. 
 
• RBI publishes figures for four alternative measures of money supply, viz. M1, M2, M3, and M4.
 
• They are defined as follows -
 
 
• M1 = Currency + Demand deposits with the banking system. 
 
• M2 = M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
 
• M3 = M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks
 
• M4 = M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organizations (excluding National Savings Certificates)
 
 
 
• M1 and M2 are narrow money. 
 
• M3 and M4 are known as broad money.
 
• These gradations are in decreasing order of liquidity. M1 is the most liquid and easiest for transactions whereas M4 is the least liquid of all. M3 is the most commonly used measure of the money supply.
 
• It is also known as aggregate monetary resources.

question: Which of the following is NOT a function of money?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Problem in storage**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**Traditional functions of money are generally classified as:

__
 
• **Medium of Exchange**: Money is used for buying and selling goods and services.
 
• **Unit of Account**: Money is used to measure the value of goods and services.
 
• **Store of Value**: Money allows the ability to defer consumption from the present into the future. It's a way to store wealth.
 
• **Standard of Deferred Payment**: It is used as a standard for future payments.

However, "problem in storage" is not related to the function of money. Actually, part of the benefit of money is that it eliminates the storage issue inherent in a barter system. Money doesn’t physically deteriorate and could be stored or saved for future use with ease. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• The concept of money and its functions is central to any study of the economy. 
 
 
• Money helps to facilitate trade, allowing a more efficient allocation of goods and services. Without money, economies would have to rely on the barter system, which is inefficient because it requires a double coincidence of wants.
 
• Money also plays a crucial role in the macro-economy. It influences important macroeconomic variables like interest rates, prices, wages, and economic growth. Central Banks — in India, it is the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) — manage the money supply to control inflation and stabilize the economy.
 
 
 
• In terms of the types of money used in the Indian economy, there are several forms:
 
 
• **Commodity Money**: This includes any commodity that is generally accepted as a medium of exchange. Until the 19th century, most transactions in India were conducted with commodities like gold, silver, copper coins, etc.
 
• **Fiat Money**: This is the money by order (fiat) of the government. Its value is not based on the material used for its manufacturing but on the trust and assurance by the government that the piece of note has a certain value. For example, Indian Rupee (INR).
 
• **Paper Money or Currency**: It represents the most commonly used form of money and includes notes issued by the Reserve Bank of India.
 
• **Bank Money**: Commercial banks in India also create money in the form of deposits, which are generated through the process of lending.
 
• **Electronic Money or Digital Money**: This form of money is recorded electronically on a storage device, such as a bank's computer or even on smart cards or mobile phones. With the progression of technology and internet penetration, online transactions are becoming more popular in India.
 
• **Near Money or Quasi-Money**: These are highly liquid assets that can be readily converted into cash, like savings accounts and time deposits, treasury bills, and other short term government bonds.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The Ministry of Finance is in charge of making Re. 1 notes and coins in India.
 
• However, the Reserve Bank of India is the only organization allowed to issue currency notes of different values, except for the one rupee note, according to the Reserve Bank of India Act.
 
• Coins in India are presently being issued in denominations of 50 paise, one rupee, two rupees, five rupees, ten rupees and twenty rupees.
 
• Coins up to 50 paise are called 'small coins' and coins of Rupee one and above are called 'Rupee Coins'.
 
• Coins can be issued up to the denomination of ₹1000 under the Coinage Act, 2011.
 
• Twenty five (25) paise coins have been withdrawn from circulation with effect from June 30, 2011 and are, therefore, no more legal tender.
 
• Rs. 75 coin, the coin’s metallic value exceeds its legal value as half of the coin is made of silver, so they are not used for transactions (legal tender).

question: The central bank may ________ to discourage credit in the economy.
solution:
The correct answer is __**increase bank rate.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__ Key Points__**

__
 
• **The bank rate** is the interest rate at which the central bank **lends money** to commercial banks.
 
• When the central bank** increases the bank rate**, it becomes **more expensive** for commercial banks to borrow money from the central bank.
 
• This, in turn,** reduces** the amount of credit that commercial banks can offer to their customers, thereby **discouraging credit** in the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Increasing **the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is another tool that the central bank can use to** discourage credit.**

 
 
• **CRR **is the amount of funds that commercial banks have to keep with the central bank as a** percentage of their deposits**.
 
• When the **CRR is decreased**, banks have more funds available to lend, which can lead to an** increase in credit** in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Buying securities** in the open market is a tool that the central bank can use to **increase liquidity** in the economy.
 
 
• When the central bank buys securities, it i**njects money** into the economy, which can lead to an** increase in credit.**
 
• Therefore, this option is** not** suitable for discouraging credit in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Reducing** the **Statutory Liquidity Ratio** (SLR) is another tool that the central bank can use to **increase the availability of funds** for banks to lend.
 
 
• SLR is the percentage of deposits that banks have to keep in the form of liquid assets such as** cash, gold, or government securities.**
 
• When the SLR is** reduced**, banks have** more funds available** to lend, which can lead to an increase in credit in the economy.

question: Under Statutory liquidity ratio, commercial banks are required to keep a fraction of __________ in form of liquid assets.
solution:
The correct answer is __**total demand and term deposits**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 __Statutory liquidity ratio(SLR) is a government term where commercial banks are mandated to keep a specific proportion of ____total demand and term deposits____ in the form of liquid assets.__

__
 
• It is determined by the RBI.
 
• It is used to control inflation and fuel growth, by decreasing or increasing the money supply.
 
• Liquid Assets, Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) and SLR Limit are the three components of SLR under Section 24 and Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act 1949.
 
• Liquid Assets:__ Here assets like gold, security bonds can be easily converted to cash.
 
• __Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL):__ It refers to the total demand and time liabilities (deposits) of the public that are held by the banks with other banks.
 
• __Demand deposits__ consist of all liabilities, which the bank needs to pay on demand. They include current deposits, demand drafts etc.
 
• __Time deposits__ consist of deposits that will be repaid on maturity.
 
• __S__LR Limit in India was a maximum of 40% and minimum of 20.75%. However, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) amended the Banking Regulation Act in January 2017 to remove the floor rate of 20.75% for SLR. This means that the RBI can now set the SLR at any level between 0% and 40%.
 
• The RBI will incur a penalty on a bank if it does not keep the required SLR ratio.
 
• SLR is calculated using the given formula: SLR rate = (liquid assets / (demand + time liabilities)) × 100%​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__** Cash reserve ratio

 
• The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a monetary policy tool used by central banks, including the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), to regulate and control the money supply in the economy.
 
• CRR is the percentage of total deposits that commercial banks are required to keep as reserves with the central bank.
 
• It is a portion of the bank's demand and time liabilities.
 
• The primary objective of implementing CRR is to ensure the liquidity and stability of the banking system while controlling inflation and managing credit growth.
 
• When the central bank increases the CRR, it reduces the amount of money available for lending by commercial banks.
 
• This helps reduce excess liquidity in the economy, controlling inflationary pressures, and curbing excessive credit expansion.
 
• On the other hand, when the central bank decreases the CRR, it increases the amount of money available for lending by commercial banks.
 
• This can stimulate credit growth, promote economic activity, and ease liquidity conditions in the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Microfinance refers to the provision of financial services to low-income individuals or those who do not have access to typical banking services.
 
• It includes a range of services such as microloans, savings, insurance, and money transfers.
 
• The primary aim of microfinance is to provide small loans to impoverished individuals to help them start or expand small businesses, thereby reducing poverty.
 
• Microfinance institutions (MFIs) play a critical role in providing these financial services, especially in developing countries.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Microloan**

 
 
• Microloans are small loans given to individuals who typically do not have access to traditional banking services.
 
• These loans are often used to start or grow small businesses and are a subset of microfinance services.
 
• Microloans can range from a few dollars to several thousand dollars, depending on the borrower's needs and the lender's policies.
 
• The concept of microloans was popularized by Nobel Laureate Muhammad Yunus and the Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
 
 
 
• **Homeloan**
 
 
• A home loan, or mortgage, is a loan given by a bank or financial institution to individuals to purchase a home or property.
 
• Home loans are typically long-term loans with a repayment period ranging from 10 to 30 years.
 
• They require collateral, usually the property being purchased, to secure the loan.
 
• Interest rates on home loans can be fixed or variable, depending on the lender's policies and the borrower's agreement.
 
 
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY)**
 
 
• PMAY is an initiative by the Government of India aimed at providing affordable housing to the urban poor.
 
• The scheme was launched on June 25, 2015, with the goal of constructing 20 million affordable houses by March 31, 2022.
 
• It has two components: PMAY-U (Urban) for the urban poor and PMAY-G (Gramin) for the rural poor.
 
• Beneficiaries under this scheme are identified through the Socio-Economic and Caste Census (SECC) of 2011.

question: The Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework (FITF) was introduced in India post the amendment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 in ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**2016**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework (FITF) was introduced in India in 2016.
 
• The amendment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 was carried out to implement the FITF.
 
• Under FITF, the primary objective of the RBI is to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth.
 
• The inflation target is set by the Government of India, in consultation with the RBI, once every five years.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT) Framework:**

 
 
• FIT is a monetary policy strategy where the central bank sets an explicit target for the inflation rate and uses interest rate changes to achieve that target.
 
• The primary goal of FIT is to anchor inflation expectations, reduce the volatility of inflation and output, and improve economic performance.
 
• Under FIT, the central bank is accountable for achieving the inflation target and must explain its actions if it fails to do so.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934:**
 
 
• The RBI Act, 1934, is the legislative foundation for the establishment and operations of the Reserve Bank of India.
 
• The Act grants the RBI the authority to regulate the issue of banknotes, maintain reserves to ensure monetary stability, and operate the currency and credit system of India.
 
• The 2016 amendment to the RBI Act introduced the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) and the Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC):**
 
 
• The MPC is a committee constituted by the RBI to determine the policy interest rate (repo rate) required to achieve the inflation target.
 
• The MPC consists of six members - three from the RBI and three appointed by the Government of India.
 
• The decisions of the MPC are taken by majority vote, with the RBI Governor having a casting vote in case of a tie.
 
 
 
• **Inflation Target:**
 
 
• The inflation target is a specific level or range of inflation that the central bank aims to achieve over a certain period.
 
• For India, the current inflation target is set at 4% with a tolerance band of +/- 2%, meaning it can range between 2% to 6%.
 
• This target is reviewed and decided once every five years by the Government of India in consultation with the RBI.

question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct option:

Assertion (A): Financial intermediaries are essential in transmitting monetary policy to the real economy.

Reason (R): They adjust lending and deposit rates in response to policy rates set by the MPC.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**1) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Assertion (A): Financial intermediaries are essential in transmitting monetary policy to the real economy.** 
 
 
• Financial intermediaries like banks and non-banking financial institutions play a vital role in the economy by connecting savers and borrowers.
 
• They ensure that monetary policy changes—such as adjustments in policy rates made by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC)—are effectively transmitted to the economy by influencing credit availability and interest rates.
 
• They act as conduits for implementing central bank policies, ensuring a smooth flow of funds across different sectors of the economy.
 
• ***Hence, Assertion (A) is correct.***
 
 
 
 
• **Reason (R): They adjust lending and deposit rates in response to policy rates set by the MPC.**
 
 
• The MPC sets benchmark policy rates such as the repo rate or reverse repo rate to manage inflation, liquidity, and growth in the economy.
 
• Financial intermediaries adjust their lending and deposit rates based on these policy rates to align with the central bank's objectives.
 
• This adjustment influences borrowing costs, consumer spending, and investment levels, thereby transmitting monetary policy to the real economy.
 
• ***Hence, Reason (R) is correct and explains Assertion (A).***
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC):** 
 
 
• The MPC is a statutory body established under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
 
• It is tasked with maintaining price stability while keeping growth in mind.
 
• The MPC sets key policy rates such as the repo rate, which is the rate at which the RBI lends to commercial banks.
 
 
 
 
• **Role of Financial Intermediaries:** 
 
 
• Financial intermediaries include banks, insurance companies, investment funds, and other institutions that facilitate the transfer of funds between savers and borrowers.
 
• They ensure that changes in monetary policy are reflected in market interest rates, credit availability, and deposit rates.
 
• Examples include commercial banks adjusting lending rates after a repo rate hike or cut.
 
 
 
 
• **Transmission Mechanism of Monetary Policy:** 
 
 
• This refers to the process through which monetary policy decisions affect the economy and inflation.
 
• The key channels include the interest rate channel, credit channel, asset price channel, and exchange rate channel.
 
• Financial intermediaries play a crucial role in these channels by ensuring the flow of credit and liquidity.
 
 
 
 
• **Impact of Policy Rates on Economy:** 
 
 
• Higher policy rates typically lead to higher lending rates, discouraging borrowing and reducing inflationary pressures.
 
• Lower policy rates encourage borrowing, investment, and consumption, stimulating economic growth.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Repo Rate:** 
 
 
• The rate at which the RBI lends money to commercial banks.
 
• It is a tool used to control inflation and liquidity in the economy.
 
 
 
 
• **Reverse Repo Rate:** 
 
 
• The rate at which the RBI borrows money from commercial banks.
 
• It is used to absorb excess liquidity from the banking system.
 
 
 
 
• **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF):** 
 
 
• It is a monetary policy tool used by the RBI to manage liquidity and short-term interest rates.
 
• It includes repo and reverse repo operations.
 
 
 
 
• **Key Objectives of Monetary Policy:** 
 
 
• Price stability, economic growth, exchange rate stability, and employment generation.

question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct option:

Assertion (A): CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) and SLR requirements increase the lending capacity of banks.

Reason (R): These requirements reduce the amount of money banks can lend to the public.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**4) A is false, but R is true.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A): CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio) and SLR requirements increase the lending capacity of banks.** - This statement is **false**. CRR and SLR requirements, instead of increasing the lending capacity, reduce the amount of money that banks can lend to the public. Banks are mandated to keep a certain percentage of their deposits as reserves, thereby limiting the funds available for lending.

• **Reason (R): These requirements reduce the amount of money banks can lend to the public.** - This statement is **true**. Both CRR and SLR are regulatory mechanisms aimed at ensuring liquidity and financial stability. By mandating banks to maintain reserves, they restrict the banks' ability to lend excessively, thus reducing the lending capacity.

• **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio):** - It is the percentage of total deposits that banks are required to keep with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as reserves. This is done to ensure liquidity in the banking system and control inflation.

• **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):** - It is the percentage of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that banks must maintain in the form of liquid assets like cash, gold, or government-approved securities. SLR ensures financial stability and liquidity.

• **Correct Explanation:** - The Reason (R) correctly explains the impact of CRR and SLR requirements on banks' lending capacity, as these requirements directly reduce the funds available for lending by the banks.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio):** 

• CRR is set by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and currently ranges between 3% to 5%, depending on the economic situation.

• Higher CRR helps control inflation by reducing liquidity, while lower CRR boosts economic growth by increasing liquidity.

• Banks do not earn any interest on the funds kept as CRR with the RBI.

• **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):** 

• SLR is also regulated by the RBI and is generally maintained between 18% to 23% of NDTL.

• Unlike CRR, banks earn returns on the assets maintained under SLR, such as government securities.

• SLR serves as a tool for regulating inflation and ensuring the financial stability of banks.

• **Key Objectives of CRR and SLR:** 

• Control liquidity in the economy.

• Ensure financial stability and prevent excessive lending by banks.

• Help the government in borrowing funds by mandating banks to invest in government securities.

• **Impact on the Economy:** 

• Both CRR and SLR play a crucial role in monetary policy implementation.

• Higher reserves reduce inflationary pressures but may slow down economic growth.

• Lower reserves increase liquidity and boost lending but may lead to inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Difference Between CRR and SLR:** 

• **CRR:** Funds are kept with the RBI; banks earn no interest.

• **SLR:** Funds are invested in liquid assets like government securities; banks earn returns.

• **Impact on Lending:** 

• Higher CRR and SLR reduce banks' ability to lend, curbing liquidity in the economy.

• Lower CRR and SLR increase lending capacity, promoting economic growth.

• **Examples of Application:** 

• During inflationary periods, CRR and SLR are increased to reduce liquidity.

• During economic slowdown, CRR and SLR are reduced to enhance liquidity and boost lending.

</ul

subject: GK
question:
Which of the following statements about factors affecting the Money Multiplier (MM) **is/are correct**?

1. Cash held by individuals acts as a leakage and reduces the money multiplier.

2. Higher reserves held by banks with the RBI increase the money multiplier.

3. A higher Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) reduces the banking system's capacity to create money.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 1 and 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Cash held by individuals acts as a leakage and reduces the money multiplier:** When individuals hold cash instead of depositing it in banks, it reduces the funds available for banks to lend. This reduces the capacity of the banking system to create credit, thereby lowering the **Money Multiplier (MM)**. *Hence, statement 1 is correct.*

• **Higher reserves held by banks with the RBI:** When banks hold higher reserves with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), it reduces the funds available for lending. However, the statement incorrectly claims that it increases the money multiplier. In reality, higher reserves restrict the money creation process, which decreases the MM. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• **Higher Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) reduces the banking system's capacity to create money:** CRR is the percentage of a bank's total deposits that must be kept as reserves with the RBI. A higher CRR reduces the funds available for lending, thereby reducing the money multiplier. *Hence, statement 3 is correct.*

• **Correct Option:** Only statements 1 and 3 are correct, making the correct answer **Only 1 and 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

__

• **Money Multiplier (MM):**

• The money multiplier measures the maximum amount of money that banks can create with a given level of reserves. It is mathematically expressed as **MM = 1/Reserve Ratio**.

• It represents the relationship between the monetary base (currency + reserves) and the total money supply.

• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR):**

• CRR is a regulatory requirement imposed by the RBI on banks to maintain a certain percentage of their deposits as reserves with the central bank.

• CRR affects the liquidity in the banking system and directly influences the money creation process.

• **Factors Affecting the Money Multiplier:**

• **Public's Preference for Cash:** If people prefer to hold more cash, the funds available for banks to lend decrease, reducing the MM.

• **Reserve Requirements:** Higher reserve requirements (CRR or Statutory Liquidity Ratio) reduce the banking system's capacity to create credit, lowering the MM.

• **Economic Environment:** In times of economic uncertainty, banks may adopt a more cautious approach, holding higher reserves and lending less, which reduces the MM.

• **Role of RBI in Money Supply:**

• The RBI regulates the money supply through tools such as CRR, Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), and Open Market Operations (OMO).

• By adjusting reserve requirements, the RBI can influence the MM and the availability of credit in the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Example of Money Multiplier:**

• If the reserve ratio is 10%, the money multiplier is **1/0.10 = 10**. This means every ₹1 in reserves can support ₹10 in total deposits.

• **Impact of Excess Reserves:**

• Banks may choose to hold excess reserves to mitigate risks, especially during economic downturns. This reduces the MM as fewer funds are available for lending.

• **Global Comparison:**

• Countries with lower reserve requirements typically have higher money multipliers, leading to greater credit creation capacity.

7c

question: The lead bank scheme was introduced in which year?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1969**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Lead Bank Scheme** (LBS) was introduced by the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** in **1969**. It was based on the recommendations of the **Gadgil Study Group**.

• The scheme aimed to address regional disparities in banking and credit accessibility by designating a specific bank as the "Lead Bank" for each district.

• The primary objective was to ensure that banking services and credit facilities reached the underserved and unbanked regions, especially rural areas, to promote **financial inclusion**.

• Under this scheme, the Lead Bank was responsible for coordinating with other banks and financial institutions in the district to prepare and implement a **District Credit Plan (DCP)**.

• The scheme contributed significantly to the rural development of India by supporting sectors like **agriculture, small-scale industries, and self-employment ventures**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Background and Objectives of the Lead Bank Scheme:**

• The scheme was launched in **1969**, coinciding with the period when the Indian government nationalized 14 major commercial banks to expand banking services.

• The **Gadgil Committee** identified the lack of banking penetration in rural and semi-urban areas as a significant hurdle to economic development.

• The main objective was to **bridge the gap** between credit supply and demand in underdeveloped regions.

• **Role of Lead Banks:**

• Each district was assigned a Lead Bank, which acted as the coordinator for all developmental and financial activities in that district.

• The Lead Bank was tasked with conducting surveys, identifying credit gaps, and preparing plans to enhance credit flow to priority sectors.

• It also promoted cooperation among banks, government agencies, and local bodies to achieve regional development goals.

• **Priority Sectors under the Scheme:**

• The scheme emphasized providing credit to sectors like **agriculture, small-scale industries, artisans, and self-employed individuals**.

• It aimed to improve the living standards of rural populations and reduce poverty by enabling access to institutional credit.

• **Evolution and Current Status:**

• Over the years, the Lead Bank Scheme has undergone several modifications to align with the changing economic and banking landscape.

• Even today, it plays a critical role in fostering financial inclusion and ensuring the availability of banking facilities in remote regions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** periodically reviews and updates the guidelines of the Lead Bank Scheme to ensure its relevance.

• Post-2005, the scheme gained further momentum with the introduction of the **Financial Inclusion Plan** and **Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY)**.

• The **District Credit Plan (DCP)** is a key component of the scheme, ensuring that credit flow aligns with district-level development goals.

• Currently, the scheme emphasizes the use of digital banking and technology to improve access to financial services in rural areas.
</ul

__

 __

• **Marginal Utility **is the change in total utility due to a one-unit change in the level of consumption.
 
• **Law of Diminishing Marginal Utility**
 
 
• It states that as** a person consumes an item or a product, the satisfaction or utility that they derive from the product declines as they consume more and more of that product.**
 
• In other words, the additional utility gained from an increase in consumption decreases with each subsequent increase in the level of consumption.
 
 
 
• **Demand curves **are downward-sloping in microeconomic models since each additional unit of a good or service is put toward a less valuable use.
 
• Marketers use the law of diminishing marginal utility because they want to keep marginal utility high for products that they sell.

subject: GK
question: According to Malthusian theory which of the following grows in geometric progression?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Population**__.

__
 
• **According to Malthusian theory, the population grows in geometric progression**__.

 __
 
• The **Malthusian Theory of Population** is the theory of exponential **population** and **arithmetic food supply growth.**
 
• The theory was proposed by **Thomas Robert Malthus**. He believed that a balance between population growth and food supply can be established through preventive and positive checks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

 
• **Malthusian Theory of Population Growth:**

 
 
• Among the most famous theories of demography is the one associated with the English political economist Thomas Robert Malthus (1766-1834).
 
• Malthus's theory of population growth - outlined in his Essay on Population (1798) - was a rather pessimistic one.
 
• He argued that human populations tend to grow at a much faster rate than the rate at which the means of human subsistence (especially food, but also clothing and other agriculture-based products) can grow. Therefore humanity is condemned to live in poverty forever because the growth of agricultural production will always be overtaken by population growth.
 
• While population rises in **geometric progression** (i.e., like 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 etc.), agricultural production can only grow in arithmetic progression (i.e., like 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 etc.).
 
• Because population growth always outstrips growth in the production of subsistence resources, the only way to increase prosperity is by controlling the growth of the population.
 
• Unfortunately, humanity has only a limited ability to voluntarily reduce the growth of its population (through 'preventive checks' such as postponing marriage or practicing sexual abstinence or celibacy).
 
• Malthus believed therefore that positive checks' to population growth - in the form of famines and diseases - were inevitable because they were nature's way of dealing with the imbalance between food supply and increasing population.

• A company's net investment is the sum of its expenditures on capital assets less the cost of depreciating those assets.

• Depreciation: It means a fall in the value of an asset because of usage or with efflux of time or due to obsolescence or accident.
 
• Appreciation: It means an increase in the value of an asset over time. This the opposite of depreciation. It is an upward adjustment of the value of an asset held on a company's accounting book.
 
• Deceleration: It is the rate at which an asset's value in the market goes down.
 
• Gross investment: It is the total amount spent on goods in order to produce other goods and services. 
 
• Net investment: It is the amount of increase in productive stock.
 
• 
 
Capital investment is the money used by a business to purchase fixed assets, such as land, machinery, or buildings. The money may be in the form of cash, assets, or loans. Without capital investment, businesses may have a hard time getting off the ground.

__
 
• In a barter exchange, goods or services are exchanged directly for other goods or services without using a medium of exchange such as money.
 
• Barter exchange is one of the oldest forms of trade and commerce, dating back to times before the invention of money.
 
• This type of exchange relies on the mutual wants of the participants; each party must have something the other party wants.
 
• Barter systems can be simple and direct, or they can be facilitated through barter exchanges or networks where multiple parties can trade goods and services.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Online Exchange**

 
 
• Online exchange refers to the process of exchanging goods, services, or currency over the internet.
 
• This type of exchange typically involves digital platforms that facilitate the buying and selling of products or services.
 
 
 
• **Credit Exchange**
 
 
• Credit exchange involves the use of credit as a medium of exchange.
 
• This can occur in various forms such as credit cards, loans, or other forms of deferred payment.
 
 
 
• **Currency Exchange**
 
 
• Currency exchange involves the conversion of one type of currency into another.
 
• This process is essential for international trade and travel, allowing individuals and businesses to transact in different currencies.
 
 
 
• **Barter Exchange**
 
 
• Barter exchange is the direct exchange of goods and services without the use of money.
 
• This system requires that the parties involved have mutually desirable goods or services to trade.

• These industries are characterized by shared ownership between the government (usually through public sector undertakings) and private companies or individuals.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following best describes the rate of natural increase of population?

options.text: It is the crude birth rate multiplied by crude death rate
It is the ratio of working population to total population
It is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate
It is the average annual growth due to migration alone

solution:
The correct answer is __**It is the difference between the birth rate and the death rate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The rate of natural increase (RNI) of a population refers to **the difference between the crude birth rate (CBR) and the crude death rate (CDR).**
 
• It measures the population growth occurring solely due to **natural factors (births and deaths)**, excluding migration.
 
• The rate of natural increase is typically expressed as a percentage or per 1,000 individuals per year.
 
• For example, if the crude birth rate is 20 per 1,000 and the crude death rate is 8 per 1,000, the RNI is 12 per 1,000 (or 1.2%).
 
• The RNI is a critical indicator in demography, as it provides insights into the natural population growth and helps in policy planning, resource allocation, and infrastructure development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)**

 
 
• Definition: The number of live births per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• Formula: (Total Live Births / Total Population) * 1,000.
 
• Significance: Indicates fertility levels and contributes to population growth. 
 
 
 
• **Crude Death Rate (CDR)**
 
 
• Definition: The number of deaths per 1,000 people in a year.
 
• Formula: (Total Deaths / Total Population) * 1,000.
 
• Significance: Reflects mortality conditions and public health, with declines often due to better healthcare and sanitation.

question:
**Consider the following statements and choose the correct option:**

Statement 1: The Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) shows the trade-offs and opportunity costs faced by an economy.

Statement 2: The PPF is used to estimate the government's total revenue and expenditure.

options.text: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct
Neither Statement 1 nor Statement 2 is correct

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1: Only Statement 1 is correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **The Production Possibility Frontier (PPF):** It represents the maximum possible combinations of goods and services that an economy can produce given its resources and technology.
 
• **Trade-offs and Opportunity Costs:** The PPF graphically demonstrates the trade-offs and opportunity costs involved in allocating resources between different products.
 
• **Efficient Resource Utilization:** Any point on the PPF curve indicates the efficient use of resources, while points inside the curve indicate underutilization, and points outside are unattainable.
 
• PPF is a cornerstone concept in economics and is used to understand how economies allocate scarce resources efficiently.
 
• Statement 1 is correct because the PPF explicitly depicts trade-offs and opportunity costs faced by an economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concept of Opportunity Cost:**

 
 
• Opportunity cost refers to the value of the next best alternative foregone when a choice is made.
 
• In the context of the PPF, when resources are reallocated from producing one good to another, the opportunity cost is the amount of the first good that must be sacrificed.
 
 
 
• **Shape of the PPF:**
 
 
• The PPF is typically concave to the origin because of the law of increasing opportunity costs. As more resources are allocated to one good, the cost of producing additional units of that good increases.
 
• However, a straight-line PPF indicates constant opportunity costs, which is less common in real-world scenarios.

__
 
• Employment is not considered a direct component of population change as it does not directly influence the size of the population.
 
• Population change is typically determined by three key factors: births, deaths, and migration.
 
• Employment affects the socio-economic structure of a population but does not contribute directly to its growth or decline.
 
• While employment may influence migration patterns indirectly (e.g., people moving to cities for jobs), it is not a standalone factor in population change.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Births:**

 
 
• Births are a primary component of population change. The birth rate measures the number of live births per 1,000 people in a given year.
 
• It plays a significant role in determining the natural increase or decrease in population.
 
• Factors such as fertility rates, healthcare services, and socio-economic conditions influence birth rates.
 
 
 
• **Deaths:**
 
 
• Deaths are another critical component of population change. The death rate measures the number of deaths per 1,000 people in a given year.
 
• Mortality rates are affected by healthcare facilities, lifestyle, nutrition, and sanitation.
 
• A decline in the death rate due to advancements in medicine and public health can lead to population growth.
 
 
 
• **Migration:**
 
 
• Migration refers to the movement of people from one region to another, either within a country or across international borders.
 
• It can be classified into immigration (in-migration) and emigration (out-migration).
 
• Migration impacts the distribution and growth of a population in specific regions rather than the total global population size.

subject: GK
question: Which curve shows all combinations of two goods that give a consumer equal satisfaction?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indifference Curve**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• An **Indifference Curve** represents all combinations of two goods that provide the same level of satisfaction or utility to a consumer.
 
• It is a graphical representation used in **microeconomics** to analyze consumer preferences and choice.
 
• Each point on the curve indicates that the consumer is indifferent between the combinations of goods, meaning they derive equal utility from them.
 
• Indifference curves are typically **downward sloping**, reflecting the trade-offs between goods, and they do not intersect.
 
• The slope of the indifference curve, known as the **Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS)**, measures the rate at which a consumer is willing to give up one good for another while maintaining the same utility level.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Budget Constraint:**

 
 
• A budget constraint represents the combinations of goods and services a consumer can purchase given their income and the prices of the goods.
 
• It is a straight line that shows the trade-off between two goods, limited by the consumer's financial resources.
 
• The slope of the budget constraint is determined by the ratio of the prices of the two goods.
 
• While the budget constraint determines what is affordable, it does not indicate preferences or satisfaction like an indifference curve does.
 
 
 
• **Isoquant Curve:**
 
 
• An isoquant curve represents all combinations of inputs (e.g., labor and capital) that produce the same level of output.
 
• It is used in production theory to analyze input combinations and efficiency, not consumer preferences.
 
• Like indifference curves, isoquants are downward sloping, but they are specific to production rather than utility.
 
• The slope of an isoquant curve reflects the **Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS)**, which measures the rate at which one input can be substituted for another while maintaining the same output level.
 
 
 
• **Marginal Cost Curve:**
 
 
• The marginal cost curve shows the additional cost incurred for producing one more unit of a good or service.
 
• It is a key concept in production and cost analysis, helping firms determine optimal production levels.
 
• Unlike indifference curves, it does not deal with consumer satisfaction but focuses on cost dynamics and efficiency in production.
 
• The marginal cost curve typically intersects with the average cost curve at its minimum point.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme - Consumer Choice Theory:**
 
 
• The indifference curve is a fundamental concept in **consumer choice theory**, which analyzes how consumers make decisions to maximize their satisfaction given constraints such as income and prices.
 
• It helps in understanding the trade-offs consumers face and the relationship between preferences, affordability, and utility.

question: Which of the following best defines the concept of 'opportunity cost'?
solution:
The correct answer is __**The next best alternative foregone**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Opportunity cost** is the value of the next best alternative that is foregone when a choice is made.
 
• It represents the benefits or value that could have been gained if the resources had been utilized in the next best alternative.
 
• The concept is a fundamental principle in economics and helps in decision-making where resources are scarce and trade-offs are inevitable.
 
• Opportunity cost is not always expressed in monetary terms; it can also include time, effort, or other non-monetary factors.
 
• This principle underlines the importance of evaluating all possible options before committing resources to a specific decision.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The cost of production**

 
 
• This refers to the total expenditure incurred by a business to produce goods or services, including costs of raw materials, labor, and overheads.
 
• It is used to determine the selling price and profitability of a product or service.
 
• Unlike opportunity cost, this focuses only on the monetary aspect of production and does not consider foregone alternatives.
 
 
 
• **The cost of labor**
 
 
• This is a specific component of production cost and refers to the wages, salaries, and benefits paid to employees for their work.
 
• It can be divided into direct labor costs (workers directly involved in production) and indirect labor costs (support staff, management, etc.).
 
• It does not encompass the broader concept of trade-offs like opportunity cost.
 
 
 
• **The total money spent**
 
 
• This phrase typically refers to the sum of all expenses made by an individual, organization, or government in a particular context.
 
• It is a straightforward accounting measure and does not account for the value of forgone alternatives.
 
• While it helps in budgeting and tracking expenditures, it does not address the economic implications of resource allocation like opportunity cost does.

question:
Consider the following statements about the book 'India on Our Minds':

1) The book offers an insightful analysis of India's economic growth and social challenges.

2) It is a fictional novel about India's freedom struggle. Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only statement 1 is correct**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• **Statement 1:** The book "India on Our Minds" offers an **insightful analysis of India's economic growth and social challenges.** This statement is correct as the book focuses on examining India's advancements in economic sectors and the hurdles faced in addressing socio-economic disparities. It provides a detailed and analytical overview of India's transformation in various domains. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.*** 
 
 
• **Statement 2:** The book is a fictional novel about India's freedom struggle. This statement is incorrect as "India on Our Minds" is a non-fictional work that delves into India's contemporary socio-economic landscape rather than being a historical or fictional account of the freedom struggle. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*** 
 
 
• Given the nature of the book and its analytical insights, it is evident that it is not a fictional novel. It is recognized for its contribution to understanding India's growth trajectory and challenges. 
 
 
• The book is an important resource for individuals interested in India's current status in global economics and its socio-political challenges. It provides a platform for critical analysis and debate regarding India's progress and future potential. 

 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is "Only statement 1 is correct."*** 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Focus of "India on Our Minds":** 
 
 
• The book examines India's **economic growth** in the context of global markets and its role as a key player in the global economy. 
 
• It provides an analysis of **social challenges** such as poverty, inequality, and access to education and healthcare. 
 
• It discusses the implications of India's policies and reforms on its citizens and on the global stage. 
 
 
 
 
• **India's Economic Growth:** 
 
 
• India has emerged as the world's **fifth-largest economy** in terms of nominal GDP and third-largest by purchasing power parity (PPP). 
 
• The country has seen significant growth in sectors such as **technology, manufacturing, and services.** 
 
• Despite this growth, challenges such as **income inequality** and rural-urban disparities persist. 
 
 
 
 
• **Social Challenges in India:** 
 
 
• India faces challenges in providing **universal access to quality education** and healthcare. 
 
• Issues such as **gender inequality** and lack of infrastructure in rural areas affect development. 
 
• Efforts such as the **National Education Policy (NEP) 2020** and Ayushman Bharat aim to address these challenges. 
 
 
 
 
• **Importance of Non-fictional Analysis:** 
 
 
• Non-fictional works like "India on Our Minds" provide a factual and analytical perspective on contemporary issues. 
 
• They serve as valuable resources for policymakers, researchers, and students interested in India's socio-economic landscape. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• **Other Books on India's Socio-economic Landscape:** 
 
 
• **"India After Gandhi"** by Ramachandra Guha: Covers India's political history and socio-economic developments after independence. 
 
• **"The Invention of India"** by Shashi Tharoor: Explores India's history, culture, and contributions to the global stage. 
 
• **"Why Nations Fail"** by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson: Includes references to India's development challenges in the context of global economic history. 
 
 
 
 
• **Key Reports and Indices:**
