question: What is the objective of the 'Doughnut Model' of development?

options.text: It envisions a world in which people and planet can thrive in balance.
It envisions total abandonment of technology to live at peace with environment
It envisions the food processing industry as the centre of development.
It envisions rapid development at environmental cost, then make up for it later

solution:
The correct answer is __**It envisions a world in which people and planet can thrive in balance**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• ** 'Doughnut Model' of development**

 
 
• The Doughnut, or Doughnut economics, is a visual framework for sustainable development – shaped like a doughnut or lifebelt – combining the concept of planetary boundaries with the complementary concept of social boundaries.
 
• **It envisions a world in which people and the planet can thrive in balance**__.
 
• The name derives from the shape of the diagram, i.e. a disc with a hole in the middle.
 __
 
• The center hole of the model depicts the proportion of people that lack access to life's essentials (healthcare, education, equity and so on) while the crust represents the ecological ceilings (planetary boundaries) that life depends on and must not be overshot.
 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• Austrian economic thought

 
 
• Austrian economic thought talks about methodological individualism or the idea that people will act in meaningful ways which can be analyzed.
 
• The Austrian school uses the logic of a priori thinking—something a person can think on their own without relying on the outside world—to discover economic laws of universal application, whereas other mainstream schools of economics, like the neoclassical school, the new Keynesians, and others, make use of data and mathematical models to prove their point objectively.
 
• In this respect, the Austrian school can be more specifically contrasted with the German historical school that rejects the universal application of any economic theorem.
 
 
 
• Keynesian Economics
 
 
• Keynesian economics is a macroeconomic economic theory of total spending in the economy and its effects on output, employment, and inflation.
 
• Keynesian economics was developed by the British economist John Maynard Keynes during the 1930s in an attempt to understand the Great Depression.
 
• Keynesian economics is considered a "demand-side" theory that focuses on changes in the economy over the short run. 
 
 
 
• Laissez-Faire
 
 
• Laissez-faire is an economic theory from the 18th century that opposed any government intervention in business affairs.
 
• Laissez-faire economics is a key part of free-market capitalism.

__
 
• Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) is a scheme launched by the government of India to provide loans up to ₹10 Lakh to non-corporate, non-farm small/micro enterprises.
 
• These loans are classified as MUDRA loans under PMMY and are given by commercial banks, RRBs, small finance banks, MFIs, and NBFCs.
 
• The scheme was launched on 8 April 2015 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
 
• MUDRA stands for Micro Units Development and Refinance Agency Limited, which provides funding support to the micro-enterprise sector.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Strategy for Financial Inclusion**

 
 
• It is a strategy prepared by the Reserve Bank of India to provide access to formal financial services in an affordable manner.
 
• The strategy aims at promoting financial education, financial literacy, and consumer protection.
 
• It includes various stakeholders like banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), micro-finance institutions (MFIs), and insurance companies.
 
• It emphasizes the need for a robust digital financial ecosystem to achieve universal financial access.
 
 
 
• **Stand Up India scheme**
 
 
• It was launched on 5 April 2016 by the Government of India.
 
• The scheme aims to promote entrepreneurship among Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes and women by providing loans between ₹10 lakh and ₹1 crore.
 
• It ensures that each bank branch provides at least one loan to SC/ST and one to women borrowers.
 
• Stand Up India scheme provides handholding support and guidance to borrowers during the loan tenure.
 
 
 
• **Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana**
 
 
• Launched on 28 August 2014, it aims to provide universal access to banking facilities with at least one basic banking account for every household.
 
• The scheme promotes financial inclusion by ensuring access to financial services such as bank savings and deposit accounts, remittance, credit, insurance, and pension.
 
• It allows direct benefit transfer (DBT) to accounts opened under PMJDY, ensuring transparency and reducing leakages.

question: What is the primary objective of the Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises Development (MSMED) Act of 2006 in India?

options.text: To focus on large-scale industries only
To increase import tariffs to protect MSMEs
To promote and facilitate the development of MSMEs

solution:
The correct answer is __**To promote and facilitate the development of MSMEs**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The primary objective of the MSMED Act, 2006 is to **promote and facilitate the development and competitiveness of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in India**.
 
• The Act provides the first-ever legal framework for the recognition of the concept of "enterprise", which comprises both manufacturing and service entities.
 
• It aims to address the policy issues affecting MSMEs as well as the coverage and investment ceiling of the sector.
 
• The Act also emphasizes on the **promotion of MSMEs through various schemes and incentives** to enhance their productivity and competitiveness.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs)**

 
 
• MSMEs are categorized based on their investment in plant and machinery or equipment and annual turnover.
 
• Micro enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 1 crore and turnover up to Rs. 5 crore.
 
• Small enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 10 crore and turnover up to Rs. 50 crore.
 
• Medium enterprises: Investment up to Rs. 50 crore and turnover up to Rs. 250 crore.
 
 
 
• **MSMED Act, 2006**
 
 
• The Act was enacted to address the diverse issues faced by the MSME sector and to promote its development.
 
• It provides for the establishment of a National Board for MSMEs to lay down policies and programs for the sector.
 
• The Act also includes provisions related to the delayed payments to MSMEs, aimed at ensuring timely payments and reducing financial stress on these enterprises.
 
 
 
• **Importance of MSMEs**
 
 
• MSMEs play a crucial role in the socio-economic development of India.
 
• They contribute significantly to the country's GDP, exports, and employment generation.
 
• MSMEs are vital for the balanced regional development of the country as they often operate in rural and semi-urban areas.
 
• The sector also fosters entrepreneurship and innovation.
 
 
 
• **Government Initiatives for MSMEs**
 
 
• Various schemes and programs have been launched to support MSMEs, such as the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme, MUDRA Yojana, and the MSME Champions Scheme.
 
• The government has also implemented measures to improve ease of doing business for MSMEs, including simplifying registration processes and providing financial incentives.

question: Which of the following correctly highlights a unique feature of India's textile industry?

options.text: It focuses only on raw material exports.
It is partially self-reliant and imports final products.
It is self-reliant across the full value chain
It only caters to domestic markets.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It is self-reliant across the full value chain**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• India's textile industry is one of the most self-reliant sectors in the country, encompassing the **entire value chain from raw materials to finished goods**. This includes cotton production, spinning, weaving, dyeing, printing, and garment manufacturing.
 
• The Indian textile sector is among the largest globally, contributing approximately **2.3% to India's GDP**, 7% to the industrial output, and 12% to the country’s export earnings.
 
• India is the **largest producer of cotton** and jute globally and ranks second in silk and polyester production, ensuring a strong foundation for raw material availability.
 
• With a balanced integration of traditional handloom techniques and advanced machinery, the textile industry caters to both **domestic and international markets**.
 
• Government initiatives such as the **Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme** for textiles and the establishment of **Mega Textile Parks** aim to further boost the self-reliance of the sector across the value chain.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Post-Independence (1948 & 1956): **Focused on public sector dominance, planned development, and import substitution, with state control over strategic industries (IPR 1956).
 
• **1991 New Industrial Policy (LPG Reforms): **Marked a major shift towards liberalization, privatization, and globalization, dismantling the License Raj, opening up sectors to private and foreign investment, and encouraging exports.
 
• **National Manufacturing Policy (NMP 2011): **Aimed to increase manufacturing's share in GDP, create jobs, promote SEZs, and develop National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs).
 
• **Make in India (2014): **Aims to make India a global manufacturing hub, improve ease of doing business, attract FDI, and boost key sectors like defense, aerospace, and electronics.
 
• **Current Focus (Post-2020): **Emphasizes Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Schemes for high-growth sectors, further deregulation, skill development, and infrastructure, seeking self-reliance (Atmanirbhar Bharat).

question:

__
 
• The National Single Window System (NSWS) is an initiative by the Government of India that facilitates investors in obtaining clearances and approvals from various departments and ministries.
 
• The NSWS is designed to reduce bureaucratic hurdles and enhance the ease of doing business in India by providing a centralized platform.
 
• It integrates multiple government systems and services across Ministries and States, providing a single interface for businesses.
 
• The system includes a common registration form, document repository, and a dashboard for real-time tracking of approvals and clearances.
 
• Contrary to the Reason (R) in the question, the NSWS is not a separate ministry. Instead, it operates under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) within the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

• It aims to reduce the compliance burden on businesses and increase transparency and accountability in government processes.
 
• The platform is designed to cater to both domestic and global investors, promoting India as a business-friendly destination.
 
 
 
• **The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT)**
 
 
• The DPIIT is a central government department under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
 
• It is responsible for formulating and implementing promotional and developmental measures for industrial growth in India.
 
• The NSWS is one of the key initiatives under DPIIT to improve ease of doing business.
 
 
 
• **Ease of Doing Business in India**
 
 
• India has made significant improvements in the World Bank's Ease of Doing Business rankings over the years, thanks to initiatives like the NSWS.
 
• These reforms aim to simplify regulatory processes, digitize services, and provide a conducive environment for businesses to thrive.

question: What is the primary aim of TIES?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Export infra development**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **TIES (Trade Infrastructure for Export Scheme)** was launched by the Government of India in March 2017 to address the gaps in export infrastructure in the country.
 
• The scheme aims to **create and upgrade export-related infrastructure** for promoting exports in India.
 
• It provides financial assistance to central and state government agencies for the development of necessary export infrastructure, such as testing labs, cold chains, warehouses, and trade promotion centers.
 
• The funding under TIES is in the form of grants-in-aid, typically not exceeding 50% of the total project cost for eligible projects.
 
• The scheme focuses on projects that have a direct impact on improving the export competitiveness of goods and services from India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cold storage for dairy (Option 2):**
 
 
• While cold storage is an essential part of the dairy supply chain, it is not directly related to the TIES scheme.
 
• Cold storage for dairy products is typically supported under other initiatives like the Pradhan Mantri Kisan SAMPADA Yojana or schemes promoted by the Ministry of Food Processing Industries.
 
• These initiatives aim to reduce food wastage, improve processing infrastructure, and ensure better returns for farmers.
 
 
 
• **PMFBY support (Option 3):**
 
 
• The Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana (PMFBY) is a crop insurance scheme launched in 2016 to provide financial support to farmers in the event of crop failure due to natural calamities.
 
• It focuses on stabilizing farmer incomes and ensuring the adoption of innovative agricultural practices.
 
• PMFBY is unrelated to TIES, as it deals with crop insurance rather than export infrastructure.
 
 
 
• **Drug pricing regulation (Option 4):**
 
 
• Drug pricing regulation in India is overseen by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA).
 
• The NPPA ensures the availability of essential medicines at affordable prices and monitors the prices of drugs under the Drug (Prices Control) Order.
 
• It is not connected to the objectives of the TIES scheme, which is focused on export infrastructure development.

question: Which government initiative aims to provide a unified platform for citizens to access various government services online?

options.text: UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance)

solution:
The correct answer is __**UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance)** is a flagship initiative by the Government of India to provide a single platform for accessing numerous government services digitally.

• It was launched on **23rd November 2017** by Prime Minister **Narendra Modi** to promote digital governance and enhance service delivery mechanisms.

• The platform integrates **200+ government services** across central and state departments, including Aadhaar, DigiLocker, EPFO, PAN services, and more, into one accessible mobile application.

• UMANG supports services in multiple Indian languages, ensuring inclusivity and accessibility for citizens across the country.

• The app is available across multiple platforms, including **Android, iOS, and web**, and is designed to provide services related to education, healthcare, finance, agriculture, and others.

• It serves as a significant step towards achieving the vision of **Digital India**, ensuring that citizens can access services conveniently without visiting government offices physically.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **DigiLocker:** 

• Launched in **2015** under the Digital India initiative, DigiLocker provides a platform for digital storage of important documents like Aadhaar, PAN, driving license, and education certificates.

• It allows users to access their documents securely and share them electronically with government agencies and other entities.

• Unlike UMANG, DigiLocker focuses solely on document storage and verification rather than offering a wide range of services.

• **MyGov:** 

• Introduced in **2014**, MyGov is an online platform enabling citizens to engage directly with the government by participating in discussions, tasks, and policy-making processes.

• It focuses on citizen engagement and crowdsourcing ideas rather than service delivery.

• **National e-Governance Plan (NeGP):** 

• Launched in **2006**, NeGP aims to make all government services accessible to citizens through electronic means.

• It provides the framework for implementing e-governance initiatives, under which projects like UMANG have been developed.

• While NeGP is a policy framework, UMANG is a practical implementation of such policies.

• **Features of UMANG:** 

• Integration with **Aadhaar** and other government systems for seamless service delivery.

• Availability of services related to **EPFO, tax payment, utility bill payments, health schemes**, and more.

• Support for **voice-based navigation** and multi-language access to make it user-friendly for diverse groups of people.

• Secure payment gateway integrated for financial transactions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Digital India Initiative:** 

• Digital India was launched in **2015** with the vision to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy.

• Key pillars include providing digital infrastructure, enhancing digital literacy, and delivering services digitally.

• UMANG is a key component of this initiative, ensuring streamlined delivery of government services.

• **UMANG Awards:** 

• UMANG has received several accolades, including the **Best m-Government Service Award** at the **World Government Summit 2018** held in Dubai.

• It is recognized globally as an exemplary model for digital governance.

• In **1950, the Planning Commission** was established with **Jawaharlal Nehru **as its chairman.

• He gave the industrial foundation of the economy the most attention.
 
• In light of this, the **1948 Industrial Policy Resolution** was revised, and a new resolution was adopted in 1956.

__
 
• In India, the share of agriculture in the country's **GDP decreased **dramatically between 1950 and 1990 (from 67.5% to 64.9%), but not the population that depended on it.
 
• **​**A monetary indicator of the market worth of all the final goods and services produced and sold (not resold) in a certain time period by nations is the **gross domestic product (GDP)**.
 
• This measurement is frequently reviewed before being regarded as a valid indicator due to its subjective and complicated character. While nominal **GDP** is more useful for comparing **national economies** on the **global market**.
 
• **GDP **(nominal) per capita does not account for variations in the cost of living and **inflation rates **of the various nations.
 
• The contribution made by each **industry **or **sector** of the economy can also be calculated as a **percentage **of the total **GDP**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Many national and **international** economic groups keep track of **GDP **definitions.
 
• The **GDP **is defined by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development** (OECD)** as "an aggregate measure of production equal to the sum of the gross values added of all resident and institutional units engaged in production and services (plus any taxes, and minus any subsidies on products not **included **in the value of their outputs)".
 
• According to an **IMF **report, "**GDP** represents the monetary value of final goods and services that are purchased by the final user **produced **in a country in a certain period of **time **(say, a quarter or a year)."

solution:

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• **Mahalanobis Model**

 
 
• **​Marxist **economists **Grigory** **Feldman** from the Soviet Union and **Prasanta** **Chandra** **Mahalanobis** from India separately developed the **Feldman-Mahalanobis model in 1953**.
 
• **Mahalanobis **ended up serving as the **Second Five Year Plan's** primary economist and was the focus of many of the country's most contentious economic discussions.
 
• The **core **of the **strategy** is a change in** industrial investmen**t patterns towards the development of a domestic **consumption goods sector.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Long-term expansion** of the nation's consumer** goods production** capacity depends on the capital goods sector having a high adequate capacity.
 
• The division between the two different categories of **goods **helped consumers better comprehend the **trade-off** between levels of immediate and** future consumption** and provided a clearer **explanation **of **Marx's **theories in** Das Kapital**.
 
• **Feldman**, an economist for the **GOSPLAN **planning committee at the time, first proposed these concepts in 1928, outlining the theoretical justifications for a** two-department growth strategy**.

(iii) Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI)
solution:

• **Industrial Finance Corporation of India (IFCI)** was set up in **1948**, making it the oldest DFI.
 
• **Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India (ICICI)** was set up in** 1955, **making it the second oldest DFI.

question: How many industries were listed in Schedule A of Industrial Policy, 1956?
solution:
The correct answer is __**17.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956** in India classified industries into three categories: **Schedule A, B, and C**.
 
• There were 1**7 industries listed under Schedule A.**
 
• The industries under Schedule A were the ones where the **state would have exclusive responsibility**.
 
• The purpose of such categorization was to help in the **systematic development** of various sectors in India.
 
• Some of the sectors under Schedule A included **arms and ammunition, atomic energy, iron and steel, heavy machinery, mineral oil, coal, etc.**
 
• The Initiative was a part of India's broader** 'socialistic pattern of society' **approach where the state played a dominant role in industrial development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Schedule B:**

 
 
• Schedule B consisted of **12 industries.**
 
• These industries were to be progressively **state-owned, but private enterprise** could also supplement the effort.
 
• This schedule included industries such as **aluminium and other non-ferrous metals, machine tools, electrical engineering, automobiles and tractors, industrial and agricultural chemicals, and more**.
 
 
 
• **Schedule C:**
 
 
• Schedule C covered the** rest of the industries,** and they were left **open to the private sector, **although the state could also venture.
 
• This implied that the** rest of the industries not specified in Schedule A or B** could be initiated and operated by private enterprises.
 
• The government could also start any new industry in this category, depending on the national interest.
 
 

This policy intended to maintain a** balance between public and private sectors,** providing ample opportunities for private entities while the State assumed responsibility for industrial development in certain sectors.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• 
 
​Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) 1956:-

 
 
• It laid the foundation for India’s second five-year plan and Industrial policy Resolution 1956, which paved the way for the development of the Public Sector and License Raj. 
 
• In accordance with the goal of the state controlling the commanding heights of the economy, the Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 was adopted. 
 
• The 1956 Policy empha­sised the need to expand the public sector and build up a large and growing coop­erative sector. 
 
• It encourages the separation of ownership and management in private in­dustries and, above all, prevents the rise of pri­vate monopolies. 
 
• This resolution formed the basis of the Second Five Year Plan, the plan which tried to build the basis for a socialist pattern of society. 
 
• **This resolution classified Industries into three categories.**
 
• The first category comprised industries that would be exclusively owned by the government; the second category consisted of industries in which the private sector could supplement the efforts of the public sector. 
 
• It was based upon the Mahalanobis Model of growth which advocated that emphasis should be laid on the heavy industries, which can increase the economic output of the country. Mahalanobis model suggested the dominance of the heavy industries. 
 
• It laid emphasis on integrated infrastructure development as a prerequisite to private investment and therefore gave priority to power, transport, and financial institutions.
 
• It gave recognition to small-scale industries such as cottage industries with respect to balanced regional growth and also gave tax concessions and subsidies.
 
• It gave impetus to industrial development in far-off of the country to increase economic growth.
 
• It considered FDI as complementary to domestic growth provided a major share in control and management was to be given to Indian hands.

question: Why is PC Mahalanobis' name talked about in the context of Five-Year Plans?

options.text: He was the chairman of the Planning Commission.
He established the Institute of Economic Growth.
He conceptualised the framework for the Second Five-Year Plan.
He was the finance minister during the First Five-Year Plan period.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis** was an **Indian statistician** who played a significant role in** formulating India's strategy for industrialization in the Second Five-Year Plan (1956–61).**
 
• The Plan, influenced by the Mahalanobis model, stressed the importance of **boosting the public sector's role **in the economy and targeted significant growth in sectors like **steel, electricity, and heavy machinery.**
 
• Although Mahalanobis was not the chairman of the Planning Commission nor the Finance Ministry during this time, his contributions were instrumental for the execution of the economic strategy during the Plan period.
 
• Therefore, his name is often mentioned alongside the development of these five-year plans in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** **Second Five year plan:**

 
• The Second Five-Year Plan, also known as the **Mahalanobis Plan**, was proposed by Indian statistician Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis in 1955. It was in effect from **1956 to 1961.**
 
• This plan focused on the development of the** public sector** and aimed to create a socialistic pattern of society.
 
• This Plan set the precedence for a predominant role of the state which would determine the **direction of the economy.**
 
• A substantial part of the plan was focused on** increasing industrialization,** with a particular emphasis on the development of heavy industries such as **steel, heavy engineering, machine making, etc.**
 
• The Plan aimed at a** 25% increase** in the national income over a period of five years and a transformation in the pattern of industrial production.
 
• However, the Plan was only partially successful in achieving its objectives, and the target growth rate of **national income (5%) was not achieved. **Still, it set a clear path for future industrial policies in India.

question: 'A Plan of Economic Development for India' is also known as ______.
solution:
The correct answer is__** the Bombay Plan.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• **The correct answer is option 4, i.e., Bombay Plan**.
 
• Bombay Plan was a **set of proposals for the economic development of India**, presented by a group of leading industrialists and economists in 1944.
 
• It was named after the city where it was drafted, i.e., Bombay (now Mumbai).
 
• The plan **aimed to create a mixed economy in India**, with a balance between the public and private sectors.
 
• It called for an increase in public investment in key sectors such as agriculture, industry, and infrastructure, while also promoting entrepreneurship and free enterprise.
 
• The Bombay Plan was seen as a response to the challenge o**f post-war reconstruction and development in India, as well as a critique of the laissez-faire policies of the colonial government.**
 
• It was also influenced by socialist and Fabian ideas, as well as the experience of planned economies in other countries.
 
• The Bombay Plan received both praise and criticism from different quarters. Some saw it as a visionary blueprint for India's future, while others criticized it as elitist, impractical, or insufficiently radical. However, it remains an important landmark in the history of economic thought and policy in India.
 
• The other options mentioned in the question are not correct because they do not refer to any actual plan of economic development for India. Delhi, Gujarat, and Surat are all cities or states in India, but they do not have any such plans named after them. Therefore, option 4, i.e., Bombay Plan, is the correct answer.

The correct answer is __**First**.__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• First Five-Year Plan

 
 
• 1st five-year plan was from 1951 to 1956.
 
• The prime target of the first five-year plan of India was the** Development of agriculture**.
 
• The target Growth was 2.1 % and the Actual Growth was 3.6 %.
 
• It was based on Harrod-Domar.
 
• The influx of refugees, severe food shortage & mounting inflation confronted the country at the onset of the first five-year plan.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3e20068b61817b168623bbf4377a66602deb382bfb1e34ae29a5e35078dcefcb.png] Additional Information__Second Five Year Plan (1956-1961)

 
• The second five-year plan is based on the so-called Mahalanobis model.
 
• This was the USSR model Indianized by PC Mahalanobis, the founder of the Indian Statistical Institute and a close aide of Nehru.
 
• This model is known to have set the statistical foundations for state-directed investments and created the intellectual underpinnings of the license-raj through an elaborate input-output model.
 
• This Model suggested that there should be an emphasis on the heavy industries, which can lead the Indian Economy to a long-term higher growth path
 
• Started Industrial Policy Resolution 1956.

Third Five-Year Plan (1961-1966)

 
• The Third 5 year Plan focused on agriculture & enhancement in the production of wheat, but the succinct Sino - Indian War in the year 1962 exposed flaws in the economy & shifted the spotlight towards the Defence industry.
 
• On May 31 & June 1, 1961, the National Development Council considered the Draft Report on the Third Plan and generally approved it.
 
• In the course of this period, India's economy must not only enlarge swiftly but must, in unison, become independent and self-generating.
 
• This long-standing approach is projected to offer a wide-ranging design of expansion for the country's natural resources, industrial advance, and agricultural changes in the social structure & an incorporated scheme of regional & national development.

Fourth Five Year Plan (1969-1974)

 
• The fourth Five Year Plan was the first plan launched by the Indira Gandhi government amid the pressure of drought, devaluation, and inflationary recession.
 
• The country was fighting with population explosion, increased unemployment, poverty, and a shackling economy. In addition, the situation in East Pakistan (now independent Bangladesh) was becoming dire as the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971 and the Bangladesh Liberation War took place.
 
• Funds earmarked for industrial development had to be used for the war effort.
 
• The result was that this plan period was also no better than the third five-year plan.

The correct answer is __**Fifth Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Fifth Five Year Plan: Its duration was 1974 to 1978. This plan focussed on Garibi Hatao, employment, justice, agricultural production, and defense.
 
• The Electricity Supply Act was amended in 1975, a Twenty-point program was launched in 1975, the Minimum Needs Programme (MNP), and the Indian National Highway System was introduced. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• First Five Year Plan: It was launched for the duration of 1951 to 1956, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. It was based on the Harrod-Domar model with a few modifications. Its main focus was on the agricultural development of the country.
 
• Second Five Year Plan: It was made for the duration of 1956 to 1961, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. It was based on the P.C. Mahalanobis Model made in the year 1953. Its main focus was on the industrial development of the country.
 
• Third Five-Year Plan: It was made for the duration of 1961 to 1966, under the leadership of Jawaharlal Nehru. This plan is also called ‘Gadgil Yojna’, after the Deputy Chairman of Planning Commission D.R. Gadgil. The main target of this plan was to make the economy independent. The stress was laid on agriculture and the improvement in the production of wheat. 
 
• Plan Holidays: Due to the failure of the previous plan, the government announced three annual plans called Plan Holidays from 1966 to 1969. The main reason behind the plan holidays was the Indo-Pakistani war and the Sino-India war, leading to the failure of the third Five Year Plan.
 
• Fourth Five-Year Plan: Its duration was from 1969 to 1974, under the leadership of Indira Gandhi. There were two main objectives of this plan i.e. growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance.
 
• Rolling Plan: After the termination of the fifth Five Year Plan, the Rolling Plan came into effect from 1978 to 1980. In 1980, Congress rejected the Rolling Plan, and a new sixth Five Year Plan was introduced. 
 
• Sixth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1980 to 1985, under the leadership of Indira Gandhi. The basic objective of this plan was economic liberalization by eradicating poverty and achieving technological self-reliance.
 
• Seventh Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1985 to 1990, under the leadership of Rajiv Gandhi. The objectives of this plan include the establishment of a self-sufficient economy, opportunities for productive employment, and up-gradation of technology.
 
• Eighth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1992 to 1997, under the leadership of P.V. Narasimha Rao. In this plan, the top priority was given to the development of human resources i.e. employment, education, and public health.
 
• Ninth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 1997 to 2002, under the leadership of Atal Bihari Vajpayee. The main focus of this plan was “Growth with Social Justice and Equality”.
 
• Tenth Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 2002 to 2007, under the leadership of Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Manmohan Singh. II. This plan aimed to double the Per Capita Income of India in the next 10 years.
 
• Eleventh Five Year Plan: Its duration was from 2007 to 2012, under the leadership of Manmohan Singh. It was prepared by C. Rangarajan.Its main theme was “rapid and more inclusive growth”. Twelfth Five Year Plan: Its duration is from 2012 to 2017, under the leadership of Manmohan Singh. Its main theme is “Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth”.

• They aimed to create a balance in the country's economy and promote steady growth in various sectors such as agriculture, industry, and services.
 
• The Planning Commission, an institution in the Government of India, was responsible for drafting and executing these plans.
 
• The First Five-Year Plan focused mainly on the agricultural sector to address the food shortage that the country was facing post-independence.
 
 
 
• **Planning Commission**
 
 
• The Planning Commission was an institution in the Government of India, which formulated India's Five-Year Plans, among other functions.
 
• It was established in March 1950 by a resolution of the Government of India.
 
• The Planning Commission was replaced by the NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) in 2015.
 
• The commission played a crucial role in allocating resources, formulating policies, and defining the direction of economic development in the country.
 
 
 
• **Economic Growth Rate**
 
 
• The economic growth rate is a measure of the increase in a country’s economic output and is often calculated as the percentage increase in the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
 
• It is an important indicator of economic health and is used by policymakers to gauge the effectiveness of economic policies.
 
• A higher growth rate indicates a thriving economy with more jobs and higher income levels, while a lower rate may suggest economic problems.

question: Harrod Domar model was the main idea behind the ________ Five Year Plan.
solution:
The correct answer is __**First**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Harrod-Domar model was the foundation for the First Five Year Plan of India.
 
• This plan was implemented between 1951 and 1956.
 
• The model emphasizes the importance of savings and investments for economic growth.
 
• It was aimed at addressing the country's immediate need for development in agriculture, irrigation, and energy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Harrod-Domar Model:**

 
 
• This model is an economic growth model that was developed independently by Sir Roy Harrod in 1939 and Evsey Domar in 1946.
 
• The model suggests that the economy's growth rate depends on the level of savings and the productivity of capital investment.
 
• The key equation of the Harrod-Domar model is: Growth Rate = Savings Ratio / Capital-Output Ratio.
 
• The model highlights the need for investment to spur economic growth and the importance of efficient use of capital.
 
 
 
• **First Five Year Plan of India:**
 
 
• Launched in 1951, the First Five Year Plan focused on the primary sector, especially agriculture.
 
• It aimed to increase food production, improve irrigation facilities, and develop transport and communication infrastructure.
 
• The plan was successful in achieving its targets and laid the foundation for future economic planning in India.
 
• It also emphasized the need for industrialization to create job opportunities and improve the standard of living.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Savings and Investments:**
 
 
• Savings provide the funds necessary for investment, which in turn leads to economic growth.
 
• Higher savings rates can lead to higher investment rates, which can enhance productive capacity and increase GDP.
 
• Efficient allocation and use of savings are crucial for maximizing the returns on investment.
 
• Government policies often aim to encourage savings and investments through various incentives and reforms.
 
 
 
• **Development Goals of the First Plan:**
 
 
• To increase agricultural production to ensure food security for the population.
 
• To develop irrigation facilities to support agriculture and manage water resources effectively.
 
• To build infrastructure such as roads, railways, and ports to facilitate trade and movement of goods.
 
• To address the immediate needs of the country in terms of employment and poverty alleviation.

The correct answer is __**Fourth Five-Year Plan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) was launched by the Government of India during the **Fourth Five-Year Plan** (1969-1974).
 
• The primary objective of DPAP was to provide **employment to people in drought-prone areas** and to ensure economic development by stabilizing the income of the people living in these areas.
 
• The program aimed at **reducing the adverse effects of drought** on the productivity of land, water resources, and overall livelihood of the people.
 
• DPAP was part of the broader strategy of the Fourth Five-Year Plan to tackle **regional disparities** and promote balanced regional development in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Five-Year Plans**

 
 
• The Five-Year Plans of India were centralized and integrated national economic programs. The first plan was launched in 1951 and subsequent plans were formulated for five-year periods.
 
• The **Fourth Five-Year Plan** (1969-1974) aimed at growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance.
 
• It focused on agriculture, including the Green Revolution, and improvements in industrial production.
 
 
 
• **Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP)**
 
 
• DPAP is one of the earliest area development programs initiated in India to address the issues of drought and desertification.
 
• The program focuses on the development of natural resources, including water conservation, afforestation, and soil conservation to reduce the impact of drought.
 
• It also aims to improve the socio-economic conditions of the people living in drought-prone areas through employment generation and infrastructure development.
 
 
 
• **Regional Disparities**
 
 
• Regional disparities refer to the differences in income, wealth, and living standards across different regions within a country.
 
• Addressing regional disparities is crucial for balanced and inclusive growth, ensuring that all regions benefit from economic development.
 
• Programs like DPAP are aimed at reducing these disparities by focusing on the development of less developed and drought-prone regions.

question: What gave a major impetus to the cotton textile industry in India after Independence?

options.text: Export of raw cotton to England

solution:
The correct answer is __**Swadeshi movement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Swadeshi movement was a significant part of the Indian independence struggle, encouraging the use of Indian-made goods and boycotting British products.
 
• It played a major role in reviving the domestic industries, including the cotton textile industry.
 
• This movement fostered a sense of national pride and self-reliance among Indians, leading to increased demand and production of Indian goods.
 
• The Swadeshi movement laid the foundation for the growth of indigenous industries, which saw major development post-independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Partition of India in 1947**

 
 
• The partition of India in 1947 led to the division of the country into India and Pakistan. While it had significant socio-political impacts, it did not directly give a major impetus to the cotton textile industry.
 
 
 
• **Export of raw cotton to England**
 
 
• During the British colonial period, India was a major exporter of raw cotton to England. However, this did not benefit the Indian cotton textile industry, as raw materials were sent to England for manufacturing finished goods.
 
 
 
• **Development of railway network**
 
 
• The development of the railway network in India did contribute to the overall industrial growth by improving transportation and connectivity. However, it was not the major driving force behind the cotton textile industry's growth post-independence.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi Movement**
 
 
• The Swadeshi movement was a part of the Indian independence movement that encouraged the boycott of British products and the use of Indian-made goods.
 
• It significantly boosted the domestic cotton textile industry by increasing the demand for Indian textiles and reducing dependence on British imports.
 
• The movement also encouraged the establishment of new textile mills in India, leading to the growth of the industry.
 
• Post-independence, the momentum gained from the Swadeshi movement continued to support the development of the Indian cotton textile industry.

question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the **correct **options:

**Assertion (A):** Global Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) indicators excluded informal sectors.

**Reason (R):** Informal enterprises are difficult to measure consistently across nations.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Global Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) indicators** measure how conducive a country's regulatory environment is for starting and operating businesses.
 
• These indicators primarily focus on formal sectors, excluding informal enterprises, as they lack consistent data across nations.
 
• Informal enterprises are **challenging to measure** due to their non-standardized structure and operations, which vary significantly across countries.
 
• The World Bank, which publishes the EoDB rankings, generally relies on data from registered businesses and government regulations, leaving out the informal sector.
 
• **Reason (R)** correctly explains the exclusion of informal enterprises, as they are difficult to assess uniformly across different nations due to inconsistencies in data collection methods and definitions of informal businesses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Ease of Doing Business Rankings and Informal Sector**

 
 
• The Ease of Doing Business rankings are published by the World Bank to compare the business environments of different countries.
 
• The rankings primarily evaluate regulations affecting registered businesses, ignoring informal sectors due to challenges in uniform data collection.
 
• Informal businesses often operate outside formal regulatory frameworks, making them difficult to assess using standardized metrics.
 
• Including informal enterprises would require developing globally consistent definitions and measurement methods, which are currently lacking.

• The Industrial Policy Resolution (IPR) of 1956 was a significant policy document that aimed to classify industries into three categories: Schedule A, Schedule B, and Schedule C.
 
• Schedule A included industries that were exclusively under state control and were regarded as essential for national defense and economic development (e.g., railways, atomic energy).
 
• Schedule B covered industries that were to be developed under joint sector arrangements, i.e., both state and private enterprises could participate in these industries.
 
• Schedule C comprised industries that were to be left for private sector operations, allowing individual entrepreneurship to thrive.
 
• The classification was designed to promote a mixed economy model and was rooted in the philosophy of socialist planning, which sought to balance private and state ownership.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Post-Independence (IPR 1948, 1956): Focused on public sector dominance and planned development.
 
• Liberalization (IPR 1991): Shifted towards opening the economy and global integration.
 
• **Recent Initiatives:**
 
 
• Make in India (2014): To make India a global manufacturing hub.
 
• Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan (2020): Aimed at self-reliance and reducing import dependency.
 
• Production-Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme (2020): Offers incentives for increased domestic production.

Read the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully and choose the **correct **option.

**Assertion (A)**: India adopted import substitution during the planning era.

**Reason (R)**: This was to protect infant domestic industries from foreign competition.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Import substitution** refers to an economic policy aimed at reducing dependency on foreign goods by promoting domestic production and industries.
 
• India adopted the policy of import substitution during the planning era, particularly during the Second Five-Year Plan (1956-61) led by P.C. Mahalanobis, to boost industrialization.
 
• The primary objective was to protect the domestic industries, which were in their nascent stages, from foreign competition and to achieve self-reliance in industrial production.
 
• Through high import tariffs, quotas, and trade restrictions, foreign goods were made less competitive, encouraging the growth of Indian industries.
 
• While this policy played a critical role in laying the foundation for India’s industrial base, it also led to inefficiencies and a lack of competition in the long run.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First** FYP (1951-56): Focused on agriculture, controlling inflation, and refugee rehabilitation (Harrod-Domar model). 
 
• **Second **FYP (1956-61): Emphasized rapid industrialization, especially heavy industries (Mahalanobis Model). 
 
• **Third **FYP (1961-66): Aimed for food self-sufficiency and increased agricultural/industrial production, but faced challenges. 
 
• **Fifth **FYP (1974-78): Key focus on Garibi Hatao (poverty alleviation), employment, and social justice. 
 
• **Sixth **FYP (1980-85): Introduced early economic liberalization and aimed for technological self-reliance. 
 
• **Eighth **FYP (1992-97): Launched after the 1991 economic crisis, promoting LPG (Liberalisation, Privatisation, Globalisation) and industrial modernization. 
 
• **Ninth **FYP (1997-2002): Focused on social sector development and equitable growth. 
 
• **Tenth **FYP (2002-07): Aimed for faster and more inclusive growth. 
 
• **Eleventh **FYP (2007-12): Focused on faster, more inclusive, and sustainable growth. 
 
• **Twelfth **FYP (2012-17): The final FYP, targeting faster, sustainable, and more inclusive growth with emphasis on education, infrastructure, and poverty reduction.

question: Which Five-Year Plan focused on heavy industries?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Second**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Second Five-Year Plan (1956-1961)** of India was focused on the rapid industrialization of the country, especially the establishment and growth of heavy industries.
 
• This plan was based on the **Mahalanobis Model**, named after P.C. Mahalanobis, which emphasized investment in the heavy industrial sector as a means to achieve long-term economic growth.
 
• Key industries such as steel, coal, and heavy machinery were given priority to build a strong industrial base for the country.
 
• The government established public sector enterprises like the **Bhilai Steel Plant, Durgapur Steel Plant**, and **Bokaro Steel Plant** under this plan.
 
• Promoting self-reliance in industrial production and reducing dependence on foreign imports was one of the main objectives of this plan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **First Five-Year Plan (1951-1956):**

 
 
• The primary focus of the First Five-Year Plan was on the **agricultural sector** to address food shortages and ensure self-sufficiency in food production.
 
• It was based on the **Harrod-Domar Model**, which emphasized increasing investment in agriculture and irrigation projects.
 
• Key projects included the construction of major dams like **Bhakra Nangal** and **Hirakud** to improve irrigation and power generation.
 
 
 
• **Third Five-Year Plan (1961-1966):**
 
 
• The Third Plan aimed to achieve self-reliance in **food production** and accelerate economic development by prioritizing both agriculture and industry.
 
• It also focused on defense production following the **1962 Indo-China War**.
 
• The plan, however, faced setbacks due to the war, drought, and economic challenges, leading to its partial success.
 
 
 
• **Fourth Five-Year Plan (1969-1974):**
 
 
• The Fourth Plan primarily focused on **stabilizing the economy** and achieving self-reliance in technology and production.
 
• It emphasized the growth of the **Green Revolution** to boost agricultural productivity and reduce dependence on food imports.
 
• Industrial growth was also pursued, but the focus shifted towards balancing agriculture and industry.

question: When was the first Industrial Policy announced in independent India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1948**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first Industrial Policy of independent India was announced in **1948**.
 
• The Industrial Policy of 1948 laid the foundational framework for India's industrial development post-independence.
 
• It categorized industries into four broad categories: (1) Industries exclusively owned by the state, (2) Mixed industries (state and private ownership), (3) Industries controlled by the state, and (4) Industries under private sector ownership.
 
• Key sectors like arms and ammunition, atomic energy, and railways were designated as exclusive government monopolies.
 
• The policy aimed to strike a balance between promoting industrialization, encouraging private entrepreneurship, and maintaining state control over critical sectors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **1950**

 
 
• No new industrial policy was announced in 1950. However, the Constitution of India came into effect on January 26, 1950, establishing the framework for governance and economic policy in the country.
 
• The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950, which played a significant role in formulating Five-Year Plans for economic development, including industrial growth.
 
 
 
• **1951**
 
 
• The **Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951**, was introduced to regulate and develop industries in the national interest.
 
• It provided a framework for licensing industries to ensure planned industrial development.
 
• Though not an industrial policy in itself, this Act was a significant step in implementing the objectives of the 1948 Industrial Policy.
 
 
 
• **1952**
 
 
• No distinct industrial policy was announced in 1952.
 
• However, the focus during this period remained on implementing the first Five-Year Plan (1951-56), which emphasized agricultural development and laid the foundation for industrial expansion.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: Industrial Policy in India**
 
 
• Industrial policies in India are statements of the government that outline strategies for industrial development and economic growth.
 
• Over time, India has introduced several industrial policies, such as those in 1948, 1956, 1977, 1980, and 1991, each reflecting changing socio-economic priorities and challenges.
 
• The primary objectives of industrial policies in India are to promote industrialization, ensure balanced regional development, encourage private sector participation, and maintain state control over critical sectors.

**Assertion (A): **Globalization led to increased inequality in India.

**Reason (R):** Growth was unevenly distributed, benefiting mostly urban elite and service sectors.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Globalization in India** has led to significant economic growth, but this growth has been unevenly distributed across different sectors and regions.
 
• The **urban elite and service sectors**, particularly in technology and finance, benefited disproportionately, leading to increased income inequality.
 
• Rural areas and agriculture-dependent populations have not seen comparable benefits, widening the urban-rural divide.
 
• The **Gini coefficient**, a measure of income inequality, has shown an upward trend in India post-globalization, indicating growing disparities.
 
• Thus, **Reason (R)** correctly explains the **Assertion (A)** that globalization led to increased inequality in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A**

 
 
• This option would be valid if globalization had led to inequality due to factors unrelated to the uneven benefits for urban elites and service sectors.
 
• However, the direct link between the uneven growth distribution and increasing inequality makes R the correct explanation of A.
 
 
 
• **Option 3: A is true but R is false**
 
 
• While A is true that globalization increased inequality, rejecting R would imply that uneven growth distribution did not play a role, which is incorrect.
 
• Uneven growth is a well-documented driver of inequality in India, especially post-1991 economic reforms.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: A is false but R is true**
 
 
• This option would suggest that globalization did not lead to inequality, which contradicts empirical evidence.
 
• R is true, but it directly supports the assertion made in A, making A valid as well.
 
 
 
• **Globalization in India**
 
 
• The liberalization of the Indian economy in 1991 opened markets to foreign investment, trade, and private-sector participation.
 
• While this has driven economic growth, it has also accentuated income disparities, especially between urban and rural areas.
 
• Key beneficiaries include IT, financial services, and real estate sectors, while traditional industries and agriculture have lagged behind.
 
• This dual-speed growth highlights the importance of inclusive policies to address inequalities arising from globalization.

question: Disinvestment involves selling stakes in?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Public enterprises**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Disinvestment** refers to the process of the government selling or diluting its ownership stakes in **public sector enterprises (PSEs)** to reduce its involvement in such businesses.
 
• The aim of disinvestment is to **improve the financial health of public enterprises**, reduce the fiscal burden on the government, and promote private sector participation in the economy.
 
• Disinvestment is often categorized into **minority disinvestment** (retaining majority ownership) and **strategic disinvestment** (transferring management control to private entities).
 
• The **Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM)** under the Ministry of Finance spearheads the disinvestment process in India.
 
• Key examples of disinvestment in India include the sale of stakes in companies such as Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) and Air India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **NGOs (Non-Governmental Organizations):**

 
 
• NGOs are private, non-profit organizations that work towards various social, cultural, or environmental causes.
 
• They operate independently of the government and are funded through donations, grants, or self-generated income.
 
• Examples include organizations like Greenpeace, the Red Cross, and CRY.
 
• Disinvestment does not involve NGOs as they are not owned or controlled by the government.
 
 
 
• **Private Firms:**
 
 
• Private firms are businesses owned by individuals or private entities rather than the government.
 
• These firms operate for profit and are not subject to government disinvestment since they are not public assets.
 
• Examples include companies like Reliance Industries, Tata Consultancy Services, and Infosys.
 
 
 
• **Trade Unions:**
 
 
• Trade unions are organizations formed by workers to promote their rights and interests, such as fair wages and safe working conditions.
 
• They are not business enterprises and therefore do not fall under the purview of disinvestment.
 
• Examples of trade unions in India include the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) and the Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC).
 
 
 
• **Public Enterprises:**
 
 
• Public enterprises are companies or corporations owned and controlled by the government, either fully or partially.
 
• Disinvestment in public enterprises aims to reduce the fiscal burden on the government and improve the efficiency and competitiveness of these enterprises.
 
• Examples of public enterprises in India include Coal India, Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL), and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL).

question: Which reform enabled MNCs to enter India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Globalisation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Globalisation** refers to the process of interaction and integration among people, companies, and governments worldwide, primarily driven by international trade and investment.
 
• In the context of India, globalisation became prominent with the **1991 economic reforms** under the New Economic Policy, which introduced liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation (LPG reforms).
 
• This reform allowed **Multi-National Corporations (MNCs)** to enter the Indian market by reducing trade barriers, opening up Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), and deregulating the economy.
 
• The Indian government encouraged globalisation to boost economic growth, improve technological advancements, and integrate with the global economy.
 
• As a result of globalisation, India became a hub for foreign investments, witnessed significant technological advancements, and developed its manufacturing and service sectors.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Land Reform**

 
 
• Land reforms in India were introduced to address issues such as **land inequality, zamindari system, and landlessness**.
 
• The main objectives were to abolish intermediaries, ensure land redistribution to landless farmers, and implement tenancy reforms.
 
• Land reforms were aimed at improving agricultural productivity and equitable distribution of resources but are unrelated to the entry of MNCs in India.
 
 
 
• **Labour Law**
 
 
• Labour laws are a set of regulations governing the rights and responsibilities of workers, employers, and trade unions.
 
• Their primary focus is on ensuring fair wages, safe working conditions, and social security for workers.
 
• Though labour reforms are critical for industrial growth, they are not directly responsible for allowing MNCs to enter India.
 
 
 
• **Swadeshi**
 
 
• The Swadeshi movement was a part of the Indian independence struggle, encouraging the boycott of foreign goods and promoting indigenous products.
 
• It aimed to revive Indian industries and reduce dependence on British-made goods.
 
• Swadeshi, being a nationalist movement, contrasts globalisation and is unrelated to the entry of MNCs into India.

Assertion (A): The disinvestment policy has been widely criticized in India.

Reason (R): It resulted in increased market monopoly by public sector undertakings.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**A is true but R is false.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Assertion (A):** The disinvestment policy in India has been widely criticized for various reasons, including concerns over undervaluation of assets, lack of transparency, and the impact on employment in public sector enterprises.
 
• **Reason (R):** The claim that disinvestment increased market monopoly by public sector undertakings (PSUs) is incorrect. In fact, disinvestment typically involves selling government stakes in PSUs to private entities, reducing the government's monopoly in those sectors.
 
• The criticism of the disinvestment policy primarily stems from fears of privatization, loss of public control over strategic sectors, and potential exploitation by private players, rather than the creation of monopolies by PSUs.
 
• Disinvestment in India aims to improve the efficiency of PSUs by introducing private participation and raising revenue for the government, not to consolidate monopolies.
 
• Therefore, while Assertion (A) is true, Reason (R) is false as it provides an incorrect explanation for the criticism of disinvestment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Disinvestment Policy in India:**

 
 
• Disinvestment refers to the process of selling or liquidating government-owned assets or stakes in public sector enterprises (PSUs).
 
• The primary objectives include reducing the fiscal burden, improving operational efficiency, and fostering private sector participation in the economy.
 
• It can take various forms, such as strategic disinvestment, minority stake sale, or outright privatization.
 
 
 
• **Monopolies and Market Competition:**
 
 
• Monopolies occur when a single entity dominates the market, limiting competition and consumer choice.
 
• Disinvestment typically reduces the monopoly of PSUs by introducing private players into the market.
 
• For instance, sectors like telecommunications and aviation saw increased competition after government disinvestment and deregulation.
 
 
 
• **Criticism of Disinvestment:**
 
 
• Critics argue that disinvestment often undervalues public assets, leading to losses for the government.
 
• Concerns about job losses and the erosion of workers' rights in privatized entities are frequently raised.
 
• There is also apprehension about private players prioritizing profits over public welfare in critical sectors like healthcare and education.
 
 
 
• **Strategic Sectors and Privatization:**
 
 
• While the government has retained control over strategic sectors such as defense, railways, and nuclear energy, it has allowed private participation in non-strategic areas.
 
• This approach aims to strike a balance between public control and private efficiency.

question: Which is NOT part of the Washington Consensus?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Export subsidies**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Washington Consensus does not include **export subsidies** as one of its policy recommendations.
 
• Export subsidies are considered distortive to market dynamics and contrary to the principles of free-market economics promoted by the Washington Consensus.
 
• The Washington Consensus advocates for policies that encourage trade liberalization and removal of barriers, rather than artificially supporting exports.
 
• Export subsidies involve direct financial support from governments to domestic industries to make their goods competitive in the global market, which can lead to trade disputes and inefficiency.
 
• International organizations like the World Trade Organization (WTO) discourage the use of export subsidies as they violate fair trade practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trade liberalisation**

 
 
• Trade liberalization refers to reducing barriers to trade, such as tariffs, quotas, and regulations, to promote free trade among nations.
 
• It is a key component of the Washington Consensus aimed at improving economic efficiency and integrating economies into the global market.
 
• Trade liberalization is believed to spur economic growth by increasing access to goods, services, and technology.
 
 
 
• **Fiscal discipline**
 
 
• Fiscal discipline involves maintaining a sustainable level of government spending and ensuring that deficits and debt levels remain manageable.
 
• The Washington Consensus emphasizes fiscal discipline as a critical measure to achieve macroeconomic stability.
 
• It prevents excessive borrowing, reduces inflationary pressures, and builds investor confidence in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Tax reform**
 
 
• Tax reform under the Washington Consensus aims to simplify the tax system, broaden the tax base, and ensure equity and efficiency in tax collection.
 
• It typically includes measures like reducing high marginal tax rates, eliminating exemptions, and improving compliance mechanisms.
 
• Tax reform contributes to fiscal stability and promotes economic growth by reducing distortions in market behavior.
 
 
 
• **Washington Consensus: Main Theme**
 
 
• The Washington Consensus is a set of 10 economic policy recommendations proposed by economist John Williamson in 1989.
 
• It was designed to address economic crises and promote growth in developing countries, especially in Latin America.
 
• The consensus advocates for free-market principles, open trade policies, privatization, and macroeconomic stability.
 
• While influential, the Washington Consensus has been criticized for its one-size-fits-all approach and the socioeconomic challenges it posed for some nations.

question: What was the main rationale for the policy of import substitution during the first seven Five Year Plans?
solution:
The correct answer is __**To protect infant domestic industries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The policy of import substitution was aimed at reducing reliance on foreign goods by fostering domestic production capabilities.
 
• It was designed to **shield infant industries** from international competition during their early stages of development.
 
• By restricting imports and promoting domestic production, the policy sought to build a self-reliant economy, especially in key sectors like manufacturing and industrial goods.
 
• Import substitution aligned with the broader goals of India's Five Year Plans, which emphasized economic self-sufficiency and industrialization.
 
• It involved protective measures such as **tariffs, quotas, and subsidies** for domestic industries to ensure their growth and competitiveness.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: To expand international trade**

 
 
• The focus of import substitution is not on expanding international trade but on reducing dependency on foreign imports.
 
• India’s economic policy during the first seven Five Year Plans prioritized self-reliance over global trade integration.
 
• While international trade was considered, it was secondary to the goal of fostering domestic industries.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: To attract foreign investors**
 
 
• Attracting foreign investors was not a primary objective of the import substitution policy during this period.
 
• In fact, the policy often discouraged foreign investment by emphasizing domestic production and limiting foreign participation in key industries.
 
• The focus was on building indigenous capabilities rather than relying on foreign capital or expertise.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: To create export dependency**
 
 
• Export dependency is the opposite of the goals of import substitution, which aimed at reducing reliance on foreign economies.
 
• The policy sought to create a balanced trade environment by ensuring that domestic industries catered to local demand first.
 
• Export promotion was considered later in India’s economic strategy, especially after liberalization in the 1990s.
 
 
 
• **Context of Import Substitution Policy**
 
 
• India adopted the import substitution strategy during its early economic planning phases (1951–1990) to accelerate industrialization and reduce foreign dependency.
 
• This policy was influenced by global economic theories such as protectionism and the idea of nurturing infant industries.
 
• Though effective in fostering domestic industries initially, the policy faced criticism for inefficiency, lack of competitiveness, and stagnant growth, leading to economic liberalization later.

• Policies such as **Make in India** and **Atmanirbhar Bharat** aim to promote the growth of heavy industries in India to reduce dependence on imports and boost self-reliance.
