• The **Logistics Performance Index (LPI)** is a benchmarking tool developed by the **World Bank** to measure a country's trade and transport logistics efficiency. 

• The LPI evaluates how effectively goods are moved into, within, and out of a country, covering aspects like **customs clearance, infrastructure, international shipments, logistics quality, tracking, and timeliness**. 

• The LPI is released every two years and ranks countries based on their logistics performance. The latest report highlights areas needing improvement for better participation in global trade. 

• Six key components are assessed: **Customs, Infrastructure, Ease of arranging shipments, Logistics competence, Tracking and tracing, and Timeliness of shipments**. 

• This index is critical for policymakers and businesses as it identifies bottlenecks in logistics chains and helps in formulating strategies for improvement. 

• The LPI is recognized globally as a standard to evaluate the competitiveness of countries in terms of **global trade facilitation**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 

• **History and Purpose of LPI:** 
 

• The **World Bank** introduced the Logistics Performance Index in **2007** to assist countries in identifying challenges and opportunities in their logistics systems. 

• The index aims to improve **global supply chain efficiency** by offering insights into logistics bottlenecks. 
 
 

• **Key Components of LPI:** 
 

• **Customs:** Efficiency of customs and border clearance processes. 

• **Infrastructure:** Quality of trade and transport-related infrastructure such as ports, railways, roads, and information technology. 

• **Ease of Arranging Shipments:** Competitiveness of pricing and ease of organizing shipments. 

• **Logistics Quality:** Competence and quality of logistics services, such as transport operators and customs brokers. 

• **Tracking:** Ability to track and trace consignments. 

• **Timeliness:** Punctuality and reliability of shipments in reaching destinations. 
 
 

• **Global Rankings in Logistics:** 
 

• Countries like **Germany, Singapore, and Sweden** often rank at the top of the LPI due to their advanced logistics infrastructure and efficient customs processes. 

• Developing nations strive to improve their logistics performance to enhance their competitiveness in the global market. 
 
 

• **Relevance for Developing Economies:** 
 

• Efficient logistics systems are vital for reducing **trade costs**, enhancing **economic growth**, and boosting **export competitiveness**. 

• For example, countries in **South Asia** and **Sub-Saharan Africa** often focus on improving logistics infrastructure to facilitate trade. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 

• **India’s Performance in LPI:** 
 

• India ranked **38th** in the **2022 LPI**, showcasing improvements in its logistics efficiency due to initiatives like **PM Gati Shakti** and the **Bharatmala Project**. 

• The introduction of **GST (Goods and Services Tax)** has also contributed to reducing transit times and improving logistics performance. 
 
 

• **Importance of LPI in Policy Making:** 
 

• The LPI helps governments identify **inefficiencies in trade processes** and prioritize investments in logistics infrastructure. 

• It also aids in aligning national logistics strategies with **global best practices** to enhance trade facilitation.

Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the correct options:

Reason (R): Allegations of data manipulation prompted the suspension.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Assertion (A): Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) report by the World Bank was discontinued in 2021.** 
• The **Ease of Doing Business (EoDB)** report was an annual flagship publication by the **World Bank**, ranking countries based on their business regulations and environment. 
• In **September 2021**, the World Bank announced the discontinuation of the report following allegations of irregularities in data and rankings manipulation. *Hence, the assertion is correct.* 
• **Reason (R): Allegations of data manipulation prompted the suspension.** 
• In 2020, the World Bank initiated an investigation into data irregularities in the **2018 and 2020 reports** following concerns raised about the rankings of certain countries. 
• The investigation revealed that data manipulation was done to benefit certain countries like **China**, raising questions about the integrity of the report. 
• This led to the permanent discontinuation of the report by the World Bank in **2021**. *Hence, the reason is correct and explains the assertion.* 
• **Correct Option:** Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Ease of Doing Business Report:** 
• The Ease of Doing Business report ranked countries based on **10 indicators**, including starting a business, dealing with construction permits, getting electricity, registering property, and paying taxes. 
• It was first published in **2003** and became a key tool for policymakers and investors to assess business environments worldwide. 
• The rankings were influential in shaping economic reforms in several countries. 
• **Reason for Data Manipulation:** 
• The investigation revealed undue pressure on World Bank staff to alter data in favor of certain countries like **China**, Saudi Arabia, and Azerbaijan. 
• This manipulation undermined the credibility of the rankings and prompted calls for greater transparency. 
• **Impact of Discontinuation:** 
• Countries now lack a global benchmark for assessing their business environments. 
• The World Bank is exploring alternative methods to measure business climates, focusing on **broader economic and social indicators**. 
• **Recent Developments:** 
• Post-discontinuation, the World Bank introduced a new initiative called **Business Enabling Environment (BEE)** to assess policies supporting private sector development. 
• BEE aims to provide a more holistic view of economic and regulatory environments. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Countries Influenced:** 
• China’s ranking was allegedly altered in the 2018 report, increasing its position from **85th to 78th**. 
• Other countries like Saudi Arabia and Azerbaijan were also reportedly favored in the rankings. 
• **Data Integrity Concerns:** 
• The manipulation of data highlighted the need for stronger governance frameworks in international organizations. 
• It also underscored the importance of ethical practices in producing global indices. 
• **Lessons Learned:** 
• Transparency and accountability are crucial for maintaining the credibility of global reports. 
• Future initiatives like BEE aim to mitigate risks associated with data manipulation.

question: What is the role of WTO with respect to globalization?

options.text: Ensure fair trade rules among nations

solution:
The correct answer is __**Ensure fair trade rules among nations**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **World Trade Organization (WTO)** is an international body established in **1995** to regulate and facilitate international trade. Its primary goal is to ensure that trade flows as smoothly, predictably, and freely as possible.
 
• The WTO works to **create and enforce fair trade rules** among nations by providing a platform for trade negotiations and resolving disputes.
 
• It oversees the implementation of trade agreements, including those concerning goods, services, and intellectual property, ensuring that member countries comply with their commitments.
 
• The WTO promotes **non-discriminatory trade practices**, such as the "most-favored-nation" (MFN) principle, which ensures equal treatment of all member nations in trade matters.
 
• Through its efforts, the WTO aims to reduce barriers to trade, such as tariffs and quotas, and prevent unfair trade practices like dumping and subsidies that distort competition.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Functions of WTO:**
 
 
• The WTO provides a platform for **trade negotiations** among its 164 member countries. These negotiations focus on reducing tariffs, eliminating trade barriers, and establishing global trade norms.
 
• It administers a set of trade agreements, including the **General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT)**, **General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS)**, and agreements on intellectual property rights.
 
• It acts as a **dispute resolution mechanism**, where member nations can bring trade disputes for impartial adjudication.
 
• The WTO conducts regular reviews of member countries' trade policies to ensure transparency and compliance with global trade rules.
 
 
 
• **Membership and Decision-Making:**
 
 
• The WTO operates on a consensus-based model where decisions require the agreement of all members.
 
• Its membership includes major economies like the **United States, European Union, China, and India**, as well as smaller developing nations, ensuring diverse representation.
 
 
 
• **Impact of WTO:**
 
 
• The WTO has contributed significantly to **global trade liberalization**, leading to increased international trade volumes and economic growth.
 
• It has supported **developing countries** by providing special provisions, technical assistance, and capacity-building programs.
 
 
 
• **Criticism of WTO:**
 
 
• The organization has faced criticism for being skewed in favor of **developed countries**, often marginalizing the concerns of poorer nations.
 
• It has also been criticized for its inability to address environmental and labor issues effectively within trade agreements.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Key Agreements under WTO:**
 
 
• **GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade):** Focuses on the trade of goods and reducing tariffs.
 
• **GATS (General Agreement on Trade in Services):** Aims to liberalize trade in services like banking, education, and healthcare.
 
• **TRIPS (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights):** Ensures the protection of intellectual property rights globally.
 
 
 
• **Key Facts:**
 
 
• The WTO was established on **1 January 1995**, replacing GATT, which was created in **1948**.
 
• It is headquartered in **Geneva, Switzerland**.
 
• The current Director-General of the WTO (as of 2023) is **Dr. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala**.

Green Revolution in India:

• After Independence, Indian policy-makers adopted all measures to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains.
 
• In the year 1965, the government of India launched the Green Revolution with the help of a geneticist, now known as the father of the Green revolution (India) M.S. Swaminathan.
 
• The movement of the green revolution was a great success and changed the country’s status from a food-deficient economy to one of the world’s leading agricultural nations.
 
• It started in 1967 and lasted till 1978.
 
• India adopted a new strategy in agriculture, which resulted in the 'Green Revolution', especially in the production of wheat and rice.
 
• Indira Gandhi, the then Prime Minister of India, officially recorded the impressive strides of the Green Revolution in agriculture by releasing a special stamp entitled 'Wheat Revolution' in July 1968.
 
• The success of wheat was later replicated in rice.

Thus, to signify the achievements of the Green Revolution, a stamp was released by the then Prime Minister Mrs. Indira Gandhi entitled as ‘Wheat Revolution’ in July 1968.

question:
Which of the followings HYV seeds is/are associated with the Green Revolution in India?

(A) Rice

(B) Wheat
solution:
The correct answer is **__Both A and B__**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Green Revolution in India : 

 
 
• At independence, about 75 per cent of the country’s population was dependent on agriculture.
 
• Productivity in the agricultural sector was very low because of the use of old technology and the absence of the required infrastructure for the vast majority of farmers.
 
• India’s agriculture vitally depends on the monsoon and if the monsoon fell short the farmers were in trouble unless they had access to irrigation facilities which very few had.
 
• The stagnation in agriculture during colonial rule was permanently broken by the green revolution.
 
• This refers to the large increase in the production of food grains resulting from the use of high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, **especially for wheat and rice. **
 
• The use of these seeds required the use of fertilizer and pesticide in the correct quantities as well as a regular supply of water; the application of these inputs in correct proportions is vital. 
 
• The farmers who could benefit from HYV seeds required reliable irrigation facilities as well as financial resources to purchase fertilizer and pesticides.
 
• As a result, in the first phase of the green revolution (the approximately mid-1960s up to mid-1970s), the use of HYV seeds was restricted to the more affluent states such as Punjab, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu.
 
• Further, the use of HYV seeds primarily benefited the wheat-growing regions only. In the second phase of the green revolution (the mid-1970s to mid-1980s), the HYV technology spread to a larger number of states and benefited more variety of crops.
 
• The spread of green revolution technology-enabled India to achieve self-sufficiency in food grains; we no longer had to be at the mercy of America, or any other nation, for meeting our nation’s food requirements.

question: Commercialisation of agriculture is an indication of _______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Marketable surplus.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Commercialisation of agriculture** refers to the process of **transforming agriculture **from a subsistence-based activity to a commercial enterprise.
 
• This involves producing **crops and goods **not only for personal consumption but also for **sale in the market.**
 
• When agriculture is commercialised, there is an increase in **marketable surplus, **which is the amount of agricultural produce that is available for sale in the market after meeting the **needs of the producers** and their families.
 
• This surplus can be sold for a** profit,** leading to an **increase in income** for the farmers.
 
• **Producers' surplus** refers to the** difference **between the price at which the producer is willing to sell a product and the **actual price** they receive in the market.
 
 
• This surplus is** maximised **when the producer is able to sell their product at a** higher price** than their cost of production.
 
 
 
• **Consumer surplus** refers to the difference between the price that **consumers are willing to pay** for a product and the actual price they pay.
 
 
• This surplus is maximised when the price of the product is **lower **than the value that consumers place on it.
 
 
 
• **Income surplus** refers to the **increase in income** that is generated as a result of commercialisation of agriculture.
 
 
• This surplus is maximised when the marketable surplus is sold at a price that is** higher than the cost of production.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The term 'commercialisation of agriculture' is often associated with the **Green Revolution**, which was a period of significant agricultural innovation and productivity growth that occurred in the **1960s and 1970s.**
 
• The Green Revolution involved the introduction of **new crop varieties, improved irrigation systems**, and the **use of fertilisers and pesticides.**
 
• These innovations led to a significant increase in **agricultural productivity** and helped to** alleviate food shortages **in many parts of the world.
 
• However, there are also concerns about the **negative environmental **and **social impacts **of commercialisation of agriculture, such as **soil degradation, water pollution,** and displacement of** small-scale farmers.**
 
• In addition to marketable surplus, commercialisation of agriculture can also lead to the** emergence of agribusinesses**, which are large-scale, commercial enterprises that are involved in various aspects of agriculture, such as** production, processing, and distribution.**

subject: GK
question: Which statement best reflects the failure of structural transformation in Indian agriculture between 1950-1990?
solution:
The correct answer is __**65% of population remained in agriculture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• While **Agricultural GDP doubled** between 1950 and 1990, it did not signify structural transformation as the workforce in agriculture remained high, and productivity gains were uneven. *This statement is correct but does not directly address structural transformation.*

• The **Agricultural workforce did not decline rapidly**; instead, it remained relatively stagnant, with a large proportion of the population relying on agriculture for their livelihood. *Hence, this statement is incorrect.*

• The **Industrial sector failed to absorb the excess labour** from agriculture, which is a key characteristic of structural transformation. Industrial and service sectors were unable to provide enough jobs to reduce dependency on agriculture. *Thus, this statement is incorrect.*

• Approximately **65% of the population remained in agriculture** by 1990, which indicates the failure of structural transformation. Despite efforts at modernization and Green Revolution initiatives, the economy did not shift a significant portion of its workforce to non-agricultural sectors. *This statement is correct and highlights the issue of structural stagnation in Indian agriculture.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Structural Transformation in Agriculture:**

• Structural transformation refers to the shift of the workforce from the agricultural sector to industrial and service sectors, accompanied by increased productivity and urbanization.

• This process is vital for long-term economic development and poverty reduction.

• In India's case, the reliance on agriculture remained high despite significant economic growth in other sectors.

• **Green Revolution in India:**

• The Green Revolution (1960s-1980s) introduced high-yielding variety (HYV) seeds, fertilizers, and irrigation techniques, leading to a significant increase in agricultural productivity.

• While it improved food security, it did not contribute significantly to reducing the agricultural workforce.

• **Challenges in Indian Agriculture:**

• Low mechanization and small landholdings prevented large-scale industrialization of agriculture.

• Insufficient rural-urban migration and lack of industrial job creation contributed to the workforce remaining in agriculture.

• **Comparison with Other Countries:**

• Countries like China and South Korea experienced rapid structural transformation through industrialization and urbanization.

• India lagged behind due to policy constraints and insufficient infrastructure development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Definition of Structural Transformation:** It is the reallocation of economic activity across sectors, leading to higher productivity and improved living standards.

• **Role of Industrialization:** Industrial and service sectors must grow rapidly to absorb surplus agricultural labour and diversify the economy.

• **Policy Implications:** Government policies like land reforms, industrial promotion, and education are critical to enabling structural transformation.

• **Current Scenario:** As of recent estimates, around 42% of India's workforce remains in agriculture, indicating slow progress in structural transformation.
</ul

subject: GK
question: The Green Revolution in its first phase (mid-1960s to mid-1970s) was largely ineffective in which of the following regions?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bihar**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Green Revolution** was introduced in the mid-1960s to increase agricultural productivity in India by using high-yield variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and advanced irrigation methods. 
• Initially, the Green Revolution was primarily implemented in regions with well-developed irrigation facilities and fertile soils. **Punjab**, **Haryana**, and **western Uttar Pradesh** benefitted significantly due to their favorable agro-climatic conditions. Hence, these regions experienced a rapid increase in crop productivity. 
• In contrast, regions such as **Bihar**, which lacked sufficient irrigation infrastructure and faced socio-economic challenges, did not benefit much from the initial phase of the Green Revolution. This made the impact in Bihar relatively ineffective during the first phase. 
• Bihar's agriculture during the mid-1960s to mid-1970s was largely dependent on monsoon rains. The absence of adequate irrigation and modern technology hindered the adoption of Green Revolution techniques. 
• **Tamil Nadu**, though not as impacted as Punjab and Haryana, had some benefits due to irrigation projects like the Mettur Dam. This placed it ahead of states like Bihar in terms of agricultural advancements during the Green Revolution era. 
• Thus, while the Green Revolution transformed agriculture in specific regions of India, its benefits were unevenly distributed, leaving out states like Bihar in the initial phase. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Green Revolution Overview:** 
• The Green Revolution in India began in the **1960s** under the leadership of **Dr. M.S. Swaminathan**, considered the "Father of the Green Revolution in India." 
• It focused on increasing the production of staple crops like **wheat** and **rice**, particularly in states with better infrastructure. 
• The use of high-yield variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilizers, and pesticides was a hallmark of this revolution. 
• **Impact on Different Regions:** 
• **Punjab and Haryana:** These regions saw a massive agricultural boom due to their well-developed irrigation systems, such as canals and tube wells, and fertile soils. 
• **Western Uttar Pradesh:** This region benefitted significantly due to its proximity to Punjab and Haryana and similar agro-climatic conditions. 
• **Bihar:** Lacked adequate irrigation and infrastructure, which made the adoption of Green Revolution techniques challenging. Socio-economic disparities and dependence on traditional farming practices further hampered progress. 
• **Tamil Nadu:** Benefitted moderately due to irrigation projects like the Mettur Dam but did not achieve the same level of success as Punjab and Haryana. 
• **Key Features of the Green Revolution:** 
• Introduction of HYV seeds for crops like wheat and rice. 
• Increased use of chemical fertilizers, pesticides, and advanced irrigation methods. 
• Focus on mechanization of agriculture, such as the use of tractors and harvesters. 
• Emphasis on agricultural research and development, supported by institutions like the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR). 
• **Challenges Faced by Bihar:** 
• **Poor irrigation facilities:** A lack of canals and tube wells restricted the adoption of HYV seeds. 
• **Socio-economic factors:** High levels of poverty and illiteracy among farmers hindered the implementation of modern farming techniques. 
• **Dependence on monsoon:** With no assured irrigation, agriculture in Bihar was largely rain-fed, making it vulnerable to droughts and floods. 
• **Land fragmentation:** Small and fragmented landholdings made it difficult to implement large-scale agricultural reforms. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• The Green Revolution significantly increased India's food grain production, transforming the nation from a food-deficit country to a food-surplus one. 
• However, its benefits were limited to regions with better infrastructure and irrigation facilities, leaving out areas like Bihar, Odisha, and eastern Uttar Pradesh in the initial phases. 
• The uneven distribution of benefits highlighted the need for more inclusive agricultural policies and reforms to address regional disparities. 
• Later initiatives like the **Eastern India Green Revolution** were introduced to address these disparities and boost agricultural productivity in neglected regions like Bihar. </ul

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the methods of national income estimation?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Banking method**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• National income is the total value of a country’s final output of all new goods and services produced in one year.
 
• Methods of measuring national income are:

 
• Expenditure Method - Under this method, we estimate the disposal of income on the purchase of final goods and services.
 
• Income Method - The Income Method measures national income from the side of payments made to the primary factors of production in the form of rent, wages, interest, and profit for their productive services in an accounting year. 
 
• Production method - In this method, national income is measured as a flow of goods and services. This method is also called an **output method**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• 
 Measurement of National Income

 
 
• 
 There are three methods to measure national income:

 
 
• **Income Method**
 
• **Production (Value-Added) Method**
 
• **Expenditure Method**
 
 
 
• 
 Measurement of National Income – Income Method

 
 
• Estimated by adding all the factors of production (rent, wages, interest, profit) and the mixed-income of self-employed.
 
• In India, one-third of people are self-employed
 
• This is the ‘**domestic**’ income, related to the production within the borders of the country
 
 
 
• Measurement of National Income – Production Method
 
 
• Estimated by adding the value added by all the firms.
 
• **Value-added** = Value of Output – Value of (non-factor) inputs
 

 
 
• This gives** GDP at Market Price (MP) – because it includes depreciation (therefore ‘gross’) and taxes (thus ‘market price’)**
 
• To reach National Income (that is, NNP at FC)
 

 
 
• Add Net Factor Income from Abroad: **GNP at MP = GDP at MP + NFIA**
 
• Subtract Depreciation:** NNP at MP = GNP at MP – Dep**
 
• Subtract Net Indirect Taxes: **NNP at FC = NNP at MP – NIT**
 
 
 
• Measurement of National Income – Expenditure Method
 
 
• The expenditure method to measure national income can be understood by the equation given below: 
 
 
• **Y = C + I + G + (X-M),**
 
• where** Y = GDP at MP, C = Private Sector’s Expenditure on final consumer goods, G = Govt’s expenditure on final consumer goods, I = Investment or Capital Formation, X = Exports, X- M = Net Exports (difference between exports (X) and imports (M))**
 
 
 
 
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points__**

 
• GDP: Gross Domestic Product is the sum of the money of all the final goods and services produced solely within the boundaries of a country, at a specific time.

 
 
• GDP includes the income of foreigners staying in the country.
 
• It excludes the income of nationals of the country staying abroad and also excludes the remittances sent from abroad.
 
 
 
• GNP: Gross National Product is the sum of the money of all the final goods and services produced both within and outside of a country by nationals during a specific period of time.
 
 
• GNP includes remittances.
 
• It excludes income generated locally by non-nationals.

question: The value of GDP at the current prevailing prices is called _______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**nominal GDP**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **The gross domestic product (GDP) **value at the most recent prices is known as **nominal GDP**.
 
• It is determined by current market pricing, without taking into account the** impact of inflation or deflation**.
 
• It shows how much money was spent on the commodities and services a nation generated within a certain fiscal year. In contrast to real GDP, which measures the rate of price rises in an economy, nominal GDP excludes changes in prices brought on by inflation.
 
• Due to the fact that real GDP only takes into account production and is unaffected by changes in prices or exchange rates, it is regarded as a reliable measure of a nation's economic progress.
 
• Growing pricing rather than an increase in the number of goods and services produced may be the cause of nominal GDP growth from year to year.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Real gross domestic product (GDP)**, which refers to the volume level of GDP, is GDP expressed at constant prices.
 
• By quantifying the values of all the goods and services produced in a given year in terms of a base period, one can derive constant price estimates of GDP.
 
• The standard measurement of the value added produced via the production of goods and services in a nation over a specific time period is the **gross domestic product (GDP)**.
 
• Consequently, it also accounts for the revenue generated by that manufacturing, or the total amount spent on finished goods and services (fewer imports).

__
 
• Net National Product (NNP):

 
 
• NNP is obtained by subtracting depreciation value (i.e. capital stock consumption) from GNP.
 
• Net National Product (NNP) = Gross National Product − Depreciation.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Gross Domestic Product (GDP):

 
 
• It is the total money value of all final goods and services produced within the geographical boundaries of the country during a given period of time.
 
• GDP = C + G + I
 
 
• C = Consumption expenditure
 
• G = Government expenditure
 
• I = Investment expenditure
 
 
 
 

 
• Gross domestic product at market prices

 
 
• Gross domestic product at market prices aims to measure the wealth created by all private and public agents in a national territory during a given period.
 
• The way of measuring GDP at market prices is the production approach as the sum of added values of all activities which produce goods and services, plus taxes and minus subsidies on products.
 
 
 
• Personal Income: 
 
 
• Income is obtained by nationals by subtracting corporate taxes and payments made for social securities provisions from national income and adding to it government transfer payments, business transfer payments and net interest paid by the government. 
 
• Personal Income = National income – undistributed profits of a corporation – payments for social security provisions – corporate tax + government transfer payments + Business transfer payments + Net interest paid by the government.

Personal income includes compensation from a number of sources, including salaries, wages, and bonuses received from employment or self-employment, dividends and distributions received from investments, rental receipts from real estate investments, and profit sharing from businesses.

question: _________ measures the aggregate production of final goods and services taking place within the domestic economy during a year.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Gross domestic product**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__****Gross domestic product (GDP)**

__
 
• It is the standard monetary measure of the value-added created through the **production of goods and services **in a country during a certain period
 
• As such, it also measures the income earned from that production or the** total amount **spent on final goods and services (fewer imports)
 
• As a broad measure of overall domestic production, its functions as a comprehensive scorecard of a given country's economic performance.
 
• In India, the GDP is released by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)**. Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation on a quarterly and yearly basis.
 
• The formula to calculate GDP is of t**hree types: Expenditure Approach, Income Approach, and Production Approach**.
 
• **Expenditure Approach**
 
 
• GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Export
 
 
 
• **Income Approach**
 
 
• GDP = Total National Income + Sales Taxes + Depreciation + Net Foreign Factor Income
 
 
 
• **Production or Value-Added Approach**
 
 
• Gross Value Added = Gross Value of Output – Value of Intermediate Consumption
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross national product (GNP) **is an estimate of the total value of all the final products and services turned out in a given period by the means of production owned by a country's residents. GNP is commonly calculated by taking the sum of personal consumption expenditures, private domestic investment, government expenditure, net exports, and any income earned by residents from overseas investments, then subtracting income earned by foreign residents. 
 
• **Net national product (NNP)** is the monetary value of finished goods and services produced by a country's citizens, overseas and domestically, in a given period. It is the equivalent of the gross national product (GNP), the total value of a nation's annual output, minus the amount of GNP required to purchase new goods to maintain existing stock.
 
• The **gross national product at factor cost** is the difference between the gross national product and net indirect taxes. It is also called gross national income. Gross national income is the total compensation of employees, operating surplus, mixed income, depreciation and net factor income from abroad.

• Consumption of fixed capital refers to the** reduction in the value of a fixed asset** due to **wear and tear, obsolescence,** or other factors.
 
• **Depreciation** is the **accounting method **used to allocate the** cost of a fixed asset** over its useful life, reflecting the consumption of fixed capital over time.
 
• Depreciation can be calculated using different methods, such as straight-line depreciation, declining balance depreciation, or sum-of-the-years' digits depreciation.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Net investment:-

 
 
• It​ refers to the difference between gross investment and depreciation, representing the actual increase in the stock of fixed assets.
 
 
 
• Appreciation:-
 
 
• It​ refers to the increase in the value of an asset over time, which is the opposite of depreciation.
 
 
 
• Gross investment:-
 
 
• It​ refers to the total amount of investment in fixed assets, including both the increase in the stock of assets and the replacement of existing assets.
 
 

9e:T

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is NOT included in domestic income?

options.text: Income earned by the residents of the country
Income earned by the non-residents outside the country
Income earned by all the employees of the country
Profit of all the industries of the country

solution:
The correct answer is __**Income earned by the non-residents outside the country**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Domestic income, also known as Gross Domestic Product, is the total income earned by all sectors (households, firms, and the government) within the geographical boundaries of a country, irrespective of whether they are residents or non-residents.
 
• However, income earned by non-residents outside the country is NOT included in the domestic income. Such income is part of the national income, not domestic income.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**: This is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders over a specific period, typically a year.
 
• **Gross National Product (GNP)**: It is the total market value of all final goods and services produced by residents of a country in a given period of time.
 
 
• **GNP = GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)**
 
• Here, **Net Factor Income from Abroad = Income earned by domestic factors of production from rest of the world - Income earned by factors of production of rest of the world from the domestic economy**
 
 
 
• **Net National Product (NNP) at Factor Cost or National Income (NI)**: This is the GNP minus depreciation.
 
 
• NNP or NI = GNP - Depreciation
 
 
 
• **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**: This is the GDP minus depreciation.
 
 
• NDP = GDP - Depreciation
 
 
 
• **Per Capita Income**: It is a measure of the amount of money earned per person in a certain area.
 
 
• Per Capita Income = National Income / Total Population
 
 
 
• **Factor Income**: It's the income that factors of production (land, labour, capital, and entrepreneurship) receive in return for their contribution to the production process.
 
• **Transfer Payments:** These are payments made without the provision of goods or services in return. Examples are social security benefits, pensions, unemployment benefits, etc. Transfer payments are not included in the computation of national income as they do not involve productive activity.

question: What is known as aggregate monetary resources?

options.text: M1 + Savings deposits with Post Office savings banks
M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks
M3 + Total deposits with Post Office savings organisations (excluding National Savings Certificates)
Currency (notes plus coins) held by the public and demand deposits held by commercial banks

solution:
The correct answer is__** M1 + Net time deposits of commercial banks.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Poin__**

__
 
• **The correct answer to the given question is option 2, which is M1 (currency in circulation + demand deposits with commercial banks) + net time deposits of commercial banks.**
 
• Aggregate monetary resources refer to the** total amount of money available in an economy.**
 
• Option 2, which is **M1 (currency in circulation + demand deposits with commercial banks) + net time deposits of commercial banks**, is known as aggregate monetary resources.
 
• M1 + savings deposits with Post Office savings banks (option 1) is known as narrow money.
 
• M3 + total deposits with Post Office savings organizations (excluding National Savings Certificates) (option 3) is known as broad money.
 
• Currency (notes plus coins) held by the public and demand deposits held by commercial banks (option 4) are known as the monetary base.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ** M1 + savings deposits with Post Office savings banks is known as narrow money**.
 
• It only includes the most liquid forms of money, i.e., the currency in circulation and demand deposits with commercial banks, along with savings deposits with Post Office savings banks.
 
• It doesn't include time deposits or other forms of deposits with commercial banks.
 
• **M3 + total deposits with Post Office savings organizations (excluding National Savings Certificates) **is known as broad money.
 
• It includes all forms of deposits with commercial banks, Post Office savings organizations (excluding National Savings Certificates), and other financial institutions.
 
• It is a broader measure of money supply than M1 and M2.
 
• ** Currency (notes plus coins)** held by the public and demand deposits held by commercial banks is known as the monetary base.
 
• It is the total amount of currency in circulation and demand deposits held by commercial banks.
 
• It doesn't include time deposits or other forms of deposits with commercial banks.

• A flow is a quantity that is measured with reference to a period of time.

• Wealth is a stock since it can be measured at a point of time.
 
• Income is a flow because it can be measured over a period of time.
 
• Salary and change in wealth is a flow because it can be measured over a period of time.

question: What is Net National Product?

options.text: The product of gross national product and depreciation is net national product.
The sum of gross national product and income of foreigners is net national product.
Net national product is equal to gross national product.
The difference between gross national product and depreciation is net national product.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The difference between gross national product and depreciation is net national product.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Net National Product is a measure of the total value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, minus the value of capital goods used up in the production process.** 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross National Product (GNP)** is the total value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, regardless of their location, in a specific period of time (usually a year). It includes the value of goods and services produced by a country's citizens and businesses, both domestically and abroad.
 
• ** Depreciation refers to the decrease in the value of capital goods (**such as machinery, buildings, and vehicles) over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, and other factors. It is subtracted from GNP to arrive at Shuddh Rashtriya Utpad, which provides a more accurate measure of a country's economic output.
 
• ** Shuddh Rashtriya Utpad is also known as Net National Product (NNP)** and represents the income earned by a country's residents from the production of goods and services. It is a key measure of a country's economic performance and is used to calculate other indicators such as per capita income and the Human Development Index.

question: Which of the followings is NOT an example of factor payment?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Pension.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Factor payment** refers to payments made to **factors of production,** which are the resources used in the **production of goods and services.**
 
• These factors include **land, labor, capital, and entrepreneurship.**
 
• **Interest, wages, rent,** are all examples of factor payments.
 
• Interest is paid to **capital**, wages are paid to **labor**, rent is paid to** land**, and pension is paid to** retired labor.**
 
• However, pension is **not a** factor payment as it is paid to retired labor and **not to active labor.**
 
• Factor payment is made to the factors of production that are **actively involved** in the production process.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Interest** is the payment made for the use of** borrowed capital.**
 
• **Wages** are the payment made to** labor for their services.**
 
• **Rent **is the payment made for the **use of land** and other** natural resources.**
 
• The most widely utilized factor in **macroeconomic analysis** is factor income, which aids governments in identifying the distinction between **GDP and GNP.**
 
• It can also be used to highlight discrepancies in the **allocation of revenue.**

subject: GK
question: Fisher’s quantity theory is explained by his famous equation given as ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**MV = PT.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fisher's quantity theory:-**

 
 
• It​ is a monetary theory that explains the relationship between** money supply, velocity of money, price level, and output**.
 
• The famous equation given by Fisher is **MV = PT, **where M is the money supply, V is the velocity of money, P is the price level, and T is the level of transactions.
 
• The equation suggests that an** increase in the money supply **(M) will lead to an **increase** in the price level (P), assuming that the velocity of money (V) and the level of transactions (T) are** constant.**
 
• The theory also implies that changes in the** money supply** have a direct impact on inflation, as an increase in the money supply leads to an **increase in the price level**, which in turn reduces the purchasing power of money.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The quantity theory of money has been subject to** criticism** over the years, with some economists arguing that it **oversimplifies the complex dynamics** of the economy.
 
• One of the criticisms is that the **velocity of money** is **not constant **and can vary significantly over time, making it difficult to predict the** impact of changes in the money supply **on the price level.
 
• Another criticism is that the theory assumes that the** level of transactions is fixed**, which is not always the case as it can be influenced by a variety of factors such as technology, demographics, and government policies.

question: What is the relationship between interest rate and demand for money?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Inverse**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• Interest rates bear an inverse relationship with the demand for money.
 
• Opportunity costs of holding money will be high when interest rates are high;
 
 
• people are losing out on possible earnings that interest-bearing investments could have generated.
 
• When interest rates are high, the opportunity cost of holding money increases because people can earn more by investing their money rather than keeping it as cash.
 
• This leads to a **lower demand for money** for transactional and speculative purposes
 
 
 
• When interest rates are low, the opportunity cost of holding money is low.
 
• People prefer holding more money for transactions or precautionary needs because the benefit of investing it is minimal.
 
• This leads to a higher demand for money.
 
• The relationship can be visualized using the liquidity preference theory by John Maynard Keynes:
 
• The demand for money (liquidity preference) decreases as the interest rate increases, and vice versa.

question: Which of the following is NOT correct with regards to the history of calculating National Income (NI) in India?

options.text: First attempt to compute NI was made by Dadabhai Naoroji.
First official attempt to compute NI was made by PC Mahalanobis.
Dadabhai Naoroji divided the Indian economy into two parts: primary sector and secondary sector.
First scientific method to compute NI was used by Dr VKRV Rao.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadabhai Naoroji divided the Indian economy into two parts: primary sector and secondary sector**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• National income is the total income of all the residents of the country.
 
• Thus, it is the total income of the country.
 
• It is considered to be one of the most important attributes for comparing the development of countries.
 
• The National Income formula equals GDP + Foreign Production by National Residents – Domestic Production by Non-National Residents.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**

 
• Dadabhai Naoroji, known as the Grand Old Man of India, was a leading figure in the early Indian independence movement and a founder of the Indian National Congress.
 
 
• His activities were mainly in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
 
• The Indian Independence League, however, was primarily active during the 1940s, significantly after Naoroji's most impactful years and following his death in 1917.
 
• This organization sought to obtain independence for India from British rule during World War II, with notable connections to Subhas Chandra Bose and the Indian National Army (INA).
 
• Naoroji founded or was associated with several organizations, like the Bombay Association (the oldest political organization in Bombay), the East India Association (established in London to discuss Indian affairs), and Gyan Prasarak Mandali (for the education of adult men in Bombay).
 
• These affiliations reflected his focus on political advocacy, economic theories (notably the Drain Theory), and social reform both in India and the UK.
 
• The Indian Independence League's context and methods, focused on leveraging the geopolitical situations during World War II for India's independence through more direct action, were distinct and not within Naoroji's lifetime or direct activities.
 
 
 
• **​PC Mahalanobis**
 
 
• The Second five-year plan was based on the Mahalanobis model, an economic development model developed by the Indian statistician Prasanta Chandra Mahalanobis in 1953.
 
• PC Mahalanobis established the Indian Statistical Institute (ISI) in Calcutta in 1931 and for the same reason, he is known as the father of Indian Statistics. He was a member of the first Planning Commission of free India.
 
• The second five-year plan was for the year 1956-1961.
 
• The second five-year plan focused on the development of the public sector and rapid Industrialisation. The plan attempted to determine a balanced allocation of investment between productive sectors in order to maximize long-run economic growth. 
 
• As a result, hydroelectric power projects across the country and five steel plants at Bhilai, Durgapur, and Rourkela were established with the help of Russia, Britain (the U.K), and West Germany respectively. Coal production was increased. More railway lines were added all over the country.
 
• The Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and Atomic Energy Commission of India was established to promote research in India.

question: The CSO adopted the concept of Gross Value Added in _____.

• The **Central Statistics Office (CSO)** adopted the concept of **Gross Value Added (GVA)** in **January 2015** as part of a major revision in the national accounts statistics.
 
• This change was implemented when the base year for GDP calculation was shifted from **2004-05 to 2011-12**.
 
• GVA measures the contribution of each sector to the economy.
 
• It reflects the value of goods and services produced in an economy after deducting the cost of inputs and raw materials.
 
• This adoption aligns India's statistical calculations with international practices and standards like those recommended by the **United Nations System of National Accounts (SNA)**.
 
• Along with the introduction of GVA, the **base year revision to 2011-12** was applied to GDP estimates.
 
• This revision ensured more accurate and updated data representation, helping policymakers assess economic performance better.

__

• **Net National Product (NNP)**

question: Which of the following statements is correct about the composition of the agriculture sector and employment in GDP post-independence?

options.text: The proportion of employment has declined significantly but not the share of the agriculture sector in GDP.
The proportion of both the agriculture sector and employment in GDP has increased significantly.
The proportion of both the agriculture sector and employment in GDP has declined significantly.
The proportion of GDP contributed by the agricultural sector declined significantly but not the employment depending on the agriculture sector.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The proportion of GDP contributed by the agricultural sector declined significantly but not the employment depending on the agriculture sector.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Post-independence, the share of agriculture in India's GDP has seen a significant decline. This is due to the growth of the industrial and service sectors.
 
• Despite the decline in the GDP contribution, a large proportion of the Indian workforce is still dependent on agriculture for their livelihood.
 
• Structural transformation in the economy is observed where the labor force shifts from agriculture to other sectors, but this transition has been slow in India.
 
• Employment in agriculture remains high due to slow industrialization and the inability of other sectors to absorb the growing workforce.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP):**

 
 
• GDP is the total monetary or market value of all the finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
 
• It serves as a comprehensive scorecard of a given country’s economic health.
 
 
 
• **Agriculture Sector:**
 
 
• This sector includes farming, fishing, and forestry, and it is a primary sector of the economy.
 
• It provides food, raw materials, and employment to a large section of the population.
 
 
 
• **Employment in Agriculture:**
 
 
• A large proportion of the workforce in developing countries like India is employed in agriculture.
 
• It includes jobs in crop production, animal husbandry, fisheries, and forestry.
 
 
 
• **Structural Transformation:**
 
 
• This refers to the shift of economic activities and labor force from agriculture to the industrial and service sectors.
 
• It is a key feature of economic development and involves changes in the structure of the economy.

subject: GK
question: What is the empirically fitted relationship between the rate of change of money, wage, and rate of unemployment known as?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Philips curve**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Philips curve represents the inverse relationship between the rate of unemployment and the rate of inflation in an economy.
 
• The concept was first introduced by economist A.W. Phillips in 1958.
 
• According to the Phillips curve, lower unemployment in an economy leads to higher wages, which in turn leads to higher inflation.
 
• This relationship suggests that policymakers face a trade-off between reducing unemployment and controlling inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Friedman's Model**

 
 
• Also known as the Monetarist Theory, it was proposed by Milton Friedman.
 
• Friedman argued that there is no long-run trade-off between inflation and unemployment, as suggested by the Phillips curve.
 
• He introduced the concept of the Natural Rate of Unemployment, which posits that the economy will always revert to this natural rate despite short-term fluctuations.
 
• Friedman emphasized the role of monetary policy in controlling inflation.
 
 
 
• **Keynesian Model**
 
 
• Developed by John Maynard Keynes, this model emphasizes total spending in the economy (aggregate demand) and its effects on output and inflation.
 
• Keynesians advocate for active government intervention to manage economic cycles.
 
• They believe that insufficient demand can lead to prolonged periods of high unemployment.
 
• In contrast to the Phillips curve, Keynesians may support policies that increase aggregate demand to reduce unemployment without necessarily causing high inflation.
 
 
 
• **Baumol Hypothesis**
 
 
• Proposed by economist William J. Baumol, it addresses the cost disease in service sectors.
 
• Baumol's hypothesis suggests that wages in labor-intensive sectors (like services) rise due to wage increases in other sectors that experience higher productivity growth.
 
• This leads to higher costs in the service sector without corresponding increases in productivity.
 
• The hypothesis is often used to explain rising costs in sectors such as healthcare and education.

subject: GK
question: If GNP is 16% higher than the last year and the rate of inflation is 9%, production in the economy has grown by:
solution:
The correct answer is __**0.07**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gross National Product (GNP) is a broad measure of a nation's total economic activity.
 
• The GNP is 16% higher than the last year, indicating overall economic growth.
 
• Inflation rate is 9%, which represents the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services is rising.
 
• The production growth rate can be determined by adjusting the GNP growth rate for inflation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross National Product (GNP)**

 
 
• GNP measures the market value of all the products and services produced in one year by labor and property supplied by the residents of a country.
 
• It includes the value of goods and services produced by a country's residents, regardless of the location of the actual production.
 
 
 
• **Inflation**
 
 
• Inflation is the rate at which the general level of prices for goods and services is rising and subsequently eroding purchasing power.
 
• Central banks attempt to limit inflation, and avoid deflation, in order to keep the economy running smoothly.
 
 
 
• **Economic Growth**
 
 
• Economic growth is an increase in the production of economic goods and services, compared from one period of time to another.
 
• It can be measured in nominal or real terms, the latter of which is adjusted for inflation.
 
 
 
• **Calculation of Production Growth Rate**
 
 
• To find the production growth rate, we adjust the GNP growth rate for inflation.
 
• Formula: Production Growth Rate = (1 + GNP Growth Rate) / (1 + Inflation Rate) - 1
 
• Using the given values: GNP Growth Rate = 16% or 0.16, Inflation Rate = 9% or 0.09
 
• Production Growth Rate = (1 + 0.16) / (1 + 0.09) - 1 = 1.16 / 1.09 - 1 = 1.0642 - 1 ≈ 0.07

subject: GK
question: What is subtracted from GDP to arrive at NDP?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Depreciation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Depreciation refers to the reduction in the value of assets over time due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors.
 
• In national accounting, GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measures the total economic output of a country.
 
• NDP (Net Domestic Product) is derived by subtracting the depreciation of the country's capital assets from its GDP.
 
• This adjustment is necessary to account for the loss in value of fixed capital and provides a more accurate measure of economic performance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**

 
 
• GDP is the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders in a given time period.
 
• It is used to gauge the economic performance of a country and make international comparisons.
 
• GDP can be calculated using three approaches: the production (or output or value added) approach, the income approach, and the expenditure approach.
 
 
 
• **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**
 
 
• NDP is calculated by subtracting depreciation from GDP.
 
• Depreciation, also known as the consumption of fixed capital, reflects the wear and tear or obsolescence of physical assets.
 
• NDP provides a clearer picture of the actual economic performance by accounting for the decrease in value of capital goods.
 
 
 
• **Subsidies**
 
 
• Subsidies are financial assistance provided by the government to individuals, businesses, or other entities to promote economic and social policy objectives.
 
• They can take various forms, including direct cash transfers, tax breaks, or price controls.
 
 
 
• **Net Indirect Taxes**
 
 
• Net Indirect Taxes are calculated as indirect taxes (like sales tax, VAT) minus subsidies.
 
• They are part of the factor cost adjustment to reach market prices in national accounting.
 
 
 
• **Net Factor Income from Abroad**
 
 
• Net Factor Income from Abroad is the difference between the income residents receive from abroad for factor services (like labor and capital) and the income paid to foreign residents for their factor services within the domestic economy.
 
• This measure is used to calculate Gross National Product (GNP) from GDP.

question: Money supply is a ____ concept.
solution:
The correct answer is __**stock**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Money supply** is considered a stock concept because it represents the total amount of money available in an economy at a specific point in time.
 
• Unlike a flow concept, which is measured over a period of time, a stock concept is measured at one particular time.
 
• The money supply includes various components such as currency in circulation, demand deposits, and other liquid assets.
 
• Central banks and government agencies typically measure the money supply to monitor and manage the economy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Stock vs. Flow Concepts**

 
 
• A **stock** concept is a quantity measured at a particular point in time. Examples include the money supply, wealth, and the number of goods in inventory.
 
• A **flow** concept is a quantity measured over a period of time. Examples include income, expenditure, and production.
 
 
 
• **Components of Money Supply**
 
 
• **M1:** This is the narrow measure of money supply, which includes currency in circulation and demand deposits (checking accounts).
 
• **M2:** This is a broader measure, which includes M1 plus savings accounts, small time deposits, and non-institutional money market funds.
 
• **M3:** This includes M2 plus large time deposits, institutional money market funds, and other larger liquid assets.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Money Supply**
 
 
• The money supply is a critical factor in determining inflation levels, interest rates, and overall economic stability.
 
• Central banks, such as the Federal Reserve or the Reserve Bank of India, use measures of the money supply to implement monetary policy.
 
• Changes in the money supply can affect the economy's performance, influencing everything from consumer spending to business investment.

question: Which of the following is Fisher's equation of exchange?
solution:
The correct answer is __**MV=PT**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fisher's equation of exchange is represented as **MV=PT**.
 
• In this equation, **M** stands for the money supply in an economy.
 
• **V** represents the velocity of money, which is the rate at which money circulates in the economy.
 
• **P** is the price level, and **T** represents the total volume of transactions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Money Supply (M)**

 
 
• The total amount of monetary assets available in an economy at a specific time.
 
• It includes various components such as currency in circulation and demand deposits.
 
• Changes in the money supply can influence inflation, interest rates, and economic growth.
 
 
 
• **Velocity of Money (V)**
 
 
• The rate at which money is exchanged from one transaction to another.
 
• It indicates the efficiency of money in an economy; a higher velocity means money is changing hands more frequently.
 
• Velocity is calculated as the ratio of nominal GDP to the money supply.
 
 
 
• **Price Level (P)**
 
 
• The average of current prices across the entire spectrum of goods and services produced in the economy.
 
• It is often measured by price indices such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or the GDP deflator.
 
• Changes in the price level reflect inflation or deflation in the economy.
 
 
 
• **Total Volume of Transactions (T)**
 
 
• The total number of transactions or the total quantity of goods and services traded in the economy.
 
• This can include consumer spending, business investments, and government expenditures.
 
• The volume of transactions is an indicator of economic activity.

question: NDP = ________.

options.text: GDP - Net factor income from abroad
GDP + Net factor income from abroad

solution:
The correct answer is __**GDP - Depreciation**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Net Domestic Product (NDP) is derived by subtracting depreciation from the Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
 
• Depreciation refers to the reduction in the value of assets over time, often due to wear and tear.
 
• GDP represents the total monetary value of all finished goods and services produced within a country's borders in a specific time period.
 
• NDP provides a more accurate reflection of an economy's actual productivity and sustainability by accounting for the depreciation of capital assets.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)**

 
 
• GDP is the total market value of all goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
 
• It includes all private and public consumption, government outlays, investments, and exports minus imports.
 
• GDP is a broad measure of a nation's overall economic activity.
 
• It is often used as an indicator of the economic health of a country.
 
 
 
• **Depreciation**
 
 
• Depreciation is an accounting method of allocating the cost of a tangible or physical asset over its useful life.
 
• It represents how much of an asset's value has been used up over time.
 
• Businesses depreciate long-term assets for both tax and accounting purposes.
 
• Depreciation can affect the net income of a business as it is listed as an expense.
 
 
 
• **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**
 
 
• NDP is an economic indicator that provides a more accurate assessment of an economy's productivity by accounting for depreciation.
 
• It is calculated as GDP minus depreciation.
 
• NDP helps in understanding the sustainability of the economic activities by indicating the net addition to the nation's wealth.
 
• It ensures that the measure of economic performance considers the wear and tear of capital assets.
 
 
 
• **Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA)**
 
 
• NFIA is the difference between the income residents receive from abroad for factor services (like labor and capital) and the income paid to foreign residents for their factor services within the domestic economy.
 
• It is used in the calculation of Gross National Product (GNP).
 
• NFIA can indicate the level of economic interaction a country has with the rest of the world.
 
• A positive NFIA means a country is earning more from its investments abroad than it is paying to foreign investors in the domestic market.

subject: GK
question: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding circular flow of income?

options.text: Savings as well as government expenditure are injections to the circular flow.
The income of one sector becomes the expenditure of the other.
In a circular flow, leakages are equal to injections.
The real flow and monetary flow move in a circular manner in an opposite direction.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Savings as well as government expenditure are injections to the circular flow.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Savings** are considered a leakage from the circular flow of income as they represent income not spent on consumption.

• **Government expenditure** is an injection into the circular flow as it represents spending that adds to the overall demand in the economy.

• In a closed economy with no government intervention, **savings** would be equal to investment.

• The correct representation would be that **investment and government spending** are injections, while savings, taxes, and imports are leakages.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Circular Flow of Income**

• The circular flow of income is a model that depicts how money flows through the economy between households and firms.

• In this model, households provide factors of production (labor, land, capital) to firms, and in return, they receive income (wages, rent, interest, profit).

• Households then use this income to purchase goods and services from firms, completing the cycle.

• **Leakages and Injections**

• **Leakages** are non-consumption uses of income, including savings, taxes, and imports. They represent money that leaves the circular flow.

• **Injections** are additions to the income of firms, including investment, government spending, and exports. They represent money entering the circular flow.

• In a balanced circular flow, the total value of leakages is equal to the total value of injections.

• **Real Flow and Monetary Flow**

• The **real flow** refers to the flow of physical goods and services and the factors of production.

• The **monetary flow** refers to the flow of money in the form of income and expenditure.

• In the circular flow model, the real flow and monetary flow move in opposite directions to each other.

question:
Read the below statements marked as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Mark the **correct **options:

**Assertion (A)**: India's rank in the Global Happiness Index is lower than most South Asian neighbours.

**Reason (R)**: India's GDP per capita is the lowest in South Asia.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:
The correct answer is __**3) A is true, but R is false.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **India's rank in the Global Happiness Index has been consistently low**, with neighboring South Asian countries like Nepal, Bhutan, and Bangladesh often ranking higher.
 
• As per the 2023 World Happiness Report, India ranked **126th out of 137 countries**, while countries like Bhutan ranked significantly higher.
 
• The Global Happiness Index considers factors such as social support, life expectancy, freedom to make life choices, and perceptions of corruption—not just economic indicators like GDP per capita.
 
• India's GDP per capita is **not the lowest in South Asia**. For example, countries like Afghanistan have a lower GDP per capita than India.
 
• Hence, while the assertion (A) is correct that India's rank is lower than most South Asian neighbors, the reason (R) is incorrect since the ranking is based on several factors beyond GDP per capita.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Factors influencing the Global Happiness Index:**

 
 
• The ranking is based on six key metrics: GDP per capita, social support, healthy life expectancy, freedom to make life choices, generosity, and perceptions of corruption.
 
• While GDP per capita is an important factor, other social and psychological well-being aspects weigh heavily in the index.
 
• Countries like Bhutan rank higher because of their focus on Gross National Happiness, despite having lower GDP per capita.
 
 
 
• **India's performance in the Global Happiness Index:**
 
 
• India's lower ranking is attributed to factors such as weak social support, perceived corruption, and lower levels of individual freedom.
 
• Efforts to improve quality of life through government initiatives like Digital India, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan, and Ayushman Bharat are aimed at addressing these issues.
 
 
 
• **GDP per capita in South Asia:**
 
 
• India's GDP per capita is higher than several South Asian nations, including Afghanistan and Nepal.
 
• However, countries like Bhutan and Maldives have higher GDP per capita due to their smaller populations and focused economic strategies.

question: What is the main reason for the decline in core inflation across most countries in 2024?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Drop in international commodity prices**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A decline in international commodity prices, such as crude oil, natural gas, and agricultural products, reduces production costs for companies, leading to lower prices for goods and services, hence contributing to a decrease in core inflation.
 
• Global economic factors, such as a slowdown in demand from major economies like China and the US, often lead to a drop in commodity prices.
 
• Lower commodity prices also impact transportation and logistics costs, further reducing price pressures across various sectors.
 
• Commodity markets are sensitive to geopolitical events, and reduced geopolitical tensions or improved supply chains often stabilize or lower commodity prices globally.
 
• Central banks closely monitor commodity price trends as they significantly influence inflation expectations and monetary policy decisions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fall in service sector productivity**

 
 
• A fall in service sector productivity can lead to higher costs for services, which may increase core inflation, rather than causing a decline.
 
• Productivity drops often result from factors like labor shortages, inadequate infrastructure, or technological inefficiencies.
 
• In most economies, the service sector contributes significantly to GDP, and its performance directly impacts employment and economic stability.
 
 
 
• **Decrease in export demand**
 
 
• A decrease in export demand affects a country’s trade balance and economic growth but does not directly contribute to a decline in core inflation.
 
• Core inflation is primarily influenced by domestic factors like consumer demand and production costs, rather than external trade dynamics.
 
• However, prolonged weak export demand can lead to reduced industrial activity and lower employment, indirectly impacting inflation trends over time.
 
 
 
• **Increase in fiscal deficit**
 
 
• An increase in fiscal deficit generally puts upward pressure on inflation due to higher government borrowing and spending.
 
• Excessive fiscal deficits can lead to increased money supply in the economy, further fueling demand-driven inflation.
 
• Fiscal policy, when unbalanced, can exacerbate inflationary trends, particularly in countries with weaker monetary policy frameworks.
