question: The Uniform Civil Code (UCC) primarily aims to:

options.text: Establish uniform laws on civil matters like marriage, divorce, inheritance

solution:
The correct answer is __**Establish uniform laws on civil matters like marriage, divorce, inheritance**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Uniform Civil Code (UCC)** aims to replace personal laws based on the scriptures and customs of each major religious community in India with a common set governing every citizen. 
• The **main purpose of UCC** is to ensure uniformity in laws related to **civil matters** such as **marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption**, regardless of religion or community. 
• **Article 44** of the Indian Constitution states that the State shall endeavor to secure a Uniform Civil Code for its citizens throughout the territory of India, indicating its constitutional backing. 
• UCC is intended to **promote equality** and remove discrepancies that arise due to the application of religious laws. It seeks to foster **secularism** in legal matters. 
• The implementation of UCC is often debated, with proponents suggesting it as a means to provide **gender justice** and equality, particularly in matters where women are disadvantaged under certain personal laws. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Historical Background:** 
• The demand for UCC was first raised during the **British colonial era**, but it was deferred due to the diversity of personal laws. 
• Post-independence, the makers of the Constitution included **Article 44** in the Directive Principles of State Policy, emphasizing the importance of UCC. 
• **Current Scenario:** 
• India currently follows separate personal laws for different communities: **Hindu Marriage Act, Muslim Personal Law, Christian Marriage Act, and Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act**. 
• These laws govern marriage, divorce, inheritance, and other civil matters, leading to variations in legal rights across religions. 
• **Arguments in Favor of UCC:** 
• It ensures **gender equality** by removing discriminatory practices like **triple talaq** and unequal inheritance rights. 
• UCC helps in promoting **national integration** by creating a uniform set of laws for all citizens. 
• It simplifies the legal process by eliminating the need for separate legal systems for different communities. 
• **Arguments Against UCC:** 
• Critics argue that it might **undermine cultural diversity** and the rights of minorities. 
• There is concern that UCC might interfere with religious practices protected under **Article 25** of the Constitution, which guarantees freedom of religion. 
• Implementation challenges include resistance from communities and lack of consensus. 
• **Examples of Civil Codes in Practice:** 
• Countries like **France** and **Turkey** have adopted Uniform Civil Codes. 
• In India, states like **Goa** have implemented a common civil code, demonstrating its feasibility. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Article 44:** Part of the Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution, it underscores the need for a Uniform Civil Code. 
• The **Law Commission of India** has periodically reviewed the feasibility of UCC. In its **2018 report**, it emphasized reforms in personal laws instead of enforcing UCC directly. 
• Recent debates on UCC have gained momentum, with various political parties expressing their views on its implementation. 
• The Supreme Court of India has, in various judgments, highlighted the importance of implementing UCC to address inequalities in personal laws. 
• **Goa Civil Code:** Goa is the only Indian state that follows a uniform civil code, applicable to all its citizens irrespective of religion. </ul

question: What makes the Goa Civil Code distinct from other personal laws in India?

options.text: It applies only to the Hindu community in Goa.
It is a uniform civil code that applies to all communities regardless of religion.
It is based on British common law.
It allows separate personal laws for different religions.

solution:
The correct answer is __**It is a uniform civil code that applies to all communities regardless of religion.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Goa Civil Code**, often referred to as the **Uniform Civil Code (UCC) of Goa**, is a set of civil laws that governs all residents of Goa, irrespective of their religion, ethnicity, or caste.

• Unlike other states in India, Goa implements a single civil law for matters such as **marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption**, which applies uniformly to all communities.

• This distinct code was derived from the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867** and was retained even after Goa's integration into India in 1961.

• The Goa Civil Code is considered a practical example of the Uniform Civil Code, as envisaged under **Article 44 of the Indian Constitution**, which encourages the state to secure a uniform civil law for all citizens.

• This code ensures **gender equality** by granting equal property rights to both sons and daughters and provides provisions for community property and fair distribution of assets in case of divorce.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Portuguese Civil Code Legacy:**

• The Goa Civil Code is based on the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**, which was implemented during the Portuguese rule in Goa.

• After Goa's liberation and integration into India in **1961**, the code was retained to preserve its unique identity.

• Unlike other Indian states, Goa did not adopt separate personal laws for different religious communities.

• **Key Features of the Goa Civil Code:**

• **Universal Application:** It applies uniformly to all residents of Goa, irrespective of religion or caste.

• **Marriage and Divorce:** Couples must register their marriage, and the code provides equal grounds for divorce for both men and women.

• **Inheritance:** The code ensures **equal inheritance rights** for sons and daughters, promoting gender equality.

• **Community Property:** Property acquired during the marriage is treated as community property and is divided equally upon divorce.

• **Uniform Civil Code in India:**

• **Article 44:** It is a Directive Principle of State Policy in the Indian Constitution, which calls for the state to secure a Uniform Civil Code for all citizens.

• At present, personal laws in most states vary based on religion, covering marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption.

• The Goa Civil Code serves as a model for the implementation of a UCC in the rest of India.

• **Comparison with Other States:**

• In other states, personal laws are governed by religious codes such as the **Hindu Marriage Act, Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act,** and **Christian Marriage Act**.

• These laws vary widely, and there is no uniformity in civil matters across communities.

• In contrast, Goa’s Civil Code ensures uniformity and equality for all its residents.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Debates on UCC:**

• The implementation of a Uniform Civil Code across India has been a subject of debate due to its potential to replace personal laws with a common set of laws for all citizens.

• Opponents argue that it might infringe upon religious freedom, as guaranteed under **Article 25 of the Constitution**.

• Proponents believe it would promote equality and simplify legal processes.

• **Goa as a Model State:**

• Goa’s Civil Code is often cited as an example of how a UCC can function effectively in a pluralistic society.

• It demonstrates how uniform laws can coexist with diverse cultural and religious practices.

• **Challenges in Implementing UCC:**

• Diverse religious practices and customs pose significant challenges to achieving consensus on a single set of laws.

• There is a need for extensive consultations with stakeholders to ensure cultural and religious sensitivities are respected.

question: Article 17 of the Constitution of India deals with the abolition of ________.
solution:
__
 
• **Article 17** of the Constitution of India deals with the **abolition of untouchability.__**
 
• Article 17 **abolishes ‘untouchability’ and forbids its practice in any form. **
 
• The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability shall be an **offence punishable by law.**
 
• It falls under the **Right to equality** enshrined under the constitution in **Articles 14–18.**
 
• It is noteworthy that the term ‘Untouchability’ is **not defined anywhere in the constitution.**
 
• But in broader sense untouchability refers to the **social disabilities imposed on certain classes of persons by reason of their birth in certain castes.**
 
• In 1976, the Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 was amended and renamed as the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955.
 
• The amendment and renaming enlarged the scope and made the penal provisions more stringent.

question: Fundamental Duties were added in the Constitution of India under the leadership of which Prime Minister of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Indira Gandhi**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• It was added to the Constitution of India under the leadership of **Indira Gandhi**.
 
• The Fundamental Duties of citizens were added to the Constitution by the** 42nd Amendment in 1976**, upon the recommendations of the **Swaran Singh Committee** that was constituted by the Government.
 
• When the Constitution was adopted in the year 1949, there were no provisions regarding Fundamental Duties to the Citizens though there was a Part III for Fundamental Rights.
 
• The Swaran Singh Committee suggested that steps needed to be taken to ensure that the individual did not overlook his duties while in the exercise of his Fundamental Rights. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

By way of the 42nd Constitution (Amendment) Act, 1976, a new Chapter IV-A which consists of only one Article i.e 51-A was added which dealt with a Code of Ten Fundamental Duties for citizens.

 
• Fundamental duties are intended to serve as a constant reminder to every citizen that while the constitution specifically conferred on them certain Fundamental Rights, it also requires citizens to observe certain basic norms of democratic conduct and democratic behavior because rights and duties are correlative.
 
• The inclusion of Fundamental Duties brought our Constitution in line with Article 29 (1) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and with provisions in several modern Constitutions of other countries.
 
• The concept of Fundamental duties was taken from the USSR.
 
• The Fundamental duties are essentially taken from Indian tradition, mythology, religions, and practices.
 
• Essentially these were the duties that are the codification of tasks integral to the Indian way of life.

Thus, we can conclude that Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution of India in 1976.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 25 to Article 28**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 25 of the Indian constitution guarantees the Right to Freedom of Religion to its citizens.
 
• It provides freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.
 
• It is a basic human right guarantee that cannot be subverted or misinterpreted in any manner.
 
• Article 25 to Article 28 of the Indian constitution deals with the Right to Freedom of Religion.
 
• The objective of the Constitutional Right to Freedom of Religion in India is to sustain the principle of secularism.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** Secularism:

 
• The term secular has been derived from the Latin word ‘seculum’ which means an age, an indefinite period, or the present age.
 
• Secularism in the Indian context means first, ‘Dharmanirapaksata’ or impartiality to religion and secondly, ‘Sarva Dharma Sama Bhava’ or equal respect for all religions based on the principle of accommodation of all religions.
 
• A Secular State does not identify itself with any particular religion but protects and respects all faiths until they become a danger to the unity and integrity of the country.
 
• The most essential factors of secularism were granting equal status to all religions in India.
 
• Indian secularism is a multi-value character and gives importance to moral reasoning and equally respecting all religions.

question: How many fundamental duties are provided in the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**11**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original constitution contained only the fundamental rights and not the fundamental duties.
 
• They incorporated the duties of the State in the Constitution in the form of Directive Principles of State Polity.
 
• In 1976 Sardar Swarna Singh committee to make recommendations about fundamental duties
 
• The 42nd Constitution amendment act in 1976 added a new part IVA 
 
• It consists of only one article that is article 51A
 
• Swarna Singh suggested 8 fundamental duties in the constitution, 42nd Constitution amendment act added 10 duties
 
• In 2002, one more Fundamental Duty was added.
 
• So, at present there are total of 11 Fundamental Duties are included in the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Fundamental Duties in the Indian Constitution are inspired by the Constitution of the erstwhile USSR.
 
• None of the Constitutions of major democratic countries like the USA, Canada, France, Germany, Australia, and so on specifically contain a list of duties of citizens.
 
• Japanese Constitution is, perhaps, the only democratic Constitution in the world that contains a list of duties of citizens.
 
• Fundamental duties are confined to citizens only and do not extend to foreigners.
 
• Fundamental duties are non-justiceable.

question: The fundamental duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to his child or, as the case may be, ward between the age of 6 and ________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**14**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• On the 26th of August 2009, the Indian Parliament passed a historic act known as the ‘Right to Education Act’ or RTE Act but the RTE Act was implemented in India with effect from 1st April 2010.
 
• It is an act that aims to *provide* free and compulsory education to all children between the age of 6 to 14 years in India under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

Features of the RTE Act - 2009 under Article 21A: 

 
• Prohibition of private tuition by teachers to equalize educational opportunities to all.
 
• Reservation of 25% seats for children belonging to economically weaker sections in private schools.
 
• 45 hours including preparation hours as the minimum number of working hours per week for the teacher.
 
• Not to deploy teachers in non-academic work except elections, population census, and disaster relief duties.
 
• Establishment of primary and upper primary schools within the distance of 1km and 3kms respectively from child's house.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• Fundamental Duties

 
 
• Respect the Indian Constitution, its goals, and its institutions, as well as the National Anthem and Flag
 
• Respect and uphold the great principles that motivated the nation's fight for freedom.
 
• Uphold and defend India's independence, unity, and integrity.
 
• When required, defend the nation and perform national service.
 
• Promote harmony and a sense of common brotherhood among all Indians, notwithstanding their differences in religion, language, area, or social class, and condemn practises that are offensive to women's dignity.
 
• Value and safeguard the rich history of the nation's diverse culture.
 
• To preserve and enhance the natural world, including its woods, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, as well as to show compassion for all living things.
 
• Develop a humanistic outlook, a scientific mindset, and a spirit of reformation.
 
• Protecting public property and avoiding violence
 
• Strive for excellence in all areas of personal and societal endeavour so that the country is always striving for greater levels of ambition and success.
 
• To his ward or child between the ages of six and fourteen, provide educational possibilities. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 added this duty.
 
• 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Indian Constitution

 
 
• The Indian Constitution is the country's highest law. The document outlines the framework that delineates the core political code, as well as the fundamental rights, guiding principles, and responsibilities of citizens.
 
• It also spells out the organisation, methods, powers, and duties of governmental institutions. It is the world's longest-written national constitution.
 
• It confers constitutional supremacy (as opposed to parliamentary supremacy, given that a constituent assembly rather than Parliament produced it), and its preamble contains a proclamation that it was ratified by the people.
 
• The constitution cannot be overruled by parliament. B. R. Ambedkar and the Indian Constitution are featured on an Indian postage stamp from 2015.
 
• On 26 November 1949, the Indian Constituent Assembly approved it, and on 26 January 1950, it went into effect.
 
• The Dominion of India became the Republic of India when the constitution took the place of the Government of India Act 1935 as the primary law governing the nation.

question: Which Article of the Constitution of India deals with the recognition of the right to education as a Fundamental Right?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 21 A.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 21 A**

 
 
• **Article 21-A,** which states that all children between the ages of **six **and **fourteen **have the fundamental right to free and compulsory education, was added to the **Indian Constitution** by the **Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act of 2002**.
 
• Every child has the right to a full-time **elementary education **of satisfactory and **equitable **quality in a formal school that complies with certain **fundamental **norms and standards.
 
• According to the** Right of Children** to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE)** Act, 2009**, which represents the consequential legislation anticipated under** Article 21-A**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The** RTE Act **and** Article 21-A** both went into force on **April 1, 2010**.
 
• The words **"free and compulsory" **are part of the **RTE **Act's title. Under the definition of** "free education,"** no child aside from a child whose parents have allowed him or her to enrol in a school that is not financially supported by the relevant government shall be required to pay any kind of **fee**, **charge**, or expense that might prevent them from pursuing and completing **elementary **education.

question: Fundamental Rights are mentioned in which part of the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __Part III__.

__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

__
 
• Fundamental Rights

 
 
• **The Fundamental Rights **are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12-35). Part III of the Constitution is described as the Magna Carta of India.
 
• ‘Magna Carta’, the Charter of Rights issued by King John of England in 1215 was the first written document relating to the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
 
• The Fundamental Rights are justiciable because when violated the aggrieved individual can move the courts for their enforcement.
 
• The Supreme Court or High Courts have the power to** issue directions, orders or writs to enforce any of the Fundamental Rights.**
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• The Constitution of India provides for six Fundamental Rights

 
 
• Right to equality (Articles 14–18)
 
• Right to freedom (Articles 19–22)
 
• Right against exploitation (Articles 23–24)
 
• Right to freedom of religion (Articles 25–28)
 
• Cultural and educational rights (Articles 29–30)
 
• Right to constitutional remedies (Article 32)
 
 
 
• Originally the Constitution also included the property right (Article 31).
 
 
• However, it was deleted from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act, of 1978.
 
• It is made a legal right under Article 300-A in Part XII of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Part IV**
 
 
• Part IV (Article 36-51) of the Indian Constitution is related to the Directive Principles of our State Policy.
 
• It is not enforceable by any court but these are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
• **The government must** apply these principles in law-making.
 
• These principles have been taken from the Constitution of Ireland.
 
 
 
• **Part VI**
 
 
• **​The Governor of a State **shall have the power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites or remissions of punishment or to suspend, remit or commute the sentence of any person convicted of any offence against any law relating to a matter to which the executive power of the State extends.
 
 
 
• **Part IX** 
 
 
• Part IX of the Indian Constitution contains provisions for the Panchayats.
 
• Part IX tells about a three-tier Panchayati Raj System which would be constituted in every state at the village level, intermediate level, and district level.
 
• 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act added Part IX to the constitution with the title “The Panchayats” covering provisions from Articles 243 to 243(O).
 
• Part VIII contains provisions for Union Territories.
 
• The fifth Schedule contains provisions for the Administration and Control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
 
• Article 244 contains provisions for the administration of Scheduled Areas and Tribal Areas.

question: Which special order of the courts means “arrested person should be presented before the court"?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Habeas corpus**__.​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **special order of the courts, Habeas corpus**, means **“arrested person should be presented before the court"**.
 
• **Habeas corpus** is a legal remedy that **allows a person to inform a court about an illegitimate arrest or imprisonment** and ask that the court compel the person's custodian—typically a prison official—to bring the prisoner to court so that the validity of the arrest can be determined.
 
• **William Blackstone **referred to the **writ of habeas corpus** as a** "great and efficient writ in all manner of illrgal confinement"**.
 
• **Habeas corpus** is a summons that has the** same legal effect as a court order**; it is** directed to the custodian and requests that a prisoner be brought before the court together with documentation of the custodian's authority** so that the court can evaluate if the custodian has the right to hold the prisoner

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• .A **judicial remedy **known as a **mandamus** is an** order from a court to any government, subordinate court, corporation, or public authority** directing them to perform (or refrain from performing) a particular act that they are legally required to perform (or refrain from performing), and which is in the nature of a public duty and, in some cases, a **statutory duty**.
 
• **Certiorari** is a legal procedure **used to ask for judicial review of a ruling made by a lower court or government** **body**.
 
• A writ of prerogative known as a **quo warranto demands that the person to whom it is addressed provide proof of their legal capacity** to exercise a right, power, or franchise.

__
 
• A citizen of India has no inherent obligation to **amass property.**
 
• According to the Indian Constitution, following traffic laws is not a Basic Responsibility.
 
• **Article 51A of Part IV-A **of the Indian Constitution lists the fundamental obligations of Indian citizens.
 
 
• Respect the national flag, national anthem, and Indian Constitution as well as all of its ideas and institutions.
 
• To uphold and adhere to the lofty values that sparked the country's fight for freedom.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• ​10 Basic Responsibilities were introduced to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
 
• Later, the 11th Basic Responsibility was included in the list by the 86th Amendment Act of 2002.
 
• In 1976, the **Swaran Singh Committee** proposed Basic Responsibilities.​
 
• The Swaran Singh Committee also advocated for the obligation to pay taxes. Yet, the Constitution did not include it.
 
• The** Constitution's Article 51A **lists the essential obligations.
 
• The **Basic Rights**, **Directive Principles of State Policy**, and** Fundamental Duties **are portions of the Indian Constitution that outline the fundamental duties and **rights of citizens** towards the state as well as the fundamental obligations of states to their inhabitants. 
 
• These articles are regarded as essential parts of the constitution, which was created during 1949 by the **Indian Constituent Assembly**.

question: Which of the following Articles states that a State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them?
solution:
The correct answer is __Article 15.__

__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 15 (1) prohibits discrimination by the state against any citizen on grounds 'only' of caste, religion, sex, race, and place of birth. 
 
• Fundamental rights are provided to every citizen of the country without any discrimination.
 
• The word "discrimination" refers to making adverse distinctions with regard to or to distinguish unfavorable from others.
 
• The term 'only' means that discrimination can be done on the basis of other grounds.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information:__**There are six fundamental rights of the Indian Constitution along with the constitutional articles:

 
• Rights to equality (Article 14-18)
 
• Rights to freedom (Article 19-22)
 
• Right against exploitation (Article 23-24)
 
• Right to freedom of religion (Article 25-28)
 
• Cultural and educational rights (Article 29-30)
 
• Rights to constitutional remedies (Article 32).

**Article 59:**

 
• Article 59 of the Constitution of India deals with of the conditions of the president’s office.
 
• Article 52 to 78 in Part V of the Constitution deals with the Union Executive.
 
• The union executive consists of the president, the vice president, the prime minister, the council of ministers, and the Attorney General of India.

**Article 25:**

 
• Article 25 guarantees all citizens the freedom of conscience, as well as the freedom to profess, practice, and propagate religion.
 
• Article 25 (1) - Subject to public order, morality, and health, as well as the other provisions of this Part, all persons have an equal right to conscience and the freedom to profess, practice, and propagate religion.
 
• Article 25 (2) - Nothing in this article shall interfere with the operation of any existing law or prevent the State from enacting new legislation.
 
 
• This regulates and limits any financial, economic, political, or other secular activity associated with any religious practice.
 
• This provides for social welfare as well as the reform or opening up of Hindu religious institutions of a public nature to all sections and classes of Hindus.
 
• This provision defines Hindus as people who practice the Sikh, Jain, or Buddhist religions, and Hindu institutions are also defined accordingly.
 
 
 
• People of the Sikh faith who wear and carry the kirpan are considered to be practicing the Sikh religion.

**Article 40:**

 
• Article 40 of the Indian constitution deals with the organization of the village panchayat.
 
• It states that
 
 
• The State shall take steps to organize village panchayats.
 
• It also endows them with such powers and authority that will enable them to function as units of self-government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 20 of the Constitution of India deals with the protection of certain rights in case of conviction for offenses.**
 
• It provides safeguards for persons who have been accused of committing a crime and are facing trial or have been convicted.
 
• The article consists of three clauses, which are:
 
 
• **Protection against ex-post facto laws: **This clause prohibits the government from passing any law that punishes a person for an act that was not an offense when it was committed.
 
• In other words, a person cannot be punished for an act that was legal at the time it was committed but later became an offense.
 
• **Protection against double jeopardy: **This clause states that no person can be prosecuted or punished for the same offense more than once.
 
• **Protection against self-incrimination:** This clause provides that no person accused of an offense shall be compelled to be a witness against himself/herself.
 
 
 
• These three clauses are fundamental protections for the rights of the accused, and they are intended to ensure that individuals are not subjected to unjust or arbitrary treatment by the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ** The protection of life and personal liberty is guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India**.

 
 
• **This article states that "No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law."**
 
• The Supreme Court of India has interpreted this article in a broad and expansive manner to include within its ambit a wide range of rights and freedoms, such as the right to privacy, the right to live with dignity, and the right to a fair trial.
 
• The protection of life and personal liberty is considered to be one of the most fundamental and important rights guaranteed by the Constitution, and it is an essential component of a democratic and just society.
 
 
 
• **The abolition of untouchability is guaranteed under Article 17 of the Constitution of India.**
 
 
• This article states that **"Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden.** **The enforcement of any disability arising out of Untouchability shall be an offense punishable in accordance with the law."**
 
• The practice of untouchability, which involves the exclusion and segregation of individuals based on their caste, is considered to be a social evil and a violation of human rights.
 
• The Constitution of India recognizes the importance of abolishing untouchability and ensures that any form of discrimination or prejudice based on caste is prohibited and punishable by law.
 
 
 
• **The right to education is guaranteed under Article 21A of the Constitution of India, which was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act in 2002.**
 
• This article states that** "The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children of the age of six to fourteen years in such manner as the State may, by law, determine."**
 
• The right to education is considered to be a fundamental right and an essential component of a democratic and just society.
 
• The Constitution of India recognizes the importance of providing access to education for all children, and it places the responsibility on the State to ensure that every child between the ages of six and fourteen has access to free and compulsory education.

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

• ** Article 51A (a) of the Constitution of India states** that it is the** fundamental duty of every citizen of India to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the national flag, and the national anthem.**
 
• This duty is considered an important aspect of **citizenship in India and reflects the commitment of citizens towards the values and principles enshrined in the Constitution.**
 
• It is the responsibility of every citizen to uphold the **democratic principles, protect the sovereignty of the country, and promote national unity and integrity.​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__** 

 
• **Secularism in a constitution** refers to the principle that the state and its institutions are separate from religion, and that the state does not favor or promote any particular religion or religious beliefs.

 
 
• This means that the state is neutral in matters of religion, and individuals are free to practice their own religion without interference or discrimination from the state.
 
 
• Many countries around the world have included secularism in their constitutions.
 
• For example, the I**ndian Constitution, which was adopted in 1950, enshrines secularism as a fundamental principle. Article 25 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practice, and propagate religion subject to public order, morality and health.**
 
 
 
 
 
• **​Socialism is an economic and political ideology** that emphasizes collective or state ownership and control of the means of **production, distribution, and exchange, as well as the goal of achieving greater economic equality and social justice.**
 
• **Democracy** is a system of government where the power is held by the people, either directly or through elected representatives. It is derived from the Greek words **"demos," meaning "people," and "kratos," meaning "rule."**
 
 
• In a **democratic society, citizens **have the right to participate in the **political process, such as voting in elections, expressing their opinions, and holding their elected officials accountable.**
 
• Democracy values the principles of** freedom, equality, and justice**. It promotes individual rights and freedoms, and allows for the peaceful resolution of conflicts through open and fair dialogue.
 
• While democracy is often associated with** Western countries**, there are various forms of democratic systems in different regions of the world, such as parliamentary, presidential, and constitutional democracies.

question: Fundamental duties were not placed in Part III of the Indian Constitution because Part III is ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Justiciable**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Fundamental Duties of Indian citizens were **not part of the original Constitution**. These were introduced later by the **42nd Amendment Act in 1976**, based on the recommendations of the** Swaran Singh Committee**. The duties are listed in **Part IVA (Article 51A)** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Fundamental Duties, as per the Indian Constitution, have been established to promote a sense of respect and responsibility amongst citizens. Importantly, these **duties are non-justiciable**—they cannot be enforced through legal proceedings. This is in stark contrast with Fundamental Rights, which are enforceable in nature.
 
• The Fundamental Duties covered under **Article 51A are ten in number** and they were later expanded to **eleven by the 86th Amendment in 2002.**
 
• The Fundamental Rights, outlined in Part III of the constitution from **Article 12 to 35**, are integral to the Indian Constitution. Drafted by Dr. Ambedkar and the other framers of the Constitution, these rights were derived from the **US Bill of Rights, the Irish Constitution, and various other sources**. These rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced through the courts. If a person feels their Fundamental Rights have been violated, they can directly approach the Supreme Court or High Courts for enforcement or protection of such rights, according to **Article 32 and Article 226** of the Constitution respectively.
 
• Fundamental Duties were not included in this part to maintain a clear demarcation between the rights that are **enforceable by law (such as the fundamental rights) and moral obligations or responsibilities (such as the fundamental duties)** that are not legally enforceable.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__****Fundamental Duties (Part IVA: Article 51A):**

 
 

 Duty
 Description
 
 
 
 

 1
 To abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem
 
 

 2
 To cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
 
 

 3
 To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India
 
 

 4
 To defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so
 
 

 5
 To promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India and to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
 
 

 6
 To value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
 
 

 7
 To protect and improve the natural environment
 
 

 8
 To foster the scientific temper, humanism, and the spirit of inquiry and reform
 
 

 9
 To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
 
 

 10
 To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity
 
 

 11 (added by 86th Amendment, 2002)
 Parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their child/ward between the ages of 6 and 14 years

• This addition was based on the recommendations of the** Swaran Singh Committee.**
 
• The committee, chaired by Swaran Singh, was tasked with **studying the feasibility of including Fundamental Duties.**

• **Santhanam Committee:**
 
 
• The Santhanam Committee, officially known as the** Committee on Prevention of Corruption, was established in 1962.**
 
• It aimed to examine measures to **combat corruption in various government departments and organizations.**

__
 
• **Right to vote:-**

 
 
• The right to vote in India is guaranteed by the Constitution and the Representation of the People Act, 1951, subject to certain limitations.
 
• Every citizen over the age of 18 has the right to vote under Article 326 of the Constitution.
 
• **The Right to vote in India is a Constitutional Right but not a fundamental right.**
 
• The 61st Amendment of the Constitution lowered the voting age of elections to the Lok Sabha and to the Legislative Assemblies from 21 to 18 years which was done by amending Article 326 of the Constitution.
 
• Article 326 of the Constitution guarantees universal adult suffrage but does not mention the right to vote.
 
• In India, voting is a legal right guaranteed by the Representation of People Act, 1950.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• ** The Right to Equality:-**

 
 
• It is one of the six fundamental rights of the Constitution. 
 
• It is contained in the Indian Constitution from Article 14 to 18. 
 
• Following are the provisions under the Right to Equality- 
 
 
• Article 14- ;equality before the law as well as equal protection of the law to all people.
 
• Article 15- prohibits discrimination on the grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth, and also gender or any of them. 
 
• Article 16- guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
 
• Article 17- Abolition of untouchability. 
 
• Article 18- Abolition of all titles except military and academic.
 
 
 
 
 
• Right to freedom of religion:-
 
 
• India is one of the most diverse nations in terms of religion.
 
• Freedom of religion in India is a fundamental right guaranteed by Article 25-28 of the Constitution of India.

question: The State of Kerala Vs Leesamma Joseph case deals with ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**persons with disabilities.**__ 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ** State of Kerala Vs Leesamma Joseph:-**

 
 
• The Supreme Court of India in its judgment on 28 June 2021 in the case of "State of Kerala vs Leesamma Joseph" affirmed that persons with disabilities have a right to reservation in promotion under Article 16(4) of the Constitution of India, 1950.
 
• While examining the constitutionality of Section 33 of the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, the Court noted that 'equality of opportunity' in matters of public employment includes provision of certain reservations in favour of persons with disabilities.
 
• Furthermore, it held that Article 16(4) of the Constitution, empowering the State to make provisions for reservation in matters of promotion in favour of any backward class of citizens, also includes persons with disabilities within its scope, regardless of the nature of their establishments, whether they belong to the public sector or the private sector.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (RPDA):

 
 
• This is the principal legislation that protects the rights of individuals with disabilities in India.
 
• It replaces and strengthens the Persons with Disabilities Act, 1995.
 
• The RPDA complies with the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, to which India is a signatory.
 
• The Act expands the list of recognized disabilities from 7 to 21, and mandates the central and state governments to take measures to ensure that persons with disabilities fully enjoy all human rights and fundamental freedoms.

question: Which of the following committees recommended for the inclusion of fundamental duties in the Constitution of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Swaran Singh Committee.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Swaran Singh Committee** was established in **1976** under the leadership of Sardar Swaran Singh, an Indian Politician.
 
• The committee was specifically constituted to study and suggest changes to the Constitution in relation to the concept of** fundamental duties**. It was the Swaran Singh Committee that suggested adding** a new part outlining citizen duties.**
 
• As a result of this committee's recommendations, **the 42nd Amendment to the Constitution in 1976** included the new** Part IVA, **which specified the fundamental duties of Indian citizens. It comprises **Article 51A from (a) to (k).**
 
• The fundamental duties include tenets like respect for the **national flag, the constitution, and institutions, promoting brotherhood, protecting the environment, and upholding scientific temper among others.**
 
• The primary aim behind the inclusion of the Fundamental Duties by this committee was to create a** balance of rights and duties** in the constitution, obliging citizens to act responsibly and assist in maintaining the spirit of democracy in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sarkaria Commission:**

 
 
• The Sarkaria Commission was established in 1983 by the central government of India.
 
• The Commission was set up to examine the relationship and balance of power between state and central governments in the country and suggest changes within the framework of the Constitution.
 
• It made 247 recommendations to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, and balance between the various levels of government in India.
 
• The report of the Sarkaria Commission is the first and the most comprehensive attempt to review Centre-State relationship.
 
 
 
• **Rajamannar Committee:**
 
 
• The Rajamannar Committee was constituted by the government of Tamil Nadu in 1969.
 
• Its task was to examine the entire question concerning state autonomy and the Centre-State relations.
 
• The committee recommended a drastic overhaul of India’s federal system, with suggestions for the constitution to emerge as a truly federal one rather than quasi-federal.
 
• The need for such changes arose because of the contention that centralization of power diminishes the effectiveness of regional governments.
 
 
 
• **Balwant Rai Mehta Committee:**
 
 
• The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee was a committee appointed by the Government of India in 1957.
 
• The aim of this Committee was to examine the working of the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953) and to suggest measures for their better working.
 
• Significantly, their recommendations led to the birth of Panchayati Raj Institutions in India, outlining a three-tier system, including village, block, and district levels.
 
• The report of the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee is considered a landmark in the evolution of local self-government (Panchayati Raj) institutions in India.

question: Part 3 of the Indian Constitution enlists how many groups of Fundamental Rights?

• The idea of fundamental rights was borrowed from the constitution of The USA.

• Part III of the Constitution is described as the* Magna Carta* of India.
 
• ‘Magna Carta’, the Charter of Rights issued by King John of England in 1215 was the first written document relating to the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
 
• The Constitution of India has 6 Fundamental rights
 
 
• Right to equality (Art 14 to Art 18)
 
• Right to Freedom {Art 19 to Art 22)
 
• Right against Exploitation (Art 23 and Art 24 )
 
• Right to Freedom of Religion (Art 25 to Art 28)
 
• Cultural and Educational Rights (Art 29 to Art 30)
 
• Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32)

• Right to property (Art 31) which was a fundamental right originally was removed from the fundamental rights by the 44th amendment,1978 and was declared a legal right under art 300-A
 
• The Part III of the constitution is termed as the *Magna Carta* of India.
 
• Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art 32) is considered the heart and soul of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• Article 16 – Equality of opportunity in relation to public employment.
 
• Article 17 – Abolish Untouchability.
 
• Article 18 – Elimination of titles.
 
 
 
• Article (19-22) – Right to Freedom
 
 
• Article 19 – Protection of certain rights in relation to the freedom of speech, expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession.
 
• Article 20 – Protection in respect of conviction for offences.
 
• Article 21 – The Safety of Life and Personal Liberty.
 
• Article 21A – Right to Education.
 
• Article 22 – In some cases security against detention.
 
 
 
• Article (23-24) – Rights against exploitation
 
 
• Article 23 – Prevention of Trafficking of humans and forced labour.
 
• Article 24 – Prevention of employment of children in factories, etc.
 
 
 
• Article (25-28) – Right to freedom of religion
 
 
• Article 25 – freedom of condolences and promotion of free professional, practice, and secularism.
 
• Article 26 – Freedom of managing trustworthy matters.
 
• Article 27 – Freedom to pay taxes for the promotion of any particular religion.
 
• Article 28 – Freedom in the form of independent instruction in independent education.
 
 
 
• Articles (29-30) – Culture and Education Rights
 
 
• Article 29 – Protection of Minority Interests
 
• Article 30 – Right to Minorities and to establish and administer the educational Institutions.
 
• Article 31 – The overall acquisition of the property (Now it is not a fundamental right)

question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about the Directive Principles of State Policy?

options.text: They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic.
These have moral and political sanctions.
They aim at establishing social and economic democracy in the country.
They are positive, as they require the State to do certain things.

solution:
The correct answer is __**They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Directive Principles of State Policy of India are the guidelines or principles given to the institutes for governing India and are provided in Part IV of the Constitution of India.
 
• Directive Principles of State Policy aim to create social and economic conditions under which the citizens can lead a good life.
 
• They also aim to establish social and economic democracy through a welfare state. Directive principles are classified under the following categories; economic, socialistic, political, executive, justice and legal, administrative, environmental, protection of monuments, peace, and security.

Hence, it can be said that the Directive Principles of State Policy are fundamental for the Governance of the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Features of DPSPs

 
 
• The phrase ‘Directive Principles of State Policy’ denotes the ideals that the State should keep in mind while formulating policies and enacting laws.
 
• These are the constitutional instructions or recommendations to the State in legislative, executive, and administrative matters. According to Article 36, the term ‘State’ in Part IV has the same meaning as in Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights.
 
• Therefore, it includes the legislative and executive organs of the central and state governments, all local authorities, and all other public authorities in the country.
 
• The Directive Principles resemble the ‘Instrument of Instructions’ enumerated in the Government of India Act of 1935.
 
• In the words of Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, ‘the Directive Principles are like the instrument of instructions, which were issued to the Governor-General and to the Governors of the colonies of India by the British Government under the Government of India Act of 1935. What is called Directive Principles is merely another name for the instrument of instruction. The only difference is that they are instructions to the legislature and the executive’.
 
• The Directive Principles constitute a very comprehensive economic, social and political program for a modern democratic State.
 
• They aim at realizing the high ideals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity as outlined in the Preamble to the Constitution.
 
• They embody the concept of a ‘welfare state’ and not that of a ‘police state’, which existed during the colonial era3. In brief, they seek to establish economic and social democracy in the country.
 
• The Directive Principles are non-justiciable in nature, that is, they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.
 
• Therefore, the government (Central, state, and local) cannot be compelled to implement them.
 
• Nevertheless, the Constitution (Article 37) itself says that these principles are fundamental in the governance of the country and it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
 
• The Directive Principles, though nonjusticiable in nature, help the courts in examining and determining the constitutional validity of a law.
 
• The Supreme Court has ruled many times that in determining the constitutionality of any law if a court finds that the law in question seeks to give effect to a Directive Principle, it may consider such law to be ‘reasonable’ in relation to Article 14 (equality before law) or Article 19 (six freedoms) and thus save such law from unconstitutionality.

question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution contains Fundamental Duties?

__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **Key Points: __**In the Constitution of India, fundamental duties are mentioned in Article 51A.

 
• There was no list of fundamental duties in the original constitution.
 
• Fundamental duties were added into the Indian constitution by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act 1976.
 
• the 42nd constitutional amendment added Part IV A and Article 51A to the Indian constitution.
 
• Fundamental duties were added to the Indian constitution on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• Initially, there were only 10 fundamental duties in the constitution.
 
• The 86th **Constitutional Amendment** Act 2002 added one more fundamental duty to the constitution.
 
• Currently, there are 11 fundamental duties in the Indian constitution.
 
• The idea of fundamental duties was borrowed from the Russian constitution.
 
• Fundamental duties are non-justiciable in nature.

The 11 Fundamental Duties listed are:

 
• Respect the National Flag, National Anthem, and the Indian Constitution's principles and institutions.
 
• Uphold and uphold the lofty principles that motivated the nation's fight for freedom.
 
• Uphold and defend India's sovereignty, unification, and integrity.
 
• Defend the nation and perform national service as required.
 
• Promote harmony and a feeling of shared brotherhood among all Indians, notwithstanding differences in religion, language, location, or section, and condemn behaviours that are demeaning to women's dignity.
 
• Appreciate and safeguard the rich cultural history of the nation as a whole.
 
• Maintaining a healthy ecosystem, including woods, lakes, rivers, and wildlife, as well as showing compassion for all living things.
 
• Foster a humanistic outlook, a scientific mindset, and a spirit of reformation
 
• Protect public property and abstain from violence
 
• Strive for excellence in all areas of personal and group endeavour so that the country continually reaches greater heights of endeavour and success.
 
• Give his kid or ward between the ages of six and fourteen the opportunity to pursue an education. The 86th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2002 added this duty.

question: Which of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty of the Indian citizens?

options.text: To develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform.
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence.
To cherish and follow the noble ideas that inspired our national struggle for freedom.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Mandatory national service of 5 years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Fundamental Duties were incorporated in the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
 
• These duties are specified in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They are a set of 11 duties that are expected to be performed by the citizens of India.
 
• Mandatory national service of 5 years is not included among these Fundamental Duties.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties**

 
 
• The Fundamental Duties are moral obligations that are intended to promote a sense of discipline and commitment among the citizens of India.
 
• These duties are modeled on the Soviet Constitution and are aimed at upholding the spirit of patriotism and unity.
 
• Some of the key Fundamental Duties include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, protecting the environment, and safeguarding public property.
 
• Though not enforceable by law, these duties serve as a constant reminder to the citizens of their responsibilities towards the nation.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**
 
 
• This amendment is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" because it brought about wide-ranging changes to the Constitution.
 
• It introduced the Fundamental Duties and made several other significant changes, including the addition of the words "Socialist" and "Secular" to the Preamble.
 
• The amendment also extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from five to six years.
 
• It strengthened the role of the central government by curtailing the powers of the judiciary and state governments.
 
 
 
• **Part IVA of the Indian Constitution**
 
 
• Part IVA was added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, and contains only one Article - Article 51A.
 
• Article 51A specifies the Fundamental Duties of every citizen of India.
 
• It lists 11 duties, including cherishing the noble ideals of freedom struggle, promoting scientific temper, and protecting the natural environment.
 
• These duties highlight the importance of active citizenship and collective responsibility in the democratic framework of India.

question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides that the State must secure a social order to promote the welfare of people?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 38**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 38** of the Indian Constitution is part of the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP).
 
• This article directs the State to secure a social order for the promotion of the welfare of the people.
 
• It emphasizes minimizing inequalities in income and endeavoring to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities, and opportunities.
 
• Article 38 has two clauses: Clause (1) and Clause (2), which specifically mention the State's responsibility in social and economic spheres.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**

 
 
• The DPSP are guidelines or principles given to the federal institutes governing the state of India, to be kept in citation while framing laws and policies.
 
• These are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable by the courts for their violation.
 
• They are mentioned in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Article 37**
 
 
• It states that the provisions contained in the DPSP shall not be enforceable by any court.
 
• It emphasizes that the principles laid down are fundamental in the governance of the country.
 
 
 
• **Article 39**
 
 
• It directs the State to ensure that the citizens, men and women equally, have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.
 
• It also covers principles for resource distribution, operation of the economic system, health and strength of workers, children, and youth, and equal pay for equal work for both men and women.
 
 
 
• **Article 36**
 
 
• This article defines the term "State" in the context of DPSP.
 
• It includes the Government and Parliament of India, the Government and Legislature of each of the States, and all other local or other authorities within the territory of India or under the control of the Government of India.

question: Which Article in the fundamental duty applies, when a construction worker takes his 8-year son to the site rather than sending him to school?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 51A (k)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 51A (k) of the Constitution of India** specifies that it is a fundamental duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to their child or ward between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
 
• This duty is in line with the objective of the Right to Education Act, which mandates free and compulsory education for children in this age group.
 
• Ensuring that children go to school instead of being involved in child labor is essential for their overall development and future prospects.
 
• Violation of this duty, such as taking a child to a construction site instead of school, can lead to legal consequences and hinder the child's right to education.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties**

 
 
• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations specified in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976, based on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• These duties emphasize the importance of citizen participation in national development and the upholding of constitutional values.
 
 
 
• **Right to Education Act (RTE)**
 
 
• The Right to Education Act was enacted in 2009 to provide free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• It is a fundamental right under Article 21A of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The Act ensures that children have access to quality education without discrimination and establishes norms for school infrastructure, teacher-student ratio, and curriculum.
 
 
 
• **Child Labor**
 
 
• Child labor refers to the employment of children in a manner that deprives them of their childhood, education, or is harmful to their health and development.
 
• The Child Labor (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, and its amendments prohibit the employment of children below 14 years in hazardous occupations and processes.
 
• Efforts to eliminate child labor involve providing education and support to families to ensure children attend school instead of engaging in work.
 
 

This source code provides a detailed solution to the question regarding the fundamental duty applicable when a construction worker takes his 8-year-old son to the site instead of sending him to school. The key points highlight the importance and implications of Article 51A (k), while the additional information section provides context on related topics such as Fundamental Duties, the Right to Education Act, and child labor

question: Which fundamental duty applies on you when you see a few school students, on their educational trip to Humayun’s tomb, writing their names on the walls?

options.text: To defend the country and render national service
To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
To protect and improve the natural environment

solution:
The correct answer is __**To safeguard public property**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The fundamental duty of safeguarding public property is enshrined in Article 51A of the Indian Constitution.
 
• This duty emphasizes the importance of protecting and preserving public assets such as monuments, buildings, and other government properties.
 
• By writing their names on the walls of Humayun's tomb, the students are defacing a historical monument, which is considered public property.
 
• Citizens are expected to prevent such actions and also report any damage to public property to the authorities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties**

 
 
• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations specified in the Indian Constitution that are expected to be followed by citizens.
 
• These duties were added by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, on the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.
 
• There are 11 Fundamental Duties listed under Article 51A of the Constitution.
 
• These duties serve as a constant reminder to citizens to uphold the spirit of patriotism and to protect the unity of India.
 
 
 
• **Humayun's Tomb**
 
 
• Humayun's Tomb is a UNESCO World Heritage Site located in Delhi, India.
 
• It was commissioned by Humayun's first wife, Empress Bega Begum, in 1565 AD.

• Vandalism and damage to public property not only diminish their aesthetic and historical value but also result in financial loss.
 
• Protecting public property ensures that future generations can also learn from and appreciate these important assets.

question: Part IV A of the Indian Constitution was inserted in the Indian Constitution through __________ Constitutional Amendment Act.
solution:
The correct answer is __**42nd Constitutional Amendment Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The 42nd Amendment Act, also known as the **Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act, 1976**, was enacted during the Emergency period in India.
 
• It is considered one of the most comprehensive amendments to the Indian Constitution and was brought in by the **Indira Gandhi government**.
 
• This amendment made significant changes to the Constitution, including the insertion of Part IV A, which deals with the **Fundamental Duties** of the citizens.
 
• The 42nd Amendment also attempted to reduce the power of the judiciary and increase the power of the Parliament.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part IV A (Fundamental Duties)**

 
 
• Part IV A was added to the Constitution of India by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976.
 
• It consists of **Article 51A** which enumerates the Fundamental Duties of the citizens of India.
 
• These duties are inspired by the Constitution of the former Soviet Union and aim to remind the citizens of their moral obligations towards the nation.
 
• There are currently **11 Fundamental Duties** listed in Article 51A.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**
 
 
• Known as a "mini-Constitution" due to its wide-ranging amendments.
 
• It made extensive changes to the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, and the structure of the executive and judiciary.
 
• This amendment curtailed the power of the judiciary and strengthened the central government.
 
• Many of the provisions of this amendment were later undone by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978.
 
 
 
• **Emergency Period**
 
 
• The Emergency in India was declared by President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed upon the advice of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi from 1975 to 1977.
 
• This period is considered one of the most controversial times in Indian political history, marked by the suspension of elections and civil liberties.
 
• The 42nd Amendment was passed during this period, and it significantly altered the balance of power between the executive, legislature, and judiciary.

question: Which of the following Articles of the Indian Constitution CANNOT be suspended even during an emergency declared on the grounds of war or external aggression?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Articles 20 and 21**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 20** of the Indian Constitution deals with the protection of certain rights in the case of conviction for offenses. It prohibits ex-post-facto laws, double jeopardy, and self-incrimination.
 
• **Article 21** guarantees the right to life and personal liberty. It states that no person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law.
 
• Both Articles 20 and 21 are fundamental rights under Part III of the Indian Constitution and remain enforceable during times of emergency.
 
• Under Article 359 of the Constitution, the President can suspend the right to move any court for the enforcement of other fundamental rights during an emergency, but Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 15 and 17**:

 
 
• Article 15 prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth.
 
• Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.
 
• These articles can be suspended during an emergency.
 
 
 
• **Article 14 and 16**:
 
 
• Article 14 ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within India.
 
• Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in matters of public employment.
 
• These articles can also be suspended during an emergency.
 
 
 
• **Article 30 and 32**:
 
 
• Article 30 provides rights of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
 
• Article 32 provides the right to constitutional remedies for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• These articles can also be suspended during an emergency.

question: Which Article in the fundamental duty is invoked when you see in a private party that the Indian flag has been used as a covering for the speaker's desk?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 51A (a)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Article 51A (a) of the Indian Constitution lays down the fundamental duty of every citizen to respect the national symbols, including the National Flag.

• It states that it is the duty of every citizen of India "to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem".

• The use of the Indian Flag as a covering for a speaker's desk at a private party is a violation of this fundamental duty.

• Respecting the National Flag is a manifestation of respect for the nation itself and its values and ideals.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Fundamental Duties**

• The Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations enumerated in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Indian Constitution.

• They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976 upon the recommendations of the Swaran Singh Committee.

• Initially, there were ten duties, but an eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment in 2002.

• These duties are intended to serve as a constant reminder to every citizen that while enjoying their rights, they have to be conscious of their duties towards the nation.

• **National Flag Code of India**

• The Flag Code of India, 2002, brings together all laws, conventions, practices, and instructions for the display of the National Flag.

• It governs the usage, hoisting, and display of the Indian Flag to ensure respect and dignity towards the national symbol.

• As per the code, the flag cannot be used for decoration or as a covering in any form.

• Violations of the Flag Code can result in legal consequences under the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971.

• **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971**

• This Act prohibits any form of disrespect or insult to the Indian National Flag, the Constitution, the National Anthem, and the National Symbols.

• Disrespect includes acts such as burning, mutilating, defacing, or showing any contempt towards the flag or national symbols.

• Offenders can face imprisonment up to three years, or a fine, or both.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The fundamental duty to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood amongst all the people of India transcending religious, linguistic, regional, or sectional diversities is crucial in maintaining unity in diversity.
 
• This duty highlights the importance of respecting and tolerating different beliefs and practices within the country.
 
• It encourages citizens to rise above narrow considerations of caste, creed, and religion and to work towards the welfare of society as a whole.
 
• Promoting harmony and brotherhood is essential for fostering an environment where different communities can coexist peacefully and contribute to national development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties:**

 
 
• Fundamental Duties are a set of moral obligations that all citizens are expected to follow and respect.
 
• These duties were added to the Indian Constitution by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, under Article 51A.
 
• Initially, there were ten fundamental duties, and later, an eleventh duty was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
 
• Although these duties are non-justiciable, meaning they are not legally enforceable, they serve as a constant reminder of the responsibilities that come with citizenship.
 
 
 
• **Promoting Harmony and Brotherhood:**

question: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT regarding Fundamental Rights?

options.text: Fundamental Rights can be enforced by Law.
Fundamental rights are derived from the Britain Constitution.
The Fundamental Rights are mentioned in constitution from article 12 to 35.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Fundamental rights are derived from the Britain Constitution.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution, from Article 12 to 35.
 
• These rights are essential for the overall development of individuals and the preservation of human dignity.
 
• Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty.
 
• Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning they can be enforced through the courts of law in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**

 
 
• Fundamental Rights are the basic human rights guaranteed to all individuals by the Constitution of India. These rights are crucial for the protection and development of individuals.
 
• They are meant to promote the ideal of political democracy and prevent the arbitrary use of power by the state.
 
• Some of the key Fundamental Rights include the Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), and the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32).
 
• These rights are enforceable by the courts, and individuals can approach the judiciary to seek protection and enforcement of their Fundamental Rights.
 
 
 
• **Enforcement of Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights are justiciable, meaning individuals can approach the courts to enforce these rights if they are violated.
 
• The Supreme Court and High Courts have the power to issue writs for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• Writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari are used to enforce these rights.
 
 
 
• **Right to Life (Article 21)**
 
 
• Article 21 of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty.
 
• This article ensures that no person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to the procedure established by law.
 
• The Right to Life under Article 21 has been interpreted by the Supreme Court to include various rights such as the right to live with human dignity, right to livelihood, right to health, right to education, and more.
