question: Which of the following is true about Fundamental Rights and DPSPs?

options.text: Both are justiciable and enforceable by courts
DPSPs override Fundamental Rights when in conflict
Fundamental Rights are justiciable, but DPSPs are not
DPSPs are guaranteed by the Constitution;Fundamental Rights are optional

solution:
The Correct answer is __**Fundamental Rights are justiciable, but DPSPs are not**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Rights** are explicitly mentioned in Part III of the **Indian Constitution**.
 
• They are enforceable by the courts, meaning individuals can approach the courts if their rights are violated. This makes them **justiciable**.
 
• The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs)**, enshrined in Part IV of the Constitution, are not enforceable by the courts, making them **non-justiciable**.
 
• DPSPs act as guidelines for the government to achieve socio-economic goals and establish a welfare state.
 
• While **Fundamental Rights** focus on individual rights and liberties, DPSPs emphasize **collective welfare** and societal development.
 
• The **Supreme Court of India** has clarified that Fundamental Rights and DPSPs must be harmonized and not seen as conflicting entities.
 
• Examples of Fundamental Rights include the **Right to Equality** (Article 14-18) and the **Right to Freedom** (Article 19-22).
 
• Examples of DPSPs include the directive to promote **equal justice** and free legal aid (Article 39A) and to ensure **living wages** for workers (Article 43).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Both are justiciable and enforceable by courts**__

 __
 
• This option is incorrect because **only Fundamental Rights** are enforceable by courts, while DPSPs are not.
 
• DPSPs serve as principles for governance and cannot be legally upheld in courts.
 
 
 
• **DPSPs override Fundamental Rights when in conflict**__
 __
 
• The **Supreme Court** has ruled that Fundamental Rights hold a higher position in cases of conflict.
 
• However, efforts have been made to harmonize both, recognizing their complementary nature.
 
 
 
• **DPSPs are guaranteed by the Constitution; Fundamental Rights are optional**__
 
 
• This is incorrect as both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are integral parts of the Constitution.
 
• Fundamental Rights are guaranteed and enforceable, while DPSPs are guidelines that cannot be enforced legally.

question: The concept of Uniform Civil Code is a part of which category of principles in the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Directive Principles of State Policy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The concept of the **Uniform Civil Code (UCC)** is enshrined in Article 44 of the Indian Constitution under the **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**.
 
• Article 44 directs the State to strive to secure a UCC for all citizens throughout the territory of India to ensure **uniformity in personal laws**.
 
• The UCC aims to replace personal laws based on the scriptures and customs of each major religious community in India with a common set governing every citizen.
 
• The DPSPs, including the provision for UCC, are **non-justiciable in nature**, meaning they are not enforceable by the courts but aim to guide the State in policymaking.
 
• The objective of the UCC is to promote **national integration and gender equality** by ensuring that personal laws do not discriminate based on religion or gender.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Indian Constitution (Articles 12-35) and are enforceable by the courts.
 
• They guarantee individual rights such as the right to equality, freedom, and protection against exploitation, and ensure cultural and educational rights for minorities.
 
• Although Fundamental Rights are enforceable, the Uniform Civil Code is not part of this category as it is non-justiciable and falls under DPSPs.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Duties**
 
 
• Fundamental Duties are incorporated in Part IV-A (Article 51A) of the Constitution and were added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
 
• They outline the moral obligations of citizens, such as respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, safeguarding public property, and protecting the environment.
 
• The UCC is not part of Fundamental Duties as it pertains to State policy and not individual duties.
 
 
 
• **Preamble Objectives**
 
 
• The Preamble serves as the introduction to the Constitution, outlining the guiding principles and objectives of the Indian State such as justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity.
 
• While the Preamble reflects the ideals of the Constitution, it is not enforceable and does not directly mention the UCC.
 
 
 
• **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)**
 
 
• DPSPs are enshrined in Part IV (Articles 36-51) of the Indian Constitution and are aimed at achieving socio-economic justice and welfare.
 
• These principles guide the State in formulating policies that ensure the socio-economic and political welfare of the citizens.
 
• While not enforceable, they are fundamental in the governance of the country and aim to create a welfare state.

question: Which of the following was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Right to Property**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Right to Property** was originally a Fundamental Right under Article 31 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights through the **44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978**, and moved to the category of legal rights under Article 300A.
 
• The amendment was implemented to curb the misuse of property rights and facilitate equitable land reforms, ensuring that the state could acquire private property for public purposes by providing compensation.
 
• As a legal right, the Right to Property is enforceable through the courts, but it no longer enjoys the same elevated status and protection as Fundamental Rights.
 
• Currently, Article 300A states: **"No person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Right to Equality** (Article 14-18)

 
 
• It ensures equality before the law and equal protection of laws for all citizens.
 
• Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth (Article 15).
 
• Abolishes untouchability (Article 17) and titles except for military or academic distinctions (Article 18).
 
 
 
• **Right to Freedom** (Article 19-22)
 
 
• Guarantees six essential freedoms, including freedom of speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession (Article 19).
 
• Protects against arbitrary arrest and detention (Article 22).
 
• However, these rights are subject to reasonable restrictions for maintaining public order, sovereignty, and security.
 
 
 
• **Right against Exploitation** (Article 23-24)
 
 
• Prohibits human trafficking, forced labor, and other forms of exploitation (Article 23).
 
• Prohibits the employment of children below the age of 14 in hazardous jobs or industries (Article 24).
 
 
 
• **Theme of the Question: Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III of the Constitution, from Articles 12 to 35, and are considered essential for the development of individuals and democracy.
 
• These rights include the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and Right to Constitutional Remedies.
 
• They are justiciable, meaning citizens can approach courts if these rights are violated.

question:
**Fill in the Blank: **

Doctrine of Severability allows the _____ part of a law to be retained.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Valid**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Doctrine of Severability refers to the ability of the judiciary to separate the **valid portions of a law** from the invalid or unconstitutional ones.
 
• It is enshrined in Article 13 of the Indian Constitution, which ensures that any law inconsistent with or violating Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of its inconsistency.
 
• Under this doctrine, only the unconstitutional or invalid parts of a legislation are struck down, while the valid parts remain enforceable.
 
• The doctrine ensures that the entire law is not invalidated but retains the **valid and constitutional provisions**.
 
• This principle is applied to protect the legislative intent and preserve the valid portions of the law wherever possible, ensuring a balance between judicial review and legislative sovereignty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Repealed:**

 
 
• When a law is repealed, it is formally revoked or annulled, either partially or fully, by legislative authority.
 
• Repealing a law completely removes its legal enforceability and existence.
 
• This is different from severability, where only the unconstitutional parts are struck down, and the rest of the law remains intact.
 
 
 
• **Inconsistent:**
 
 
• The term "inconsistent" refers to provisions in a law that conflict with or violate the Constitution, particularly Fundamental Rights.
 
• As per Article 13 of the Indian Constitution, laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are declared void to the extent of their inconsistency.
 
• However, inconsistent provisions are not retained under the Doctrine of Severability; only valid ones are upheld.
 
 
 
• **Unconstitutional:**
 
 
• Any law, policy, or action that contravenes the provisions of the Constitution is deemed unconstitutional.
 
• Unconstitutional laws are struck down by courts during judicial review. The Doctrine of Severability ensures that only unconstitutional parts of a law are invalidated, preserving the valid portions.

question: Through which Constitutional Amendment was Article 21A introduced, mandating free and compulsory education as a Fundamental Right for children between 6 and 14 years of age?
solution:
The correct answer is __**86th Amendment Act**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002**, inserted **Article 21A** into the Indian Constitution, making education a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• This amendment also brought changes to Article 45, which now directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years of age.
 
• Additionally, it added Clause (k) to Article 51A, which made it a Fundamental Duty of parents or guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children between the ages of 6 and 14 years.
 
• The 86th Amendment Act paved the way for the **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009**, commonly known as the RTE Act, which operationalized Article 21A.
 
• This historic amendment was a milestone in India's efforts to achieve universal primary education and combat illiteracy among children.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **42nd Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Enacted in 1976, it is also known as the "Mini-Constitution" of India due to the extensive changes it brought to the Constitution.
 
• It made India a "socialist", "secular", and "integrity" State by amending the Preamble.
 
• Transferred subjects like Education, Forests, and Protection of Wild Animals and Birds from the State List to the Concurrent List.
 
• Strengthened the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSPs) and inserted provisions like Article 48A (environment protection) and Article 43A (worker participation in industries).
 
 
 
• **93rd Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Enacted in 2005, it inserted Clause (5) to Article 15, enabling the State to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes (SCs), and Scheduled Tribes (STs).
 
• This amendment allowed for the reservation of seats in educational institutions, including private unaided institutions, except for minority institutions under Article 30(1).
 
• It laid the foundation for the implementation of the 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) in central educational institutions.
 
 
 
• **44th Amendment Act:**
 
 
• Enacted in 1978, it reversed some provisions of the controversial 42nd Amendment Act.
 
• It restored the right to property as a legal right under Article 300A, removing it from the list of Fundamental Rights.
 
• It ensured that Articles 20 and 21, dealing with protection in respect of conviction for offenses and the right to life and personal liberty, could not be suspended even during an emergency.

question: The concept of "**Reasonable Classification**" as a limitation to the Right to Equality (Article 14) was established in which case?

options.text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Golakhnath Case v. State of Punjab & Anrs.

solution:
The correct answer is __**State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The concept of "Reasonable Classification" as a limitation to the Right to Equality under Article 14 of the Indian Constitution was established in the **State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar case (1952).**
 
• In this landmark case, the Supreme Court declared that Article 14 prohibits class legislation but allows reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia and a rational nexus to the object sought to be achieved.
 
• The court invalidated the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, as it failed the test of reasonable classification since it gave unfettered power to the government to selectively prosecute individuals without clear guidelines.
 
• This judgment laid the foundation for the doctrine of reasonable classification, which continues to guide interpretations of Article 14 in subsequent cases.
 
• The case emphasized that any classification must not be arbitrary and should be founded on substantial distinctions that justify differential treatment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973):**

 
 
• This case established the **"Basic Structure Doctrine"** of the Indian Constitution, which states that Parliament cannot amend the Constitution in a way that destroys its basic structure.
 
• It dealt with the extent of the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution under Article 368.
 
• While it did not directly relate to Article 14, it is considered one of the most important cases in Indian constitutional law.
 
 
 
• **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978):**
 
 
• This case expanded the scope of Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty) and established a close connection between Articles 14, 19, and 21.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that any law violating personal liberty must be just, fair, and reasonable, thereby upholding the principle of non-arbitrariness under Article 14.
 
• Although it reinforced the principles of equality, it did not specifically address the concept of reasonable classification.
 
 
 
• **Golakhnath v. State of Punjab (1967):**
 
 
• This case dealt with the power of Parliament to amend fundamental rights under the Constitution.
 
• The Supreme Court held that fundamental rights cannot be amended by Parliament under Article 368.
 
• While it had a significant impact on constitutional law, it did not address Article 14 or reasonable classification.

question: Which Article of the Constitution confers the right to constitutional remedies, and how is it linked to Fundamental Rights?

options.text: Article 32; it is called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution
Article 226; it is a protective mechanism for Directive Principles
Article 21; it deals with personal liberty only
Article 14; it ensures equality before law

solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 32; it is called the "heart and soul" of the Constitution**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Article 32** of the Indian Constitution provides the right to constitutional remedies, empowering individuals to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• It is referred to as the **"heart and soul"** of the Constitution by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, as it ensures the protection and enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
 
• This article gives the Supreme Court the authority to issue writs like **habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari** for the enforcement of rights.
 
• Article 32 guarantees the right to approach the highest court in case of a violation, making it a cornerstone of the Indian judiciary's role in safeguarding the Constitution.
 
• It is a fundamental part of the framework to ensure that citizens' rights are protected and upheld against arbitrary actions by the state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 226**

 
 
• Article 226 empowers the High Courts to issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights and for other purposes.
 
• It has a wider jurisdiction compared to Article 32, as it allows High Courts to address matters beyond Fundamental Rights, including statutory and legal rights.
 
• While Article 32 is limited to the Supreme Court, Article 226 provides individuals with an additional route to seek redressal at the state level.
 
 
 
• **Article 21**
 
 
• Article 21 guarantees the protection of life and personal liberty, stating that no person shall be deprived of these except according to a procedure established by law.
 
• It is one of the most expansive and interpreted articles, covering rights like the right to privacy, the right to live with dignity, and the right to a clean environment.
 
• However, it focuses specifically on personal liberty and life, not on constitutional remedies.
 
 
 
• **Article 14**
 
 
• Article 14 ensures equality before the law and equal protection of the laws within the territory of India.
 
• It prohibits discrimination by the state and upholds the principles of fairness and equal treatment in governance.
 
• While it is a critical Fundamental Right, it does not directly deal with remedies for the violation of rights.

question: In which year were the 73rd and 74th amendments passed by the Parliament?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1992**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments were passed by Parliament in December 1992.
 
• **73rd Amendment Act:**
 
 
• 73rd Amendment Act, 1992 has added a new part IX consisting of 16 Articles and the Eleventh Schedule to the Constitution.
 
• The 73rd Amendment envisages the Gram Sabha as the foundation of the Panchayat Raj System to perform functions and powers entrusted to it by the State Legislatures. 
 
• The Constitution was amended by the 73rd *Amendment **to make the three-tier of democracy* more powerful and effective.
 
• It empowered local governments rural, as constitutional entities and initiated a new chapter in the process of democratic decentralization in India. 
 
• The provisions of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, To hold regular elections under the local government bodies have been made compulsory. 
 
 
 
• 74th Amendment Act:
 
 
• Part IXA in the Constitution, which deals with Municipalities in an article **243 P to 243 ZG,** has been introduced under the 74th Amendment Act.
 
• The act provides for a five-year term of office for every municipality from the date of its first meeting.
 
• The elections to constitute a municipality shall be completed before the expiry of its duration of five years. 
 
• However, it can be dissolved before the completion of its term.
 
• If the municipality is dissolved before the expiry of its term, the elections for constituting a new municipality must be **completed within 6 months from the date of its dissolution.**
 
• A municipality constituted after its premature dissolution shall continue only for the remainder of the term.
 
• If the remainder of the period is less than 6 months it is not necessary to hold elections for the remaining period but a fresh election for the entire term is mandated.
 
• Persons who have attained the age of 21 years are eligible to contest the municipal elections i.e no person shall be disqualified if he is less than 25 years of age and has attained 21 years of age to contest in municipal elections.

__State Finance Commissions (SFCs):__

 
• The State Finance Commission (SFC) is created by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments to manage State level fiscal relations in India.

• It allocates resources to Panchayati Raj institutions at all three levels in terms of taxes, duties and levies to be collected by the state and the local bodies.

• If a Panchayat is dissolved, elections are to be held within six months from the date of dissolution.
 
• The term Panchayati Raj in India signifies the system of rural local self-government.

• This Panchayati Raj faced a major constitutional amendment in 1992 that brings back the three-tier system again.
 
• This amendment added a new part to the Constitution, namely, added Part IX titled The Panchayats.
 
• This amendment adds a Three-tier system of panchayats at the village, intermediate Mandal, and district levels except in States with a population is below 20 lakhs (Article 243B)

• The role of the State Election Commissioner is primarily defined under Article 243K of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It is a crucial constitutional and administrative figure responsible for conducting and supervising elections within a particular state or union territory in India.
 
• **The State Election Commissioner is usually appointed by the Governor of the state. **

question: The finance commission of India is required to make recommendations to the __________.
solution:
The correct answer is __**President of India**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Finance Commissions are commissions periodically constituted by the President of India under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution to define the financial relations between the central government of India and the individual state governments.

 
 
• Its core responsibility is to:

 
 
• Evaluate the state of finances of the Union and State Governments
 
• Recommend the sharing of taxes between them
 
• Lay down the principles determining the distribution of these taxes among States.
 
 
 
 
 
• The Finance Commission is required to make **recommendations to the President of India.​**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• Functions of the Finance Commission:

 
 
• The distribution of the net proceeds of taxes to be shared between the Centre and the states, and the allocation between the states of the respective shares of such proceeds.
 
• The principles that should govern the grants-in-aid to the states by the Centre (i.e. out of the consolidated fund of India).
 
• The measures needed to augment the consolidated fund of a state to supplement the resources of the panchayats and the municipalities in the state on the basis of the recommendations made by the state finance commission.
 
• Any other matter referred to it by the president in the interests of sound finance.
 
 
 
• Composition of the Finance commission:
 
 
• The Finance Commission consists of a chairman and four other members to be appointed by the President.
 
• They hold office for five years as specified by the president in his order. They are eligible for reappointment.
 
• The Constitution authorise the Parliament to determine the qualifications of members of the commission and the manner in which they should be selected.
 
• Accordingly, the Parliament has specified the qualifications of the chairman and members of the commission.
 
 
• The chairman should be a person having experience in public affairs.
 
• The four other members should be selected from amongst the following:
 
 
• A judge of a high court or one qualified to be appointed as one.
 
• A person who has specialized knowledge of finance and accounts of the government.
 
• A person who has wide experience in financial matters and in administration.
 
• A person who has special knowledge of economics.

• It oversees the management of government accounts and preparation of the Union Government's financial statements.

question: In which of the following years was the Election Commission of India founded?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1950**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Election Commission of India (ECI) was established on **25th January 1950**.
 
• It is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India at both the national and state levels.
 
• The ECI ensures the conduct of free and fair elections in the country, which is a fundamental aspect of the democratic framework of India.
 
• The Election Commission operates under the authority of the Constitution per Article 324, and subsequently enacted Representation of the People Acts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Election Commission of India (ECI)**

 
 
• The ECI is responsible for the superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of President and Vice President held under the Constitution.
 
• The body administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies in India, and the offices of the President and Vice President in the country.
 
• It was originally a one-member body but was made a three-member body in 1989.
 
• The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) heads the Election Commission of India.
 
 
 
• **Article 324 of the Indian Constitution**
 
 
• Article 324 vests the power of superintendence, direction, and control of elections in an independent body, which is the Election Commission.
 
• The Election Commission has the power to take all necessary steps to ensure free and fair elections.
 
 
 
• **Representation of the People Acts**
 
 
• The Representation of the People Act, 1950 provides for the allocation of seats in the House of the People and in the Legislative Assemblies, the delimitation of constituencies for elections, the qualifications of voters at such elections, and other related matters.
 
• The Representation of the People Act, 1951 provides for the actual conduct of elections in India, the qualifications and disqualifications for membership of Parliament and State Legislatures, and the resolution of election disputes.

question: Which committee recommended Constitutional recognition for the local government bodies in 1989?
solution:
The correct answer is __**PK Thungon Committee**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The PK Thungon Committee was formed in **1988** to review the working of the Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• The committee recommended **Constitutional recognition** for the local government bodies.
 
• It suggested the establishment of **three-tier Panchayati Raj system** in the states.
 
• The recommendations led to the **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments**, which were enacted in 1992 and came into effect in 1993.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj System**

 
 
• The Panchayati Raj system is a form of local self-government in rural India.
 
• It was introduced by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992.
 
• The system consists of three levels: the Gram Panchayat (village level), the Panchayat Samiti (block level), and the Zila Parishad (district level).
 
• This system aims to decentralize the administration and promote local governance.
 
 
 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act**
 
 
• It was enacted in 1992 and came into effect on 24 April 1993.
 
• This amendment provided a constitutional status to the Panchayati Raj institutions.
 
• It introduced Article 243 to 243O in Part IX of the Constitution.
 
• The Act mandates the establishment of Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels in all states and Union territories.
 
• It also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.
 
 
 
• **74th Constitutional Amendment Act**
 
 
• It was enacted in 1992 and came into effect on 1 June 1993.
 
• This amendment provided a constitutional status to the Urban Local Bodies (ULBs).
 
• It introduced Article 243P to 243ZG in Part IXA of the Constitution.
 
• The Act mandates the establishment of Municipalities in urban areas.
 
• It also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.

question: Which part of the Constitution deals with the Panchayats?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Part IX**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Part IX** of the Indian Constitution is titled "The Panchayats" and covers Articles 243 to 243O.
 
• It was introduced by the **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992**.
 
• This part provides a detailed framework for the creation, structure, and functioning of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in India.
 
• It aims to promote decentralized governance and ensure people's participation in rural development.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992**

 
 
• This amendment added Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule to the Indian Constitution, effective from April 24, 1993.
 
• It mandates the establishment of a three-tier system of Panchayati Raj for all states having a population of over 20 lakhs.
 
• The three tiers are: Gram Panchayat at the village level, Mandal Parishad or Block Samiti at the intermediate level, and Zilla Parishad at the district level.
 
• The Act also provides for the reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, and women.
 
 
 
• **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**
 
 
• PRIs are institutions of rural local governance in India.
 
• They are responsible for the administration of rural areas and are involved in the implementation of various developmental programs.
 
• The structure, functions, and powers of PRIs are defined by the state legislatures in accordance with the Constitutional provisions.
 
 
 
• **Decentralized Governance**
 
 
• Decentralized governance refers to the distribution of power and decision-making authority to lower levels of government, closer to the people.
 
• It aims to make governance more responsive, accountable, and inclusive.
 
• In the context of PRIs, it means empowering local bodies to make decisions about local development and administration.

__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

question: Which of the following states is one of those states that have no Panchayati Raj Institution at all?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Nagaland**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Nagaland does not have Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) due to its unique traditional and customary laws.
 
• The Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978 governs local governance in the state instead of the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• The Constitution (Seventy-Third Amendment) Act, 1992, which introduced the Panchayati Raj system in India, does not apply to Nagaland.
 
• Nagaland's traditional village councils and customary practices are protected under Article 371(A) of the Indian Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)**

 
 
• Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) are a system of rural local self-government in India.
 
• The system was institutionalized through the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992.
 
• This act provides a three-tier system of Panchayati Raj for all states having a population of over 2 million, consisting of:
 
 
• Gram Panchayat at the village level
 
• Panchayat Samiti at the intermediate level
 
• Zila Parishad at the district level
 
 
 
• The objective of PRIs is to ensure democracy at the grassroots level and empower rural India.
 
 
 
• **Article 371(A)**
 
 
• Article 371(A) of the Indian Constitution provides special provisions with respect to the state of Nagaland.
 
• It ensures that no act of Parliament in respect of religious or social practices, Naga customary law and procedure, administration of civil and criminal justice involving decisions according to Naga customary law, ownership and transfer of land and its resources shall apply to Nagaland unless the Legislative Assembly of Nagaland by a resolution so decides.
 
• This article preserves the unique social and cultural practices of Nagaland.
 
 
 
• **Nagaland Village and Area Councils Act, 1978**
 
 
• This act provides for the establishment of village councils in Nagaland.
 
• Village councils are responsible for administration, development, and maintaining law and order in villages.
 
• The members of the village councils are selected according to the traditional customs and practices of the Naga tribes.
 
• This act ensures that local governance in Nagaland respects and incorporates the traditional and customary laws of the Naga people.

question:
**Read the following statements regarding K. Sanjay Murthy's recent appointment as Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India:**

1. He took office as the CAG in November 2024 after the term of Girish Chandra Murmu.

2. The CAG is a constitutional office, which is appointed by the President under Article 148 of the Indian Constitution.

3. The CAG's term is only five years and cannot be repeated. Which of the above is/are **correct?**
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1) 1 and 2 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **K. Sanjay Murthy** has not been appointed as Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) of India as of October 2023. The question contains an incorrect timeline for the assumed appointment in November 2024.
 
• The **CAG is a constitutional authority** and is appointed by the President of India as per Article 148 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• The CAG is responsible for auditing the accounts of the Union and State governments and public sector organizations to ensure accountability.
 
• The **term of the CAG is six years**, or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, as per the Constitution. There is no restriction on repeat appointments.
 
• Statement 1 is incorrect, as it refers to a fictional event, while Statement 2 is correct regarding the constitutional provisions of the CAG’s appointment.

• Inquiring into disputes between states.
 
• Discussing subjects of common interest.
 
• Making recommendations for policy formulation and implementation.

question: Which of the following statements correctly applies the weighted voting mechanism under Article 279A(9) of the Indian Constitution?

options.text: The Centre holds 75% of the voting power in the GST Council.
A GST Council decision can be passed solely with the support of the Centre and one State.
The States collectively have twice the voting weight of the Centre in the GST Council.
Each State has equal weightage as the Centre in GST Council voting.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The States collectively have twice the voting weight of the Centre in the GST Council.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 279A of the Indian Constitution establishes the GST Council, which is a federal body tasked with making key decisions related to the Goods and Services Tax (GST).
 
• The voting structure in the GST Council is designed to balance the interests of the Centre and States.
 
• As per Article 279A(9), the Centre holds a voting weight of one-third (33.33%) of the total votes.
 
• The States collectively hold two-thirds (66.67%) of the total voting weight in the GST Council.
 
• A decision in the GST Council requires a three-fourths (75%) majority of the weighted votes, ensuring that the States play a significant role in decision-making.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: The Centre holds 75% of the voting power in the GST Council**

 
 
• This statement is incorrect as the Centre holds only one-third (33.33%) of the total voting power in the GST Council.
 
• The remaining two-thirds (66.67%) of the voting power is collectively held by the States.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: A GST Council decision can be passed solely with the support of the Centre and one State**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect as decisions in the GST Council require a three-fourths (75%) majority of the weighted votes.
 
• Since the Centre has only one-third (33.33%) of the voting power, it cannot pass a decision unilaterally or with the support of just one State.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: Each State has equal weightage as the Centre in GST Council voting**
 
 
• This statement is also incorrect. While each State has equal voting power among themselves, the collective weightage of all States is two-thirds (66.67%), which is twice that of the Centre's one-third (33.33%).
 
• The Centre does not hold equal voting weight as an individual State; instead, its voting weight is predefined as one-third of the total.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: GST Council and Its Voting Mechanism**
 
 
• The GST Council is a constitutional body formed under Article 279A to make recommendations on various aspects of GST, such as tax rates, exemptions, and procedural rules.
 
• The council consists of the Union Finance Minister as the Chairperson, the Union Minister of State for Finance, and State Finance Ministers.
 
• The unique voting structure ensures cooperative federalism by giving States a collective upper hand while maintaining the Centre's significant say in decisions.

question: Which of the following statements about the Finance Commission of India is correct?

options.text: Its recommendations are binding on the Union and State governments.
Its members enjoy a fixed tenure protected from executive removal.
Its recommendations are advisory in nature and not legally binding.
It submits its report directly to the Parliament for enactment.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Its recommendations are advisory in nature and not legally binding.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Finance Commission of India is a constitutional body established under Article 280 of the Indian Constitution to make recommendations on the distribution of tax revenues between the Union and the States.
 
• The recommendations made by the Finance Commission are advisory in nature, meaning they are not legally binding on the government but hold persuasive value for policy formulation.
 
• The President of India appoints the Finance Commission every five years or earlier if required, and its main role is to ensure a fair and equitable distribution of financial resources.
 
• The Commission provides suggestions on grants-in-aid to states and other financial matters, keeping in view the objective of maintaining fiscal stability.
 
• The government, however, has the discretion to accept, modify, or reject the recommendations made by the Finance Commission.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: Its recommendations are binding on the Union and State governments**

 
 
• This statement is incorrect. The recommendations of the Finance Commission are not binding on the Union or State governments. They are advisory in nature and serve as guidance for financial distribution.
 
• While the recommendations are generally respected due to their importance in maintaining fiscal balance, governments have the discretion to accept or reject them.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: Its members enjoy a fixed tenure protected from executive removal**
 
 
• This statement is also incorrect. The tenure of the members of the Finance Commission is not fixed in the Constitution, and their removal is governed by rules prescribed by the President of India.
 
• Members are appointed by the President and serve for the duration of the Commission's term, which is typically five years or as specified in their appointment order.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: It submits its report directly to the Parliament for enactment**
 
 
• This statement is incorrect. The Finance Commission submits its report to the President of India, not directly to the Parliament.
 
• The report is then tabled in both Houses of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum detailing the actions taken by the government on its recommendations.
 
 
 
• **About the Finance Commission of India:**
 
 
• The Finance Commission is tasked with defining the financial relations between the Union and the States in India.
 
• Its functions include recommending the distribution of net proceeds of taxes between the Centre and the States and determining the principles governing grants-in-aid to states.
 
• The Commission also reviews the financial position of the States and suggests measures to improve their financial stability and efficiency.

question: In February 2022, the Delhi High Court reserved judgement on a series of Public Interest Litigations (PILs) challenging which exception in Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC)?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Marital rape.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **PILs challenge** the **exception clause** in **Section 375** which **excludes marital rape** from the definition of rape.
 
• The challenge is significant as it could lead to the** criminalization of marital rape** and provide more protection to women against **sexual violence within marriage.**
 
• **Physical torture, dowry death, and suicide** are **not exceptions** in Section 375, but they are related to crimes against women in India.
 
• **Physical torture and dowry death** are often associated with** domestic violence **and **dowry-related crimes, r**espectively.
 
• Suicide is **not a crime**, but it is often linked to **mental health issues** and **social pressures** faced by women in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Section 375 **of the Indian Penal Code deals with the **offence of rape.**
 
• The exception being challenged in the** PILs is the exception clause **which states that sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being **under fifteen years of age,** is not rape.
 
• **Marital rape** refers to any **unwanted sexual acts** by a spouse or ex-spouse that is committed **without the other person's consent.**
 
• **Physical torture** refers to any act of violence that causes** physical harm or injury** to a person.
 
• **Dowry death** refers to the **murder or suicide of a woman** who is unable to meet the demands of her husband or his family for a dowry.

question: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA) places emphasis on the use of technology to ensure the authenticity of evidence. This is particularly relevant for:
solution:
The correct answer is __**Digital and electronic evidence**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA)**, or the Indian Evidence Act, emphasizes the importance of using technology to ensure the **authenticity and reliability of evidence**.
 
• It is particularly relevant for **digital and electronic evidence**, as such evidence can be tampered with or altered without proper mechanisms to ensure its integrity.
 
• **Digital evidence** includes data obtained from electronic devices such as computers, smartphones, hard drives, and cloud-based storage systems. Examples include emails, SMS messages, call logs, and CCTV footage.
 
• The Act includes provisions for the **admissibility of electronic records** under Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, where certified electronic records are treated as evidence in courts.
 
• This emphasis on technology aligns with global judicial trends where digital evidence plays a **crucial role in solving crimes** ranging from cybercrimes to financial fraud and organized crime.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Digital and Electronic Evidence:**

 
 
• It includes all forms of evidence that are stored or transmitted in a digital format. Examples: emails, social media posts, digital documents, and server logs.
 
• Key features: It is highly prone to tampering, requires proper authentication, and necessitates the use of advanced forensic techniques for validation.
 
• Under **Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act**, electronic records are treated as valid evidence if they meet certain technical criteria, like certification by a responsible official.
 
 
 
• **Physical Exhibits:**
 
 
• This refers to tangible objects obtained from crime scenes, such as weapons, clothing, or fingerprints.
 
• Physical evidence is crucial but is not typically subject to the same scrutiny as digital evidence in terms of authenticity checks because of its material nature.
 
 
 
• **Hand-Written Diaries:**
 
 
• This type of evidence is considered under traditional documentary evidence and does not involve technology for validation.
 
• Handwriting experts may be used for authentication.
 
 
 
• **Oral Confessions:**
 
 
• These are verbal statements made by a suspect or accused during interrogation.
 
• Such evidence is admissible under Indian law but must be corroborated with other evidence to ensure reliability.
 
 
 
• **Admissibility of Digital Evidence Globally:**
 
 
• The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) has emphasized the importance of digital evidence in combating transnational crimes.
 
• Countries like the USA and the UK also have laws in place, such as the Federal Rules of Evidence in the USA, that govern the admissibility of digital evidence.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Section 65B Certification:** A certificate is required for the admissibility of electronic records, which ensures that the evidence was generated and stored in a reliable manner.
 
• **Electronic Evidence Forensics:** Advanced forensic tools are used to extract and analyze data while maintaining its integrity.
 
• **Challenges:** The dynamic nature of digital evidence, jurisdictional issues (e.g., data stored overseas), and encryption can complicate its use in legal proceedings.
 
• **Role in Modern Crimes:** Digital evidence is indispensable in solving cybercrimes, financial fraud, and even traditional crimes where technology plays a role, such as using CCTV footage in robbery cases.
 
• **Judicial Precedents:** Indian courts have increasingly relied on digital evidence, with landmark cases such as **Anvar P.V. v. P.K. Basheer** (2014) setting important precedents for admissibility.

question: Which of the following changes has Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS) brought to criminal procedure?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Video-recorded confessions**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS)** replaces the **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)**, focusing on modernizing criminal procedure laws in India to align with contemporary requirements.
 
• The introduction of **video-recorded confessions** ensures transparency and enhances the reliability of evidence presented in courts. This provision aims to eliminate coercion and safeguard the rights of the accused.
 
• The initiative reflects a move toward digitization and technological integration in judicial processes, ensuring accountability and reducing malpractices.
 
• BNSS does not include provisions like **presumption of guilt** or **scrapping of bail rights**, as these would violate fundamental rights under the **Constitution of India**. Hence, these statements are incorrect.
 
• BNSS does not replace all **IPC sections**. It specifically deals with procedures rather than substantive criminal laws. Hence, this statement is also incorrect.
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is video-recorded confessions.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS):**

 
 
• The BNSS, enacted in **2023**, aims to enhance efficiency in criminal procedures and ensure justice delivery in a time-bound manner.
 
• The law emphasizes **digital integration**, including the use of **technology** for evidence recording, case management, and monitoring judicial processes.
 
• The BNSS also facilitates victim-centric justice by ensuring their active participation in the legal process and introducing provisions for victim compensation.
 
 
 
• **Video-recorded confessions:**
 
 
• This provision is aligned with global best practices, enhancing the credibility of the judicial system and ensuring compliance with **Article 21 of the Constitution**, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.
 
• It addresses concerns related to custodial torture or forced confessions by ensuring that statements are recorded in a transparent and impartial manner.
 
 
 
• **Key Principles of Criminal Procedure:**
 
 
• The principles of criminal procedure emphasize **fair trial**, presumption of innocence, and adherence to fundamental rights.
 
• BNSS retains these principles, reinforcing the importance of due process and equality before the law.
 
 
 
• **Indian Penal Code (IPC):**
 
 
• The IPC, enacted in **1860**, is the primary criminal code in India, addressing substantive criminal law.
 
• BNSS focuses exclusively on procedures, ensuring streamlined processes for investigation, trial, and sentencing.
 
 
 
• **Constitutional Provisions:**
 
 
• **Article 22** protects against arbitrary arrest and detention, ensuring safeguards for the accused during criminal proceedings.
 
• BNSS aligns with constitutional mandates to uphold justice, transparency, and the rule of law.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Digitization in Criminal Justice:**

 
 
• The use of technology, such as **video recording**, reduces the scope for manipulation and ensures transparency in judicial proceedings.
 
• India's judicial reforms, including BNSS, aim to integrate digital tools to expedite case disposal and improve access to justice.
 
 
 
• **International Best Practices:**
 
 
• Several countries, including the **United States** and **United Kingdom**, have implemented video-recorded confessions to ensure the integrity of legal processes.
 
• India's adoption of such practices reflects its commitment to modernizing its judicial system in line with global standards.
 
 
 
• **Victim-Centric Justice:**
 
 
• BNSS incorporates provisions to ensure timely justice for victims and safeguard their rights during legal proceedings.
 
• Compensation mechanisms under BNSS aim to reduce the financial burden on victims and their families.

• **Section 50:**

• It mandates that a person being searched has the right to have the search conducted in the presence of two independent witnesses.
 
• This provision aims to ensure transparency and prevent any misconduct by the authorities during the search process.
 
 
 
• **Section 62:**
 
 
• Section 62 focuses on the procedural guidelines for the arrest of individuals.
 
• It outlines the rights of the arrested person, such as the right to be informed about the reasons for the arrest and the right to legal representation.
 
• It ensures that arrests are conducted lawfully and in compliance with the principles of natural justice.
 
 
 
• **Section 176:**
 
 
• Section 176 deals with the investigation of custodial deaths and disappearances.
 
• It mandates that such cases should be investigated by a judicial magistrate or an executive magistrate to ensure impartiality and accountability.
 
• This provision is crucial for addressing concerns related to custodial violence and ensuring justice for victims.
 
 
 
• **Theme of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS):**
 
 
• The BNSS is a comprehensive reform of the Indian criminal laws, replacing the colonial-era Indian Penal Code (IPC), Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), and Indian Evidence Act.
 
• It aims to modernize the criminal justice system, focusing on transparency, accountability, and the protection of citizens' rights.
 
• The reforms emphasize the use of technology, such as video recording, to enhance the efficiency and fairness of criminal investigations and trials.

__
 
• The Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita (BNS), 2023, is aimed at consolidating and amending laws related to **Criminal Substantive Law** in India.
 
• BNS is designed as a replacement for the Indian Penal Code (IPC), 1860, which was drafted during British colonial rule in India.
 
• The primary objective of the BNS is to modernize and reform criminal laws to align with the changing socio-economic and technological landscape of the country.
 
• It seeks to simplify criminal laws, ensure speedy justice, and address contemporary challenges such as cybercrime and organized crime.
 
• The Bharatiya Nyaya Samhita Bill, 2023, was introduced in Parliament in August 2023 as part of a broader initiative to overhaul colonial-era legal frameworks, including the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and the Indian Evidence Act.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Civil Procedure Law**

 
 
• Civil Procedure Law governs the procedures and practices in civil courts, such as filing lawsuits, conducting trials, and enforcing judgments.
 
• The primary legislation governing this branch in India is the **Civil Procedure Code (CPC), 1908**.
 
• Civil laws deal with private disputes between individuals or organizations, such as property disputes, contracts, or family matters.
 
 
 
• **Evidence Law**
 
 
• The law of evidence deals with the rules and principles that determine what evidence is admissible in courts.
 
• The **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**, is the governing framework for evidence-related matters in Indian courts.
 
• It specifies the type and manner of evidence that can be presented in civil or criminal cases, including oral, documentary, and circumstantial evidence.
 
 
 
• **Contract Law**
 
 
• Contract law governs agreements between parties that are enforceable by law.
 
• The primary legislation in India is the **Indian Contract Act, 1872**, which outlines the essentials of a valid contract, including offer, acceptance, consideration, and capacity to contract.
 
• It also covers specific contracts such as indemnity, guarantee, bailment, agency, and partnership agreements.

question: In Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS), which court may grant default bail after time limit lapses?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Magistrate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS)**, a Magistrate has the authority to grant default bail to an accused if the investigation agency fails to file a chargesheet within the stipulated time frame.
 
• The time limit for filing a chargesheet is generally **60 days** for cases where the offense is punishable with imprisonment up to 10 years and **90 days** for offenses punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding 10 years.
 
• **Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)**, which is incorporated under BNSS, mandates that a Magistrate must release the accused on default bail if the prosecution fails to meet these deadlines.
 
• Default bail is considered a statutory right of the accused and is not dependent on the merits of the case; it ensures procedural safeguards against unlawful detention.
 
• The Magistrate can impose reasonable conditions while granting default bail, such as requiring the accused to furnish a bail bond or adhere to certain restrictions during the bail period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **District Court**

 
 
• District Courts are subordinate courts in the judicial hierarchy and primarily function as trial courts for civil and criminal cases.
 
• They lack the jurisdiction to directly grant default bail unless the case has been escalated from the Magistrate's court.
 
• District and Sessions Judges handle cases involving serious offenses, appeals, and revisions against the orders of Magistrates.
 
 
 
• **High Court**
 
 
• The High Court is the apex judicial body at the state level and primarily deals with appeals, writs, and revisions.
 
• While the High Court can grant bail in exceptional cases, default bail is generally processed through the Magistrate’s court as per procedural norms.
 
• The High Court can intervene if there is procedural illegality or denial of statutory bail by lower courts.
 
 
 
• **Gram Nyayalaya**
 
 
• Gram Nyayalayas are village-level courts established under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008, to provide speedy and accessible justice in rural areas.
 
• They primarily deal with minor civil and criminal cases and do not have jurisdiction over major offenses or default bail matters.
 
• Their objective is to reduce the burden on regular courts while ensuring justice at the grassroots level.
 
 
 
• **About Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS)**
 
 
• The BNSS is part of the set of bills introduced to replace the colonial-era laws like the Indian Penal Code (IPC), CrPC, and the Indian Evidence Act.
 
• It seeks to modernize India’s criminal laws to ensure justice delivery is more efficient and citizen-friendly.
 
• The provisions related to default bail under BNSS aim to uphold individual liberty while maintaining procedural discipline in criminal investigations.

• The **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita**, introduced as a replacement for the Indian Penal Code (IPC), includes provisions aimed at modernizing the judicial process in India.

• The reform emphasizes **efficiency, transparency, and accessibility** by leveraging technology to reduce pendency in courts and make justice delivery more effective. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__

• The Indian judiciary has been adopting digital reforms such as the **e-Courts Mission Mode Project**, which aims to computerize courts and enhance their functioning. 
 
• Virtual court hearings are part of this broader initiative, enabling remote access and reducing the time taken for proceedings. 
 
• Such reforms promote a paperless environment, improving efficiency and reducing costs. 
 
 
 
• **Impact of Virtual Hearings:** 
 
 
• Virtual hearings have made justice delivery more inclusive by allowing individuals from **remote and rural areas** to participate in proceedings without incurring significant travel expenses. 
 
• They are particularly beneficial for cases involving **environmental disasters, pandemics, or other emergencies**.

• The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita emphasizes **streamlining procedures**, such as fast-tracking cases and introducing time limits for specific processes. 
 
• The focus on **using digital evidence** highlights the importance of technology in modern justice delivery. 
 
 
 
• **Technological Integration in Judiciary:** 
 
 
• Besides virtual hearings, the judiciary is exploring the use of tools like **Artificial Intelligence (AI)** for case management and legal research. 
 
• Other technological advancements include **online case filing, digital case records, and e-payment systems** for court fees.

• **Online registration for judges:** While technology is used for administrative tasks, this specific option is not directly related to the reforms under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. 
 
• **Abolition of police reports:** This is incorrect as police reports (FIRs) are a critical part of the criminal justice system in India. 
 
 
 
• **Examples of Virtual Hearings:** 
 
 
• During the **COVID-19 pandemic**, the Supreme Court and several High Courts in India conducted virtual hearings to ensure continuity in justice delivery. 
 
• Countries like the **United States and the United Kingdom** have also adopted virtual court systems to modernize their judiciary.

question: Under the BSA, 2023, oral evidence must be:

options.text: Direct and related to what the witness saw or heard

solution:
The correct answer is __**Direct and related to what the witness saw or heard**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Under the BSA, 2023**, oral evidence must be **direct**, meaning it should pertain to what the witness personally observed or heard, rather than relying on assumptions or hearsay. 
• Oral evidence plays a crucial role in the judicial process, as it provides firsthand accounts that can help establish the facts of the case. 
• Evidence based on assumptions or speculation is inadmissible under the law, as it lacks reliability and factual accuracy. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.* 
• Language is not a criterion for admissibility of oral evidence under the BSA, 2023. Evidence can be recorded in any language, provided it is accurately translated if necessary. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.* 
• **Hearsay evidence**, or evidence not based on direct observation, is typically inadmissible except under certain exceptions outlined in the law. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.* 
• Direct evidence is considered more reliable and credible in legal proceedings compared to indirect or hearsay evidence, as it is firsthand and less prone to distortion or misinterpretation. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Direct Evidence:** 
• Direct evidence is testimony or information provided by a witness who has personally experienced the event in question. 
• It is considered highly credible and is admissible in court without requiring further corroboration. 
• **Example:** A witness testifying that they saw a person commit a crime. 
• **Hearsay Evidence:** 
• Hearsay evidence refers to information that a witness heard from someone else, rather than directly observing the event. 
• It is generally inadmissible under the legal framework, except in specific exceptions such as dying declarations or admissions. 
• **Example:** A witness stating that they were told by another person about the crime. 
• **Exceptions to Hearsay Rule:** 
• Certain exceptions allow hearsay evidence to be admitted, such as statements made under imminent fear of death (**dying declaration**). 
• Other exceptions include business records, statements against interest, or declarations made during the course of business. 
• **Importance of Oral Evidence:** 
• Oral evidence is a key element in trials, as it provides the court with a direct account of events. 
• It must be scrutinized for reliability, consistency, and credibility during cross-examination. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Admissibility Criteria:** 
• Oral evidence must be relevant, material, and directly related to the facts of the case. 
• It is subject to cross-examination to test the witness's credibility and the accuracy of their testimony. 
• **Legal Basis:** 
• The **Indian Evidence Act, 1872** governs admissibility and relevance of oral evidence in India. 
• Similar provisions exist globally, ensuring that direct evidence is prioritized for reliability. </ul

question: Which of the following is a cybercrime related to identity theft under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023?

 __ 
• **Identity theft** is a cybercrime where someone steals another individual's personal information, such as their name, date of birth, Aadhaar number, or financial details, to impersonate them for fraudulent purposes. This is explicitly covered under the **Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023**. 
• The act of **stealing personal details** to create fake identities is used to commit crimes such as financial fraud, obtaining unauthorized access to services, or engaging in illegal activities, making it a punishable offense under the new legal framework. 
• Under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, identity theft is categorized as a serious offense. It is dealt with under provisions that aim to safeguard individuals' personal and digital information. 
• Cybercriminals often exploit stolen identities to commit crimes like phishing, applying for loans fraudulently, or making unauthorized transactions. Such activities have a high impact on victims, both financially and emotionally. 
• Other options such as using public Wi-Fi, downloading free music from unofficial websites, or posting harmless pictures on social media do not constitute identity theft or fall under serious cybercrime categories unless they involve illegal intent or misuse. *Hence, these statements are incorrect.* 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Key Characteristics of Identity Theft:** 
• **Age Group:** Anyone can be a victim of identity theft, but individuals with a high online presence are at greater risk. 
• **Methods Used:** Phishing emails, social engineering tactics, hacking, and data breaches are common techniques used by cybercriminals. 
• **Impact:** Victims may face financial losses, damage to their credit score, and legal issues if their identity is used in illegal activities. 
• **Prevention:** Using strong passwords, avoiding public Wi-Fi for sensitive transactions, and being cautious about sharing personal information online are effective preventive measures. 
• **Other Cybercrimes Addressed Under Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023:** 
• **Phishing:** Deceptive attempts to acquire sensitive information like usernames, passwords, or credit card details. 
• **Hacking:** Unauthorized access to computer systems to steal or manipulate data. 
• **Cyberstalking:** Persistent harassment of an individual through digital platforms. 
• **Data breaches:** Unauthorized access to and exposure of sensitive data stored in digital systems. 
• **Implications of Identity Theft:** 
• Victims may take years to recover from the financial and reputational damage caused by identity theft. 
• Law enforcement agencies face challenges in tracking cybercriminals due to their use of advanced technologies and anonymity tools.

__

• Under the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (Indian Evidence Act), 1872**, electronic records can be considered admissible as evidence only if they meet certain conditions.

• The **certificate requirement** is specified under **Section 65B(4)** of the Act, which mandates that a certificate must accompany any electronic record submitted as secondary evidence.

• This certificate must include details about the electronic device used to produce the record, confirming its authenticity and the method by which the data was generated.

• The certificate is typically issued by a person in charge of the device (like a system administrator) and must be signed, providing assurance that the electronic record has not been tampered with.

• Without this certificate, the electronic record cannot be admitted as secondary evidence, even if it is relevant to the case.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Section 65B of the Indian Evidence Act:**

• This section deals with the admissibility of electronic records as evidence in legal proceedings.

• It specifies that for electronic records to be admissible, they must meet the conditions outlined in the section, including the requirement of a certificate under **Sub-section 4**.

• This provision ensures that the integrity and reliability of electronic evidence are maintained.

• **Purpose of the Certificate:**

• The certificate serves as a safeguard against forgery, manipulation, or alteration of electronic records.

• It confirms that the information in the electronic record was produced by a reliable device and process.

• It provides details about the person responsible for the operation of the device and the accuracy of the record.

• **Other Relevant Provisions:**

• **Section 65A:** Introduces the concept of electronic records as evidence under specific circumstances.

• **Section 3:** Defines the term "evidence" to include all documents, including electronic records, produced for the inspection of the court.

• **Section 67A:** Discusses the proof of digital signatures and their verification.

• **Examples of Admissible Electronic Records:**

• Emails, text messages, and chat logs accompanied by a valid Section 65B certificate.

• Printed copies of financial records generated from computer systems with an authenticated certificate.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Relevance of Electronic Records:** With the rise of digital transactions, electronic records have become crucial in legal cases involving contracts, financial transactions, and communications.

• **Judicial Precedent:** In the landmark judgment **Anvar P.V. vs. P.K. Basheer (2014)**, the Supreme Court of India ruled that electronic records without a Section 65B certificate are inadmissible as evidence.

• **Global Practices:** Many countries, including the **United States** and **United Kingdom**, have similar provisions for the admissibility of electronic evidence to ensure its reliability and authenticity.

• **Exceptions:** If the electronic record is presented as primary evidence (e.g., the original hard drive or device), the certificate requirement may not apply.

question: What does the term "Zero FIR" imply under the new law?

options.text: FIR can be filed at any police station, regardless of jurisdiction
FIR can be withdrawn at zero cost
FIR can be digitally deleted if not verified
FIR can be filed without police verification

solution:
The correct answer is __**FIR can be filed at any police station, regardless of jurisdiction**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Zero FIR** refers to an **FIR (First Information Report)** that can be filed at any police station, **irrespective of the location or jurisdiction** where the incident occurred. This is intended to ensure quick reporting of crimes without jurisdictional delays. 
• Once a Zero FIR is filed, it is the responsibility of the police station to **transfer the FIR** to the appropriate police station under whose jurisdiction the crime falls. 
• The concept of Zero FIR is particularly important in cases of **serious crimes** like rape, murder, or sexual harassment, where immediate action and investigation are critical. 
• The provision for Zero FIR is mentioned in the **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013**, which was enacted following the Nirbhaya case in 2012 to make the justice system more responsive to victims of crime. 
• This system ensures that victims are not turned away by police stations citing jurisdictional issues and that their complaints are registered without delay. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Importance of Zero FIR:** 
• Empowers victims to register complaints **immediately** without worrying about jurisdictional boundaries. 
• Ensures that no crime goes unreported due to **bureaucratic hurdles**. 
• Strengthens the legal framework for victims, especially in cases of **gender-based violence**. 
• **Legal Basis:** 
• The provision for Zero FIR was formalized through the **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013**. 
• While the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** and **Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC)** do not explicitly define "Zero FIR," the concept stems from the duty of police officers to register complaints under Section 154 of the CrPC. 
• **Distinction Between Regular FIR and Zero FIR:** 
• **Regular FIR:** Filed at the police station that has jurisdiction over the area where the crime occurred. 
• **Zero FIR:** Can be filed at any police station, and it will be **transferred** to the concerned jurisdictional police station for further investigation. 
• **Challenges in Implementation:** 
• Lack of awareness among the public about their right to file a Zero FIR. 
• Reluctance or refusal by some police officers to register Zero FIRs, despite legal provisions. 
• Need for training and sensitization of police personnel to handle such cases effectively. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Key Differences Between FIR and Zero FIR:** 
• In a **Regular FIR**, the jurisdiction of the police station is important, whereas in a **Zero FIR**, jurisdiction is not a constraint. 
• A Zero FIR is numbered as "0" until it is transferred to the appropriate police station, where it is assigned a regular FIR number. 
• **Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013:** 
• Introduced several provisions to enhance the safety and security of women, including the concept of Zero FIR. 
• Added stringent penalties for crimes like rape, acid attacks, and stalking. 
• **Real-Life Examples:** 
• The Nirbhaya case in 2012 highlighted the need for immediate registration of complaints without jurisdictional delays. 
• The Zero FIR provision ensures that such cases are promptly acted upon. </ul
