question: In BNSS, what provision strengthens witness protection during trial?

options.text: Use of video conferencing and identity concealment for vulnerable witnesses
Witnesses can choose to record statements via SMS
Witnesses are not required to attend trial

solution:
The correct answer is __**Use of video conferencing and identity concealment for vulnerable witnesses**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Video conferencing and identity concealment** are provisions that enhance the protection of vulnerable witnesses during trials. These measures ensure that witnesses can provide testimony without being physically present, reducing the risk of intimidation or harm. 
• Identity concealment is a critical safeguard for witnesses who may be threatened or coerced due to their participation in legal proceedings. It helps maintain their anonymity, ensuring their safety and encouraging truthful testimony. 
• Such provisions are particularly important in cases involving sensitive matters, organized crime, or instances where witnesses face threats from powerful entities. 
• The system allows witnesses to testify from secure locations, ensuring that they are shielded from direct confrontation with the accused or their associates. 
• These measures align with the broader goal of ensuring justice while protecting individuals who play an instrumental role in legal processes. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Witness Protection Scheme, 2018:** 
• This scheme was introduced by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, to provide adequate protection to witnesses in sensitive cases. 
• The scheme emphasizes the confidentiality of identity, relocation of witnesses, and other measures to ensure their safety. 
• It categorizes witnesses into three categories based on the threat perception and provides necessary protection accordingly. 
• **Use of Technology in Courts:** 
• Video conferencing is increasingly used to conduct hearings, particularly in cases involving vulnerable witnesses or during emergencies like the COVID-19 pandemic. 
• Technology minimizes logistical challenges and provides a secure environment for witnesses to testify. 
• It also enhances judicial efficiency by reducing delays caused by witness unavailability. 
• **International Practices:** 
• Countries like the **United States** and **United Kingdom** have adopted similar measures for witness protection, including the use of video conferencing and voice modulation technologies. 
• The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) also advocates for witness protection mechanisms as part of its guidelines for criminal justice reform. 
• **Legal Provisions in India:** 
• The **Indian Evidence Act, 1872**, and the **Criminal Procedure Code** have been amended to incorporate provisions for witness protection. 
• Section 161 of CrPC allows for recording witness statements through electronic means, ensuring flexibility and security. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Anonymous Jury System:** 
• This concept is not prevalent in India but is used in certain international jurisdictions to protect jury members in high-risk cases. 
• It involves concealing the identities of jury members to safeguard them from external pressures. 
• However, this option does not address witness protection directly, making it less relevant to the Indian context. 
• **SMS Statement Recording:** 
• This is not a recognized method for recording witness statements as per Indian legal standards. 
• While it might seem convenient, it lacks the safeguards necessary to ensure authenticity and reliability. 
• **No Attendance Requirement:** 
• Witnesses are generally required to attend trials unless provisions like video conferencing are used. 
• Absence of attendance without alternative arrangements can compromise the integrity of judicial proceedings. 
• **Role of Judiciary:** 
• The judiciary plays a pivotal role in implementing witness protection measures, ensuring a fair trial while safeguarding the rights and safety of witnesses. 
• Landmark judgments like **State of Maharashtra v. Dr. Praful B. Desai** have upheld the use of video conferencing for witness testimonies. </ul

solution:

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__**

__
 
• The preamble is the introductory part of the Constitution which sets out the principles on which the Constitution is based.
 
• **The preamble declares India to be a sovereign, socialist, secular and democratic republic.**
 
• The word **Federal is nowhere mentioned in the Indian** constitution.
 
• The ideals behind the Preamble to India’s Constitution were laid down by **Jawaharlal Nehru’s Objectives Resolution,** adopted by the** Constituent Assembly on January 22, 1947**.
 
• The date is mentioned in the preamble when it was adopted i.e. **November 26, 1949.**

**Keywords in Preamble**__

 
• **We, the people of India: **

 
 
• It indicates the ultimate sovereignty of the people of India.
 
 
 
• **Sovereign:**
 
 
• The term means that India has its own independent authority and it is not a dominion of any other external power.
 
 
 
• **Socialist:**
 
 
• The term means the achievement of socialist ends through democratic means.
 
• It holds faith in a mixed economy where both private and public sectors co-exist side by side.
 
• **It was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.**
 
 
 
• **Secular:**
 
 
• The term means that all the religions in India get equal respect, protection and support from the state.
 
• It was incorporated into the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.
 
 
 
• **Democratic:**

question: How many Schedules did the Constitution of India contain as of April 2021?

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **There are 12 Schedules in the Constitution of India as of April 2021.**
 
• One of the first mentions of Schedules was made in the Government of India Act, 1935 which it included 10 Schedules.
 
• Later, when the **Indian Constitution was adopted in 1949, it consisted of 8 Schedules.**
 
• Today, with the amendments in the Indian Constitution, there are a total of** 12 Schedules.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
 

 Schedules
 Mention
 
 
 
 

 First Schedule of Indian Constitution
 Name of States and Union Territories Territorial Jurisdiction of states is also included
 
 

 Second Schedule of Indian Constitution
 Provisions in relation to allowances, privileges, emoluments of, President of India Governors of Indian States etc
 
 

 Third Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 It contains the forms of oath and affirmation for Union Ministers of India Parliament Election Candidates Members of Parliament (MPs) Supreme Court Judges etc
 
 

 Fourth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 It contains the provisions in relation to the allocation of seats for States and Union Territories in the Rajya Sabha
 
 

 Fifth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 It contains provisions in relation to the administration and control of scheduled areas and scheduled tribes
 
 

 Sixth Schedule of Indian Constitution
 It contains provisions in relation to the administration of tribal areas in the states of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
 
 

 Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 Schedule deals with the three legislative lists: Union State Concurrent
 
 

 Eight Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 It deals with the 22 official languages recognized by the Constitution of India: Assamese Bengali Bodo Dogri (Dongri) Gujarati Hindi Kannada etc.
 
 

 Ninth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 
 
It deals with the state acts and regulations of that deal with land reforms and the abolition of the zamindari system. It also deals with the acts and regulations of the Parliament dealing with other matters.

 
Note: 1st Amendment Act 1951 added the Ninth Schedule

 
 
 

 Tenth Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 
 
It contains provisions relating to disqualification of the members of Parliament and State Legislatures on the ground of defection.

 
Note:

 
This schedule was added by the 52nd Amendment Act of 1985, also known as Anti-defection Law

 
 
 

 Eleven Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 
 
It contains the provisions that specify the powers, authority and responsibilities of Panchayats. It has 29 matters.

 
Note:

 
This schedule was added by the 73rd Amendment Act of 1992

 
 
 

 Twelve Schedule of the Indian Constitution
 
 
It deals with the provisions that specify the powers, authority and responsibilities of Municipalities. It has 18 matters.

 
Note:

 
This schedule was added by the 74th Amendment Act of 1992

subject: GK
question: The Constitution of India is a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic with a _________ system of government.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Parliamentary**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Parliamentary system**

 
 
• The **Constitution of India** is a sovereign socialist secular democratic republic with a **parliamentary system of government**.
 
• **India **has a parliamentary system of **government **with federal and unitary components.
 
• It is a sovereign** socialist, secular, **and **democratic** **republic**.
 
• The **Prime Minister** serves as the head of the **Council of Ministers**, which provides advice to the **President**, who is the nation's constitutional leader.
 
• The** Indian Constitution**, which was approved by the Constituent Assembly on** November 26, 1949**, and took effect on **January 26, 1950**, governs the **Country**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **​**The **head **of state in a **parliamentary system **is often a different person from the head of **government**. In contrast, in a presidential system, the executive branch does not receive its democratic legitimacy from the legislative and the head of state frequently doubles as the head of **government**.
 
• A **parliamentary** **system**, sometimes known as a parliamentarian democracy, is a form of democratic government in which the executive branch obtains the backing of the legislative, usually a **parliament**, to whom it is answerable.

question: In which of the following years was the Citizenship Act passed by the Indian Parliament?
solution:
The correct answer is 1955.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Citizenship Act of 1955** was amended by the **Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA act)**, which was first introduced in** Lok Sabha in 2016.**
 
• **A Joint Parliamentary Committee** was given this act, and it later produced a report that was delivered on January 7, 2019.
 
• The **Lok Sabha** passed the **Citizenship Amendment Act** on January 8, 2019, but it expired with the dissolution of the **16th Lok Parliament.**
 
• **Amit Shah**, the minister of home affairs, reintroduced this bill on December 9 in the** 17th Lok Sabha**, and it was later approved on December 10.
 
• On December 11th, the** Rajya Sabha** also approved the **legislation**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Citizenship Amendment Act**

 
 
• ​The Act aims to amend the **Citizenship Act of 1955** to offer **citizenship** to illegal immigrants from **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, and Pakistan** who are **Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, and Christian** words, the Act aims to facilitate **Indian citizenship** for persecuted individuals from India's neighbouring nations.
 
• Those who were "forced or compelled to seek sanctuary in India due to persecution on the basis of religion" are covered by the law. It tries to safeguard these individuals from** illegal immigration processes.**
 
• For applicants who practise one of these six religions, the change reduces the naturalisation requirement from 11 to 5 years.
 
• The applicant must have arrived in India on or before December 31, 2014, which is the deadline for **citizenship**.

• Secular: The term means that all the religions in India get equal respect, protection, and support from the state. 
 
• The preamble was amended by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act in 1976, in which three new words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity were added.
 
• It was incorporated in the Preamble by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment, 1976.

• Republic: The term indicates that the head of the state is elected by the people.
 
• In India, the President of India is the elected head of the state.
 
• The preamble was amended by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act in 1976, in which three new words Socialist, Secular, and Integrity were added.
 
• It secures justice, liberty, equality to all citizens of India and promotes fraternity amongst the people.
 
• It has been widely regarded as soul of the constitution.

question: Which part of the Constitution of India contains the provisions of Union Executive?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Part V**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Union Executive of India's Constitution is covered in Part V.
 
• This part, ranging from article 52 to 151, lays out the roles and powers of the President, Vice-president, Council of Ministers, Attorney General of India, Comptroller and Auditor General, and other executive functions of the Central Government of India.
 
• Additionally, it details processes such as the appointment, terms of office, and the conditions of service of these posts.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points __**

 
 

 Part I – The Union and its Territories
 1 – 4
 
 

 Part II – Citizenship
 5 -11
 
 

 Part III – Fundamental Rights
 12 – 35
 
 

 Part IV – Directive Principles of State Policy
 36 – 51
 
 

 Part IV A – Fundamental Duties
 51A
 
 

 Part V – The Union
 52 – 151
 
 

 Part VI – The States
 152 – 237
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

 
• President (Article 52-62): The President is the head of the Union Executive and also the first citizen of India. Articles describe the election, qualifications, term of office, Oath, conditions of the President's office, and the process in the event of impeachment.
 
• Vice-President (Article 63-71): The Constitution provides for a Vice-President and outlines the manner of their election, their role (especially as the ex-officio Chairman of Rajya Sabha), and the process for removal from office.
 
• Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head (Article 74-75): Article 74 mandates a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister as the head to aid and advise the President. Article 75 provides details on who appoints the Prime Minister and other ministers, their responsibilities, the oath of office, etc.
 
• Attorney General (Article 76): The Attorney General is the highest law officer in the country. Article 76 outlines the qualifications, appointment, duties and rights of the Attorney General.
 
• Comptroller and Auditor General (Article 148-151): The CAG audits all expenditures from the Consolidated Fund of India. Details about the office, appointment, removal, and duties of the CAG are provided here.

**Points to ponder**

 
• The President has the power to seek advice from the Supreme Court (Article 143).
 
• The Vice-President acts as President during any vacancies or when the President is unable to fulfill their duties.
 
• The Prime Minister has a pivotal role in the functioning of the Union Government. The President exercises his/her powers on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.
 
• Article 77 lays down the procedure for the work of the Government of India - it should be done in the name of the President.
 
• The Attorney General, though not a member of the parliament, has the right to participate in its proceedings.
 
• The CAG reports to the President, who places these reports before both Houses of the Parliament.

question: Which of the following is mentioned in Article 1 of the Indian constitution?

options.text: India that is Bharat as federation of states
India that is Bharat as parliamentary democracy
India that is Bharat shall be a Union of states
India that is Bharat as presidential form of democracy

solution:
The correct answer is __**India that is Bharat shall be a Union of states**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 1 of the Indian Constitution states that "India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States."
 
• This signifies that India is a single entity with a union of states rather than a federation of states.
 
• The term "Union of States" implies that states have no right to secede from the union.
 
• It defines India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union of States**

 
 
• The phrase "Union of States" was chosen to indicate that the Indian union is not a result of an agreement among the states like the American federation.
 
• It emphasizes the indestructible nature of the Indian Union, where states cannot secede from the union.
 
 
 
• **Sovereign**
 
 
• The term "sovereign" means that India is independent and free from any external control.
 
• It has the power to legislate on all matters, both internal and external.
 
 
 
• **Socialist**
 
 
• Although the word "socialist" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976, it reflects the commitment to social and economic justice.
 
• It aims to reduce income inequality and ensure a fair distribution of wealth.
 
 
 
• **Secular**
 
 
• The term "secular" was also added by the 42nd Amendment Act of 1976.
 
• It means that the state does not have an official religion and treats all religions equally.
 
 
 
• **Democratic Republic**
 
 
• "Democratic" indicates that the government is elected by the people, and "Republic" means that the head of the state is elected and not a hereditary monarch.
 
• India is committed to the democratic principles of liberty, equality, and fraternity.

question: When did a States Reorganisation Commission was set up, which recommended the creation of linguistic States on the basis of larger linguistic groups?
solution:
The correct answer is __**December 1953**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The States Reorganisation Commission (SRC) was formed in **December 1953**.
 
• The Commission was tasked with recommending the reorganization of state boundaries based on linguistic lines.
 
• The SRC was headed by **Fazal Ali** and its other members were H.N. Kunzru and K.M. Panikkar.
 
• The recommendations of the SRC led to the passage of the States Reorganisation Act in 1956, which redefined the boundaries of Indian states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **States Reorganisation Commission (SRC):**

 
 
• The SRC was constituted by the Government of India in 1953 to address demands for the reorganization of India's states on linguistic lines.
 
• The SRC's primary objective was to ensure that state boundaries were redrawn to reflect the linguistic and cultural identities of the populations within them.
 
• The Commission's final report was submitted in 1955, and it recommended the reorganization of states primarily on linguistic lines.
 
• The recommendations of the SRC were implemented through the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, which led to the creation of 14 states and 6 union territories.
 
 
 
• **Fazal Ali:**
 
 
• Fazal Ali was an Indian civil servant and politician who served as the head of the States Reorganisation Commission.
 
• He played a crucial role in the reorganization of Indian states based on linguistic lines.
 
• His leadership and contributions were instrumental in shaping the modern political map of India.
 
 
 
• **States Reorganisation Act, 1956:**
 
 
• The States Reorganisation Act was a major reform of the boundaries and governance structures of Indian states, implemented in 1956.
 
• This act led to the creation of several new states and union territories, primarily based on linguistic and cultural commonalities.
 
• It aimed to address the demands for statehood from various linguistic and regional groups within India.
 
• The Act marked a significant step towards accommodating the diverse linguistic and cultural identities within the Indian union.

question: Which part of the Indian Constitution deals with the Election Commission?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Part XV**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Part XV of the Indian Constitution** deals with elections, which includes provisions related to the Election Commission of India.
 
• It encompasses **Articles 324 to 329**, which provide the framework for the conduct of elections in the country.
 
• Article 324 specifically **vests the power of superintendence, direction, and control of elections** in an independent Election Commission.
 
• The Election Commission is responsible for conducting elections to the Parliament, state legislatures, and offices of the President and Vice-President in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Part XII** of the Indian Constitution deals with finance, property, contracts, and suits. It includes provisions related to the distribution of revenue between the Union and the States.
 
• **Part IV** contains the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are guidelines for the framing of laws by the government. These principles aim to create social and economic conditions under which citizens can lead a good life.
 
• **Part XI** deals with the relations between the Union and the States, defining the distribution of legislative and administrative powers between the two.
 
• The Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional authority responsible for administering election processes in India at both national and state levels. The body administers elections to the Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, and State Legislative Assemblies in India, as well as the offices of the President and Vice President in the country.
 
• Being a constitutional body, the Election Commission operates independently of the government to ensure free and fair elections. Its autonomy and impartial functioning are crucial for the democratic structure of the country.

question:
**Consider the following statements: **

1. The Concurrent List allows both Centre and States to legislate.

2. In case of conflict, State law prevails over Union law. Which of the above is/are **correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statement 1 is correct:** The Concurrent List in the Indian Constitution allows both the Centre and States to legislate on matters included in it. Examples include education, marriage, adoption, etc.
 
• The Concurrent List is one of the three lists under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, the others being the Union List and State List.
 
• Legislation on the Concurrent List ensures cooperation between the Centre and States while addressing shared responsibilities.
 
• In case of a conflict between Union and State laws on the same subject, the **Union law prevails**, as provided under Article 254 of the Constitution of India.
 
• Thus, Statement 2 is incorrect because the Union law overrides State law in case of conflict.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Union List:**

 
 
• Subjects under the Union List are exclusively legislated by the Parliament.
 
• Examples include defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy, railways, and currency.
 
• It contains 97 subjects (originally) as per the Constitution of India.
 
 
 
• **State List:**
 
 
• Subjects under the State List are exclusively legislated by the State Legislatures.
 
• Examples include police, public health, agriculture, and local government.
 
• The State List originally contained 66 subjects.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List:**
 
 
• It contains subjects where both the Centre and States can legislate.
 
• It originally consisted of 47 subjects, which include criminal law, education, forests, and marriage.
 
• In case of conflict, Union law prevails as per Article 254 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Article 254:**
 
 
• If there is an inconsistency between laws made by the Parliament and laws made by State Legislatures on a Concurrent List subject, the law enacted by Parliament prevails.
 
• The only exception is if the State law has received Presidential assent, then it can prevail in that state.

question:
**Arrange the following judicial events chronologically:**

1. Berubari Union case

2. Kesavananda Bharati case

3. S.R. Bommai case
solution:
The correct answer is __**1, 2, 3 (Berubari Union case, Kesavananda Bharati case, S.R. Bommai case)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Berubari Union Case (1960):** This case addressed the interpretation of the Indian Constitution regarding the transfer of territory to another country. It clarified that a constitutional amendment under Article 368 is required for transferring any part of Indian territory.
 
• **Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973):** This landmark case established the doctrine of the Basic Structure of the Constitution, which restricts Parliament's power to amend the Constitution in a way that alters its fundamental framework.
 
• **S.R. Bommai Case (1994):** This case is a significant judgment regarding the scope and limitations of Article 356 (President's Rule). It emphasized the principle of federalism and judicial review of the imposition of President's Rule.
 
• The chronological order of these cases is essential in understanding the evolution of constitutional law in India.
 
• This question highlights milestones in India's judicial history that have shaped governance and federalism in the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Berubari Union Case (1960):**

 
 
• The issue arose following the Nehru-Noon Agreement (1958) between India and Pakistan to divide Berubari Union territory.
 
• The Supreme Court opined that the transfer of territory to Pakistan required a constitutional amendment, as it involved altering India's territorial integrity.
 
• This case clarified the interpretation of Article 3 and Article 368 regarding the alteration of India's boundaries.
 
 
 
• **Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973):**
 
 
• In this case, Swami Kesavananda Bharati challenged the Kerala government's land reform laws, questioning the extent of Parliament's power to amend the Constitution.
 
• The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament could amend the Constitution but could not alter its "Basic Structure," such as democracy, secularism, federalism, and judicial independence.
 
• This judgment is regarded as a cornerstone of constitutional law in India.
 
 
 
• **S.R. Bommai Case (1994):**
 
 
• This case arose when the Karnataka state government, led by S.R. Bommai, was dismissed by the central government under Article 356.
 
• The Supreme Court laid down guidelines for imposing President's Rule and emphasized that it cannot be used arbitrarily.
 
• It upheld the importance of federalism and judicial review in safeguarding democracy.

question:
Consider the following statements:

1. Criminal law is exclusively under the Union List.

2. Agriculture is a State subject.

3. Trade and commerce within a State falls under the State List.

Which of the above is/are **correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 2: 2 and 3 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Agriculture** is a subject under the **State List**, as per Schedule VII of the Indian Constitution. States have exclusive authority to legislate on matters related to agriculture.
 
• **Trade and commerce within a state** is also listed under the **State List**. This gives states the power to regulate trade and commerce within their territorial boundaries.
 
• **Criminal law**, however, is not exclusively under the Union List. It is part of the **Concurrent List**, meaning both the Union and State governments can legislate on it.
 
• The Concurrent List allows overlapping legislative powers between the Union and States, which includes subjects like criminal law, marriage, bankruptcy, and more.
 
• Therefore, Statements 2 and 3 are correct, while Statement 1 is incorrect, making Option 2 the right choice.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Statement 1: Criminal law is exclusively under the Union List**

 
 
• This is incorrect. Criminal law is part of the **Concurrent List (Entry 1)**, meaning both the Union and State legislatures can make laws on this subject.
 
• However, in case of any conflict between the central and state laws, the central law prevails (as per Article 254 of the Indian Constitution).
 
• Examples of criminal laws include the Indian Penal Code (IPC) and the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), which apply uniformly across the country.
 
 
 
• **Statement 2: Agriculture is a State subject**
 
 
• This is correct. Agriculture falls under the **State List (Entry 14)** in Schedule VII of the Indian Constitution.
 
• States have the exclusive power to legislate on issues such as land tenure, irrigation, crop insurance, agricultural education, and farm policies.
 
• However, the Union government plays a role in framing national agricultural policies and schemes, such as the PM-KISAN scheme.
 
 
 
• **Statement 3: Trade and commerce within a State falls under the State List**
 
 
• This is correct. Trade and commerce within a state is included under the **State List (Entry 26)**.
 
• States have the power to regulate markets, taxation on goods and services, and local trade policies.
 
• However, inter-state trade and commerce are regulated by the Union government under the Union List (Entry 42).
 
 
 
• **Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution**
 
 
• The Seventh Schedule divides legislative powers between the Union and State governments into three lists:
 
 
• **Union List:** Subjects of national importance (e.g., defense, foreign affairs, atomic energy).
 
• **State List:** Subjects of state and local importance (e.g., police, public health, agriculture).
 
• **Concurrent List:** Subjects where both Union and State governments can legislate (e.g., education, criminal law, marriage).
 
 
 
• This division ensures a federal structure while allowing cooperation between different levels of government.

question:
**Fill in the blanks: **

The _____ List in Schedule VII deals solely with matters of national importance like defence and foreign affairs.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Union**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Union List** in **Schedule VII** of the **Indian Constitution** consists of subjects of national importance that require uniform policy across the country. 

• It includes **97 items** (originally 100), such as **defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, railways, banking, and currency**, which are exclusively under the legislative jurisdiction of the **Parliament of India**. 

• The subjects in the Union List are of such nature that they require centralized decision-making to ensure uniformity in administration and functioning across the nation. ***Hence, matters like defence and foreign affairs are included in this list.*** 

• **Article 246** of the Constitution specifies that Parliament has the exclusive power to make laws on any subject enumerated in the Union List. 

• Examples of topics in the Union List include **naval, military, and air forces**, **international treaties**, and **interstate trade and commerce**. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **State List:** 

• The **State List** in Schedule VII contains subjects of local or state importance, such as **police, public health, and agriculture**. Only the state legislatures can make laws on these matters. 

• It originally consisted of **66 items**, but some subjects have been moved to other lists. 

• Examples of State List topics include **markets and fairs, burial grounds, and libraries**. 
 
 

• **Concurrent List:** 

• The **Concurrent List** contains subjects of common interest to both the Union and States, such as **education, marriage, and adoption**. 

• Both Parliament and state legislatures can legislate on these subjects, but in case of conflict, the **Union law prevails**. 

• It originally consisted of **47 items**. 
 
 

• **Residuary Powers:** 

• Any subject not mentioned in the Union, State, or Concurrent Lists comes under the **residuary powers**, which are vested exclusively in the **Parliament**. 

• This provision ensures that unforeseen or new subjects like **cybersecurity** fall under the Union Government’s jurisdiction. 
 
 

• **Separation of Powers:** 

• The division of powers between the Union and State governments is a hallmark of India’s **federal structure**. 

• This separation ensures a balance of governance, with the Union List focusing on national interests and the State List catering to regional needs. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Historical Context:** 

• The division of powers was heavily influenced by the **Government of India Act, 1935**, which served as the blueprint for Schedule VII. 

• The framers of the Constitution intended to create a system ensuring both **autonomy to states** and **strong central governance**. 
 
 

• **Amendments to Schedule VII:** 

• The Union, State, and Concurrent Lists have undergone changes through **Constitutional Amendments**, reflecting evolving governance needs. 

• For instance, subjects like **education** have been moved from the State List to the Concurrent List. 
 
 

• **Judicial Interpretation:** 

• The judiciary often interprets disputes related to the scope of legislative powers under different lists, ensuring the **constitutional balance of power**. 
 
 

• **Examples of Union List Usage:** 

• The Union List has been invoked for national-level initiatives like the **Goods and Services Tax (GST)** and **international agreements**.

question: The Banking Regulation Act was passed in India in ________.
solution:
__
 
• The Banking Regulation Act was passed in India in the year **1949**__.

question: The _________ considers a marriage as complete and binding at the completion of the Saptapadi ritual.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Section 7 in The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 says:-**

 
• A** Hindu marriage may be solemnized in accordance with the customary rites and ceremonies **of either party.
 
• **Rites and ceremonies include the saptapadi.**
 
• It is a ritual of **taking seven steps by the bridegroom and the bride jointly before the sacred fire**.
 
• The **marriage becomes complete and binding when the seventh step is taken.​**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points__**

__
 
• **The Saptapadi ceremony:**

 
 
• **Establishes the commitment the couple** makes to each other during the Hindu wedding ceremony.
 
• Saptapadi quite literally** translates from Sanskrit to ‘seven steps’.**
 
• The **couple takes seven full circles,** walking clockwise around the ceremonial fire.
 
• **Circles represent the seven principles and promises they make to each other.​**
 
 
 
• **​**Hindu Marriage Act, 1955
 
 
• India is mainly a Hindu-dominated country.
 
• Therefore, Hindu marriages are mainly governed by “The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.”
 
• ​The Act came into force on May 18, 1955
 
• It is applicable to the whole of India except the state of Jammu & Kashmir.
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **​​Indian Christian Marriage Act, 1862:**

 
 
• Act consolidates the law related to the **solemnizing of Indian Christian Marriage.**
 
• **Enacted on 18th July 1872.**
 
• Applicable to the** whole of India except Cochin, Manipur, and Jammu & Kashmir.**
 
• The **act contains 88 Sections in 8 Parts and 4 Schedules. ​**
 
 
 
• **Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936:**
 
 
• **​Parsis **are governed in the matters of **marriage and divorce by the Parsi Marriage and Divorce Act, 1936.**
 
• The **Act is divided into six chapters.**
 
• It **deals with marriage between Parsis,** matrimonial courts, matrimonial suits, children of the parties, and miscellaneous provisions.
 
• **Section 2(7) of the Act says a ‘Parsi’ means a Parsi Zoroastrian.**
 
 
 
• **Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937​**
 
 
• ​The **Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act was passed in 1937.**
 
• The** aim was to formulate an Islamic law code for Indian Muslims.**
 
• For the Muslims on the other hand, the writings in the Quran would be of foremost importance.
 
• **Shariat Application Act, 1937 mandates aspects of Muslim social life such as marriage, divorce,** **inheritance, and family relations.**
 
• The Act lays out that in matters of a personal dispute the State shall not interfere.

• The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 was intended to secure the rights of marriage for the bride and groom who are Hindus and are bound under the sacred bond of marriage under any ceremony.

• Verification of all the documents is carried out on the date of application and thereafter Marriage is registered on the same working day by the registrar of marriage appointed by the Govt. of India and a marriage certificate is issued.
 
• **Section 5** of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 makes a marriage lawful only if the groom has attained the age of 21 years at the time of marriage and the bride has attained the age of 18 years at the time of marriage.

__
 
• **The Competition (Amendment) Bill, 2022 **proposes to reduce the timeline for the CCI to pass an order on transactions from **210 days to 150 days.**
 
• It seeks to amend the **Competition Act, 2002.**
 
• The Act prohibits any person or enterprise from entering into a combination which may cause adverse effect on competition.
 
• Combinations mean mergers, acquisitions, or amalgamation of enterprises.
 
• The Act defines control as control over the affairs or management by one or more enterprises over another enterprise or group.
 
• The Act specifies that any combination shall not come into effect until the CCI has passed an order or 210 days have passed from the day when an application for approval was filed.
 
• **CCI** may initiate proceedings against enterprises on grounds of entering into anti-competitive agreements and abuse of dominant position.
 
• The Act empowers the central government to appoint a **Director General to CCI.**
 
• It states required qualification of members of **CCI.**
 
• The Bill changes the nature of punishment for certain offences from imposition of fine to penalty.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Competition Commission of India**

 
 
• ​The objectives of the Act are sought to be achieved through the Competition Commission of India, which has been established by the Central Government with effect from 14th October 2003.
 
• The Competition Commission of India's goal is to create and sustain fair competition in the economy that will provide a ‘level playing field’ to the producers and make the markets work for the welfare of the consumers.
 
• CCI consists of a Chairperson and 6 Members appointed by the Central Government. 
 
• It is the duty of the Commission to eliminate practices having an adverse effect on competition, promote and sustain competition, protect the interests of consumers and ensure freedom of trade in the markets of India. Hence, option 4 is correct.

question: Which of the following does NOT come under the Fundamental Duties in the Constitution of India?

options.text: Safeguard public property and to abjure violence
Cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
Uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India

solution:
The correct answer is the __**Exercise adult franchise.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The** Fundamental Duties** are enshrined in **Part IV-A **of the Constitution and were added by the **42nd Amendment in 1976.**
 
• There are **11 Fundamental Duties** listed in** Article 51-A,** which are **non-justiciable **in nature, meaning that they **cannot be enforced** by law.
 
• The exercise of the adult franchise is** not** a Fundamental Duty, but rather a Right given to citizens under **Article 326** of the Constitution.
 
• **51(A)(a)**: Abide by the Constitution, respect its ideals, the National Flag, and the National Anthem.
 
• **51(A)(b):** Cherish and follow ideals from the national struggle for freedom.
 
• **51(A)(c):** Uphold the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India.
 
• **51(A)(d): **Defend the country and render national service when required.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Exercise adult franchise **refers to the **right to vote** in elections, which is a key feature of a **democratic system.**
 
• **Safeguarding public property and abjuring violence** is important for maintaining **law and order** in the country.
 
• **Cherishing and following the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom** is a way of paying **homage to the leaders** and movements that fought for India's independence.
 
• **Upholding and protecting the sovereignty, unity, and integrity of India** is crucial for maintaining **national security and preventing any threats** to the country's territorial integrity.

question: In which of the following years was the Right of Persons with Disabilities Act passed?
solution:
The correct answer is __**2016**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Right of Persons with Disabilities Act was passed in the year **2016**.
 
• This act replaced the earlier Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights, and Full Participation) Act, 1995.
 
• The act aims to give effect to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which India ratified in 2007.
 
• The act covers a range of rights and entitlements for persons with disabilities, including education, employment, and social security.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights, and Full Participation) Act, 1995**

 
 
• This was the first comprehensive law in India concerning the rights of persons with disabilities.
 
• It provided for equal opportunities and full participation of persons with disabilities in society.
 
• The act focused on prevention and early detection of disabilities, education, employment, and non-discrimination.
 
 
 
• **United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD)**
 
 
• The UNCRPD is an international human rights treaty aimed at protecting the rights and dignity of persons with disabilities.
 
• Adopted on 13 December 2006 and entered into force on 3 May 2008.
 
• India signed the convention on 30 March 2007 and ratified it on 1 October 2007.
 
• The convention requires countries to promote, protect, and ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disabilities.
 
 
 
• **Right of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016**
 
 
• This act was enacted to comply with the UNCRPD and to address the gaps in the 1995 Act.
 
• It recognizes 21 types of disabilities, compared to 7 in the 1995 Act.
 
• The act mandates that persons with disabilities have the right to equality, life with dignity, and respect for their integrity.
 
• It includes provisions for reservation in education and employment, social security, and accessibility.

question:
Consider the following statements related to the Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) handbook.

1.It will be launched by the Ministry of Science and Technology.

2.ODR is the resolution for cases outside courts using digital technology and techniques of Alternative Dispute Resolution

(ADR), such as negotiation, mediation and arbitration.

3.The development of ICT and increased use of internet has played a major role for ODR.

Which of the given statements is/are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Only 2 and 3**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• Statement 2 is correct because ODR refers to resolving disputes outside the courts using digital technology and techniques such as negotiation, mediation, and arbitration.

• Statement 3 is correct because the development of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) and increased use of the internet have significantly contributed to the growth and implementation of ODR.

• Statement 1 is incorrect because the ODR handbook is not launched by the Ministry of Science and Technology. It is typically associated with the Ministry of Law and Justice or other relevant legal bodies.

• Therefore, only statements 2 and 3 are correct.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Online Dispute Resolution (ODR)**

• ODR is a mechanism for resolving disputes via the internet and other digital means, bypassing the need for physical presence in a courtroom.

• ODR often involves the use of Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) techniques such as negotiation, mediation, and arbitration.

• It aims to make the dispute resolution process more efficient, accessible, and cost-effective.

• ODR can be particularly beneficial for cross-border disputes, where parties are located in different countries.

• **Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR)**

• ADR encompasses various methods for resolving disputes outside traditional judicial processes.

• Common ADR techniques include negotiation, mediation, arbitration, and conciliation.

• ADR is favored for its ability to provide more flexible, speedy, and amicable solutions compared to court litigation.

• It is often less formal, less expensive, and can be tailored to the specific needs of the parties involved.

• **Information and Communication Technology (ICT)**

• ICT refers to technologies that provide access to information through telecommunications.

• It includes the internet, wireless networks, cell phones, and other communication mediums.

• ICT has revolutionized how information is accessed, shared, and utilized, significantly impacting various sectors, including dispute resolution.

• The growth of ICT has enabled the development of platforms and tools that facilitate ODR.

• Advanced techniques like molecular breeding and genetic engineering are also being employed to accelerate the development of superior sugarcane varieties.

• Research areas include crop improvement, soil health, pest and disease management, water use efficiency, and sustainable farming practices.
 
• Institutions like ICAR, State Agricultural Universities (SAUs), and Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) play a vital role in conducting and disseminating agricultural research.
 
• Collaborative efforts with international organizations and the private sector also contribute to the advancement of agricultural research in the country.

• **Tarak Nath Das** was an Indian revolutionary and a professor of political science. He was one of the key members of the Indian independence movement against British rule.

• Various revolutionary activities were carried out both within India and in other parts of the world where Indians resided, including Europe and North America.
 
 
 
• **Ghadar Party**
 
 
• The Ghadar Party was an organization founded by Indian immigrants in the United States and Canada with the aim of securing India's independence from British rule.
 
• It was established in 1913 and played a significant role in mobilizing Indians abroad to support the cause of Indian independence.
 
• Many members of the Ghadar Party were involved in revolutionary activities and sought to incite rebellion against British authorities in India.

question: The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 empowers the ________ to establish authorities charged with the mandate of preventing environmental pollution in all its forms.

The correct answer is __**Central Government**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, is an Act of the Parliament of India, enacted in the wake of the Bhopal Gas Tragedy.
 
• The Act empowers the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution and to establish authorities for the purpose.
 
• It provides the Central Government with the authority to take all necessary measures to protect and improve the quality of the environment.
 
• It encompasses a wide range of regulations and standards to control pollution and manage hazardous substances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986**

 
 
• The Act was passed in response to the need for overarching legislation to protect and improve the environment.
 
• The Act gives the Central Government the power to take measures for environmental protection, such as setting standards for emissions or discharge of environmental pollutants from various sources.
 
• It provides a framework for coordinating the activities of various central and state authorities established under other laws to ensure environmental protection.
 
• The Act also includes provisions for penalties for contravention of the standards and restrictions set by the government.
 
 
 
• **Key Provisions of the Act**
 
 
• **Section 3:** Empowers the Central Government to take measures to protect and improve the environment and to prevent, control, and abate environmental pollution.
 
• **Section 6:** Empowers the Central Government to make rules to regulate environmental pollution, including standards for the quality of the environment, and the maximum allowable concentrations of various pollutants.
 
• **Section 15:** Provides for penalties for non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, including imprisonment and fines.
 
• **Section 19:** Allows any person to file a complaint in a court of law against anyone who fails to comply with the Act's provisions.
 
 
 
• **Importance of the Act**
 
 
• The Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, serves as a comprehensive framework for the protection and improvement of the environment in India.
 
• It addresses the need for a unified approach to environmental regulation and management.
 
• The Act empowers the government to take proactive measures to prevent environmental degradation and to respond effectively to environmental emergencies.
 
• It plays a crucial role in ensuring sustainable development and safeguarding public health and well-being.

• It is not solely governed through annual Heads of State Summits but includes several ministerial meetings, working groups, and collaborative initiatives to ensure effective coordination and implementation.

question: Which mechanism did India operationalize in 2024 to strengthen regional financial resilience within SAARC?
solution:
The correct answer is __**SAARC Currency Swap Framework (2024-27)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The SAARC Currency Swap Framework (2024-27) was operationalized by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to enhance financial cooperation and stability among SAARC member nations.
 
• Under this mechanism, India provides short-term financial assistance in foreign currency to SAARC member countries facing liquidity constraints.
 
• The total corpus for the framework is USD 2 billion, with each eligible member country allowed to withdraw up to USD 400 million within specified limits.
 
• The framework aims to strengthen regional financial resilience, mitigate balance of payment crises, and promote economic stability within the SAARC region.
 
• The currency swap facility is offered in major international currencies (e.g., USD, EUR) or Indian Rupees to support member nations in times of financial distress.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **SAARC Development Fund (SDF) capital increase**:

 
 
• The SAARC Development Fund was established in 2010 to promote regional integration and economic development in SAARC member states.
 
• It primarily funds projects under its three windows: Social, Economic, and Infrastructure development.
 
• Although increasing the SDF's capital has been proposed, it is not directly linked to the financial resilience mechanisms implemented in 2024.
 
 
 
• **About SAARC**:
 
 
• The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was established in 1985 to promote economic, social, and cultural cooperation among its eight member states: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan, and Sri Lanka.
 
• SAARC initiatives aim to foster regional integration, address common challenges, and promote sustainable development within South Asia.

question: Fill in the blanks: Established in 1961 within the former Palace of the Maharaja of Patiala, the National Institute of Sports was later renamed as the Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports (NSNIS) on ______ .
solution:
The correct answer is __**23rd January 1973**__.

__
 
• The National Institute of Sports (NIS) was established in 1961 within the premises of the historic Palace of the Maharaja of Patiala, Punjab.
 
• It was renamed as the **Netaji Subhas National Institute of Sports (NSNIS)** on **23rd January 1973**.
 
• The renaming was done in honor of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, a prominent leader in India’s freedom struggle, whose birth anniversary falls on January 23rd.
 
• NSNIS is widely regarded as the "Mecca" of Indian sports, providing professional training and technical education in various sports disciplines.
 
• It functions under the aegis of the **Sports Authority of India (SAI)** and plays a pivotal role in nurturing and developing athletes and sports coaches in the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Institute of Sports (NIS) and its importance**:

 
 
• The institute offers advanced training programs for athletes and coaches in a range of disciplines, including athletics, hockey, football, boxing, and wrestling.
 
• It also conducts diploma and certification courses in sports coaching, equipping individuals with the skills to train athletes effectively.
 
• NSNIS has played a key role in producing several Olympians and international-level athletes for India.
 
• It continues to be a hub for sports research and the development of modern training methodologies.

question: Bharatiya Nagarik suraksha Samhita(BNSS) ensures access to FIR through which portal?
solution:
The correct answer is __**CCTNS**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS)** is a comprehensive and integrated system for effective policing through e-Governance.
 
• It was launched by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), Government of India, in 2009 as part of the national e-governance initiative.
 
• CCTNS facilitates a nationwide networked infrastructure for tracking crime and criminals in real-time, ensuring seamless sharing of information between police stations and higher police authorities.
 
• The system also enables citizens to access police services such as lodging FIRs, tracking case status, and obtaining verification certificates online.
 
• As of now, most states and union territories in India use the CCTNS platform to provide services like digital filing of FIRs, improving transparency and efficiency in policing activities.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Crime Portal**

 
 
• It is not a specific portal but often refers to platforms like the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) website.
 
• The NCRB is responsible for collecting and analyzing crime data as mandated by the Ministry of Home Affairs but does not directly allow citizens to lodge FIRs.
 
 
 
• **BHAVISHYA**
 
 
• BHAVISHYA is an online Pension Sanction and Payment Tracking System launched by the Government of India.
 
• It is designed to cater to retiring employees for tracking their pension process, ensuring transparency and timely disbursal.
 
• This portal is unrelated to crime or police services.
 
 
 
• **DIGI-FIR**
 
 
• DIGI-FIR is a concept introduced in some states like Madhya Pradesh to allow citizens to lodge FIRs online.
 
• While it serves a similar purpose, it is not implemented nationwide or as comprehensively as CCTNS.
 
 
 
• **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Samhita (BNSS)**
 
 
• The BNSS is a proposed draft legislation aimed at replacing the existing Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to modernize and streamline the criminal justice system in India.
 
• One of its key features is enabling citizens to access FIRs and other police services online, which aligns with the goals of CCTNS.

question:
**Consider the following statements:**

1. Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill.

2. Every Financial Bill is a Money Bill.

Which of the above statements is/are **correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• A Money Bill is a specific type of Financial Bill under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill because it contains provisions exclusively dealing with financial matters such as taxation, borrowing, expenditure, or other money-related issues.
 
• However, not every Financial Bill is a Money Bill. Financial Bills can also include provisions beyond the scope of Article 110, requiring approval from both Houses of Parliament.
 
• A Money Bill can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha and requires the certification of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
 
• Thus, Statement 1 is correct, and Statement 2 is incorrect, making Option 1 the correct answer.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Money Bill**:

 
 
• A Money Bill is defined under Article 110 of the Indian Constitution.
 
• It contains provisions exclusively related to taxes, borrowing of money by the government, withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund or Contingency Fund, and appropriation of funds.
 
• It must be introduced in the Lok Sabha with the recommendation of the President.
 
• The Rajya Sabha can suggest amendments but cannot amend or reject a Money Bill. It has to return the bill to the Lok Sabha within 14 days.
 
 
 
• **Financial Bill**:
 
 
• Financial Bills are broader in scope and include Money Bills as a subset. There are two types of Financial Bills:
 
• **Category A:** These contain provisions related to financial matters and provisions not covered under Article 110. They need the President's recommendation and must be introduced in the Lok Sabha.
 
• **Category B:** These involve only incidental financial provisions and do not require the President's recommendation.

• The framework aims to simplify and enhance the efficiency of the Indian criminal justice system.

question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act is often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" due to the extensive changes it introduced to the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**42nd Amendment Act, 1976**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, is often referred to as the "Mini-Constitution" due to the extensive changes it introduced to the Indian Constitution.
 
• It was passed during the Emergency period under the leadership of Prime Minister **Indira Gandhi**.
 
• This amendment brought significant changes to the **Preamble**, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles of State Policy, and the powers of the Parliament and judiciary.
 
• It introduced terms like "**Socialist**" and "**Secular**" in the Preamble of the Constitution.
 
• It curtailed the power of the judiciary and strengthened the authority of the Parliament, especially in the context of amending the Constitution.
 
• The 42nd Amendment also extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from 5 to 6 years, though this was later reversed by the 44th Amendment.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **44th Amendment Act, 1978**:

 
 
• This amendment was enacted to undo the excesses of the 42nd Amendment, restoring the balance between the executive, legislature, and judiciary.
 
• It restored the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies to 5 years.
 
• It also ensured that Fundamental Rights like the Right to Property were no longer included as part of Fundamental Rights but rather as a legal right under Article 300A.
 
• Additionally, it introduced safeguards against the misuse of emergency provisions by requiring stricter conditions for the proclamation of national emergencies.
 
 
 
• **52nd Amendment Act, 1985**:
 
 
• This amendment introduced the **anti-defection law** in India by adding the Tenth Schedule to the Constitution.
 
• The purpose was to curb defections by legislators to ensure the stability of the government and uphold the integrity of the democratic process.
 
• It laid down conditions under which a legislator could be disqualified on grounds of defection.
 
 
 
• **86th Amendment Act, 2002**:
 
 
• This amendment made education a Fundamental Right under Article 21A of the Constitution.
 
• It mandated free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 years.
 
• It also altered the Directive Principles of State Policy by adding a new clause under Article 45, directing the state to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years of age.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are **correct**?

1) If a State law on a Concurrent List subject is reserved for the President and receives assent, it overrides the existing Union law on the same subject in that state.

2) Parliament can later nullify such a State law by passing another law on the same subject.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 3 (Both 1 and 2)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Statement 1:** When a State law on a subject from the Concurrent List is reserved for the President and receives his/her assent, it overrides the Union law on the same subject within that particular State. This provision is mentioned under Article 254(2) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• **Statement 2:** Parliament retains the power to nullify such a State law by passing another law on the same subject. This ensures the supremacy of Parliament as per Article 254(1) of the Constitution.
 
• The Concurrent List allows both the Union and State legislatures to make laws on certain subjects. However, in case of conflict between State and Union laws, Union law usually prevails unless the State law is specifically reserved for Presidential assent.
 
• Presidential assent under Article 254(2) enables State laws to have precedence over Union laws within the State, but this is not absolute. Parliament retains overriding powers to enact a law to nullify or supersede the State law.
 
• This mechanism ensures a balance between centralization and decentralization within India's federal structure, promoting cooperation between the Union and State governments.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Concurrent List:**

 
 
• The Concurrent List is one of the three lists in the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, alongside the Union List and the State List.
 
• It contains subjects on which both the Union and State governments can legislate, such as education, marriage, adoption, and bankruptcy.
 
• In case of conflict between Union and State laws, Article 254(1) ensures that Union law prevails unless the State law has received Presidential assent under Article 254(2).
 
 
 
• **Article 254 – Conflict of Laws:**
 
 
• Article 254 deals with conflicts between Union and State laws made on subjects listed in the Concurrent List.
 
• Clause 1: If there is an inconsistency between Union and State laws, the Union law prevails.
 
• Clause 2: A State law inconsistent with Union law can prevail within the State only if it is reserved for the President's consideration and receives assent.
 
• This article ensures that the federal structure is maintained while granting limited precedence to State laws under specific conditions.
 
 
 
• **Supremacy of Parliament:**
 
 
• Despite the autonomy granted to States in certain cases, Parliament retains overriding legislative powers over the Concurrent List subjects.
 
• Parliament can enact new laws or amend existing ones to nullify or supersede State laws, ensuring that national interests are prioritized.
 
• This highlights the unitary bias within India's federal system, where the Union has more legislative control than States.
 
 
 
• **Legislative Process in India:**
 
 
• Legislation in India is governed by the division of powers outlined in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution.
 
• The Union List grants exclusive legislative powers to Parliament, while the State List empowers State legislatures.
 
• The Concurrent List promotes cooperative federalism, allowing both levels of government to legislate while preserving Union supremacy in case of conflicts.

question:
**Consider the following statements:**

1. Delegated legislation is made by administrative authorities.

2. It cannot be challenged in a court of law.

Which of the above statements is/are **correct**?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1: Only 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Delegated legislation** refers to laws made by an administrative authority under powers delegated to it by the legislature.
 
• It is typically used to fill in the details of legislation that the primary law enacted by the legislature cannot cover comprehensively.
 
• Administrative authorities, such as government ministers or departments, are empowered to make rules, regulations, or orders under this framework.
 
• Delegated legislation allows for flexibility and expertise in lawmaking, especially in technical areas where detailed knowledge is required.
 
• While delegated legislation is legal, its validity may be challenged in a court of law if it exceeds the powers given by the parent act or violates constitutional provisions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Delegated Legislation: **

 
 
• Delegated legislation is essential to handle technical and specialized areas that require detailed rules and regulations.
 
• It saves time for the legislature by allowing experts and administrative bodies to draft specific provisions.
 
• However, it requires oversight to prevent misuse of power, and judicial review serves as an important safeguard.

question:
Which of the following statements regarding the constitutional responsibility of the Council of Ministers (CoM) is/are **correct**?

1) The Union Council of Ministers is collectively accountable to the Lok Sabha.

2) In states with bicameral legislatures, the State CoM is collectively responsible to the Legislative Council.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Option 1**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, as stated under Article 75(3) of the Indian Constitution.
 
• Collective responsibility means that the entire Council of Ministers shares responsibility for any decision or action taken by the government.
 
• They remain in office as long as they enjoy the confidence of the Lok Sabha. A vote of no-confidence can lead to their resignation.
 
• This principle ensures accountability of the executive (Council of Ministers) to the legislature (Lok Sabha) in a parliamentary system of government.
 
• Option 2 is incorrect because in states with bicameral legislatures, the State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly, not the Legislative Council, as per Article 164(2).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Article 164(2): Responsibility of State CoM**

 
 
• At the state level, the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly, not the Legislative Council, even in states with bicameral legislatures.
 
• This ensures that the executive at the state level remains accountable to the directly elected house of the legislature.
 
 
 
• **Vote of No Confidence**
 
 
• A government loses power if it fails to maintain the confidence of the Lok Sabha through a majority vote.
 
• A no-confidence motion can be moved against the government, and its passage results in the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers.
 
 
 
• **Bicameral Legislature**
 
 
• In India, a bicameral legislature refers to a legislative body with two houses: the Legislative Assembly (lower house) and the Legislative Council (upper house).
 
• The Legislative Assembly is the directly elected body, while the Legislative Council is partly elected and partly nominated.
 
• Collective responsibility applies only to the Legislative Assembly as it represents the will of the people.

question: What is the maximum detention period a Magistrate can authorize under Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita(BNSS), 2023, for offences punishable with less than 10 years, before default bail applies?
solution:
The correct answer is __**60 days**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, a Magistrate can authorize detention for a maximum period of 60 days for offences punishable with less than 10 years of imprisonment before default bail becomes applicable.
 
• Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), which is mirrored in the BNSS, governs the detention period authorized by a Magistrate.
 
• The 60-day period applies to cases where the offence is not punishable with death, life imprisonment, or imprisonment exceeding 10 years.
 
• If the investigation is not completed within 60 days, the accused becomes entitled to default bail as per the provisions of the law.
 
• This provision ensures the protection of individual liberty and prevents unnecessary prolonged detention without trial.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, is a comprehensive legislation replacing the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
 
• It aims to streamline criminal procedures and ensure justice delivery while safeguarding the rights of the accused and victims.

question: When was the Amateur Athletics Federation of India (AAFI) established?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1946**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Amateur Athletics Federation of India (AAFI)** was established in the year **1946** as the apex body for athletics in India.
 
• The AAFI was founded with the goal of promoting and regulating athletics in the country and ensuring the participation of Indian athletes in international competitions.
 
• It is now known as the **Athletics Federation of India (AFI)** and serves as the governing body for athletics in India.
 
• AFI is affiliated with the **World Athletics** (formerly known as the International Association of Athletics Federations or IAAF), which governs athletics worldwide.
 
• The Athletics Federation of India organizes various national-level athletic events, trains athletes, and ensures their participation in global competitions, such as the Olympics, Asian Games, and Commonwealth Games.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **1936**
 
 
• The year 1936 is historically significant for Indian athletics as it marks the participation of Indian athletes in the **Berlin Olympics**. However, the AAFI had not been established at this time.
 
• During the 1936 Olympics, Indian hockey team won gold, and the event was notable for the legendary athlete Jesse Owens' remarkable performance.
 
 
 
• **1956**
 
 
• The year 1956 is significant in Indian sports history as India participated in the **Melbourne Olympics**.
 
• Indian athletes competed in various events, but this year is not related to the establishment of the AAFI.
 
 
 
• **1966**
 
 
• In 1966, the **Asian Games** were held in Bangkok, Thailand, where Indian athletes won several medals.
 
• This year also saw the progress of Indian sports on the global stage, but it is unrelated to the founding of the AAFI.
 
 
 
• **Amateur Athletics Federation of India (AAFI)**
 
 
• The AAFI was established to promote and develop athletics at grassroots, national, and international levels in India.
 
• It was renamed as the **Athletics Federation of India (AFI)** in later years to better reflect its evolving role and responsibilities.
 
• AFI works towards organizing championships, selecting and training athletes, and ensuring adherence to international standards in competitions.
 
 
</ul
