 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Raja Rammohun Roy was a prominent social and educational reformer in India during the early 19th century.
 
• He founded the Atmiya Sabha in 1814, which later became the Brahmo Samaj, to promote social and religious reforms.
 
• The Atmiya Sabha was established to fight against the social evils such as caste discrimination, and to promote monotheism and rational thinking.
 
• Rammohun Roy is often called the "Father of the Indian Renaissance" for his efforts to modernize Indian society.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Raja Rammohun Roy:**

 
 
• Born on May 22, 1772, in Radhanagar, Bengal, Rammohun Roy was a pioneer in the Indian social reform movement.
 
• He opposed practices such as sati (the burning of widows), child marriage, and caste discrimination, advocating for women's rights and education.
 
• Rammohun Roy was also instrumental in the establishment of the Hindu College in Calcutta in 1817, which later became Presidency College.
 
• His efforts in advocating for the abolition of sati led to the regulation banning the practice in 1829 by the British Governor-General, Lord William Bentinck.
 
 
 
• **Atmiya Sabha:**
 
 
• Founded in 1814, the Atmiya Sabha was an organization that aimed to discuss and propagate the ideas of monotheism and rationality.
 
• The Sabha's meetings involved discussions on the Upanishads, Vedas, and other scriptures to interpret them in a way that promoted a monotheistic view.
 
• It served as a platform for intellectuals to debate and discuss various social issues and the need for reforms in Hindu society.
 
• The Atmiya Sabha's activities laid the foundation for the later establishment of the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, which continued the reformist agenda.
 
 
 
• **Brahmo Samaj:**
 
 
• Founded by Raja Rammohun Roy in 1828, the Brahmo Samaj was a socio-religious reform movement that aimed to purify Hinduism and promote monotheism.
 
• The Brahmo Samaj sought to eliminate social evils such as caste discrimination, child marriage, and the dowry system.
 
• It emphasized the importance of education, especially for women, and supported widow remarriage.
 
• The movement had a significant impact on the Indian society and influenced many later reformers and movements.
 
 
 
• **Social Reform in India:**
 
 
• The early 19th century saw the emergence of several social reform movements in India aimed at addressing various social issues and promoting modernization.
 
• Reformers like Raja Rammohun Roy, Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, and Swami Vivekananda played crucial roles in advocating for change and improving the status of women and marginalized communities.
 
• These movements laid the groundwork for future social and political developments in India, including the struggle for independence.
 
• The reforms also contributed to the development of a more progressive and inclusive society in India.

• He founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828 in Calcutta with the aim of reforming and modernizing Indian society by promoting **monotheism and rationalism**.

question: In which year was the temple entry movement started by Bhimrao Ambedkar?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1927**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The temple entry movement was started by Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar in the year **1927**.
 
• This movement was aimed at allowing untouchables or Dalits to enter Hindu temples.
 
• Dr. Ambedkar led several Dalits to enter the Kalaram Temple in Nashik, Maharashtra, which was significant for its religious importance.
 
• The movement was part of a broader effort by Dr. Ambedkar to fight against the caste system and for the rights of Dalits.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dr. Bhimrao Ambedkar**

 
 
• Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was an Indian jurist, economist, politician, and social reformer who inspired the Dalit Buddhist movement and campaigned against social discrimination towards the untouchables (Dalits).
 
• He was the principal architect of the Constitution of India and served as the first Law and Justice Minister of independent India.
 
• Ambedkar’s efforts to eradicate social evils like untouchability and caste restrictions were profound and were recognized by the nation, which posthumously awarded him the Bharat Ratna, India’s highest civilian award.
 
 
 
• **Temple Entry Movement**
 
 
• The Temple Entry Movement was part of the broader Dalit movement in India aimed at securing equal rights for untouchables.
 
• It was a social movement aimed at ensuring that Dalits had the right to enter temples and participate in religious activities, which were traditionally denied to them due to caste-based discrimination.
 
• The movement was significant in highlighting the issues faced by Dalits and in pushing for social reforms.
 
 
 
• **Kalaram Temple Satyagraha**
 
 
• The Kalaram Temple Satyagraha was a landmark protest led by Dr. Ambedkar in 1930, where he and his followers attempted to enter the Kalaram Temple in Nashik.
 
• The protest was aimed at challenging the traditional prohibitions that barred Dalits from entering temples.
 
• Though the attempt faced significant resistance, it marked a crucial step in the fight against caste-based discrimination and temple entry restrictions.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Movement**
 
 
• The Temple Entry Movement significantly contributed to the social reforms in India, paving the way for the eventual abolition of untouchability.
 
• It also helped in raising awareness about the plight of Dalits and inspired future generations to continue the fight for equality and justice.
 
• The movement laid the groundwork for legal and social changes, including the enactment of laws that prohibited untouchability and discrimination.

question: The Regulating Act of 1773 primarily introduced changes in the Company's administration in which two distinct areas?

options.text: Company's Judicial system and revenue collection.
Company's Military strategy and trade regulations.
Company's constitution at home and territorial control in India.
Company's relations with princely states and foreign policy.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Company's constitution at home and territorial control in India**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Regulating Act of 1773** was the first significant legislative intervention by the British Parliament in the affairs of the **East India Company**, aimed at restructuring its administrative framework both in India and in Britain.
 
• This act brought changes to the **Company’s constitution at home** by subordinating its commercial activities to the British Parliament, thus ensuring better oversight. The **Board of Control** was established to supervise the Company’s operations.
 
• In India, the act introduced changes in the **territorial control** by centralizing administration under the Governor-General of Bengal. **Warren Hastings** was appointed as the first Governor-General, with supervisory power over the presidencies of Bombay and Madras.
 
• It aimed to address issues of corruption and inefficiency within the Company’s administration in India, with the establishment of the **Supreme Court of Judicature at Calcutta** to oversee judicial matters.
 
• The act marked the beginning of the British government’s intervention in Indian affairs, establishing the foundation for the future **Parliamentary system of governance in India**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Provisions under the Regulating Act of 1773:**

 
 
• The Governor of Bengal was designated as the **Governor-General of Bengal** with a council comprising four members to assist in administrative matters.
 
• A **Supreme Court** was established at Calcutta in 1774, which was the first British court in India to administer justice.
 
• Direct control was established by the British Crown over the Company’s policies, marking the beginning of the dual system of governance.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Act:**
 
 
• It limited the autonomy of the East India Company by ensuring its accountability to the British Parliament.
 
• The act also prohibited Company officials from engaging in private trade or accepting gifts, reducing corruption.
 
• The revenue from India was to be disclosed to the British government.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Territorial Control in India:**
 
 
• By centralizing power, the act reduced administrative conflicts between the presidencies of **Bombay, Madras, and Bengal**.
 
• This centralization laid the groundwork for the British government’s consolidation of its hold over Indian territories.
 
 
 
• **Significance of the Act:**
 
 
• The act was the first step towards **regulating the affairs of the East India Company** and marked the beginning of British administrative control in India.
 
• It also reflected Britain’s emerging interest in Indian governance, which eventually culminated in the **Government of India Act of 1858**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Distinction Between Options:**

 
 
• **Option 1:** The act focused on governance rather than judicial system reforms or revenue collection, which were addressed in later acts like the **Pitt’s India Act of 1784**.
 
• **Option 2:** Military strategy and trade regulations were not the primary focus of the Regulating Act but were instead managed by the Company’s policies during that period.
 
• **Option 4:** Relations with princely states and foreign policy were not directly influenced by this act but were later addressed in the 19th century.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:** The act was a response to reports of corruption and mismanagement by the East India Company, particularly after its financial crisis in the 1770s.

__
 
• The Age of Consent Act, 1891, was enacted during British rule in India to address the issue of child marriages and improve the condition of women.
 
• It raised the minimum age of consent for marital relations for girls from 10 years to 12 years.
 
• It was introduced following the tragic death of an 11-year-old girl, Phoolmoni Dasi, due to marital rape, which led to widespread outrage and calls for reform.
 
• The Act aimed to protect young girls from forced sexual relations and exploitation within marriage.
 
• Though the Act faced opposition from orthodox sections of society, it marked a significant step in the social reform movement of colonial India.

• On **December 4, 1829**, Lord William Bentinck passed the **Bengal Sati Regulation, 1829**, which declared the practice of Sati as **illegal and punishable by criminal courts**. 
 
• The regulation applied initially to the **Bengal Presidency** but was later extended to other regions of British India. 
 
• This decision was supported by prominent social reformers like **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**, who actively campaigned against Sati and advocated for women's rights in India.

__

• He was a prominent **social reformer** during the 19th century in India and played a key role in the abolition of Sati. 
 
• He founded the **Brahmo Samaj** in 1828, which aimed to reform Hindu society by eliminating practices like Sati, child marriage, and caste discrimination. 
 
• Raja Ram Mohan Roy also argued that the practice of Sati was not mandated by Hindu scriptures and was against the principles of humanity. 
 
 
 
• **Lord William Bentinck's Reforms:** 
 
 
• In addition to abolishing Sati, Lord William Bentinck introduced several other reforms during his tenure as Governor-General. 
 
• He worked on improving **education** by promoting English as the medium of instruction and supporting missionary schools. 
 
• He also reformed the judicial system by introducing measures to curb corruption and ensure fairness in the administration of justice. 
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Abolition of Sati:** 
 
 
• The abolition of Sati was a **landmark reform** that marked the beginning of a series of social changes in India during British rule. 
 
• It set a precedent for future reforms targeting other social evils, such as child marriage and untouchability. 
 
• Although there was some opposition to the law, it was widely regarded as a progressive step towards gender equality and women's empowerment. 
 
 
 
• **Other British Governors-General:** 
 
 
• **Lord Dalhousie:** Known for his policies of annexation, such as the Doctrine of Lapse, and his role in modernizing India with the introduction of railways, telegraphs, and postal systems.

question: Under which Act was a Law Commission first established in India to codify and consolidate Indian laws?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Charter Act, 1833**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• The **Charter Act, 1833** was a landmark legislation passed by the British Parliament, marking significant changes in the administration of India.

• It was the first act that provided for the establishment of a **Law Commission** in India with the purpose of **codifying and consolidating Indian laws**.

• The Law Commission was headed by Lord Macaulay, who played a major role in drafting the **Indian Penal Code (IPC)** and introducing English as the medium of legal and administrative education. 

• The Act centralized legislative authority in India by vesting all law-making powers with the **Governor-General of India in Council**, aiming to unify laws across British-controlled territories. 

• The main objective of the Law Commission was to ensure a uniform system of laws for India, which would replace diverse systems of customary laws and local practices. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Charter Act, 1833:**

• The Act abolished the trading rights of the East India Company, transforming it into a purely administrative body.

• It introduced **civil services examinations** to recruit officials in British India, laying the foundation for modern bureaucracy.

• Under this Act, **Lord William Bentinck** was appointed as the first Governor-General of India, unifying the administration of Bengal, Madras, and Bombay under one authority.

• The Act aimed to promote the idea of **legal uniformity**, eventually influencing the codification of Indian laws like the IPC and CPC.

• **Law Commission of India:**

• The first Law Commission was established in **1834** under the Charter Act, 1833, with Lord Macaulay as its chairman.

• It played a pivotal role in drafting laws that still exist in modern Indian legal systems, such as the **Indian Penal Code (1860)**, the **Code of Civil Procedure (1859)**, and the **Criminal Procedure Code (1861)**.

• **Indian Penal Code (IPC):**

• The IPC was drafted by the first Law Commission and came into force in **1860**.

• It is the primary criminal code in India, providing detailed provisions for crimes, punishments, and procedural safeguards.

• The code is structured into 23 chapters and 511 sections, covering offenses ranging from theft to murder and cybercrimes.

• **Other Relevant Legislative Acts:**

• **Regulating Act, 1773:** Introduced the first attempt at regulating the East India Company's affairs but did not include provisions for law codification.

• **Government of India Act, 1858:** Transferred administrative control from the East India Company to the British Crown but was not responsible for establishing the Law Commission.

• **Indian Councils Act, 1861:** Marked the beginning of legislative councils but had no role in codifying laws.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Impact of the Charter Act, 1833:**

• The Act centralized legislative powers and paved the way for a unified legal system in India.

• It laid the foundation for modern legal and bureaucratic systems that continue to influence Indian governance.

• **Lord Macaulay's Contribution:**

• As chairman of the Law Commission, Lord Macaulay was instrumental in drafting the IPC and shaping modern Indian law.

• He advocated the use of English for legal and administrative purposes, fostering a uniform system of governance.

question: The Ilbert Bill controversy of 1883-84 was related to:

options.text: The imposition of new taxes on agricultural produce.

solution:

__

• The **Ilbert Bill**, introduced in **1883** by the then Viceroy of India, **Lord Ripon**, sought to allow Indian judges to preside over cases involving European offenders in criminal matters.

• During the colonial period, European residents in India were subject to a separate legal framework, which barred Indian judges from trying them. The Ilbert Bill aimed to remove this racial distinction in the judiciary system.

• The bill faced severe opposition, especially from the European community in India, who viewed it as a threat to their perceived racial superiority. This led to widespread protests and debates.

• The controversy highlighted the deep-seated racial tensions in colonial India and revealed the discriminatory practices prevalent in the British administration.

• The opposition forced the British government to amend the bill by introducing a compromise, where European offenders could opt to be tried by a jury consisting of at least 50% Europeans. This diluted the original intent of the bill.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Historical Context:**

• The Ilbert Bill was part of a series of reforms introduced by **Lord Ripon**, who is often referred to as the "Father of Local Self-Government in India."

• It was introduced at a time when Indians were increasingly demanding equality and justice under British rule.

• **Impact on Indian Society:**

• The Ilbert Bill controversy brought Indians together, as they saw this as an opportunity to demand equality in the judiciary system.

• It helped to strengthen the nascent **Indian National Movement**, as leaders like **Surendranath Banerjee** and others used this issue to mobilize public opinion against colonial injustice.

• **Racial Discrimination in Colonial India:**

• The opposition to the Ilbert Bill revealed the inherent racial biases of the British administration, where Europeans were placed above Indian citizens in matters of law and governance.

• It emphasized the need for a fair and impartial judiciary that treated all citizens equally, irrespective of their race.

• **Outcome of the Controversy:**

• Although the bill was amended and diluted, the controversy surrounding it became a significant milestone in India's struggle for independence.

• The Ilbert Bill controversy also demonstrated the power of collective action, as both Indians and Europeans organized protests to voice their opinions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Lord Ripon's Reforms:**

• Lord Ripon is known for introducing the **Local Self-Government Act** in 1882, which empowered local bodies such as municipalities and district boards.

• His tenure was marked by progressive policies aimed at involving Indians in administrative roles and promoting education.

• **European Opposition:**

• The European community in India argued that Indian judges were not competent to try Europeans due to cultural and racial differences.

• This opposition was rooted in the belief in the racial superiority of Europeans over Indians.

• **Legacy of the Ilbert Bill:**

• The controversy set the stage for future debates on equality and justice in colonial India.

• It also exposed the limitations of British liberalism, which claimed to promote equality but often failed to apply it in practice.

• **Pitt's India Act of 1784:**

• The Act was introduced by British Prime Minister **William Pitt the Younger** to rectify the shortcomings of the Regulating Act of 1773.

• It divided the Company’s functions into **commercial and political spheres**, with political activities coming under the control of the Board of Control.

• The Act also strengthened parliamentary oversight of the Company’s affairs in India.

• **Dual System of Control:**

• The governance of India was divided between the **Board of Control** (representing the British Crown) and the **Court of Directors** (representing the East India Company).

• **Impact of Pitt's India Act:**

• The Act paved the way for the gradual centralization of authority in British India.

question: The Government of India Act of 1935 primarily aimed to:

options.text: Establish a Dominion status for India.
Provide for a federal structure with provincial autonomy.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Provide for a federal structure with provincial autonomy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• The **Government of India Act, 1935** was a significant step towards the establishment of a federal structure in India by providing for a federation of Indian provinces and princely states.

• It introduced **provincial autonomy**, making provinces largely autonomous in their internal administration. This was a major shift from the earlier system of governance under the Government of India Act, 1919.

• Under this Act, the Governor's role in provinces was largely ceremonial, while elected provincial legislatures and ministries held significant powers. Hence, provincial autonomy was a key feature.

• This Act also proposed a bicameral legislature at the Centre, consisting of the **Federal Assembly** and the **Council of States**.

• It did not grant complete independence to India but laid the groundwork for a more decentralized and representative government. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*

• It did not establish Dominion status for India, as the British government retained control over defense and foreign affairs. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• The Act did not introduce universal adult suffrage. Voting rights were still limited to a small proportion of the population based on property, tax, or education qualifications. *Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Federal Structure:**

• The Government of India Act, 1935, was the first attempt to introduce a federal structure in India. While the federation was never fully implemented due to the lack of agreement among princely states, it laid the foundation for the federal system in the Constitution of India (1950).

• The Act divided powers between the Centre and the provinces into three lists: **Federal List, Provincial List, and Concurrent List**. This division of powers influenced the Indian Constitution.

• **Provincial Autonomy:**

• Provincial autonomy allowed elected representatives in provinces to take charge of their respective ministries and administrative functions without interference from the Centre.

• This autonomy was a step towards self-governance and gave Indians some experience in running their own government.

• **Key Features of the Act:**

• The Act abolished the diarchy introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919, at the provincial level, but introduced it at the Centre.

• It extended the system of communal representation by providing separate electorates for **Scheduled Castes, women, and laborers**.

• **Limitations of the Act:**

• The Act did not grant India independence or Dominion status, as ultimate power still rested with the British Crown.

• The Governor-General retained control over defense, foreign affairs, and certain reserved subjects, limiting the autonomy of the federal government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Background:**

• The Act was a result of deliberations at the **Round Table Conferences** held in London (1930-32), where Indian leaders demanded greater autonomy.

• It was the longest and most detailed legislation enacted by the British Parliament for India, consisting of **321 sections and 10 schedules**.

• **Influence on Indian Constitution:**

• Many features of the Government of India Act, 1935, were adopted in the Indian Constitution, including the federal structure, division of powers, and the concept of a bicameral legislature.

• The Concurrent List and the provision for emergency powers were also inspired by this Act.

• **Impact:**

• The Act was criticized for not granting full independence but was significant in providing Indians with experience in governance, which played a crucial role in preparing for independence.

• It marked a shift in British policy, indicating a gradual transfer of power to Indians, even though it was limited in scope.

</ul

• In 1875, farmers attacked a marketplace where many moneylenders lived.
 
• They burnt account books and looted grain shops. They also torched the houses of people who were both traders and moneylenders.
 
• The farmers’ main motive was to destroy the account books of the moneylenders and they resorted to violence only when these books were not handed over to them.
 
• The movement also got support from the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha co-founded by M G Ranade.
 
• Accordingly, the Deccan Riots Commission was set up which presented a report to the British Parliament in 1878.
 
• In 1879, the Agriculturists Relief Act was passed which ensured that the farmers could not be arrested and imprisoned if they were unable to pay their debts.

• **Ryotwari system:-**

 
 
• The Ryotwari system​ **of revenue collection** in India was introduced by the **British **during their colonial rule.
 
• This system was based on the** Ricardian theory of rent, **which states that rent is the** surplus income** earned by landowners due to the** differential fertility of land.**
 
• Under the Ryotwari system, individual farmers or ryots were directly responsible for **paying land revenue **to the government.
 
• This system was prevalent in areas where** landownership was fragmented** and there were no intermediaries between the government and the farmers.

• **Smith's theory :-**

 
 
• It​** **is based on the idea that rent is **paid for the use of land **that has a** fixed supply and is immobile.**
 
 
 
• **Malthusian theory :-**
 
 
• It suggests that as **population growth increases**, land becomes scarce and rents increase, leading to a **decline in living standards. **
 
 
 
• **Marx's theory :-**
 
 
• It​** **is based on the idea that rent is a** form of exploitation of the labor of tenant farmers **by landowners who hold a monopoly on land.

subject: GK
question:
The question consists of two statements, namely, Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Use them to choose the correct alternative.

**Assertion (A):** During the British rule, India’s exports exceeded the imports leading to surplus of balance of trade.

**Reason (R):** The surplus of balance of trade was used for growth and development of India.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true and R is false

solution:
The correct answer is __**A is true and R is false**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**Explanation**:

**Assertion (A)**: India did **indeed have a surplus in its balance of trade during most of the British Raj**.

 
• This means that the value of its exports exceeded the value of its imports.
 
• This was due to several factors, including:
 
 
• **Forced cultivation of cash crops**: The British forced Indian farmers to grow crops like** indigo and cotton for export**, even if it meant neglecting food production for domestic consumption.
 
• **Deindustrialization**: British policies **destroyed India's traditional industries, making the country more dependent on imported manufactured goods**.
 
• **Drain of wealth**: A significant portion of the trade surplus was not reinvested in India, but sent back to Britain as tribute and profits for British companies.
 
 

**Reason (R)**: However, the statement that the surplus of the balance of trade was used for the growth and development of India is **false**.

 
• The benefits of the trade surplus primarily accrued to the British, while India suffered from:
 
 
• **Underdevelopment**: The drain of wealth and focus on cash crops over food production stunted India's economic development and exacerbated poverty.
 
• **Exploitation**: **Indian farmers** and laborers were often **exploited by British companies and landowners, receiving meager wages and working in poor conditions**.
 
• **Lack of infrastructure**: Despite the trade surplus, the British invested **very little in India's infrastructure**, such as roads, railways, and education, which further hampered development.
 
 

 

Therefore, while it is true that **India had a positive balance of trade under British rule**, the **surplus was not used for its growth and development**, but rather benefited the British at the expense of the Indian people.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Permanent Settlement was introduced by the East India Company during the tenure of Lord Cornwallis in 1793.
 
• It was an agreement between the East India Company and Bengali landlords to fix revenues to be raised from land.
 
• This system was primarily implemented in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa.
 
• Under this system, the Zamindars were recognized as the owners of the land and were responsible for collecting and paying the fixed revenue to the Company.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Permanent Settlement**

 
 
• The Permanent Settlement was also known as the Zamindari System.
 
• The Zamindars were required to pay a fixed amount of revenue to the East India Company, irrespective of the agricultural yield.
 
• This system aimed to ensure a stable revenue for the Company and incentivize Zamindars to improve agricultural practices.
 
• However, it led to the exploitation of peasants and did not significantly improve agricultural productivity.
 
 
 
• **Lord Cornwallis**
 
 
• He was the Governor-General of India from 1786 to 1793.
 
• He introduced several reforms in the administration, judiciary, and revenue systems of India.
 
• The Cornwallis Code, introduced in 1793, aimed to overhaul the administrative structure in British India.
 
• He is credited with laying the foundation of a structured administration in India.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Permanent Settlement**
 
 
• The system led to the emergence of a new class of landlords who were loyal to the British.
 
• It created a stark divide between the Zamindars and the peasants, leading to widespread poverty and indebtedness among the latter.
 
• The rigidity of the revenue demand often led to the transfer of land ownership and distress sales.
 
• The system was criticized for its failure to promote agricultural development and for exacerbating social inequalities.

question: ‘Drain of Wealth’, a critique of the colonial exploitation, was given by which of the following nationalist leaders?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Dadabhai Naoroji**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji, also known as the "Grand Old Man of India", was an early Indian political leader, merchant, scholar, and writer.
 
• He is best known for his work in the Indian National Congress and his influential economic writings on the drain theory, which criticized British economic policies in India.
 
• In his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India", he detailed how the British were draining India of its wealth.
 
• Naoroji's economic analysis and advocacy laid the groundwork for Indian economic nationalism and inspired future leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Drain of Wealth Theory**

 
 
• The "Drain of Wealth" theory proposed by Dadabhai Naoroji argued that Britain was systematically transferring Indian wealth to Britain.
 
• Naoroji highlighted that a significant portion of India's wealth and resources were being drained to Britain without any adequate economic or material returns to India.
 
• This theory was primarily articulated through his writings and speeches, particularly in his seminal work "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India".
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**
 
 
• Founded in 1885, the Indian National Congress was one of the first political movements to demand greater autonomy and self-governance for India.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was one of the founding members and served as the President of the INC three times.
 
• The INC played a crucial role in the Indian independence movement, advocating for civil rights, representation, and eventually complete independence from British rule.
 
 
 
• **Economic Nationalism**
 
 
• Economic nationalism is a body of policies that emphasize domestic control of the economy, labor, and capital formation, often advocating protectionism and import substitution.
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji's critique of British economic policies laid the foundation for economic nationalism in India, influencing the Swadeshi movement and later economic policies post-independence.

solution:
The correct answer is __Osman Ali__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Seven Nizams, who were also known as Asaf Jahis, ruled Hyderabad – the seventh, Asaf Jah Nawab Mir Osman Ali Khan Bahadur reigned till 1948**__.

 __
 
• From 1724 to 1948, Hyderabad underwent immense growth, both culturally and economically.
 
• The Nizam chose not to join the Indian Union after India gained independence in August 1947.
 
• However, his rule ended in September 1948, when the Indian Army launched Operation Polo under the leadership of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the then Home Minister and Deputy Prime Minister of India.
 
• The State of Hyderabad was invaded and the Nizam was forced to step down.
 
• The Asaf Jahis were allowed to keep their titles even after their reign ended.
 
• Asaf Jah VII chose his grandson Nawab Mir Barakat Ali Khan Bahadur Mukarram Jah as his successor, but he was Nizam only in name.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Nasir Jung**

 
 
• Mir Ahmed Ali Khan Siddiqi Bayafandi, Nasir Jung, was the son of Nizam-ul-Mulk by his wife Saeed-un-Nisa Begum.
 
• He was born on 26 February 1712. He succeeded his father as the Nizam of Hyderabad State in 1748.
 
• He had taken up a title of Humayun Jah, Nizam ud-Daula, Nawab Mir Ahmad Ali Khan Siddiqi Bahadur, Nasir Jung, Nawab Subadar of the Deccan. However, he is most famously known as **Nasir Jung.**
 
• The Mughal Emperor Muhammad Shah bestowed him with the title Nasir Jung and later the next Mughal Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur appointed him as the Subedar of the Deccan and bestowed him with the title Nasir-ud-Daula.
 
• **His official name was Humayun, Nizam ud-Daula, Nawab Mir Ahmad Ali Khan Siddiqi Bayafandi Bahadur, Nasir Jang, Nawab Subadar of the Deccan.**
 
• He ruled Hyderabad State in India from 1 June 1748 to 1750.
 
 
• He was appointed as his father's Deputy during his absence in Delhi from 1737 to 1741.
 
• In 1741 he attempted to seize power but was defeated by his father at the Eid Gah Maidan in Aurangabad, on 23 July 1741.
 
• After his father's death, he ascended the throne on 2 June 1748 at Burhanpur.

question: On 21 October 1943, Subhash Chandra Bose proclaimed the formation of the Provisional Government of Free India in ________.
solution:
The correct answer is **__Singapore.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• On **21 October 1943**, Subhash Chandra Bose proclaimed the formation of the Provisional Government of Free India in **Singapore.**
 
• It was also called **Azad Hind or Free India**.
 
• It was established with financial, political and military support from Imperial Japan.
 
• **The Indian National Army (INA)** was the army of the Azad Hind government.
 
• Azad Hind had diplomatic ties with** Nazi Germany**, **the Italian** **Socialist Republic, the Empire of Japan, Thailand, Burma, Croatia, Manchukuo and the Second Philippine Republic**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Subhas Chandra Bose was born on **23rd January 1897, in Cuttack**, Orissa Division, Bengal Province, to Prabhavati Dutt Bose and Janakinath Bose.
 
• His Jayanti is celebrated as** 'Parakram Diwas'** on **23rd January**.
 
• At **Rangoon and Singapore**, Subhash Chandra Bose established two Indian National Army Headquarters.
 
• **The Rani Jhansi regiment **was created as a women's unit. **Lakshmi Sehgal** was in charge of the regiment.

question: The Poona Pact of 1932 was an agreement between Mahatma Gandhi and ______.
solution:
The correct answer is __**BR Ambedkar.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **On 24 September 1932, the Poona Pact was sealed between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B R Ambedkar in the Yerwada Central Jail, Pune. **
 
• Gandhiji was undertaking a fast against the British government’s decision to grant separate electorates for the ‘Depressed classes’.
 
• The separate electorate for Dalits was a topic upon which Gandhi and Ambedkar could not agree.
 
• **In the First Round Table Conference held in 1930, Dr. Ambedkar had demanded a separate electorate for the ‘Depressed classes’ whom he was representing.**
 
• Gandhi and the Congress Party were against the idea of separate electorates for any class as it was seen as a means to weaken and divide Indian society.
 
• The the**n British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald granted the ‘Communal Award’ to minority communities** including the ‘Depressed classes’.
 
• **Gandhi protested against this award** (also known as the MacDonald Award) **by undertaking a fast unto death **whilst in jail in Poona.
 
• **When Gandhi started his fast, there was public pressure on Ambedkar to step in and stop the fast. This resulted in the Poona Pact.​**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Provisions of the Poona Pact**__

 
 
• **Seats would be reserved for the ‘Depressed classes’ in the Provincial Councils.**
 
• The number of seats reserved for the provinces depended on the strength of the provinces:
 
 
• **Madras: 30; Punjab: 8; Bombay and Sindh: 15; Central Provinces: 20; Bihar and Orissa: 18; Bengal: 30; United Provinces: 20; and Assam: 7 (Total reserved: 148)**
 
 
 
• In the** Central Legislature, 19% of the seats would be reserved** for the Depressed Classes.
 
• The members of the depressed classes who were eligible to vote would form an electoral college. This College would elect four candidates among the depressed classes on the basis of a single vote.
 
• This** principle of ‘Joint electorate and reserved seats’** was to be followed in the Central Assembly too.
 
• It was** agreed that this system would continue for ten years **unless it was ended by mutual consent sooner.
 
• It was also agreed upon to allocate a** certain portion of money from the educational grant for the education of the depressed classes **in all the provinces.
 
• **Nobody would be discriminated against because they belonged to the depressed classes in the matter of election to the local bodies or appointment to government service.**

question: Who among the following became a part of the Constituent Assembly from Madras Constituency in 1946?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Ammu Swaminathan.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ammu Swaminathan was elected to the Constituent Assembly from the Madras Constituency in 1946. **
 
• **She spoke on fundamental rights and directive principles.**
 
• Ammu Swaminathan was** born in 1894 in Palakkad, Kerala.**
 
• **In 1917, she worked** with Kamaladevi Chattopadhyay, Annie Besant, Muthulakshmi Reddy, and others** to set up the Women’s India Association (WIA) at Adyar, Madras.**
 
• Swaminathan **was involved in the Quit India Movement in 1942** which led to her imprisonment a year later.
 
• Post-independence** she was elected to the first Lok Sabha in 1952 and subsequently to the Rajya Sabha in 1954.​**

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] Important Points__**

__
 
• **Kamla Chaudhry**

 
 
• Kamla Chaudhry was** one of those 15 women who were a part of the Constituent Assembly.**
 
• She was also** a talented short story writer and freedom fighter.**
 
• Kamla actively **took part in the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930.**
 
• She was** jailed several times **for her participation in the movement for independence.
 
• During the movement, **she joined Indian National Congress.**
 
• **She was the senior Vice-Chairperson during the fifty-fourth session of the All India Congress Committee.**
 
 
 
• **Hansa Jivraj Mehta​**
 
 
• ​Mehta was **one of the 15 women framers of the Indian Constitution.**
 
• She was **elected to the Constituent Assembly from Bombay** under a Congress Party ticket.
 
• In the Assembly, she **strongly argued in favor of women’s rights** and intervened in** debates on uniform civil code and reservations.**
 
• Mehta **participated in the non-cooperation and swadeshi movements.**
 
• Her** involvement with India’s freedom struggle** got her arrested in 1932.
 
 
 
• **Begum Aizaz Rasul**
 
 
• ​Rasul **stepped into electoral politics in 1937 **when she was **elected as a member of the U.P. Legislative Assembly.**
 
• She **continued to be a member of the U.P. Assembly until 1951.**
 
• Rasul was among the very few women, legislators to be** elected from a non-reserved province in British India- a remarkable achievement.**
 
• She was a strong opponent of **reservation for minorities in legislative assemblies, the partition of India, and feudal practices like the zamindari system. ​**
 
 

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

__
 
• Formation of the constituent assembly

 
 
• ​__Under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946, elections were held for the Constituent Assembly.
 
• The members were elected by the members of the provincial assemblies by the method of a single transferable vote of proportional representation.
 
• In the beginning, there were 389 members. But after the partition of the country into India and Pakistan, the number came down to 299
 
 
• 229 were from the British Indian provinces while the remaining 70 were from the princely states.
 
 
 
• The seats to the British Indian provinces and princely states were allotted in the proportion of their respective population and were to be divided among Muslims, Sikhs and the rest of the communities.

solution:
The correct answer is __**General Dyer.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **General Dyer British officer issued the infamous ‘crawling order’ whereby Indians had to crawl on all fours to pass an alley**.
 
• The crawling order of the British government is related to the Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
 
• The Jallianwala Bagh massacre, also known as the Amritsar massacre.
 
• Took place at Amritsar, Punjab on **13th April 1919.**
 
• General Reginald Dyer was the Brigadier (Acting) who ordered troops of the British Indian Army to fire into a crowd of unarmed Indian civilians.
 
• This incident shocked Rabindranath Tagore and he renounced his knighthood.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Warren Hastings:**

 
 
• He became th**e first Governor-General of Bengal in 1773.**
 
 
 
• **Lord Curzon (1899-1905):**
 
 
• He formed a Police commission in 1902 under the leadership of Sir Andrew Fraser.
 
• It recommended a separate Training centre for officers and constables.
 
• It introduced provincial police service and also at the same time made the Indian Army a modern fighting force then Commander-in-chief Lord Kitchener made reform in the Indian Military.
 
• He passed the Calcutta Corporation Act in the year 1899.
 
• He was the Viceroy who passed a law for protecting Ancient Indian monuments.
 
• He passed the law in 1904 that made the destruction of Ancient Monuments an offence and directed officials to collect and preserve ancient monuments.
 
• In India, the British Viceroy Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal (1905) despite strong Indian nationalist opposition.
 
• The government announced the partition in January 1904.
 
• Bengal was divided into two new provinces 'Bengal' (which comprises western Bengal and the province of Bihar and Orissa) and Eastern Bengal and Assam, with Dacca as the capital of the latter.
 
 
 
• **Lord Irwin (1926 AD-1931 AD): **Important Events
 
 
• Simon Commission visited India in 1928.
 
• Nehru Report, 1928.
 
• Lahore Session of the Congress, (1929) and Poorna Swaraj, declaration.
 
• Civil Disobedience Movement, 1930 started.
 
• Dandi March (12 March 1930).
 
• Gandhi-Irwin Pact, 5 March 1931.
 
• Sharda Act, 1929, under which the marriageable age of girls (14 years) and boys (18 years) was raised.
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhash Chandra Bose founded the Independence of India League.

The correct answer is __**Kaushal Konwar**__.

• He pledged to remain a **vegetarian and accepted the ShrimadBhagawad Gita as his only companion**.

question: ____________ announced the bifurcation of the British Indian Empire into a secular India and Islamic Pakistan.
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Louis Mountbatten.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Lord Louis Mountbatten** announced the **bifurcation of the British Indian Empire **into a **secular India** and** Islamic Pakistan** on **June 3, 1947.**
 
• The plan was known as the** Mountbatten Plan **or the **3 June Plan.**
 
• The main aim of the plan was to address the demand for a **separate Muslim state** in India, which was advocated by the **All India Muslim League** led by **Muhammad Ali Jinnah.**
 
• The plan proposed the creation of** two independent dominions** of **India and Pakistan**, which would have their **own constitutions and governments,** but would remain within the **British Commonwealth.**
 
• **Lord Ripon, Lord Dalhousie, and Lord Curzon** were also British officials who served as** Viceroy of India** during the British Raj but did not announce the bifurcation of the British Indian Empire.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Ripon **served as **Viceroy of India** from **1880 to 1884** and introduced various reforms, including the** Local Self-Government Act**, which provided for the establishment of** local self-government institutions** in India.
 
• **Lord Dalhousie** served as **Viceroy of India** from **1848 to 1856 **and was known for his** policy of annexation**, which led to the annexation of several **princely states** in India.
 
• **Lord Curzon** served as** Viceroy of India** from **1899 to 1905** and was known for his **administrative reforms,** including the** partition of Bengal** in **1905**, which was later revoked due to protests.
 
• Hence, the **correct answer **is option **3**, Lord Louis Mountbatten.

question: The famous scientist, Albert Einstein, was inspired by whose idea of non - violence?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Albert Einstein was known to greatly admire the philosophy and principles advocated by Mahatma Gandhi, particularly the concept of non-violence or "ahimsa".
 
• He had corresponded with Gandhi and expressed his admiration.
 
• There is a famous quote attributed to Einstein about Gandhi: "Generations to come, it may well be, will scarce believe that such a man as this one ever in flesh and blood walked upon this Earth".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vardhaman Mahavira**

 
 
• Born in 599 BCE in Kundalagrama, Bihar, in a royal family of the Kshatriya clan.
 
• Mahavira means "Great Hero" – a title he earned through his teachings. He's often referred to as 'Jain' since his followers are called 'Jains'.
 
• Became the 24th Tirthankara (religious teacher) of Jainism at around age 42 after 12 years of rigorous ascetic practices.
 
• He propagated the principle of Ahimsa (non-violence), truth, asceticism, and righteousness.
 
• His teachings included the central tenet of Jainism: the Three Jewels, or right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct.
 
• Mahavira is traditionally believed to have been born in 599 BCE and to have achieved Nirvana (release from the cycle of birth and death) in 527 BCE.
 
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**
 
 
• Born on 2nd October 1869, in Porbandar, Gujarat is celebrated as the International Day of Non-Violence.
 
• Led famous movements against the British rule, such as Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22), Civil Disobedience Movement (1930), and Quit India Movement (1942), which resulted in India's independence in 1947.
 
• Assassinated on 30th January 1948, by Nathuram Godse.
 
• His philosophy of peaceful resistance, known as Satyagraha, has inspired civil rights movements worldwide.
 
 
 
• **Gautam Buddha**
 
 
• Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, was the founder of Buddhism.
 
• He was born as a prince in Lumbini (present-day Nepal) but renounced his royal life when confronted with the realities of human suffering.
 
• His teachings, known as Dhamma in Buddhism, includes the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, which articulate the reality of suffering and the path to the cessation of suffering.
 
• Established the Sangha, an order of monks, for the spread of his teachings.
 
• Buddha is believed to have attained Nirvana (Enlightenment) under the Bodhi tree at Bodhgaya, Bihar, India.
 
 
 
• **B. R. Ambedkar**
 
 
• Full name Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, often known as Babasaheb, he was an Indian jurist, economist, and social reformer.
 
• He played a pivotal role in drafting the Indian constitution and is widely known as the "Father of the Indian Constitution."
 
• As a leading activist and social reformer, Ambedkar campaigned against social discrimination towards the untouchables (Dalits).
 
• He led the Mahad Satyagraha on 20th March 1927 to allow untouchables to use water from a public tank in Mahad, Maharashtra.
 
• As the first Minister of Law and Justice of India, he played a key role in drafting the Indian Constitution.
 
• He was also the one to lead Dalit Buddhist Movement in 1956 in India for the rights and upliftment of Dalits. His death anniversary on 6th December is observed as "Mahaparinirvan Diwas" across India.

question: 'Hind Swaraj' or 'Indian Home Rule' is written by which of the following freedom fighters?
solution:
The correct answer is__** Mahatma Gandhi.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Hind Swaraj:-**

 
 
• Hind Swaraj was written by Mahatma Gandhi in 1909.
 
• In this book, Gandhiji declared that British rule was established in India with the cooperation of Indians and had survived with their cooperation only.
 
• He added that if Indians had refused to cooperate, British rule would have collapsed and led to Swaraj.
 
 
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi:-**
 
 
• Mahatma Gandhi was a social reformist and leader of the Indian Independence Movement who introduced the idea of nonviolent resistance called Satyagraha.
 
• Birth: 2nd October 1869 in Porbandar (Gujarat)
 
• Brief Profile: Lawyer, politician, social activist, and writer who became the leader of the nationalist movement against the British rule of India. 
 
• Death: He was shot dead by Nathuram Godse on 30th January 1948.
 
• 30th January is observed as Martyrs' Day.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji:-**

 
 
• He was also known as the "Grand Old Man of India,"
 
• Naoroji was a Parsi intellectual, educator, cotton trader, and an early political and social leader.
 
• He was one of the founding members of the Indian National Congress.
 
• Naoroji served as a Member of Parliament (MP) in the United Kingdom House of Commons as a Liberal Party member.
 
• He is also credited with the founding of the concept of "Drain of Wealth" that held that Britain was taking away India's resources, leading to India's impoverishment.
 
 
 
• **Bal Gangadhar Tilak:-**
 
 
• He is known as Lokmanya Tilak.
 
• He was an Indian nationalist, teacher, and an eminent independence activist.
 
• He was the first leader of the Indian Independence Movement and is best known for his slogan "Swaraj (Self-rule) is my birthright and I shall have it!" adopted by the Indian independence movement.
 
• Tilak was one of the first and strongest advocates of "Swaraj" and a strong radical during the Indian Independence Movement.
 
• He is known for his attempts to mobilize Indian masses through religious symbolism, such as turning the annual domestic festival into a grand public event.
 
 
 
• **Annie Besant:-**
 
 
• She was born in Britain, Besant was a social reformer, women's rights activist, writer, orator, educationist, and prominent theosophist.
 
• She moved to India in 1893 and became a leader in the Indian National Congress.
 
• She launched the Home Rule League in 1916, aiming for dominion status for India.
 
• Besant was the first woman president of the Indian National Congress.

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi returned back to India in January 1915.**
 
• He returned from South Africa, where he fought the racist regime through the method of mass agitation.
 
• He called the method of mass agitation- Satyagraha.
 
• After arriving in India, he led various Satyagrahas in different states of the country.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Important years related to Mahatma Gandhi:-**

 
 
• 
 
1869: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi was born on October 2 in Porbandar, Gujarat, India.

 
 
• 
 
1888: Gandhi travelled to England to study law at University College London and was admitted to the inner Temple with the intention of becoming a barrister.

 
 
• 
 
1893-1914: Gandhi spent twenty-one years in South Africa, where he developed his political views, ethics, and political leadership skills. He experienced and witnessed racial discrimination, which was instrumental in developing his social activism.

 
 
• 
 
1915: Gandhi returned to India from South Africa.

 
 
• 
 
1919: Gandhi launched his first large-scale protest, the Satyagraha campaign against the proposed Rowlatt Act.

 
 
• 
 
1920-1922: Gandhi led the Non-Cooperation Movement against the British rule.

 
 
• 
 
1930: Gandhi led the Salt March, also known as the Dandi March, a 240-mile march to the Arabian sea to protest against the British salt tax.

 
 
• 
 
1942: Gandhi launched his last major campaign against British rule, the Quit India Movement.

 
 
• 
 
1947: India gained independence from British rule on August 15.

 
 
• 
 
1948: Gandhi was assassinated on January 30 in New Delhi by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.

question: Who among the following signed the Poona pact with Mahatma Gandhi?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhimrao Ambedkar.**__ [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Bhimrao Ambedkar:-**

 
 
• He​** **signed the** Poona pact** with **Mahatma Gandhi **in **1932.**
 
• The Poona pact was an agreement between the** leaders of the Dalit community** and the** Indian National Congres**s.
 
• It aimed to secure **reserved seats for Dalits **in the provincial legislative councils.
 
 
 
• **Poona Pact:-**

question: Which party formed the government in Britain in the year 1945?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Labour Party**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• In the 1945 general election, the Labour Party won a landslide victory, securing 393 seats out of 640.
 
• This election marked a significant turning point in British political history, with the Labour Party forming its first majority government.
 
• The Labour Party, led by Clement Attlee, implemented numerous social reforms, including the establishment of the National Health Service (NHS).
 
• The 1945 election is often seen as a mandate for post-war reconstruction and the creation of a welfare state.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Labour Party**

 
 
• The Labour Party is a centre-left political party in the United Kingdom.
 
• It was founded in 1900, growing out of the trade union movement and socialist parties of the 19th century.
 
• The party's platform has historically included policies aimed at reducing inequality and promoting social welfare.
 
• The Labour Party's 1945 victory is often credited to its promises of widespread social reform and economic recovery following World War II.
 
 
 
• **Clement Attlee**
 
 
• He was the leader of the Labour Party from 1935 to 1955 and served as Prime Minister from 1945 to 1951.
 
• Attlee's government is known for nationalizing major industries and public utilities and establishing the NHS.
 
• Under his leadership, the Labour government implemented extensive social reforms, laying the foundations for the modern British welfare state.
 
 
 
• **National Health Service (NHS)**
 
 
• The NHS was established in 1948, providing healthcare to all UK residents based on need rather than the ability to pay.
 
• It was one of the major social reforms introduced by the post-1945 Labour government.
 
• The creation of the NHS is considered one of the Labour Party's most significant achievements.
 
 
 
• **1945 General Election**
 
 
• The election was held on 5 July 1945, with the results declared on 26 July after votes from servicemen overseas were counted.
 
• It was the first general election to be held in Britain since 1935, as elections had been suspended during World War II.
 
• The Labour Party's victory ended nearly a decade of Conservative government under Winston Churchill.

The correct answer is __**1869**__.

__
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi** was born on **2nd October 1869**.
 
• His full name was **Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi**.
 
• Gandhi is widely recognized as the **Father of the Nation** in India.
 
• He played a key role in **India's independence movement** against British rule through his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **National Festivals of India**

 
 
• India celebrates three national festivals: **Republic Day** (26th January), **Independence Day** (15th August), and **Gandhi Jayanti** (2nd October).
 
• Gandhi Jayanti is observed to commemorate the birth anniversary of Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• On this day, various events and activities are organized across the country to honor his contributions and teachings.
 
• It is also celebrated as the **International Day of Non-Violence** by the United Nations.
 
 
 
• **Philosophy of Mahatma Gandhi**
 
 
• **Ahimsa**: Non-violence, the principle of not causing harm to any living being.
 
• **Satyagraha**: The policy of passive political resistance, especially that advocated by Mahatma Gandhi against British rule in India.
 
• **Swadeshi**: The focus on self-sufficiency and the use of domestic goods.
 
• **Sarvodaya**: The welfare of all, a concept aiming for the progress and upliftment of all sections of society.
 
 
 
• **Important Events in Gandhi's Life**
 
 
• **Salt March** (1930): A nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly.
 
• **Quit India Movement** (1942): A movement demanding an end to British rule in India.
 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement** (1920-22): A mass protest demanding self-governance and full independence.
 
• **Assassination**: Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated on 30th January 1948 by Nathuram Godse.

solution:
The correct answer is __**1931**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed on **5 March 1931** between Mahatma Gandhi and the then Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin.
 
• This pact marked the end of the **civil disobedience movement** led by the Indian National Congress against British rule in India.
 
• Under the terms of the pact, the British Government agreed to **release all political prisoners** who had been detained during the civil disobedience movement.
 
• Mahatma Gandhi, representing the Indian National Congress, agreed to **discontinue the civil disobedience movement** and participate in the **Second Round Table Conference** in London.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Gandhi-Irwin Pact**

 
 
• The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was a political agreement signed by Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy of India, Lord Irwin, in 1931.
 
• It was a significant event in the Indian freedom struggle, which led to the cessation of the civil disobedience movement that was initiated against the British Salt Tax.
 
• The pact included several concessions by the British Government, such as the withdrawal of all ordinances and prosecutions, release of prisoners arrested for participating in the salt march, and the return of confiscated properties of the satyagrahis.
 
• Gandhi agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference in London as the sole representative of the Indian National Congress.
 
 
 
• **Civil Disobedience Movement**
 
 
• Launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930, the Civil Disobedience Movement aimed at disobeying certain laws, demands, and commands of the British government, particularly the Salt Act.
 
• The movement began with the Dandi March, where Gandhi and his followers marched to the Arabian Sea coast to produce salt from seawater in defiance of British laws.
 
• This movement attracted widespread participation from various sections of Indian society and was a crucial step towards India's independence.
 
• The movement saw significant government repression, including the arrest of thousands of protesters and leaders.
 
 
 
• **Second Round Table Conference**
 
 
• The Second Round Table Conference was held in London in September 1931 and was attended by Mahatma Gandhi as the representative of the Indian National Congress.
 
• The conference aimed to discuss constitutional reforms in India and the future governance of the country.
 
• Despite the discussions, the conference did not result in any significant agreements, leading to Gandhi's return to India and the resumption of the civil disobedience movement.
 
• The failure of the conference highlighted the deep divisions between the British authorities and Indian leaders regarding India's political future.

• **Round Table Conferences**

• Key leaders included Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, and many others who contributed to India's fight for independence.

• **Mahatma Gandhi**

• The party contested the Bombay Legislative Assembly elections held in 1937 and won 15 seats.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Independent Labour Party (ILP)**

 
 
• The Independent Labour Party was established by BR Ambedkar on 15 August 1936 in Bombay.
 
• The ILP was formed to address the issues faced by the working class and the marginalized sections of society, particularly the Dalits.
 
• The party's manifesto emphasized the need for state socialism in the sphere of industry and agriculture.
 
• It also advocated for labor rights, including fair wages, decent working conditions, and social security measures for workers.
 
 
 
• **BR Ambedkar**
 
 
• Born on 14 April 1891, Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was a prolific scholar and an influential leader of the Dalit community in India.
 
• He played a crucial role in drafting the Indian Constitution and was a strong advocate for the rights of the oppressed and marginalized.
 
• Ambedkar's efforts led to significant social reforms, including the abolition of untouchability and the promotion of education and employment opportunities for Dalits.
 
• He embraced Buddhism in 1956 along with many of his followers, which marked a significant movement in the Dalit community towards religious and social empowerment.
 
 
 
• **Social Reform Movements in India**
 
 
• Social reform movements in India aimed at eradicating social evils and injustices prevalent in society, such as caste discrimination, gender inequality, and child marriage.
 
• Prominent social reformers included Raja Ram Mohan Roy, who worked towards the abolition of Sati, and Jyotirao Phule, who fought for the rights of the lower castes and women's education.
 
• These movements laid the foundation for a more equitable and just society in India by challenging traditional norms and advocating for progressive changes.
 
• The contributions of leaders like BR Ambedkar were instrumental in shaping modern India's social and political landscape.

question: Pingali Venkayya is widely credited for his significant contribution to the design of which national symbol of India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**The National Flag**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 

__ 
 
• Pingali Venkayya, a freedom fighter and a visionary, is credited with designing the **Indian National Flag**. 
 
• He presented his design for the flag in **1921** to Mahatma Gandhi during a session of the Indian National Congress held in **Bezwada (now Vijayawada)**, Andhra Pradesh. 
 
• The initial design by Pingali Venkayya consisted of two primary colors, **red** and **green**, symbolizing two major communities in India—**Hindus and Muslims**. Later, Gandhi suggested adding a white stripe to represent **all other communities** and a **spinning wheel (Charkha)** to symbolize self-reliance. 
 
• The current form of the Indian National Flag was adopted on **July 22, 1947**, with modifications to include three horizontal stripes of **saffron, white, and green** with the **Ashoka Chakra** in navy blue at the center. 
 
• Pingali Venkayya is often referred to as the **‘Designer of the Indian National Flag’**, and his contributions hold great significance in India's struggle for independence. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 

__ 
 
• **Pingali Venkayya’s Life and Contributions:** 
 
 
• Born on **2nd August 1876** in Bhatlapenumarru, near Machilipatnam, Andhra Pradesh. 
 
• He was a **Gandhian**, an educationist, and an agriculturist. 
 
• He was well-versed in **geology, agriculture, and languages**, and authored several research papers. 
 
• Pingali Venkayya actively participated in **India’s freedom struggle** and was closely associated with Mahatma Gandhi. 
 
 
 
• **Significance of the National Flag:** 
 
 
• The Indian National Flag is a symbol of **sovereignty, unity, and pride** for the nation. 
 
• The three colors of the flag represent: 
 
 
• **Saffron:** Courage, sacrifice, and selflessness. 
 
• **White:** Truth, peace, and purity. 
 
• **Green:** Faith, fertility, and prosperity. 
 
 
 
• The **Ashoka Chakra**, with 24 spokes, symbolizes the **eternal wheel of law (Dharma)**. 
 
 
 
• **Adoption of the National Flag:** 
 
 
• The flag went through several iterations before its final adoption in **1947**. 
 
• The Constituent Assembly of India adopted it on **22nd July 1947**, just a few weeks before India gained independence. 
 
 
 
• **Honoring Pingali Venkayya:** 
 
 
• In recognition of his contributions, the Government of India issued a **commemorative postage stamp** in his honor in **2009**. 
 
• His birthplace, Bhatlapenumarru, has become an important site for honoring his legacy. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

 
 
• The Indian National Flag must adhere to the **Flag Code of India, 2002**, which governs its usage and display. 
 
• The flag is made of **khadi (hand-spun cloth)**, a fabric promoted by Mahatma Gandhi during the independence movement. 
 
• The **design and proportions** of the flag are prescribed by the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). 
 
• The **first public hoisting** of the tricolor took place on **15th August 1947**, by India’s first Prime Minister, **Jawaharlal Nehru**, at the Red Fort in Delhi.

question:
Jayaprakash Narayan's concept of Total Revolution included which of the following components?

1. Social reforms to eradicate corruption

2. Political reforms to decentralize power

3. Armed struggle against the government

4. Economic reforms focusing on privatization

Which of these are correct?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1 and 2 only**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Jayaprakash Narayan's concept of Total Revolution** was a comprehensive movement aimed at transforming various aspects of Indian society, governance, and economy to build a just and corruption-free system.
 
• **Social reforms:** Jayaprakash Narayan advocated for the eradication of corruption, upliftment of marginalized communities, and fostering equality in society. This was a key component of Total Revolution. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Political reforms:** He emphasized decentralization of power, giving more authority to local self-governments such as Panchayati Raj institutions, and making governance more participatory. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***
 
• **Armed struggle:** Jayaprakash Narayan was a proponent of peaceful, non-violent methods for bringing change and explicitly opposed armed struggle. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Economic reforms:** He focused on economic equality and self-reliance but did not advocate for privatization. Instead, he supported Gandhian principles of local economies and self-sufficient villages. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***
 
• ***Thus, the correct answer is 1 and 2 only.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **About Jayaprakash Narayan:**
 
 
• Jayaprakash Narayan, popularly known as JP, was a prominent Indian independence activist, socialist, and political leader.
 
• He is best known for leading the **Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti)** movement during the 1970s against corruption, authoritarianism, and social injustice.
 
• He played a key role in the formation of the **Janata Party** and was instrumental in the movement that led to the end of the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975.
 
 
 
• **Key Components of Total Revolution:**
 
 
• **Social reforms:** Addressing issues like caste discrimination, economic inequality, and social justice.
 
• **Political reforms:** Advocating for participatory democracy, decentralization of power, and greater transparency in governance.
 
• **Economic reforms:** Promoting self-reliant villages, equitable resource distribution, and Gandhian principles of economy.
 
• **Education reforms:** Emphasizing value-based education to instill a sense of responsibility and civic duty in citizens.
 
• **Cultural and ethical reforms:** Fostering moral and ethical values in society to build a corruption-free and harmonious nation.
 
 
 
• **Non-violence and Peace:**
 
 
• JP believed in the principles of non-violence and peaceful protest, inspired by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• He rejected violent methods or armed struggles to achieve socio-political change.
 
 
 
• **Legacy:**
 
 
• Jayaprakash Narayan's contributions to Indian politics and society have left a lasting impact, particularly in the areas of grassroots democracy and anti-corruption movements.
 
• He was posthumously awarded the **Bharat Ratna**, India's highest civilian award, in **1999**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Emergency Period (1975-1977):** Jayaprakash Narayan became the face of resistance against the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi.
 
• **Role in Opposition Unity:** JP's call for Total Revolution united opposition parties, leading to the formation of the **Janata Party** and its victory in the **1977 General Elections**.
 
• **Influence on Youth:** His movement inspired a generation of young Indians, particularly students, to actively participate in politics and social reforms.
 
• **Books and Biographies:** Several books and biographies have been written on Jayaprakash Narayan's life and ideology, such as **"Jayaprakash Narayan: A Biography" by Bimal Prasad**.

question: C. Rajagopalachari led the Salt Satyagraha in which of the following states?
solution:
The correct answer is **__Tamil Nadu.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **C Rajagopalachari** led the Salt Satyagraha protest in **Tamil Nadu.**
 
• Inspired by the Dandi March by Mahatma Gandhi, a group of **100 men** led by C Rajagopalachari marched to **Vedaranyam and extracted salt from seawater in April 1930 to break the salt law imposed by the British**.
 
• He began his march from** Tiruchi on April 13 and reached Vedaranyam on April 28**.
 
• The Salt Satyagraha was an act of civil disobedience led by Mahatma Gandhi to protest British rule in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Salt March or Dandi March or Salt Satyagraha, was started by Mahatma Gandhi in the year 1930 in the March-April period.
 
• It was the protest of the Indian people against Britain’s Salt Act of 1882 which prohibited Indians from collecting or selling salt, a staple in their diet.
 
• Gandhi declared resistance to British salt policies to be the unifying theme for his new campaign of “satyagraha,” or mass civil disobedience.
 
• First, Gandhi sent a letter on March 2, 1930, to inform the Viceroy Lord Irwin that he and the others would begin breaking the Salt Laws in 10 days. Then, on March 12, 1930, Gandhi set out from his ashram, or religious retreat, at Sabarmati near Ahmedabad with several dozen followers on a trek of some 240 miles to the coastal town of Dandi on the Arabian Sea.
 
• In April, Gandhiji was joined with the tens of thousands of followers for their salt satyagraha.

question: In which of the following years was the civil disobedience campaign completely ceased?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1934.**__

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

 
• On March 12, 1930, Gandhiji inaugurated the civil disobedience movement with the Dandi Salt March.
 
• He broke the Salt Laws imposed by the British Government.
 
• The civil disobedience movement broadened into people refusing to buy foreign goods, a refusal to pay taxes and not attending office and school.
 
• Disturbed by this movement the British imprisoned Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.
 
• By the end of 1930, thousands of Indians, were in jail and the movement had generated worldwide publicity.
 
• Lord Irwin (British viceroy from1926–31) was looking for a way to end it.
 
• Gandhiji was released from custody in January 1931, and the two men began negotiating the terms of the pact.
 
• The Gandhi-Irwin pact was signed on March 5, 1931, and the two main clauses of the pact were to ensure Congress's participation in the Round Table Conference and the end of the civil disobedience movement.
 
• The **Second Round Table Conference in London** which Gandhiji attended with Sarojini Naidu, proved to be futile as the British did not honour their demands.
 
• The Viceroy, Lord Willingdon, in the absence of Gandhiji, adopted the policy of repression, the Gandhi-Irwin Pact was violated and the Viceroy took to the suppression of the INC. 
 
• Gandhiji resumed the movement in January 1932 and appealed to the country to join in.
 
• Gandhiji realised that the second phase of the civil disobedience movement lacked the organisation that marked its first phase, even though the entire nation put up a tough fight.
 
• The movement continued for six months. Gandhiji began a fast for 21 days on May 8, 1933, to make amends for the sins committed against the untouchables.
 
• He withdrew the mass Satyagraha on July 14, 1933, but the movement ceased completely on April 7, 1934.
 
• **Hence Civil disobedience campaign completely ceased in 1934.**
