question: Who was the founder of Harijan Sevak Sangh founded in 1932?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Mahatma Gandhi**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The All India Harijan Sevak Sangh is an independent national-level non-profit voluntary Organisation with Branches in 26 States.
 
• It was founded in September 1932 in the wake of Gandhiji's Epic Fast at Yervada Jail, Pune, resulting in the historic Poona Pact.
 
• The immediate historical background dates back to the Second Round Table Conference in London in 1931 when Gandhi Ji opposed the segregation of the depressed classes of the Hindu community into a separate electoral group.
 
• Gandhi Ji saw in it a sinister device of the British government to create a split in the Hindu community in furtherance of its policy of divide and rule.
 
• The Sangh was established to combat untouchability and a new weekly paper, the Harijan, was started.
 
• Harijan means children of God, it was Gandhi Ji's name for the untouchables.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
 

 Jawaharlal Nehru 
 
 
 
• Early Life and Education: Jawaharlal Nehru was born on November 14, 1889, in Allahabad, India.
 
• Role in the Indian National Congress: Nehru served as the President of the Indian National Congress several times before India achieved independence. He was the presiding officer at the Lucknow session in 1936, Faizpur session in 1937, etc.
 
• Imprisonment: Nehru was sent to jail multiple times by the British Government due to his role in the Civil Disobedience Movements of 1930 and 1932.
 
• First Prime Minister of Independent India: After India achieved independence on August 15, 1947, Nehru became the first Prime Minister. He held the prime minister-ship from 1947 until his death in 1964, which is the longest term so far in India's history.
 
• Role in the Non-Aligned Movement: Nehru was one of the initial leaders who advocated the policy of non-alignment in the Cold War politics and was instrumental in the formation of the Non-Aligned Movement, strengthening India's international standing.
 
• Death: Nehru died of a heart attack on May 27, 1964. His death marked the end of an era in Indian politics.
 
 
 
 

 Jyotiba Phule 
 
 
 
• Jyotirao Govindrao Phule was born on April 11, 1827, in Pune, Maharashtra, India. He was a merchant and also a member of the municipal council. He was inspired by a book called "The Rights of Man" by Thomas Paine.
 
• Phule believed that the only way to get rid of social problems was to educate women and people from lower castes. He started schools for girls and taught his own wife as well. He wrote important books like "Gulamgiri" (meaning "Slavery") and "Shetkarayacha Aasud" (meaning "Cultivator’s Whipcord"). "Gulamgiri" criticized the caste system and was translated into English as "Slavery".
 
• In 1873, he founded the "Satya Shodhak Samaj" to promote equality in society. He even started an orphanage for needy children, making him the first Hindu to do so.
 
 
 
 

 BR Ambedkar
 
 
 
• Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was the first minister of Law and Justice of India.
 
• He is known as the 'Father of the Indian Constitution.
 
• His Political Party: Scheduled Caste Federation, Independent Labor Party, Republican Party of India.
 
• His social Organization: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha, Samata Sainik Dal.

__
 
• **Moplahs:-**

 
 
• **The Moplahs, also known as Mappilas, are a Muslim community indigenous to the Malabar Coast of Kerala, India. **
 
• They are believed to have descended from Arab traders who settled in the region in the 9th century and intermarried with the local population.
 
• The Moplahs have a distinct culture and language, which is a mix of Malayalam and Arabic.

• It​ was the culmination of a series of riots by Moplahs (Muslims of Malabar) in the 19th and early 20th centuries against the British and the Hindu landlords in Malabar (Northern Kerala). 
 
• Most Moplahs were predominantly converted Hindus during Tipu Sultan's capture of Malabar.
 
• The prominent leaders of the rebellion were Ali Musaliyar and Variyankunnath Kunjahammed Haji.
 
• In November 1921, 67 Moplah prisoners were killed when they were being transported in a closed freight wagon from Tirur to the Central Prison in Podanur. They died of suffocation. This event is called Wagon Tragedy.

• Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was a prominent peasant leader in India and was deeply involved in the peasant movement.
 
• He founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) in 1929 to address the issues of peasants and farmers in Bihar.
 
• The BPKS played a crucial role in mobilizing peasants against the zamindari system and for the rights of tenant farmers.

• **Peasant Movement in India:**

• These movements were significant in shaping the agrarian policies of the country and addressing issues like land reforms, tenancy rights, and fair wages.
 
 
 
• **Zamindari System:**
 
 
• The Zamindari system was a traditional land revenue system in India where landlords or zamindars collected rent from the peasants and paid a portion to the British colonial government.
 
• This system led to the exploitation of peasants, high rents, and forced labor, causing widespread agrarian distress.
 
 
 
• **All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS):**
 
 
• The AIKS was formed in 1936 as a national organization to address the issues faced by peasants across India.
 
• It worked towards the abolition of the zamindari system, fair land distribution, and better living conditions for agricultural workers.
 
 
 
• **Swami Sahajanand Saraswati's Contributions:**
 
 
• He was a key figure in the peasant movement and worked tirelessly for the upliftment of the agrarian community.
 
• His efforts led to significant reforms in the agrarian sector, and he is remembered as a champion of peasant rights in India.

question: In which of the following cities did Mahatma Gandhi lead the peasant movement against the imposed indigo cultivation by the British planters?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Champaran**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Champaran is famous for the Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 where Mahatma Gandhi led a movement against the British planters who forced local farmers to grow indigo under harsh conditions.
 
• This movement marked Gandhi's first active involvement in the Indian freedom struggle and was a significant milestone in India's path to independence.
 
• The success of the Champaran movement brought Gandhi to the forefront of the Indian independence movement.
 
• The indigo planters in Champaran were exploiting the farmers by forcing them to grow indigo on a portion of their land and sell it at fixed prices, which was economically detrimental to the farmers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mahatma Gandhi**

 
 
• Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, popularly known as Mahatma Gandhi, was a prominent leader of the Indian independence movement against British rule.
 
• He is known for his philosophy of non-violence (Ahimsa) and civil disobedience, which he employed to lead India to independence.
 
• Gandhi's methods inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world.
 
• He is often referred to as the "Father of the Nation" in India for his pivotal role in the country's struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Indigo Cultivation**
 
 
• Indigo was a valuable dye in the textile industry during the colonial period.
 
• British planters in India forced local farmers to grow indigo under the Tinkathia system, where farmers had to grow indigo on 3/20th (or roughly 15%) of their land.
 
• This system was highly exploitative as the indigo crop depleted the soil, and the farmers received very low prices for their produce.
 
• The Champaran Satyagraha was a protest against this system and highlighted the plight of the farmers.
 
 
 
• **Satyagraha**
 
 
• Satyagraha is a form of nonviolent resistance or civil resistance.
 
• The term was coined and developed by Mahatma Gandhi during the Indian independence movement.
 
• Satyagraha is based on the principle of nonviolence and seeks to bring about social and political change through passive resistance and peaceful protests.
 
• It emphasizes the power of truth and the need to adhere to ethical principles in the face of injustice.

question: Who was the Viceroy of India when Mahatma Gandhi started Dandi March on 12 March 1930?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Irwin**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Lord Irwin served as the Viceroy of India from 1926 to 1931.
 
• During his tenure, Mahatma Gandhi launched the Salt March, also known as the Dandi March, on 12 March 1930.
 
• The Dandi March was a pivotal event in the Indian independence movement, protesting against the British salt monopoly.
 
• Lord Irwin was known for his efforts to engage with Indian leaders, leading to the historic Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Dandi March:**

 
 
• The Dandi March, also known as the Salt March, was a 24-day, 240-mile (390 km) march led by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• It began on 12 March 1930 and ended on 5 April 1930.
 
• It was a direct action campaign of tax resistance and nonviolent protest against the British salt monopoly.
 
• The march was a significant event in the Indian independence movement, garnering worldwide attention and inspiring numerous Indians to join the struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Gandhi-Irwin Pact:**
 
 
• Signed on 5 March 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Irwin, the then Viceroy of India.
 
• The pact marked the end of the civil disobedience movement in India.
 
• As part of the agreement, the British agreed to release all political prisoners, and Gandhi agreed to discontinue the Salt Satyagraha.
 
• The pact paved the way for Gandhi to attend the Round Table Conference in London to discuss India's future constitutional status.
 
 
 
• **Lord Irwin:**
 
 
• Lord Irwin, later known as Lord Halifax, was the Viceroy of India from 1926 to 1931.
 
• His tenure was marked by significant events like the Simon Commission, the Nehru Report, and the Salt March.
 
• He played a crucial role in negotiations with Indian leaders and was instrumental in the signing of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
 
• Lord Irwin's tenure is often remembered for his attempts to reconcile British interests with Indian aspirations for self-governance.

question: The Non-Cooperation Movement was called off after which of the following incidents?

options.text: Outbreak of the First World War

solution:
The correct answer is __**Chauri-Chaura incident**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Chauri-Chaura incident occurred on February 5, 1922, in the Chauri-Chaura town of the Gorakhpur district in the United Provinces (now Uttar Pradesh), British India.
 
• During this incident, a large group of protesters participating in the Non-Cooperation Movement clashed with police, who opened fire. In retaliation, the demonstrators attacked and set fire to a police station, killing all of its occupants.
 
• In response to the violence, Mahatma Gandhi, the leader of the Non-Cooperation Movement, called off the movement on February 12, 1922, emphasizing his principle of non-violence (Ahimsa).
 
• The Chauri-Chaura incident marked a significant turning point in the Indian independence movement, highlighting the challenges of maintaining non-violent discipline among the masses.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement**

 
 
• Launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1920, the Non-Cooperation Movement aimed to resist British rule in India through non-violent means.
 
• It was a significant phase of the Indian independence movement, advocating for Swaraj or self-governance.
 
• Key strategies included the boycott of British goods, institutions, and services, and the promotion of Indian-made goods and institutions.
 
• The movement saw widespread participation but was suspended after the Chauri-Chaura incident to prevent further violence.
 
 
 
• **Gandhian Principles**
 
 
• Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy centered around non-violence (Ahimsa) and truth (Satya).
 
• Gandhi believed in the power of peaceful protest and civil disobedience as tools for social and political change.
 
• He emphasized the importance of self-reliance, community solidarity, and ethical living.
 
 
 
• **Chauri-Chaura Town**
 
 
• Chauri-Chaura is a town in the Gorakhpur district of Uttar Pradesh, India.
 
• The town gained historical significance due to the incident of February 1922, which had a profound impact on India's struggle for independence.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Indian Independence Movement**
 
 
• The suspension of the Non-Cooperation Movement led to a period of reflection and re-strategizing within the Indian National Congress.
 
• It underscored the need for disciplined, non-violent resistance and influenced future movements, such as the Civil Disobedience Movement and the Quit India Movement.
 
• The incident also highlighted the complexities of leading a mass movement and the potential for deviations from non-violent principles.

question: The Salt Satyagraha of 1930 was a direct civil disobedience movement against which British policy?

options.text: The imposition of heavy taxes on land revenue.
The British monopoly on the manufacture and sale of salt.
The restrictions on the movement and assembly of Indians.
The introduction of separate electorates for different communities.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The British monopoly on the manufacture and sale of salt**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Salt Satyagraha, led by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930, was a nonviolent protest against the British monopoly on salt production and its taxation, which affected every Indian household.
 
• The British government imposed a salt tax and prohibited Indians from collecting or making their own salt, forcing them to buy it from government sources.
 
• On March 12, 1930, Gandhi and his followers began a 24-day march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, covering 240 miles, to produce salt from seawater as an act of civil disobedience.
 
• The march and subsequent acts of defiance against the salt laws galvanized nationwide support, symbolizing the broader struggle for Indian independence.
 
• The Salt Satyagraha became a turning point in the Indian independence movement, showcasing the power of nonviolent resistance and gaining international attention.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **The imposition of heavy taxes on land revenue**

 
 
• The British introduced systems like the Zamindari, Ryotwari, and Mahalwari to collect land revenue.
 
• These systems often resulted in exorbitant taxes, leading to widespread poverty and exploitation of farmers.
 
• While this issue caused significant unrest, it was not the direct cause of the Salt Satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **The restrictions on the movement and assembly of Indians**
 
 
• The British government implemented several restrictive laws, such as the Rowlatt Act, which curtailed civil liberties like freedom of assembly and movement.
 
• These restrictions led to protests like the Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919 but were not the primary focus of the Salt Satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **The introduction of separate electorates for different communities**
 
 
• The British introduced separate electorates for Muslims, Sikhs, and other minority communities through acts like the Government of India Act, 1919 and 1935.
 
• This policy was aimed at dividing Indian society along communal lines but was unrelated to the Salt Satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **Overall Theme: The Salt Satyagraha**
 
 
• The Salt Satyagraha was part of Gandhi's broader strategy of nonviolent resistance (Satyagraha) against British colonial rule.
 
• It demonstrated the ability of Indians to challenge unjust laws through peaceful means, inspiring similar movements worldwide.
 
• The movement emphasized self-reliance, unity, and the rejection of oppressive policies imposed by colonial rulers.

question: Who was the prominent leader during the Quit India Movement, remembered for hoisting the Indian flag at the Gowalia Tank Maidan in Mumbai in 1942?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Aruna Asaf Ali**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Aruna Asaf Ali** was a prominent leader during the **Quit India Movement**, which began on **8 August 1942**, under the leadership of Mahatma Gandhi.

• She is famously remembered for **hoisting the Indian National Flag** at the **Gowalia Tank Maidan** in Mumbai, defying British authorities and marking the commencement of the movement.

• The act of flag hoisting made her a symbol of resistance and courage, earning her the title of the **"Heroine of the 1942 Quit India Movement."**

• Despite the British crackdown and arrests of key leaders, including Mahatma Gandhi, Aruna Asaf Ali continued to inspire people and mobilize support for India's independence.

• She played an instrumental role in organizing underground activities and publishing revolutionary literature, including the **Congress Radio**, which broadcasted news and messages to keep the freedom struggle alive.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Quit India Movement:** 

• Launched by Mahatma Gandhi during the **Bombay session** of the Indian National Congress on **8 August 1942**.

• The movement called for the immediate withdrawal of British rule from India, with the slogan **"Do or Die."**

• It was a mass civil disobedience movement, involving strikes, protests, and boycotts across the country.

• The British responded with severe repression, including arrests, violence, and the disruption of communication channels.

• **Gowalia Tank Maidan:** 

• Renamed as **August Kranti Maidan**, it holds historical significance as the venue where the Quit India Movement was launched.

• The flag hoisting by Aruna Asaf Ali at this location became a symbolic act of defiance against colonial rule.

• **Aruna Asaf Ali’s Contribution:** 

• She was a staunch advocate for India's independence and actively participated in various movements, including the **Salt March** and **Quit India Movement**.

• She served as a member of the Indian National Congress and later joined the **Socialist Party** and **Communist Party of India**.

• Post-independence, she continued her activism, focusing on social welfare and education reforms.

• **Legacy:** 

• She was awarded the **Bharat Ratna** posthumously in **1997**, recognizing her contributions to India's freedom struggle.

• Her courage and determination make her a celebrated figure in Indian history and a role model for women in leadership.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Sucheta Kriplani:** 

• She was the first woman Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh and a prominent freedom fighter.

• She played an active role in the Quit India Movement but is not associated with the flag hoisting at Gowalia Tank.

• **Annie Besant:** 

• A British socialist, theosophist, and supporter of Indian self-rule, she contributed to India's freedom struggle but was not directly involved in the Quit India Movement.

• **Vijayalakshmi Pandit:** 

• The sister of Jawaharlal Nehru, she was an important political leader and diplomat but did not participate in the flag hoisting at Gowalia Tank.

solution:
The correct answer is **__Dadabhai Naoroji.__**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• First Indian elected to the British House of Commons, **Dadabhai Naoroji** contested on the ticket of **Liberal Party.**
 
• Dadabhai Naoroji was also known as the **"Grand Old Man of India" and "Unofficial Ambassador of India"**.
 
• He was an Indian political leader, merchant, scholar and writer who was a Liberal Party Member of Parliament in the **United Kingdom House of Commons between 1892 and 1895.**
 
• Naoroji is honoured for his work in the Indian National Congress, of which he was one of the founding members and thrice - **in 1886,1893, and 1906 - elected president.**
 
• His** authored book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India** brought attention to his theory of the Indian **"wealth drain"** into Britain.
 
• India Post showing Naoroji on stamps in** 1963, 1997 and 2017.​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Liberal Party**:

 
 
• Liberal Party, a British political party that emerged in the** mid-19th century as the successor to the historic Whig Party.**
 
• It was the major party in opposition to the Conservatives until **1918, after which it was supplanted by the Labour Party**.
 
• The Liberals continued as a minor party until** 1988** when they **merged with the Social Democratic Party to form what is now called the Liberal Democratic Party.**
 
• Through its long history, the Liberal Party included various schools of thought, but all Liberals were united by the conviction that the source of progress lay in the free exercise of individual energy.
 
 
 
• **Labour Party**:
 
 
• Labour Party, **a British political party whose historic links with trade unions have led it to promote an active role for the state in the creation of economic prosperity and in the provision of social services.**
 
• In opposition to the Conservative Party, it has been the **major democratic socialist party in Britain since the early 20th century.**
 
• In 1900 the **Trade Union Congress (the national federation of British trade unions) cooperated with the Independent Labour Party(founded in 1893) to establish a Labour Representation Committee,** which took the name Labour Party in 1906.
 
 
 
• **Conservative Party**:
 
 
• **Conservative Party, byname Tories, in the United Kingdom,** a political party whose guiding principles include the promotion of private property and enterprise, the maintenance of a strong military, and the preservation of traditional cultural values and institutions.
 
• Since World War I the Conservative Party and its principal opponent, the Labour Party, have dominated British political life.
 
• The name Conservative was first used as a description of the party by **John Wilson Croker writing in the Quarterly Review in 1830.**
 
 
 
• **Communist Party:**
 
 
• ** The Communist Party of Britain (CPB) is a communist political party in Great Britain idealized to Marxist-Leninist theory.**
 
• The party came out from a dispute between Eurocommunists and Marxist-Leninists in the Communist Party of Great Britain in 1988.
 
• Ex-members included General Secretaries of three organisations:
 
• **Bob Crow of the RMT union, Ken Gill of the Manufacturing.**
 
• **Science and Finance (MSF) union and member of the TUC General Council.**
 
• **Kate Hudson of the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND). **

question: Who was the Mughal emperor, when a massive rebellion against british rule broke out in 1857?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bahadur Shah Zafar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Bahadur Shah Zafar was the last Mughal emperor in the Indian subcontinent.
 
• After the death of Bahadur Shah Zafar, none of his descendants was recognized as kings.
 
• Bahadur Shah Zafar was the son of Akbar II.
 
• **The entry of Bahadur Shah Zafar to the 1857 rebellion gives courage, hope, and confidence to ordinary people.**
 
• **British forces recaptured Delhi from the rebel forces in September 1857.**
 
• The last Mughal emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar was **trialled **in court and sentenced to life imprisonment.
 
• The British exiled him to Rangoon following his involvement in the** Indian Rebellion of 1857.**
 
• Bahadur Shah Zafar and his wife Begum Zinat Mahal were sent to prison in Rangoon in 1858.
 
• Bahadur Shah Zafar died in the Rangoon jail in 1862.
 
• After the death of Bahadur Shah Zafar, his family was shifted out of the Red Fort and given another place in Delhi to reside.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The Revolt of 1857 was the first rebellion against the British East India Company.
 
• The first war of Indian Independence started on 10th May 1857.
 
• The revolt was started at Meerut.
 
• It began as a revolt of the sepoys of the British East India Company’s army but eventually secured the participation of the masses.
 
• The issue of greased cartridges and military grievances has been over-emphasized, as the factor for the Revolt of 1857.
 
• In March 1857, Mangal Pandey, a sepoy in Barrackpore, refused to use the cartridge and attacked his senior officers.
 
• He was hanged to death on 8th April 1857.
 
• On 9th May 1857, 85 soldiers in Meerut refused to use the new rifle and were sentenced to ten years imprisonment.
 
• The revolt is known by several names: the Sepoy Mutiny (by British Historians), the Indian Mutiny, the Great Rebellion (by Indian Historians), the Revolt of 1857, the Indian Insurrection, and the First War of Independence (by Vinayak Damodar Savarkar).
 
• Lord Canning is the British viceroy during the revolt of 1857.

• Chittaranjan Das was a prominent Indian freedom fighter and political leader known as 'Deshbandhu', which means 'Friend of the Nation'.
 
• He played a significant role in the Non-Cooperation Movement against British rule in India.
 
• Chittaranjan Das was the founder of the Swaraj Party along with Motilal Nehru, which aimed at attaining self-governance within the British Empire.
 
• He was also a renowned lawyer and defended Aurobindo Ghosh in the Alipore Bomb Case, further establishing his reputation as a key figure in the Indian independence movement.

• The movement saw widespread participation across India with actions like boycotting British goods, institutions, and services.
 
• Chittaranjan Das played a crucial role in galvanizing support for the movement, especially in Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Swaraj Party**
 
 
• Founded by Chittaranjan Das and Motilal Nehru in 1923, the Swaraj Party aimed to achieve self-governance within the British Empire.
 
• The party sought to enter legislative councils through elections to obstruct and eventually end British rule from within the system.
 
• This was a strategic shift from Gandhi's non-cooperation approach and aimed at more direct political engagement.
 
 
 
• **Alipore Bomb Case**
 
 
• In 1908, Aurobindo Ghosh and several others were arrested for their alleged involvement in a conspiracy to bomb a British magistrate's carriage.
 
• Chittaranjan Das defended Aurobindo Ghosh, and his eloquent defense played a significant role in the acquittal of Ghosh.
 
• This case was a landmark in the Indian legal history and highlighted the role of Indian lawyers in the freedom movement.

__
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru was a prominent leader of the Indian National Congress and a key figure in the Indian independence movement.
 
• He was the one who called for complete independence from British rule during the Lahore session of the Indian National Congress in 1929.
 
• The demand for complete independence (Purna Swaraj) was officially adopted by the Indian National Congress at this session.
 
• The resolution for complete independence was passed on December 31, 1929, and January 26, 1930, was declared as the Independence Day, which was later celebrated as Republic Day after India became independent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• It was the principal party behind the demand for self-rule and later complete independence from British colonialism.
 
• Leaders like Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose, and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel were prominent figures associated with INC.
 
 
 
• **Lahore Session of 1929**
 
 
• The Lahore session of the INC in December 1929 was a pivotal moment in the Indian independence movement.
 
• During this session, the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) was officially adopted.
 
• Jawaharlal Nehru was elected as the President of the INC during this session.
 
• The INC decided to celebrate January 26, 1930, as Independence Day, marking the beginning of a direct action campaign for complete independence.
 
 
 
• **Purna Swaraj (Complete Independence)**
 
 
• Purna Swaraj means complete self-rule or full independence from British rule.
 
• The resolution for Purna Swaraj was a declaration that the Indian people would fight for complete independence and not settle for anything less.
 
• This declaration intensified the struggle for independence and led to various civil disobedience movements and protests against British rule.
 
 
 
• **Republic Day**
 
 
• January 26 was chosen as the Republic Day to honor the date on which the Declaration of Independence was proclaimed in 1930.
 
• On January 26, 1950, the Constitution of India came into effect, making India a sovereign, democratic republic.
 
• Republic Day is celebrated every year with grand parades and festivities across the country.

• In his book "Poverty and Un-British Rule in India," Naoroji presented a detailed critique of the British economic policies in India, arguing that they were responsible for the widespread poverty in the country.
 
• Naoroji's work laid the foundation for the Indian nationalist movement and inspired future leaders like Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India**

 
 
• This book, published in 1901, is a seminal work by Dadabhai Naoroji in which he systematically examined the economic impacts of British rule on India.
 
• Naoroji introduced the concept of "Drain Theory," which argued that a significant portion of India's wealth was being drained to Britain without adequate returns, leading to persistent poverty in India.
 
• The book provided statistical evidence to support Naoroji's claims, making a compelling case for economic reforms and self-governance.
 
• It was one of the first works to use economic analysis to critique colonial policies, influencing both Indian and British policymakers.
 
 
 
• **Dadabhai Naoroji**
 
 
• He was born on 4th September 1825 in Mumbai and was educated at Elphinstone College.
 
• Naoroji was also the first Indian to be elected to the British Parliament, representing the Liberal Party for Finsbury Central from 1892 to 1895.
 
• He played a key role in bringing the economic grievances of Indians to the attention of the British public and Parliament.
 
• Besides his political career, Naoroji was an educator, co-founding the University of Mumbai, and a businessman involved in the cotton trade.
 
 
 
• **Indian National Congress (INC)**
 
 
• Founded in 1885, the INC was the first modern nationalist movement to emerge in the British Empire in Asia and Africa.
 
• The Congress became the principal leader of the Indian independence movement, with its influence spreading from the Indian subcontinent to the rest of the world.
 
• It played a significant role in the independence struggle, leading to India gaining independence in 1947.
 
• Prominent leaders associated with the Congress include Mahatma Gandhi, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Subhas Chandra Bose.

question: When was the All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) established?

The correct answer is __**1920**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was **established on 31 October 1920**.
 
• It is the **first national trade union in India**.
 
• AITUC played a significant role in the Indian labour movement and is affiliated with the Communist Party of India.
 
• The founding conference of AITUC was held in Bombay (now Mumbai) with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first president.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Trade Union**

 
 
• A trade union is an organization of workers formed to protect and advance their rights and interests.
 
• Trade unions negotiate with employers on behalf of their members on issues such as wages, working conditions, and benefits.
 
• They also provide legal representation and support to members in disputes with employers.
 
• Trade unions play a crucial role in advocating for labor laws and policies that benefit workers.
 
 
 
• **AITUC's Role in Indian Independence**
 
 
• AITUC was actively involved in the Indian independence movement.
 
• It organized strikes and protests to challenge British colonial rule and demand better working conditions for Indian workers.
 
• Many prominent leaders of the independence movement, including Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru, supported the activities of AITUC.
 
• After independence, AITUC continued to advocate for workers' rights and social justice in independent India.
 
 
 
• **Communist Party of India (CPI)**
 
 
• The Communist Party of India is one of the oldest political parties in India, founded in 1925.
 
• The CPI has historically been aligned with the Soviet Union and promoted Marxist-Leninist ideologies.
 
• The party played a significant role in the labor and peasant movements in India.
 
• AITUC is closely associated with CPI, and many of its leaders have been prominent members of the party.

question: Which of the following groups/parties was started in San Francisco, United States of America during the Indian National Movement?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ghadar Party**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ghadar Party was an Indian revolutionary organization primarily founded by expatriate Indians in the United States and Canada with the aim of securing India's independence from British rule.
 
• It was established in 1913 in San Francisco, California, by Punjabi Indians of the Sikh faith and other Indians living in the United States.
 
• The party used the weekly paper, "Ghadar," which was published in multiple languages including Punjabi, Hindi, Urdu, and English, to promote their cause and encourage Indians to rise against British rule.
 
• The Ghadar Party played a significant role in the Indian independence movement by organizing mutinies in India during World War I and seeking international support for their cause.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)**

 
 
• The HSRA was a revolutionary organization in India which aimed to overthrow British rule through armed struggle.
 
• It was founded in 1928 by young Indian revolutionaries including Bhagat Singh, Chandrasekhar Azad, Sukhdev, and others.
 
• The organization believed in socialist principles and aimed to establish a republic in India.
 
• The HSRA is famously known for the bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly in Delhi by Bhagat Singh and Batukeshwar Dutt in 1929.
 
 
 
• **Swaraj Party**
 
 
• The Swaraj Party was established in 1923 by Motilal Nehru and Chittaranjan Das in response to the suspension of the non-cooperation movement by Mahatma Gandhi.
 
• The party aimed to attain self-governance for India through constitutional means within the framework of British rule.
 
• It sought to enter legislative councils to obstruct British policies and advocate for Indian interests.
 
• The Swaraj Party played a pivotal role in the Indian legislative councils during the 1920s.
 
 
 
• **Khilafat Committee**
 
 
• The Khilafat Committee was formed in 1919 in India to support the Ottoman Caliphate and oppose the dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire by the Allied forces after World War I.
 
• The movement was led by prominent Muslim leaders like Maulana Mohammad Ali, Shaukat Ali, and Abul Kalam Azad.
 
• It sought to build solidarity between Indian Muslims and the broader Muslim world and was allied with the Indian National Congress in the Non-Cooperation Movement.
 
• The Khilafat Movement declined after the abolition of the Caliphate by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1924.

question: Who among the following was the key leader of the Khongjom War (1891) against British annexation of Manipur?

options.text: Tikendrajit Singh commanded the Manipuri army and was later executed.
Rani Gaidinliu led resistance against the British in Naga regions post-1930s.
U Kiang Nangbah led uprisings in Jaintia Hills against colonial intrusion.
Veer Surendra Sai resisted the British in Sambalpur for over four decades.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Tikendrajit Singh commanded the Manipuri army and was later executed**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Tikendrajit Singh**, also known as Senapati (General), was a key figure in the **Khongjom War of 1891**, which marked Manipur's resistance against British annexation.
 
• As the Commander of the Manipuri Army, Tikendrajit led the defense forces of Manipur in their fight against the British Empire.
 
• The war culminated in the Battle of Khongjom, where Manipuri forces faced overwhelming British forces but displayed exemplary valor.
 
• Following the defeat, Tikendrajit was arrested by the British and executed publicly on **13 August 1891**, becoming a martyr for India’s freedom struggle.
 
• The Khongjom War is commemorated annually in Manipur as **Khongjom Day** to honor the sacrifices of Manipuri warriors like Tikendrajit Singh.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Rani Gaidinliu**

 
 
• Rani Gaidinliu was a Naga spiritual and political leader who led resistance against British rule in the 1930s.
 
• She was associated with the Heraka religious movement, which sought to revive traditional Naga culture and religion.
 
• She was arrested by the British in 1932 and sentenced to life imprisonment but was released after India’s independence in 1947.
 
• She was honored with the title of **‘Rani’** by Jawaharlal Nehru for her role in the freedom struggle.
 
 
 
• **U Kiang Nangbah**
 
 
• U Kiang Nangbah was a freedom fighter from the Jaintia Hills (present-day Meghalaya) who led a rebellion against British colonial rule in the 1860s.
 
• He opposed the imposition of taxes and the erosion of traditional Khasi-Jaintia governance by the British.
 
• Captured by the British, he was executed in 1862, becoming a symbol of resistance in the region.
 
 
 
• **Veer Surendra Sai**
 
 
• Veer Surendra Sai was a prominent freedom fighter from Odisha who led resistance against British rule in Sambalpur for over four decades.
 
• He fought against the annexation of Sambalpur under British policies and defended tribal rights and local governance.
 
• His prolonged resistance lasted until his capture in 1864; he was imprisoned for the rest of his life.
 
 
 
• **The Khongjom War (1891)**
 
 
• The Khongjom War was the last war of independence fought by the Kingdom of Manipur against British annexation.
 
• Despite the advanced weaponry of the British, the Manipuri soldiers fought bravely to protect their sovereignty.
 
• It marks a significant chapter in India’s freedom struggle, highlighting the resilience of smaller kingdoms against colonial powers.

question: V.O. Chidambaram Pillai, also known as 'Kappalottiya Thamizhan', was a pioneer of the Swadeshi movement who started which enterprise?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **V.O. Chidambaram Pillai**, also known as **'Kappalottiya Thamizhan'**, was a renowned freedom fighter and a significant figure in the **Indian Swadeshi Movement.**

• He founded the **Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (SSNC) in 1906** to challenge the monopoly of the British-owned **British India Steam Navigation Company** (BISNC).

• The company was established to provide shipping services between **Tuticorin and Colombo** and to promote indigenous enterprise and self-reliance in the shipping industry.

• SSNC was the first shipping company in India to be owned and operated entirely by Indians, symbolizing **economic independence** and resistance against British colonial rule.

• V.O. Chidambaram Pillai mortgaged his personal property to acquire ships for the company, demonstrating his commitment to the Swadeshi cause.

• The company faced severe opposition from the British, and V.O.C. was eventually arrested and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment, marking him as a martyr of economic freedom.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Swadeshi Movement:**

• The Swadeshi Movement was part of the larger **Indian independence movement** and promoted the use of **indigenous goods** and boycotting British products.

• It was initiated during the **partition of Bengal in 1905** as a method to protest against the British policies and strengthen India's economic backbone.

• The movement involved promoting Indian industries, including textiles, handlooms, and other cottage industries.

• **V.O. Chidambaram Pillai's Contribution:**

• He was a lawyer by profession and also a leader of the Indian National Congress.

• He is remembered for his efforts to promote industrial and economic self-reliance among Indians through initiatives like the **Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company.**

• He was jailed for his nationalist activities, during which he endured harsh conditions and later became a symbol of resistance.

• **British India Steam Navigation Company (BISNC):**

• The BISNC was a British-owned shipping company that held a monopoly over shipping services in colonial India.

• It symbolized British economic dominance and exploitation of Indian resources and trade routes.

• **Impact of the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company:**

• The establishment of SSNC inspired other Indian entrepreneurs to start indigenous enterprises in various sectors.

• It highlighted the importance of economic independence as a key aspect of the freedom struggle.

• Despite its short-lived operation due to British sabotage, it left a lasting legacy in India's industrial history.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **V.O.C.'s Ships:** The two ships acquired by the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company were named **SS Gallia** and **SS Lawoe.**

• **Arrest and Imprisonment:** V.O. Chidambaram Pillai was arrested in **1908** under sedition charges and sentenced to **40 years of imprisonment**, later reduced to 6 years.

• **Legacy:** He is commemorated as a symbol of India's fight for economic freedom, with several institutions and places named after him in Tamil Nadu.

• **Swadeshi Enterprises:** Similar enterprises inspired by the Swadeshi Movement included textile mills, banks, and educational institutions aiming to reduce dependence on British resources.
</ul

question: The Simon Commission, appointed in 1927, was boycotted by the Indian National Congress because:

options.text: It recommended the immediate granting of full independence to India.
It proposed the complete abolition of separate electorates.
It did not include any Indian members.
It advocated for the continuation of dyarchy in the province

solution:
The correct answer is __**3) It did not include any Indian members.**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Simon Commission** was appointed by the British Government in **1927** to review the working of the Government of India Act, 1919, and to suggest reforms in the Indian administration. 
• The Commission had **seven British members**, but it did not include a single Indian representative. This exclusion was considered an insult to the Indian population and its leaders. 
• The **Indian National Congress** and several other political organizations opposed the Commission, as they believed that Indians should have been included to represent their own interests in the review process. 
• The Commission was boycotted across India, and protests were organized by prominent leaders like **Lala Lajpat Rai**, who led a protest in Lahore and was injured in police action during the demonstration. 
• One of the slogans raised during the protests against the Simon Commission was **"Simon Go Back."** The exclusion of Indians from the Commission demonstrated the British Government's unwillingness to grant Indians a meaningful role in governance. 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is 3) It did not include any Indian members.*** 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Simon Commission:** 
• It was formally known as the **Indian Statutory Commission** and was chaired by **Sir John Simon**. 
• The Commission arrived in India in **1928** and faced widespread opposition due to the absence of Indian members. 
• The Commission suggested reforms in provincial governance but upheld the concept of separate electorates, which were already criticized for dividing Indian society. 
• The final report of the Simon Commission led to the Government of India Act, 1935, which introduced provincial autonomy but was seen as inadequate by Indian leaders. 
• **Lala Lajpat Rai:** 
• He played a key role in opposing the Simon Commission by organizing protests in Lahore. 
• During one such protest, he was severely injured in a police lathi charge and later succumbed to his injuries. His death became a rallying point for the freedom struggle. 
• **Historical Context:** 
• The exclusion of Indians from the Simon Commission highlighted the British Government's lack of commitment to granting Indians a genuine role in self-governance. 
• This led to increased calls for complete independence, culminating in the **Purna Swaraj Resolution** adopted by the Indian National Congress in **1930**. 
• **Key Outcomes:** 
• The Simon Commission and its exclusionary policies intensified the Indian struggle for independence. 
• The protests against the Commission marked a significant phase in India's freedom movement, strengthening the demand for self-governance and representation. 
• The Commission's report ultimately led to the Government of India Act, 1935, but it failed to address the aspirations of the Indian population fully. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Government of India Act, 1919:** 
• It introduced **dyarchy** (dual governance) in provinces, dividing subjects into reserved and transferred categories. 
• The Act was criticized for providing limited autonomy to Indians and retaining significant powers with the British authorities. 
• **Separate Electorates:** 
• The concept of separate electorates was introduced by the British to divide Indian society along religious and communal lines. 
• It allowed specific communities to elect their representatives, which led to divisions and weakened national unity. 
• **Purna Swaraj Resolution:** 
• Adopted by the Indian National Congress in **1930**, it marked the demand for complete independence from British rule. 
• The resolution was passed under the leadership of **Jawaharlal Nehru** during the Lahore Session of the Congress. 
• **Protests Against Simon Commission:** 
• Protests were widespread and included leaders from different political ideologies, uniting Indians against British policies. 
• These protests strengthened the Indian independence movement and highlighted the need for self-representation in governance. </ul

question: Which of the following describes the role of Aruna Asaf Ali in Indian history?

options.text: She was elected as India's first female judge.
She hoisted the Indian flag during the Quit India Movement.
She led a military regiment during the 1857 revolt.
She participated in drafting the Constitution.

solution:
The correct answer is __**She hoisted the Indian flag during the Quit India Movement.**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Aruna Asaf Ali** played a significant role in India's freedom struggle during the **Quit India Movement**, which began in **August 1942**. 
• She is famously known for **hoisting the Indian National Flag** at the **Gowalia Tank Maidan** in Bombay (now Mumbai) on **9 August 1942**, marking the launch of the movement. 
• This act of defiance turned her into a **prominent symbol of resistance** against British rule. 
• Her actions inspired many Indians to join the movement, and she became known as the "**Heroine of the Quit India Movement**." 
• Aruna Asaf Ali continued her efforts for India's independence and was also active in post-independence India, advocating for various social and political causes. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Quit India Movement:** 
• Launched by **Mahatma Gandhi** on **8 August 1942** during the Bombay session of the **All India Congress Committee**. 
• Its primary aim was to demand an end to British rule in India and achieve complete independence. 
• The movement's slogan, "**Do or Die**," urged Indians to act decisively against colonial rule. 
• **Aruna Asaf Ali's Legacy:** 
• She was born on **16 July 1909** in Kalka, Haryana, and married **Asaf Ali**, a prominent lawyer and freedom fighter. 
• She was awarded the **Bharat Ratna**, India's highest civilian honor, in **1997** for her contributions to the nation. 
• She also received the **International Lenin Peace Prize** for her efforts towards world peace. 
• **Role of Women in Freedom Struggle:** 
• Women like **Aruna Asaf Ali**, **Sarojini Naidu**, and **Kamala Nehru** played crucial roles in mobilizing support and leading protests against British rule. 
• They participated in activities such as picketing foreign goods, organizing rallies, and spreading nationalist ideas. 
• **Gowalia Tank Maidan:** 
• Located in Mumbai, this place is historically significant as the site where the **Quit India Movement** was officially launched. 
• Today, it is known as the "**August Kranti Maidan**" in honor of the movement. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Other Contributions of Aruna Asaf Ali:** 
• She was the first mayor of **Delhi** post-independence in **1958**. 
• She co-founded the **National Federation of Indian Women** in **1954**, advocating for women's rights and social justice. 
• Her life and work remain a source of inspiration for generations of Indians. </ul

question: Which significant political move by Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi ensured that Assam remained a part of India and not East Pakistan during the Cabinet Mission Plan's proposal in 1946?

options.text: Opposing the grouping of Assam with Bengal
Launching the Quit India Movement in Assam

solution:
The correct answer is __**Opposing the grouping of Assam with Bengal**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __

• **Lokpriya Gopinath Bordoloi**, the first Chief Minister of Assam, played a pivotal role in ensuring that Assam remained a part of India during the turbulent period of the **Cabinet Mission Plan's proposal in 1946**.

• He opposed the British plan to **group Assam with Bengal** in a single administrative unit. This grouping was seen as a precursor to Assam potentially being included in East Pakistan during Partition.

• Bordoloi’s opposition was based on the belief that Assam had a distinct cultural identity and should remain independent of Bengal's influence. This move safeguarded Assam’s **territorial and cultural integrity**.

• His efforts included lobbying at the national level and engaging with Congress leaders like **Jawaharlal Nehru** and **Vallabhbhai Patel** to ensure Assam’s interests were protected.

• Ultimately, Bordoloi’s firm stance and negotiations resulted in Assam being excluded from the proposed grouping, ensuring its integration into India and avoiding its annexation into East Pakistan.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __

• **Cabinet Mission Plan (1946):** 

• The Cabinet Mission Plan was proposed by the British government to discuss and plan the transfer of power to Indian leadership.

• It suggested a grouping of provinces into three sections, with Assam and Bengal forming Group C. This grouping was opposed by many as it diluted Assam's autonomy.

• The plan also laid the groundwork for India’s partition, with the creation of Pakistan becoming increasingly likely.

• **Gopinath Bordoloi’s Leadership:** 

• As the leader of Assam, Bordoloi championed the cause of Assamese culture and opposed any attempt to merge Assam with Bengal or Pakistan.

• He mobilized public opinion and worked with both local and national leaders to safeguard Assam’s interests.

• **Assam’s Strategic Importance:** 

• Assam, rich in natural resources and with a unique cultural heritage, was considered a vital region in India’s northeastern frontier.

• Its inclusion in East Pakistan would have significantly altered the political and geographical landscape of the region.

• **Outcome:** 

• Due to Bordoloi’s efforts, Assam was kept out of the grouping with Bengal, ensuring its integration into India post-Independence.

• He was later awarded the **Bharat Ratna** posthumously in 1999 for his contributions to the nation.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 

• **Other Options Analysis:** 

• **Launching the Quit India Movement in Assam:** While the Quit India Movement was significant, it was not directly related to Assam’s exclusion from East Pakistan. Hence, this is incorrect.

• **Signing the Assam Accord:** The Assam Accord was signed in 1985, much after Independence, and was unrelated to the events of 1946. Hence, this is incorrect.

• **Rejecting the Instrument of Accession:** The Instrument of Accession was related to princely states joining India or Pakistan post-Independence, not the grouping under the Cabinet Mission Plan. Hence, this is incorrect.

question: Jinnah: His Successes, Failures and Role in History' was authored by?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Ishtiaq Ahmed**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Dr. Ishtiaq Ahmed** is the author of the book titled **"Jinnah: His Successes, Failures and Role in History."** The book provides an in-depth analysis of **Muhammad Ali Jinnah**, the founder of Pakistan.

• The book was published in **2020** and critically examines Jinnah's political journey, his successes, failures, and his role in shaping the subcontinent's history.

• **Ishtiaq Ahmed** is a renowned political scientist and historian of Pakistani origin. He is an Emeritus Professor of Political Science at **Stockholm University, Sweden**.

• The book highlights Jinnah's transformation from a staunch advocate of Hindu-Muslim unity to the leader of the **Muslim League**, advocating for the creation of Pakistan.

• It delves into key historical events such as the **Lucknow Pact (1916)**, **Pakistan Resolution (1940)**, and the eventual **Partition of India (1947)**, analyzing Jinnah's role in each.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **About the Author:**

• **Dr. Ishtiaq Ahmed** has written extensively on South Asian politics, history, and the partition of India. His works are known for their **neutral and factual approach**.

• He has contributed significantly to the understanding of the complex relationship between India and Pakistan through his academic and research work.

• **Key Themes of the Book:**

• The book explores how **Jinnah's political ideology** evolved over time, from being a liberal secularist to a leader advocating for a separate nation for Muslims.

• It critically examines Jinnah's failures, such as his inability to prevent communal violence during the partition.

• The book also sheds light on the internal workings of the **Muslim League** and its strategy to achieve the goal of Pakistan.

• **Important Historical Context:**

• The **partition of India in 1947** led to the creation of two nations, India and Pakistan. Jinnah played a pivotal role in this process as the leader of the Muslim League.

• The book discusses how Jinnah's vision of Pakistan as a secular state was later overshadowed by religious and political factors.

• **Other Works on Jinnah:**

• Books like **"Jinnah of Pakistan"** by **Stanley Wolpert** and **"The Sole Spokesman"** by **Ayesha Jalal** also provide significant insights into Jinnah's life and politics.

• However, Dr. Ishtiaq Ahmed's work stands out for its comprehensive analysis and critical approach.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Muhammad Ali Jinnah:**

• Born on **25 December 1876** in Karachi, Jinnah was a barrister by profession and became the leader of the **All-India Muslim League**.

• He is often referred to as the **"Quaid-e-Azam"** (Great Leader) in Pakistan.

• Jinnah's leadership played a crucial role in the passage of the **Pakistan Resolution** in **1940**.

• **Partition of India:**

• The partition in **1947** was one of the largest mass migrations in history, resulting in significant loss of life and property.

• Jinnah's demand for a separate homeland for Muslims was based on the **Two-Nation Theory**, which argued that Hindus and Muslims were distinct nations with their own customs, religion, and traditions.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Uprising of Khurda, also known as the Paika Rebellion, took place in the Khurda region of Odisha.
 
• It was led by Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar, the commander of the forces of the Raja of Khurda.
 
• The rebellion was a response to the British East India Company's oppressive policies and land revenue systems.
 
• The Paikas, the traditional warrior class of Odisha, played a significant role in the uprising, showcasing their valor and resistance against British colonial rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Uprising of Khurda:**

 
 
• The Uprising of Khurda in 1817 is also known as the Paika Rebellion.
 
• The Paikas were the landed militia of Odisha, who were rendered landless by the policies of the British East India Company.
 
• The rebellion was one of the earliest organized armed rebellions against British rule in India.
 
• It was led by Bakshi Jagabandhu Bidyadhar, who mobilized the Paikas and other sections of society against the British.
 
• The revolt was primarily a reaction to the British land revenue policies, which were exploitative and led to widespread discontent among the peasants and landed gentry.
 
• The Paikas attacked British establishments, looted the treasury, and set fire to government buildings as a mark of their protest.
 
• Though the rebellion was eventually suppressed by the British, it is remembered for its significant impact on the resistance movements against colonial rule in India.
 
 
 
• **Odisha:**
 
 
• Odisha is an eastern state of India known for its rich history, culture, and heritage.
 
• The state was known as Kalinga in ancient times and has a long history of resistance against external invasions, including that of the Maurya Empire.

__
 
• On 1 July 1909, in London Curzon Wyllie was assassinated by the Indian revolutionary Madan Lal Dhingra, who was a member of India House in London
 
• Sir William Hutt Curzon Wyllie was a British Indian army officer.
 
• **Madan Lal Dhingra** claimed that he had murdered Curzon-Wyllie as a patriotic act and in revenge for the inhumane killings of Indians by the British Government in India.

• ​**Madan Lal Dhingra was born on 18 February 1883 in Amritsar, India, and died on 17 August 1909**.
 
• He was an Indian revolutionary, pro-independence activist, while studying in England, **he assassinated William Hutt Curzon Wyllie**.
 
• Curzon Wylie had joined the British Army in 1866 and the Indian Political Department in 1879. In 1901, he was selected to be Political Aide-de-Camp to the Secretary of State for India.
 
• He was also the head of the Secret Police and had been trying to obtain information about Savarkar and his fellow revolutionaries.
 
• **On the evening of 1 July 1909**, Madan Lal Dhingra, along with a large number of Indians and Englishmen had gathered to attend the annual 'At Home' function **hosted by the Indian National Association at the Imperial Institute**.

 __

solution:
The correct answer is __**Ardhendu Destidar**__.

__** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] Key Points__**

__
 
• **Ardhendu Destidar** belonged to the second group, In his early teens, he left the roof of his father due to a difference of opinion on political matters with him.
 
• **He became an active member of the revolutionary party of Chittagong under the table, the leadership of Master-da (Surya Sen).**
 
• Just a few weeks before the storming of the** Armoury**, he got severely burnt due to an accident in manu­facturing picric acid powder meant for high explosive bombs.
 
• He had not fully recovered from his injuries when he joined the party that carried out the raid on the Police Line on the** 18th,** With the main body of the raiders, he retired to** Jalalabad Hill**.
 
• He happened to be the **sixth man **to be wounded in the exchange of bullets with the British soldiers.
 
• He received a deadly wound in his abdomen from the enemy's bullet which rendered him unconscious and he was left on the field as dead.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**** **__**Chittagong Armoury Raid**__

 
• The Chittagong armoury raid, also known as the **Chittagong uprising, was an attempt by armed Indian independence fighters led by Surya Sen on 18 April 1930 to raid the Chittagong armoury **of police and auxiliary forces in the Bengal Presidency of British India (now Bangladesh).
 
• The raiders were members of the revolutionary** Indian Republican Army, **which advocated for armed uprisings to free India from British colonial rule.
 
• They were inspired by the** 1916 Easter Rising in Ireland**.
 
• Sen devised a plan to cut Chittagong off from Calcutta by capturing the** two main armouries, destroying the telegraph and telephone office, and kidnapping members of the European Club as hostages.**
 
• Imperial banks in Chittagong were to be looted in order to raise funds for future uprisings, and various imprisoned revolutionaries were to be released.
 
• A group of revolutionaries led by Ganesh Ghosh captured the police armoury in Dampara's Police Line, while another group of ten men led by** Lokenath Bal took the Auxiliary Forces armoury** (**now the old Circuit House**).
 
• A total of** 65 people **were involved in the raid, which was carried out in the name of the Indian Republican Army, Chittagong Branch.
 
• They were unsuccessful in their search for ammunition, but they were successful in cutting telephone and telegraph wires and disrupting train movements.

__
 
• The Indian National Army (INA) was formed during World War II in Singapore.
 
• The INA was initially formed under the leadership of Mohan Singh in 1942 with the aim of securing Indian independence from British rule.
 
• It was later reorganized and led by Subhas Chandra Bose, who took command in 1943.
 
• Singapore served as a strategic location for the INA due to its significant Indian population and its occupation by the Japanese forces at the time.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian National Army (INA)**

 
 
• The Indian National Army (INA) was an armed force formed by Indian nationalists in 1942 in Southeast Asia during World War II.
 
• The aim of the INA was to secure Indian independence from British rule, a cause that garnered significant support among Indian expatriates and prisoners of war.
 
• Mohan Singh initially formed the INA with Indian prisoners of war captured by the Japanese during the Malayan Campaign and the Battle of Singapore.
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose, a prominent leader in the Indian independence movement, took charge of the INA in 1943 and restructured it significantly.
 
 
 
• **Subhas Chandra Bose**
 
 
• Subhas Chandra Bose, also known as Netaji, was a prominent Indian freedom fighter who played a crucial role in the Indian independence movement.
 
• Bose was a charismatic leader who advocated for radical action against British rule and sought foreign alliances to achieve Indian independence.
 
• Under his leadership, the INA sought to liberate India from British control with the assistance of the Axis powers during World War II.
 
• Bose's efforts and his call for complete independence inspired many Indians and left a lasting legacy in India's history.
 
 
 
• **World War II and Southeast Asia**
 
 
• World War II, which lasted from 1939 to 1945, involved major global powers and was marked by significant military campaigns in various regions, including Southeast Asia.
 
• Southeast Asia was strategically important during the war, with countries like Singapore, Malaya, and Burma witnessing major battles.
 
• The Japanese occupation of Southeast Asia during the war provided an opportunity for Indian nationalists to seek support for their cause against British colonial rule.
 
• The INA's formation and activities in Southeast Asia were part of the broader context of anti-colonial struggles and the global impact of World War II.

question: What was the key contribution of Baikuntha Shukla in the Indian freedom struggle?
solution:
The correct answer is __**He assassinated a government approver**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Baikuntha Shukla** played a key role in the Indian freedom struggle by assassinating **Phanindranath Ghosh**, a government approver who betrayed revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev.
 
• Phanindranath Ghosh had turned into a British informant, leading to the arrest and execution of several revolutionary leaders.
 
• Shukla carried out the assassination on **9 November 1932** to uphold the revolutionary spirit and discourage betrayal within the freedom movement.
 
• He was associated with the revolutionary organization **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA)**, which was instrumental in fighting British colonial rule through armed resistance.
 
• Baikuntha Shukla was arrested, tried, and eventually hanged on **14 May 1934**, making him one of the youngest martyrs of the Indian independence movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Champaran Satyagraha (Option 1):**

 
 
• The Champaran Satyagraha of 1917 was led by **Mahatma Gandhi** and marked his first significant involvement in the Indian freedom struggle.
 
• It was initiated to address the grievances of farmers in Bihar who were forced to grow indigo under oppressive conditions imposed by British landlords.
 
• This non-violent movement resulted in the abolition of the exploitative tinkathia system and marked Gandhi's emergence as a mass leader in India.
 
 
 
• **Protest against Simon Commission (Option 2):**
 
 
• The Simon Commission, formed in 1927, was a British initiative to review constitutional reforms in India, but it lacked Indian representation.
 
• The commission was met with widespread protests, and the slogan "**Simon Go Back**" became popular.
 
• Lala Lajpat Rai suffered fatal injuries during a protest against the commission in 1928, further igniting nationalist sentiments.
 
 
 
• **Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (HSRA) (Option 4):**
 
 
• The HSRA was a revolutionary organization formed in 1928 by leaders like **Chandrasekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, and Sukhdev**.
 
• The group aimed to overthrow British rule through direct action, including armed resistance and political assassinations.
 
• HSRA members carried out significant actions, such as the assembly bombing in 1929 and the assassination of British police officer J.P. Saunders in 1928.
 
 
 
• **Baikuntha Shukla and the Revolutionary Movement:**
 
 
• Baikuntha Shukla's actions reflect the dedication and sacrifices of revolutionaries who believed in armed struggle as a means to achieve independence.
 
• His martyrdom serves as a reminder of the diverse strategies employed in India's fight against colonial oppression, ranging from non-violent satyagraha to armed resistance.

• She led an armed rebellion against British colonial rule and fought to preserve Naga culture and independence.

• After India's independence, she was awarded the **Padma Bhushan** in **1982** for her contributions.

• Heraka means "pure religion" and was a spiritual reform movement among the Zeliangrong Nagas.

• It advocated monotheism, the rejection of superstitions, and cultural unity among the Nagas.

• He envisioned a Naga Raj (Naga Kingdom) and resisted British colonial rule.

• He was executed by the British in **1931**, prompting Rani Gaidinliu to take over the leadership.

• The freedom movement in Northeast India was marked by socio-religious reforms and resistance against British colonial policies.

• Leaders like Rani Gaidinliu and Jadonang played key roles in preserving indigenous cultures while fighting for independence.

• Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta was founded on July 29, 1876, by Dr Mahendra Lal Sircar, IACS is the oldest institute in India devoted to the pursuit of fundamental research in the frontier areas of basic sciences.

• Jyotiba Phule founded Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune, Maharashtra, on 24th September 1873.
 
• It was a reformational society that promoted education and increased social rights, justice, and political access in the deprived sections.
 
• Moreover, its primary focus was on uplifting and supporting Dalits, Shudras, and women in Maharashtra.
 
• Jyotiba Phule’s wife, Savitribai, used to administer the social activities for the women’s section.
 
• Jyotirao established it to stand against the unfair caste system and orthodox, illogical Brahminical status in this society.
 
• He challenged the Brahmins who claimed themselves to be God’s messenger and a connecting medium to the almighty.
 
• The Samaj rejected the approach of Vedic culture, Upanishad, and the predominance of Aryan society. Instead, according to him, Aryan society tries to suppress and deprive the non-Aryans, which he protested.
 
• Shahu Maharaj, a Maratha ruler of the princely state Kolhapur, continued the movement after the death of Phule.
 
• Later, Bhaurao Patil and other Maratha leaders like Nana Patil, Keshavrao Jedhe, Madhavrao Bagal, and Khanderao Bagal kept this movement alive.
 
• However, the Samaj gradually dissolved during the 1930s as these leaders started to join the Indian National Congress.

• He wrote the play 'Nil Darpan' in 1860-61, which portrays the plight of indigo farmers under British rule in Bengal.

• The rebellion highlighted the exploitation by British planters and led to reforms in the indigo cultivation practices.

• It encompasses a wide range of genres, including poetry, drama, novels, short stories, and essays.
 
• Notable figures in Bengali literature include Rabindranath Tagore, Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay.
 
 
 
• **British Colonial Rule in India:**
 
 
• British colonial rule in India lasted from 1858 to 1947, following the transfer of power from the East India Company to the British Crown after the Revolt of 1857.
 
• During this period, India was subjected to economic exploitation, cultural changes, and political reorganization.

• The law was a result of the extensive campaign led by Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar, who used his knowledge of Hindu scriptures to argue that widow remarriage was sanctioned by ancient texts.
 
• This reform was an important step towards gender equality and improving the social status of women in India.

• Vidyasagar's advocacy for women's rights, including widow remarriage and female education, marked him as a pioneer in the fight for social justice in India.

subject: GK
question: The revolution of 1857 started in May from which of the following cantonments in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Meerut**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The revolution of 1857, also known as the First War of Indian Independence, started from the cantonment of **Meerut**.
 
• The revolt began on May 10, 1857, when Indian soldiers in Meerut rebelled against the British officers.
 
• The immediate cause of the revolt was the introduction of new rifle cartridges rumored to be greased with cow and pig fat, offending both Hindu and Muslim soldiers.
 
• Meerut was one of the largest military cantonments in India at the time, making it a significant starting point for the uprising.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Causes of the Revolt**

 
 
• **Political Causes:** The annexation policies of the British, such as the Doctrine of Lapse, created widespread resentment among Indian rulers.
 
• **Economic Causes:** The heavy taxation and exploitation of Indian farmers, artisans, and the destruction of traditional industries led to economic distress.
 
• **Social and Religious Causes:** The British social reforms, which were seen as interference in traditional customs and religious practices, angered many Indians.
 
 
 
• **Spread of the Revolt**
 
 
• After Meerut, the revolt quickly spread to other parts of India, including Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, and Gwalior.
 
• Many Indian rulers and soldiers joined the rebellion, seeing it as an opportunity to regain their lost power and territories.
 
 
 
• **Suppression of the Revolt**
 
 
• The British used superior military force and strategic alliances with some Indian rulers to suppress the revolt.
 
• By 1858, the British had regained control over most of the rebellious areas, marking the end of the revolt.
 
 
 
• **Consequences of the Revolt**
 
 
• The revolt led to the end of the East India Company's rule in India, and the British Crown took direct control of the Indian administration.
 
• The British government made several administrative and military reforms to prevent any future rebellions.
 
• The revolt also marked the beginning of a stronger nationalistic movement in India, leading to the eventual struggle for independence.
