question: Which of the following best describes the role and personality traits of Shaheed Kanhu and Sidhu Murmu during the Santhal Rebellion of 1855?

options.text: Visionary tribal leaders who united the Santhal community to resist exploitation with courage and strategic acumen.
Passive intermediaries who negotiated peace treaties between the British and Santhals without resorting to conflict.
Religious preachers who inspired rebellion solely through spiritual teachings without active participation in battles.
Local zamindars who switched allegiance from British rulers to lead a revolt for personal gains.

solution:
The correct answer is __**Visionary tribal leaders who united the Santhal community to resist exploitation with courage and strategic acumen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Shaheed Kanhu and Sidhu Murmu** were prominent leaders of the **Santhal Rebellion** of **1855-56**, which was one of the most significant tribal uprisings against the British colonial rule and local zamindars.

• They united the **Santhal community**, predominantly located in the present-day regions of **Jharkhand, Bihar, and West Bengal**, to rise against the **exploitative practices of British officials, moneylenders, and landlords**.

• The rebellion was driven by their vision to establish a society free from oppression, usury, and unjust land revenue systems. They were known for their **courage and strategic acumen** in organizing and leading their community.

• The rebellion began in **June 1855**, with Kanhu and Sidhu rallying **10,000 Santhals** under the banner of resistance, declaring their independence from British rule and landlords.

• Their leadership was characterized by their ability to inspire collective action, employing indigenous methods of warfare and mobilizing their community with a strong sense of unity and purpose.

• The uprising was eventually suppressed by the British using military force, but their sacrifice is remembered as a symbol of resistance and tribal pride.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Santhal Rebellion:**

• The **Santhal Rebellion**, also known as the **Santhal Hul**, was a tribal revolt against the exploitative practices of zamindars, moneylenders, and the British East India Company.

• It began on **30 June 1855** in the village of **Bhognadih**, led by Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu.

• The rebellion was rooted in the grievances of the Santhals, who faced **economic exploitation**, loss of traditional land, and oppressive revenue systems.

• **Role of Kanhu and Sidhu Murmu:**

• Sidhu and Kanhu declared their intent to establish a **self-governed region**, free from British interference.

• They believed in **restoring tribal autonomy** and protecting their cultural identity.

• The rebellion showcased their exceptional **organizational skills and leadership** in uniting thousands of Santhals for a common cause.

• **Outcome of the Rebellion:**

• The uprising was brutally suppressed by the British, who deployed an army and used advanced weaponry against the poorly armed Santhals.

• While the rebellion failed to achieve its immediate goals, it highlighted the **plight of tribal communities** and forced the British to reconsider their policies towards them.

• **Legacy:**

• Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu are celebrated as **freedom fighters and martyrs** in India.

• Their struggle is commemorated annually in tribal regions, especially in Jharkhand, Bihar, and West Bengal.

• Their story serves as a powerful reminder of the indigenous communities' resilience and their fight for justice and autonomy.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Key Characteristics of the Santhal Rebellion:**

• The rebellion was one of the earliest tribal uprisings against British colonial rule in India.

• It was marked by the use of traditional weapons like bows, arrows, and spears, as well as guerrilla tactics.

• The rebellion was a response to the unjust practices of **moneylenders, revenue officials, and landlords**, who exploited the Santhals through high taxes and loans.

• **Santhal Parganas:**

• After the rebellion, the British government created a separate administrative region called **Santhal Parganas** in 1856 to address the grievances of the Santhal community.

• This area was designated to provide a degree of autonomy to the Santhals and protect their rights over land.

• **Commemorations:**

• The contributions of Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu are celebrated during the annual **Hul Diwas** in memory of the rebellion.

• Statues, memorials, and educational institutions have been established in their honor across India.

</ul

question: Rani Gaidinliu, a prominent freedom fighter, is best known for her leadership in which movement during British India?

options.text: Joined the Heraka movement, mobilizing Naga tribes against British missionaries
Peasant uprising in Bengal against zamindari oppression.
Armed revolt in Punjab supporting the Ghadar Party's cause
Non-cooperation movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in Andhra Pradesh

solution:
The correct answer is __**Joined the Heraka movement, mobilizing Naga tribes against British missionaries**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__

• **Rani Gaidinliu** was a prominent freedom fighter from the **state of Manipur** in northeastern India.

• She joined the **Heraka movement**, a socio-religious movement, which aimed to revive the traditional Naga religion and culture while opposing the influence of **British missionaries**.

• The Heraka movement, under the leadership of **Jadonang** (her cousin), became a platform for rebellion against the **British colonial rule** in the Naga Hills.

• After Jadonang's execution by the British in **1931**, Rani Gaidinliu took over the leadership of the movement and expanded its reach to mobilize the **Naga tribes** for armed resistance.

• Her efforts earned her the title of "**Rani**" from **Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru**, as a mark of respect for her courage and leadership in the fight against British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Heraka Movement:**

• The Heraka movement was a religious reform movement that originated among the **Zeliangrong tribes** of Manipur, Nagaland, and Assam.

• It sought to revive the traditional Naga religion, which was under threat from British missionary activities promoting Christianity.

• The movement gradually turned into a political struggle against British oppression and became a significant part of India's freedom struggle.

• **Rani Gaidinliu's Role:**

• She was only **16 years old** when she assumed leadership of the Heraka movement after Jadonang's execution.

• Under her leadership, the movement adopted a more militant approach, organizing armed resistance and guerrilla warfare against British authorities.

• She was captured by the British in **1932** and sentenced to **life imprisonment**. She was released in **1947** after India's independence.

• **Honors and Legacy:**

• Rani Gaidinliu is remembered as a symbol of **resistance and empowerment** in northeastern India.

• The Government of India issued a **commemorative stamp** in her honor and established a museum dedicated to her life and contributions.

• The **Rani Gaidinliu Tribal Freedom Fighters Museum** was inaugurated in **Manipur** to showcase her contributions to India's freedom struggle.

• **Other Options Explained:**

• **Peasant uprising in Bengal:** This refers to movements like the **Indigo Rebellion** or **Tebhaga Movement**, which were not associated with Rani Gaidinliu.

• **Armed revolt in Punjab:** This relates to the **Ghadar Party** and their activities, which were centered in Punjab and had no connection to the Naga Hills or Rani Gaidinliu.

• **Non-cooperation movement in Andhra Pradesh:** This was part of Mahatma Gandhi's national movement and unrelated to Rani Gaidinliu's localized struggle in the Naga region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Jadonang:** Known as a precursor to Rani Gaidinliu, he envisioned a Naga kingdom free from British rule and laid the foundation of the Heraka movement.

• **British Repression:** The colonial authorities were alarmed by the Heraka movement's growth and arrested Rani Gaidinliu, viewing her as a threat to their control in the region.

• **Post-Independence:** After her release in 1947, Rani Gaidinliu continued to advocate for tribal rights and preservation of indigenous culture.

• **Recognition:** She was awarded the **Padma Bhushan** by the Government of India in recognition of her immense contribution to the nation.
</ul

question: Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion in the 1920s, mobilizing tribal communities against British rule. He primarily operated in which modern-day Indian state?

The correct answer is __**Andhra Pradesh**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Alluri Sitarama Raju** was a prominent freedom fighter who led the **Rampa Rebellion** in the 1920s, a tribal uprising against British rule. The rebellion took place in the regions that now form part of **modern-day Andhra Pradesh**. 
• The rebellion primarily occurred in the **Godavari Agency area**, which is located in the **Eastern Ghats**. This area was heavily populated by tribal communities. 
• Alluri Sitarama Raju mobilized the tribal population against the oppressive policies of the British, especially against the **Forest Act**, which restricted the rights of the tribals to use forest resources. 
• His leadership in guerrilla warfare strategies against the British made him a revered figure among the tribal communities and earned him the nickname "**Manyam Veerudu**" (Hero of the Jungle). 
• The rebellion ended in **1924** when Alluri Sitarama Raju was captured and executed by the British, but his legacy continues to inspire freedom movements and tribal rights advocacy. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Rampa Rebellion:** 
• The rebellion occurred in the **1922-1924** period and was centered in the **Rampa region** of the Godavari districts in Andhra Pradesh. 
• It was a tribal revolt against British colonial oppression, particularly against the restrictions imposed by the **Madras Forest Act of 1882**. 
• The act limited the tribals' access to the forest, which was their primary source of livelihood, pushing them into hardship and poverty. 
• **Alluri Sitarama Raju:** 
• Born on **4th July 1897**, in Pandrangi village in the Visakhapatnam district of Andhra Pradesh. 
• He was inspired by the ideals of the **Indian freedom struggle** and was deeply moved by the plight of tribal communities under British rule. 
• His leadership in armed rebellion against the British made him a **folk hero** among tribals. 
• He was captured and executed by the British in **1924**, but his efforts laid the groundwork for future tribal movements. 
• **Impact of the Forest Act:** 
• The **Madras Forest Act** restricted the usage of forest resources, including grazing, collecting firewood, and hunting, which were integral to the tribal way of life. 
• The act alienated the tribal communities from their traditional lands and pushed them into economic distress, leading to widespread resentment. 
• This resentment culminated in revolts like the Rampa Rebellion, which aimed to restore tribal rights and autonomy. 
• **Guerrilla Warfare Strategy:** 
• Alluri Sitarama Raju adopted **guerrilla warfare tactics** to fight against the British forces. 
• He led surprise attacks on British police stations, seized arms, and disrupted their administration in the tribal areas. 
• His deep knowledge of the terrain and support from tribal communities made these tactics highly effective. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Legacy:** Alluri Sitarama Raju is remembered as a symbol of tribal resistance and patriotism. His life and sacrifices continue to inspire movements advocating for tribal rights and environmental protection. 
• **Recognition:** The Indian government has honored his contributions by naming institutions and projects after him, such as the **Alluri Sitarama Raju University**. 
• **Regional Significance:** The rebellion is seen as a pivotal moment in the history of Andhra Pradesh and is celebrated annually in the region. 
• **Tribal Movements:** The Rampa Rebellion is part of a larger context of tribal uprisings during British rule, such as the **Santhal Rebellion** and **Munda Rebellion**, highlighting the widespread discontent among indigenous communities. </ul

question: Identify the tribal leader who led the Kol Revolt (1831-1832) in Chotanagpur against British exploitation.

Raghunath Mahato initiated a farmers' revolt against forced taxation.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Budhu Bhagat** was a prominent tribal leader who mobilized the tribal peasantry in the **Chotanagpur region** during the **Kol Revolt** of **1831-1832**. 
• The Kol Revolt was an uprising led by the **Kol tribal community** against British exploitation, oppressive revenue policies, and the encroachment of their lands. 
• Budhu Bhagat became the face of the resistance, organizing the tribal peasants to fight against the colonial forces and their local collaborators, including zamindars. 
• The movement was marked by guerrilla warfare tactics, with tribal warriors attacking British establishments and symbols of exploitation in the **Chotanagpur Plateau**.

 __ 
• **Kol Revolt (1831-1832):** 
• The Kol Revolt was primarily triggered by the exploitation of tribal communities, including high land taxes, forced labor, and the loss of their ancestral lands. 
• It was a significant uprising that involved various tribal groups, including the Kols, Mundas, and Oraons. 
• The revolt spread across regions of modern-day **Jharkhand** and parts of Bihar, impacting British administrative control in these areas.

• **Geographical Context:** 
• The Kol Revolt was concentrated in the **Chotanagpur Plateau**, which is rich in mineral resources and has historically been home to tribal communities. 
• British exploitation of these resources and imposition of zamindari systems disrupted the traditional tribal way of life. 
• **Impact of the Kol Revolt:** 
• Although the revolt was suppressed, it forced the British to reconsider their revenue and administrative policies in tribal regions. 
• The uprising laid the foundation for subsequent tribal revolts, such as the **Munda Rebellion (1899-1900)** led by **Birsa Munda**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Tribal Movements in India:** 
• Tribal revolts were often triggered by the loss of autonomy, exploitation by landlords, and oppressive colonial policies. 
• Prominent uprisings include the **Santal Rebellion** (1855-1856), the **Munda Rebellion** (1899-1900), and the **Chuar Revolt** (1767-1809). 
• These movements were typically localized but were critical in shaping the narrative of resistance against colonial rule. 
• **Role of Tribal Leaders:** 
• Tribal leaders like **Budhu Bhagat**, **Birsa Munda**, and **Sidu-Kanhu** became symbols of resistance and are still revered as heroes in their communities.

• **The first English factory in Bengal was set up on the banks of the river "Hugli" in 1651.**
 
• The factory was established by the East India Company and was located in the village of Hooghly, which was then a part of the **Bengal Subah of the Mughal Empire.**
 
• The factory was initially used as a trading post for the** Company's goods, particularly textiles and spices.**
 
• Over time, the English established more factories in the region, including in** Calcutta (now Kolkata), which became the Company's headquarters in Bengal.**

• ** The East India Company was a British joint-stock company that was formed in 1600 for the purpose of trading with India and Southeast Asia.**
 
• The Company had a monopoly on English trade with these regions and was granted extensive privileges and powers by the British Crown, including the right to establish its own army and navy, negotiate treaties with local rulers, and administer justice in its own territories.
 
• Over time, the Company became increasingly involved in Indian politics and began to exert its influence over local rulers and territories.
 
• The Company's domination of Indian trade and its political power eventually led to the colonization of India by the British Empire.
 
• The Company's rule in India came to an end in** 1858,** when the British Crown assumed direct control over India following the Indian Rebellion of **1857.**

question: Ramakrishna Gopal Bhandarkar and Mahadev Govind Ranade carried out their work of religious reforms in Maharashtra through which of the following organisations?
solution:
The correct answer is Prarthana Samaj.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Prarthana Samaj:**-

 
 
• The Prarthana Samaj was founded in 1867 in Bombay by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang.
 
• It was an off-shoot of Brahmo Samaj.
 
• It was a reform movement within Hinduism and Justice M.G.
 
• **Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar joined it in 1870 and infused new strength to it.**
 
• **Mahadev Govind Ranade also ran the Deccan Education Society.**
 
• Several members of the Prarthana Samaj had earlier been active in the Paramhansa Mandali.
 
• This Samaj denounced idolatry, priestly domination, caste rigidities, and preferred monotheism.
 
• It also concentrated on social reforms like inter-dining, inter-marriage, widow remarriage, and the uplift of women and depressed classes.
 
• Apart from Hindu sects, it also drew upon Christianity and Buddhism.
 
• It sought truth in all religions.
 
• Drawing inspiration from the Maratha Bhakti saints of the medieval period, Ranade sought to establish the concept of one compassionate God.
 
• Veeresalingam Pantulu was the Telugu reformer who encouraged the Prarthana Samaj in South India.​
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Atmiya Sabha:-**

 
 
• It tried to initiate social and religious reforms in society. 
 
• The association was a philosophical discussion circle in India.
 
• They used to conduct debate and discussion sessions on philosophical topics and also used to promote free and collective thinking and social reform.
 
• The foundation of Atmiya Sabha in 1815 is considered the beginning of the modern age in Kolkata.
 
 
 
• **Theosophical Society:-**
 
 
• It was founded by Madam HP Blavatsky and Col HS Olcott in New York in 1875.
 
• In 1882, its headquarters were shifted to Adyar (Tamil Nadu). 
 
• Theosophical Society of India was founded by Annie Beasant.
 
• The Theosophical Society sought inspiration from Indian thought and culture.
 
• It advocated the revival and strengthening of ancient religion of Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism.
 
 
 
• **Brahmo Samaj:-**
 
 
• It was formed in 1828
 
• It prohibited all forms of idolatry and sacrifice, believed in the Upanishads, and forbade its members from criticising other religious practices.
 
• It critically drew upon the ideals of religions – especially of Hinduism and Christianity – looking at their negative and positive dimensions.
 
• Brahmo ;Samaj discarded faith in divine Avatars.

• **Annie Besant** was a **British socialist, women's rights activist, and theosophist **who played a significant role in India's struggle for independence from British rule.
 
• She promoted the studies of **ancient Indian religions, philosophies, and doctrines** through the Theosophical Society.
 
• Annie Besant became the **President** of the **Theosophical Society in 1907,** which was founded in **New York in 1875.**
 
• The Theosophical Society aimed to promote the study of **comparative religion, philosophy, and science, **and to investigate the unexplained laws of nature and the powers latent in humanity.
 
• Besant believed that ancient **Indian wisdom** had much to offer the world, and she worked tirelessly to promote the **study of Hinduism, Buddhism,** and other **Eastern religions** through the Theosophical Society.
 
• She also co-authored a book called **'The Secret Doctrine'** with the founder of **Theosophical Society, Madame Blavatsky, **which explored the origins of the universe and humanity's place in it.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Arya Samaj**

 
 
• Arya Samaj was founded by **Swami Dayanand Saraswati** in **1875 in Bombay.**
 
• It aimed to promote the **study of the Vedas **and to **reform Hinduism** by rejecting **idol worship and caste system.**
 
• Although Arya Samaj promoted the study of ancient Indian religions, it **did not **have a significant influence on Annie Besant's work.
 
 
 
• 
 **Paramhans Mandali **

 
 
• Paramhans Mandali was a religious and social reform organization** founded by Dadoba Pandurang in 1840 in Bombay (now Mumbai).**
 
• It aimed at abolishing caste distinctions and promoting social equality.
 
• Advocated for the study and interpretation of Vedanta philosophy.
 
• Emphasized rational thinking and education..
 
 
 
• **Prarthana Samaj**

subject: GK
question: British Parliament introduced Indian High Courts Act in which year?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1861**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Indian High Courts Act was introduced by the British Parliament in the year **1861**.
 
• This act led to the establishment of High Courts in India for the first time, replacing the older Supreme Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• The High Courts were given extensive original and appellate jurisdiction, marking a significant shift in the Indian judicial system.
 
• These High Courts were modeled after the English judicial system and were intended to provide a higher level of judicial administration in the major cities of India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Indian High Courts Act 1861**

 
 
• The Indian High Courts Act 1861 was an act of the British Parliament that led to the creation of High Courts in India in the three Presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• Before this act, the judicial system in these cities was managed by Supreme Courts, which were established under the Charter Act of 1774.
 
• The new High Courts were granted original civil and criminal jurisdiction, appellate jurisdiction, and supervisory jurisdiction over the lower courts.
 
• This act was significant as it brought uniformity and improvement in the judicial administration of British India.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Courts of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras**
 
 
• These courts were established under the Regulating Act of 1773 and subsequent acts, and they functioned until the High Courts were established in 1861.
 
• They were the highest courts in British India and had both original and appellate jurisdiction.
 
• The Supreme Courts were replaced by the High Courts to streamline and improve the judicial system.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Administration in British India**
 
 
• The British introduced several reforms to the judicial system in India to make it more efficient and aligned with British legal principles.
 
• The High Courts Act was a part of these reforms, which aimed to enhance the administration of justice in the colonies.
 
• These reforms were crucial in shaping the modern Indian judicial system.

question: Sido and Kanhu were leaders of which of the following tribal rebellions?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Santhal Rebellion**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Santhal Rebellion, also known as the Santhal Hool, was a tribal rebellion in present-day Jharkhand, India, against both British colonial authority and zamindari system.
 
• The rebellion was led by the four Murmu Brothers - Sidhu, Kanhu, Chand, and Bhairav.
 
• The Santhals were an indigenous tribal community that faced exploitation and oppression under the British rule and local landlords.
 
• The rebellion began on 30th June 1855 and lasted until the suppression of the uprising by the British in 1856.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Moplah Rebellion**

 
 
• The Moplah Rebellion of 1921 was an armed revolt by the Mappila Muslims of Kerala against British authority and the Hindu landlords.
 
• The rebellion was part of the Khilafat Movement and was characterized by communal violence between Mappilas and Hindus.
 
• The British suppressed the rebellion with considerable violence, and it is considered one of the significant uprisings against colonial rule in India.
 
 
 
• **Kol Rebellion**
 
 
• The Kol Rebellion (1831-32) was a revolt by the Kols, a tribal community in the Chotanagpur region against British rule and local landlords.
 
• The rebellion was primarily against the introduction of new revenue policies and exploitation by moneylenders and landlords.
 
• The British eventually suppressed the rebellion, but it remains a significant event in the history of tribal resistance in India.
 
 
 
• **Munda Rebellion**
 
 
• The Munda Rebellion (1899-1900) was led by Birsa Munda, a tribal leader, against British colonial rule in the Chotanagpur Plateau area.
 
• The rebellion aimed to establish Munda Raj and remove British government and missionaries from the region.
 
• The British suppressed the rebellion, but Birsa Munda is remembered as a prominent tribal freedom fighter in Indian history.

question: Which of the following Acts introduced 'provincial autonomy' by discontinuing the application of dyarchy?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Government of India Act, 1935**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935, introduced the concept of 'provincial autonomy' in British India.
 
• This Act marked the end of the system of dyarchy introduced by the Government of India Act, 1919.
 
• Under provincial autonomy, provinces were given more authority and independence in their internal administration.
 
• Indian ministers, chosen by provincial legislatures, were given authority in provincial governments, reducing the British governors' power.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Government of India Act, 1919**

 
 
• Also known as the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.
 
• Introduced the concept of dyarchy in the provinces, splitting the provincial subjects into reserved and transferred subjects.
 
• Reserved subjects were administered by the Governor and his Executive Council, while transferred subjects were administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislative council.
 
 
 
• **Charter Act of 1813**
 
 
• It ended the East India Company's commercial monopoly in India, opening trade to private British merchants.
 
• Asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Indian territories held by the Company.
 
• Provided for the promotion of education in India.
 
 
 
• **India Council Act, 1909**
 
 
• Also known as the Morley-Minto Reforms.
 
• Introduced separate electorates for Muslims, a measure designed to provide representation to minorities.
 
• Increased the size of the legislative councils at both the central and provincial levels.

question: Which of the following Sikh reform movements was started in 1873 in Amritsar?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Singh Sabha Movement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Singh Sabha Movement was a Sikh reform movement started in **1873 in Amritsar**.
 
• It aimed at reforming the Sikh community by promoting education and a return to the teachings of the Sikh Gurus.
 
• The movement was a reaction to the proselytizing activities of Christian missionaries and the Arya Samaj, which were seen as a threat to Sikhism.
 
• It played a significant role in the revival of Sikh institutions, literature, and the Punjabi language.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Babbar Akali Movement:**

 
 
• This was a militant movement in the 1920s aimed at freeing India from British rule.
 
• The Babbar Akali Dal was formed by a group of Sikh farmers in Punjab.
 
• They were against British policies and sought to restore Sikh sovereignty.
 
• It was named "Babbar" (lion) to denote the fierce nature of the movement.
 
 
 
• **Akali Movement:**
 
 
• The Akali Movement (also known as the Gurudwara Reform Movement) was a campaign in the early 20th century to reform the management of Sikh gurudwaras.
 
• It aimed at removing corrupt mahants (custodians) appointed by the British government.
 
• The movement led to the formation of the Shiromani Gurudwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC).
 
• The SGPC now oversees the management of gurudwaras in Punjab, Haryana, and Himachal Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Gurudwara Movement:**
 
 
• This movement is synonymous with the Akali Movement mentioned above.
 
• It focused on freeing Sikh places of worship from the control of corrupt mahants.
 
• The movement gained momentum in the 1920s and led to significant reforms in the management of Sikh religious institutions.
 
• It was a major milestone in the history of the Sikhs and their religious autonomy.

question: In which of the following years was VD Savarkar sent to Andaman Jail by the British?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1911**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, also known as Veer Savarkar, was a prominent freedom fighter, social reformer, and writer.
 
• In 1910, Savarkar was arrested by the British for his involvement in revolutionary activities against the colonial regime.
 
• He was subsequently tried and sentenced to two life terms of imprisonment totaling fifty years and was deported to the Andaman Islands in 1911.
 
• The Cellular Jail in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, also known as Kala Pani, was where he was imprisoned. This jail was notorious for its harsh conditions and was used by the British to exile political prisoners.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Vinayak Damodar Savarkar:**

 
 
• He was born on May 28, 1883, in Bhagur, a village near Nashik in Maharashtra, India.
 
• He was a staunch advocate of Hindutva and is credited with founding the ideology.
 
• Savarkar wrote several books, including "The First War of Indian Independence 1857," which presented the uprising of 1857 as a unified and national effort against British rule.
 
• After his release from prison, he continued his activities as a social reformer and political activist, although he was kept under strict surveillance by the British authorities.
 
 
 
• **Cellular Jail (Kala Pani):**
 
 
• The Cellular Jail is located in Port Blair, the capital of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
 
• It was constructed by the British between 1896 and 1906 to exile political prisoners.
 
• The jail is known for its solitary confinement cells, which were designed to isolate prisoners from each other and prevent them from communicating.
 
• Many prominent Indian freedom fighters, including Batukeshwar Dutt, Yogendra Shukla, and more, were imprisoned here.
 
• Today, the Cellular Jail is a national memorial monument.

question: Where was the first official summit of the Non-Aligned movement held?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Yugoslavia**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The first official summit of the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in September 1961.
 
• The summit was a significant event as it marked the formal establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement.
 
• The NAM was founded during the Cold War as a group of states that were not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc.
 
• The movement aimed to create an independent path in world politics that would not be aligned with any major power bloc, particularly the United States or the Soviet Union.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)**

 
 
• The Non-Aligned Movement is a forum of 120 developing world states that are not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc.
 
• After the United Nations, it is the largest grouping of states worldwide.
 
• It originated in the Bandung Conference of 1955, and its first summit was held in Belgrade, Yugoslavia, in 1961.
 
• Key principles of NAM include mutual respect for territorial integrity and sovereignty, mutual non-aggression, mutual non-interference in domestic affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
 
 
 
• **Bandung Conference**
 
 
• The Bandung Conference, also known as the Asian-African Conference, was a meeting of Asian and African states, most of which were newly independent.
 
• It took place on 18-24 April 1955 in Bandung, Indonesia.
 
• The conference aimed to promote Afro-Asian economic and cultural cooperation and to oppose colonialism or neocolonialism by any nation.
 
• The conference was an important step in the establishment of the Non-Aligned Movement.
 
 
 
• **Cold War**
 
 
• The Cold War was a period of geopolitical tension between the Soviet Union and the United States and their respective allies, the Eastern Bloc and the Western Bloc, after World War II.
 
• The period is generally considered to span from 1947, the year the Truman Doctrine was announced, to 1991, the year the Soviet Union collapsed.
 
• It was marked by a rivalry between the two superpowers, which did not result in direct large-scale fighting between the two, but involved proxy wars, the arms race, and ideological competition.

question: In which year was the battle of Buxar fought?
solution:
The correct answer is __**1764**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Battle of Buxar was fought on 22 October 1764.
 
• It was a significant battle between the British East India Company and the combined forces of the Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II, Nawab of Awadh Shuja-ud-Daula, and Nawab of Bengal Mir Qasim.
 
• The victory of the British East India Company in the Battle of Buxar solidified their position in India and paved the way for their eventual control over large parts of the Indian subcontinent.
 
• This battle is considered a pivotal point in Indian history as it marked the beginning of British colonial rule in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **British East India Company**

 
 
• The British East India Company was an English company formed for the exploitation of trade with East and Southeast Asia and India, incorporated by royal charter on December 31, 1600.
 
• It eventually came to rule large areas of India with its own private armies, exercising military power and assuming administrative functions.
 
 
 
• **Mughal Empire**
 
 
• The Mughal Empire was an empire in the Indian subcontinent, founded in 1526.
 
• It was established and ruled by a Muslim dynasty with Turko-Mongol Chagatai roots from Central Asia and lasted until the mid-19th century.
 
 
 
• **Nawab of Bengal**
 
 
• The Nawab of Bengal was the hereditary ruler of Bengal and Bihar, with the capital at Murshidabad.
 
• The last independent Nawab of Bengal, Mir Qasim, was a key figure in the Battle of Buxar.
 
 
 
• **Nawab of Awadh**
 
 
• The Nawab of Awadh was the hereditary ruler of the state of Awadh (Oudh) in northern India.
 
• Shuja-ud-Daula, the Nawab of Awadh, was one of the key figures in the Battle of Buxar, fighting against the British East India Company.

• Swami Dayanand Saraswati was a renowned Hindu religious scholar, reformer, and the founder of the Arya Samaj.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The movement's slogan is "Krinvanto Vishwam Aryam" which means "Make the world noble".

• Arya Samaj has been instrumental in promoting education, especially for women, and eradicating social evils like child marriage and caste discrimination.

• **Swami Dayanand Saraswati**

• Born as Mool Shankar Tiwari on February 12, 1824, in Tankara, Gujarat.

• He was a staunch critic of idolatry and ritualistic worship and advocated for a return to the teachings of the Vedas.

• His notable work, "Satyarth Prakash" (The Light of Truth), outlines his vision of a reformed society.

• He was a Hindu philosopher and religious reformer, associated with the Brahmo Samaj.

• He was the father of Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore.

• Though not directly related to the Arya Samaj, he played a significant role in the religious and social reform movements in Bengal.

• **Swami Vivekanand**

• Born as Narendranath Datta on January 12, 1863, he was a chief disciple of the 19th-century Indian mystic Ramakrishna.

• He founded the Ramakrishna Mission and the Ramakrishna Math.

• He is best known for his speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago in 1893, where he introduced Hinduism to the Western world.

• **Raja Ram Mohan Roy**

• He was a prominent social and educational reformer who is often called the "Father of the Indian Renaissance".

• He founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828, which played a key role in reforming and modernizing Indian society.

question: Who is called the father of Local Self-Government in India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Lord Ripon**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Lord Ripon** is known as the father of local self-government in India for his efforts to introduce local governance reforms.
 
• In 1882, he passed a resolution that laid the foundation for local self-governance in India.
 
• His resolution allowed for the formation of local bodies with elected representatives, marking a significant step towards decentralization.
 
• Lord Ripon's reforms aimed to improve administrative efficiency and encourage public participation in local governance.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lord Cornwallis**

 
 
• Lord Cornwallis served as the Governor-General of India from 1786 to 1793.
 
• He is known for his role in the establishment of the Permanent Settlement of Bengal in 1793, which introduced a new land revenue system.
 
• This system had long-lasting effects on the agrarian structure of Bengal and other parts of India.
 
 
 
• **Lord Wellesley**
 
 
• Lord Wellesley served as the Governor-General of India from 1798 to 1805.
 
• He is known for his aggressive expansionist policies and the establishment of British supremacy in India through the policy of Subsidiary Alliances.
 
• His tenure saw the defeat of Tipu Sultan in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War and the annexation of large territories.
 
 
 
• **Lord William Bentinck**
 
 
• Lord William Bentinck served as the Governor-General of India from 1828 to 1835.
 
• He is known for his social and administrative reforms, including the abolition of Sati and suppression of Thuggee.
 
• He also introduced English as the medium of instruction in Indian education.
 
 
 
• **Local Self-Government**
 
 
• Local self-government refers to the administration of local areas by elected representatives who are accountable to the local community.
 
• It aims to decentralize administrative functions and promote public participation in governance.
 
• Local self-governance in India includes institutions like Panchayats in rural areas and Municipalities in urban areas.
 
• These institutions play a crucial role in the delivery of basic services, local development, and civic engagement.

question: What was the primary objective of the Ring-Fencing Policy adopted by the British in India during the 18th century?

options.text: To expand British territory by annexing Indian states
To economically exploit coastal trading companies
To create buffer states to defend British territories
To impose direct rule over all princely territories

solution:
The correct answer is __**To create buffer states to defend British territories**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Ring-Fencing Policy was primarily aimed at creating buffer states to protect British territories in India, particularly from external threats like the Marathas and Afghan invasions.
 
• It was implemented during the late 18th century under Governor-General Warren Hastings' administration, as the British East India Company sought to secure its territorial acquisitions.
 
• States such as Awadh (Oudh) were turned into buffer zones through alliances or treaties, ensuring that these regions bore the brunt of invasions before they could threaten core British territories like Bengal.
 
• The policy involved maintaining a strong military presence and entering into subsidiary alliances to control the external policies of the Indian princely states while allowing them nominal sovereignty.
 
• This strategy laid the groundwork for the subsequent Subsidiary Alliance system introduced by Lord Wellesley, which further tightened British control over Indian states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1: To expand British territory by annexing Indian states**
 
 
• This was not the primary objective of the Ring-Fencing Policy. Territorial expansion became a more prominent strategy later under policies like the Doctrine of Lapse (introduced by Lord Dalhousie) and outright annexation through military conquest.
 
• The Ring-Fencing Policy was more about securing existing territories rather than expanding them aggressively.
 
 
 
• **Option 2: To economically exploit coastal trading companies**
 
 
• This option does not align with the core objective of the Ring-Fencing Policy, which was focused on military and territorial security.
 
• Economic exploitation of India by the British was carried out through trade monopolies, land revenue systems like the Permanent Settlement, and later, industrial policies. However, these were separate from the Ring-Fencing Policy.
 
 
 
• **Option 4: To impose direct rule over all princely territories**
 
 
• The Ring-Fencing Policy did not aim at imposing direct British rule over princely states. Instead, it sought to maintain the sovereignty of buffer states while controlling their external affairs.
 
• Direct rule over princely states was achieved later through policies like the Subsidiary Alliance and the Doctrine of Lapse.
 
 
 
• **Main Theme: The Ring-Fencing Policy**
 
 
• The Ring-Fencing Policy was one of the earliest strategies employed by the British East India Company to secure its territories in India.
 
• It was a defensive strategy focusing on the containment of threats from external powers like the Marathas, Afghans, and other regional rulers.
 
• It marked the beginning of British interference in the internal affairs of Indian princely states, paving the way for eventual domination over the Indian subcontinent.
 
 
</ul

question: Which major constitutional feature was first introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935 and later adopted in the Indian Constitution?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Federal structure with Provincial Autonomy**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Government of India Act, 1935, introduced the concept of a** federal structure** in India, dividing powers between the Centre and the Provinces.
 
• It provided for** Provincial Autonomy**, giving elected provincial legislatures and governments significant control over provincial subjects.
 
• Under this Act, the provinces were granted the right to legislate on subjects listed in the Provincial List without interference from the Centre.
 
• It marked the first time that Indian provinces were allowed to administer their own affairs independently, albeit under the overarching supervision of the British government.
 
• This federal principle, with a division of powers between the Centre and states, was later adopted and expanded in the Indian Constitution of 1950.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Fundamental Duties**
 
 
• Fundamental Duties were not part of the original Indian Constitution. They were added by the 42nd Amendment Act in 1976.
 
• They are enshrined in Part IVA (Article 51A) of the Constitution and outline the moral obligations of citizens to promote a spirit of patriotism and uphold the unity of India.
 
• Examples include respecting the Constitution, safeguarding public property, and protecting the natural environment.
 
 
 
• **Parliamentary Sovereignty**
 
 
• Parliamentary Sovereignty refers to the concept where the Parliament is the supreme legal authority, capable of creating or ending any law.
 
• This concept is a feature of the British Parliamentary system but is not fully applicable to India as the Indian Constitution is supreme and Parliament operates within its limits.
 
• In India, Parliament is not sovereign due to the system of judicial review and the federal structure of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Universal Adult Franchise**
 
 
• Universal Adult Franchise guarantees that every adult citizen, irrespective of caste, gender, religion, or economic status, has the right to vote in elections.
 
• This was adopted in India with the commencement of the Constitution on January 26, 1950.
 
• It was not introduced by the Government of India Act, 1935, but rather was a decision made during the drafting of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
</ul

question:
**Fill in the blank: **

The Federal Court of India, as provided under the Government of India Act 1935, was established in the year ____.
solution:
The correct answer is __**1937**__.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 
__ 

• The **Federal Court of India** was established under the provisions of the **Government of India Act, 1935**, which was a landmark legislation enacted by the British Parliament to provide a new constitutional framework for India. 

• The Federal Court was formally inaugurated on **1 October 1937**, making it the first apex court of India before the Supreme Court was established post-independence. 

• The court had jurisdiction to resolve disputes between provinces and princely states, as well as to hear appeals against decisions of the High Courts in certain cases. 

• It comprised a Chief Justice and not more than six judges. The first Chief Justice of the Federal Court was **Sir Maurice Gwyer**. 

• The Federal Court functioned until **28 January 1950**, when it was replaced by the **Supreme Court of India** under the Constitution of India. 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 
__ 

• **Government of India Act, 1935**: 
 

• The act is regarded as the most comprehensive legislation enacted by the British Parliament for governing India. It introduced significant constitutional reforms, including the establishment of the Federal Court. 

• It provided for a federal structure, dyarchy at the provincial level, and direct elections for legislative bodies. 
 
 

• **Jurisdiction of the Federal Court**: 
 

• The Federal Court had **original jurisdiction** to settle disputes between the provinces and princely states. 

• It also had **appellate jurisdiction** over decisions of the High Courts in cases involving the interpretation of the Government of India Act, 1935. 

• However, decisions of the Federal Court could be appealed to the **Judicial Committee of the Privy Council** in London. 
 
 

• **Composition**: 
 

• The Federal Court consisted of the Chief Justice and a maximum of six other judges appointed by the British Crown. 

• The judges were selected based on their legal expertise and experience in judicial service. 
 
 

• **Replacement by Supreme Court**: 
 

• With the enforcement of the **Constitution of India** on **26 January 1950**, the Federal Court ceased to exist and was replaced by the **Supreme Court of India**. 

• The Supreme Court inherited the jurisdiction and functions of the Federal Court, along with additional powers outlined in the Constitution. 
 
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
 

• **Sir Maurice Gwyer**, the first Chief Justice of the Federal Court, played a pivotal role in shaping the judicial legacy of the Federal Court and establishing its independence. 

• The Federal Court served as an important precedent for the creation of the independent judiciary in India, highlighting the concept of separation of powers and the rule of law. 

• The Federal Court's original jurisdiction was limited, as it primarily dealt with inter-governmental disputes and constitutional matters under the 1935 Act. 

• Though the Federal Court was an important institution, its decisions were often subject to review by the **Privy Council**, reflecting the colonial nature of governance during that period.

question: **Fill in the blank**: The Factory Act 1881 primarily regulated ____.

options.text: working hours of women and children
night shifts hours for men only
minimum wage for women and children

solution:
The correct answer is __**working hours of women and children**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Factory Act of 1881** was introduced during British rule in India to regulate working conditions in factories, particularly focusing on the **working hours of women and children**.
 
• The Act limited the number of working hours for children under the age of **12** to **9 hours per day**, aiming to prevent exploitation and ensure their welfare.
 
• It also mandated that children working in factories were to receive **four holidays in a month** and adequate rest intervals during work hours.
 
• For women, the Act aimed to regulate working hours to ensure they were not subjected to long or harsh working hours, which could negatively impact their health and family responsibilities.
 
• The Factory Act of 1881 was significant because it marked the beginning of **legislative efforts** to regulate labor conditions in India, paving the way for future labor reforms. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Important Provisions of Factory Act 1881:**

 
 
• The Act was introduced by the British government as a response to social reform efforts aimed at improving labor conditions.
 
• It was applicable to factories employing **100 or more workers**, focusing on industries where exploitation of labor was rampant.
 
• The Act mandated the provision of **ventilation, lighting, and sanitary conditions** in factories to improve worker health.
 
• It required factory owners to maintain **records of child workers** to ensure compliance with age and working hour restrictions.
 
 
 
• **Subsequent Developments:**
 
 
• The **Factory Act of 1891** further enhanced the provisions of the 1881 Act by reducing working hours for children and introducing restrictions on night work for women.
 
• Later, the **Indian Factories Act of 1948** replaced earlier legislations and introduced comprehensive measures for labor welfare, including safety, working conditions, and health regulations.
 
 
 
• **Impact on Labor Welfare:**
 
 
• The Factory Act of 1881 was the first step toward improving labor conditions in India, though its scope was limited to specific industries and regions.
 
• It raised awareness of the need for **labor laws** in India and led to increased focus on worker rights and welfare in subsequent decades.
 
 
 
• **Similar Laws in Other Countries:**
 
 
• In England, the **Factory Acts** of the 19th century aimed to improve working conditions, especially for women and children, setting an example for India.
 
• Other countries, such as the United States, also passed labor laws during the Industrial Revolution to regulate working hours and ensure safety in factories.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Historical Context:** The Factory Act of 1881 was introduced during the tenure of **Lord Ripon**, who is known for his reform-oriented policies in India.
 
• **Age Restrictions:** The Act defined a child worker as someone under the age of **12 years**, marking an early attempt to regulate child labor.
 
• **Industrial Revolution Influence:** The Act was inspired by similar labor laws enacted in Britain during the **Industrial Revolution**.
 
• **Social Impact:** While the Act was limited in scope, it marked an important step toward addressing labor exploitation and improving working conditions in colonial India.

question: The revolutionary Bagha Jatin (Jatindranath Mukherjee) was known for his valiant fight and for inspiring revolutionaries in which Indian state?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Bengal**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Bagha Jatin**, also known as **Jatindranath Mukherjee**, was a prominent revolutionary leader during the Indian freedom struggle.

• He hailed from the state of **Bengal**, which played a pivotal role in the revolutionary activities against British rule.

• Bagha Jatin earned his moniker "Bagha" (meaning tiger) after he killed a tiger single-handedly in **1906**, showcasing his unparalleled bravery.

• He was a key figure in organizing revolutionary groups in **Bengal**, including the **Jugantar Party**, which actively worked against British imperialism.

• Bagha Jatin's valiant fight against the British forces in **1915** at **Balasore, Odisha**, remains one of the most heroic episodes of India's struggle for independence.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Bengal's Role in Revolutionary Activities:**

• **Bengal** emerged as a hub for revolutionary activities during the early 20th century due to widespread dissatisfaction with British policies like the **Partition of Bengal in 1905**.

• Several revolutionary organizations such as the **Jugantar** and **Anushilan Samiti** were established in Bengal to challenge British authority.

• Prominent revolutionaries like **Bagha Jatin, Surya Sen, Khudiram Bose, and Prafulla Chaki** hailed from Bengal and contributed significantly to India's independence movement.

• **Life and Legacy of Bagha Jatin:**

• **Born:** Jatin was born on **7 December 1879** in **Kushtia, Bengal Presidency** (now in Bangladesh).

• He was deeply influenced by **Swami Vivekananda**, who inspired him to dedicate his life to the service of the nation.

• Jatin played a crucial role in procuring arms and organizing revolutionary activities aimed at overthrowing British rule.

• His famous last words, "Amra morbo, jagat jagbe" (We shall die so that the world may awaken), reflect his selfless sacrifice for the nation.

• **Other States in the Context of Revolutionaries:**

• **Punjab:** Punjab was known for revolutionaries like **Bhagat Singh, Lala Lajpat Rai, and Udham Singh**, who played pivotal roles in India's struggle for freedom.

• **Uttar Pradesh:** Uttar Pradesh was home to leaders like **Chandrashekhar Azad** and served as a significant center for revolutionary activities, including the Kakori Train Robbery.

• **Bihar:** Bihar contributed leaders like **Jayaprakash Narayan** and revolutionary activities during the Quit India Movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Jugantar Party:** Founded in **1906**, this revolutionary group aimed to overthrow British rule through armed resistance.

• **Partition of Bengal (1905):** A British policy aimed at dividing Bengal along religious lines, which led to widespread protests and the rise of revolutionary movements.

• **Balasore Battle (1915):** Bagha Jatin and his associates fought valiantly against British forces but were ultimately outnumbered and defeated, leading to Jatin's martyrdom.

• **Legacy:** Jatin's life continues to inspire generations of Indians, symbolizing courage and patriotism in the face of oppression.
</ul

• The Writers' Building was targeted because it housed key British administrative offices, making it a significant symbol of colonial power. 
• During the attack, the trio entered the building disguised as civilians and assassinated **Colonel N.S. Simpson**, the Inspector General of Prisons, known for his oppressive measures against political prisoners.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• The **Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919** introduced the system of **dyarchy (dual government)** in the provinces of British India. This was a major constitutional reform aimed at increasing Indian participation in governance. 
• Under dyarchy, the provincial subjects were divided into two categories: **Transferred** and **Reserved**. 
• **Transferred subjects**: These included areas like education, public health, agriculture, and local government, which were administered by Indian ministers responsible to the legislative councils. 
• **Reserved subjects**: These included areas like finance, police, and revenue, which were controlled by the British Governor and his executive council. 
• The reforms were based on the **Montagu-Chelmsford Report of 1918**, authored by Edwin Montagu (Secretary of State for India) and Lord Chelmsford (Viceroy of India). 
• The objective of the reforms was to gradually introduce a **responsible government** in India while retaining British control over vital areas of administration. 
• The system of dyarchy, however, was heavily criticized due to its complexity and inefficiency. It failed to meet the aspirations of Indian leaders and was eventually replaced by provincial autonomy under the **Government of India Act of 1935**. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **The Indian Councils Act of 1861:** 
• This Act marked the beginning of **legislative devolution** by allowing Indians to be included in the law-making process as non-official members in the Viceroy's council. 
• It laid the foundation for **representative institutions** in India but did not introduce dyarchy. 
• **The Morley-Minto Reforms of 1909:** 
• Also known as the **Indian Councils Act of 1909**, this reform introduced the concept of **separate electorates** for Muslims. 
• It allowed for greater Indian representation in legislative councils but did not involve the division of subjects or dyarchy. 
• **The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919:** 
• Introduced dyarchy in provinces, which was a significant shift towards **self-governance**. 
• It also expanded the legislative councils and introduced direct elections for some seats. 
• This reform emphasized the principle of **increasing Indian participation** in governance. 
• **The Government of India Act of 1935:** 
• This Act replaced dyarchy with **provincial autonomy**, granting full control of provincial administration to Indian ministers. 
• It also proposed the establishment of a **federation** of British India and princely states, though this was never implemented. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Dyarchy:** 
• It was the first step towards **decentralization of power** in British India. 
• The system was criticized because the reserved subjects, controlled by the British, were often the more critical and resource-intensive areas. 
• **Failures of the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms:** 
• The division of subjects created confusion and inefficiency in governance. 
• Indian leaders criticized the reforms for not providing full self-governance or addressing key issues like taxation and economic exploitation. 
• **Historical Context:** The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms were introduced in the aftermath of World War I when India contributed significantly to the war effort. The reforms were a response to increasing demands for **political reforms** and self-governance. 
• **Legacy:** Though the dyarchy system was short-lived, it laid the groundwork for future reforms, eventually leading to India's independence in 1947. </ul

question:

**Assertion (A)**: Alluri Sitarama Raju led the Rampa Rebellion against the British.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• **Assertion (A):** Alluri Sitarama Raju led the **Rampa Rebellion** against the British in the early 1920s. This statement is **correct**.

• **Reason (R):** The rebellion was primarily a response to the **forest laws** imposed by the British, which severely restricted tribal access to their traditional resources such as forests and agricultural land. This statement is **correct**.

• The Rampa Rebellion, also known as the **Manyam Rebellion**, took place in the tribal areas of Andhra Pradesh, where Alluri Sitarama Raju emerged as a leader fighting for tribal rights.

• The forest laws imposed by the British disrupted the livelihood of the tribal people, who were heavily dependent on forest resources for their survival. This was one of the main causes of the rebellion.

• ***Hence, both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__

• **Alluri Sitarama Raju:**

• **Born:** 1897 in Andhra Pradesh, India.

• He was a revolutionary freedom fighter who fought against British colonial rule, particularly focusing on tribal rights.

• He advocated the use of guerrilla warfare tactics and led tribal people in armed resistance against British forces.

• **Rampa Rebellion:**

• The rebellion occurred between **1922 and 1924** in the Rampa region of present-day Andhra Pradesh.

• It was triggered by oppressive forest policies that deprived tribal communities of their traditional rights to use forest resources.

• The rebellion involved armed resistance against the British and was a significant event in the history of India's freedom struggle.

• **Forest Laws:**

• The British colonial government implemented forest laws to gain control over forest resources, restricting access for local communities.

• These laws included measures like prohibiting shifting cultivation, banning grazing, and limiting access to forest produce.

• These policies led to widespread discontent among tribal populations who depended on forests for their livelihood.

• **Legacy of Alluri Sitarama Raju:**

• He is remembered as a hero and martyr of India's freedom movement.

• In honor of his contributions, various institutions and places have been named after him, including statues and memorials.

• His efforts showcased the role of tribal communities in resisting colonial oppression.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• **Guerrilla Warfare:** Alluri Sitarama Raju adopted guerrilla tactics to fight against British forces, utilizing the dense forest terrain to his advantage.

• **Impact of Forest Policies:** The forest policies disrupted the economic and social fabric of tribal communities, making them central to the freedom struggle in Rampa.

• **Arrest and Execution:** In **1924**, Alluri Sitarama Raju was captured and executed by the British, marking the end of the rebellion.

question: Tana Bhagat led a unique tribal movement in the early 20th century, emphasizing reforms and non-violence against the British and local landlords among the Oraon community in which modern-day state?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Jharkhand**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Tana Bhagat Movement** was a tribal uprising led by **Tana Bhagat** in the early 20th century among the **Oraon community** residing in what is now the state of **Jharkhand**. 
• The movement began as a response to the oppression faced by the Oraon community under the **British colonial rule** and the local landlords (zamindars). 
• The movement was unique as it emphasized **non-violence** and sought reforms in the tribal society, such as **abstinence from alcohol**, adopting cleanliness, and rejecting superstitions. 
• The Tana Bhagat movement also had a **religious dimension**, as followers adopted practices inspired by Hindu rituals and Mahatma Gandhi’s ideals, including wearing khadi and boycotting British goods. 
• The movement gained momentum in the region that is today known as **Jharkhand**, which became a separate state in **2000** after being carved out of Bihar. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Oraon Community:** 
• The **Oraons** are one of the major tribal communities in India, primarily inhabiting the **Chotanagpur Plateau** region, which includes present-day **Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Odisha**. 
• Their traditional livelihood is based on **agriculture**, and they have a rich cultural heritage with unique dance, music, and festivals. 
• The Oraon community faced exploitation under the **British revenue system** and local zamindars, which led to several tribal uprisings, including the Tana Bhagat movement. 
• **Significance of the Tana Bhagat Movement:** 
• The movement was inspired by **Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy** of non-violence and self-reliance, making it one of the few peaceful tribal uprisings during British rule. 
• It sought to bring social and religious reform within the tribal community, emphasizing cleanliness, sobriety, and a rejection of traditional practices considered regressive. 
• The movement also had a political dimension, as it opposed the **oppression of the British** and their policies affecting the tribal population. 
• **Other Tribal Movements in Jharkhand:** 
• **Santhal Rebellion (1855-56):** The Santhals revolted against the British and zamindars due to economic exploitation and land alienation. 
• **Birsa Munda Uprising (1899-1900):** Led by **Birsa Munda**, this movement aimed at establishing Munda Raj and resisting British policies that disrupted the tribal way of life. 
• **Kol Rebellion (1831-1832):** The Kols revolted against the British and local landlords for their exploitative practices. 
• **Formation of Jharkhand:** 
• The state of **Jharkhand** was formed on **15th November 2000**, coinciding with the birth anniversary of tribal leader **Birsa Munda**. 
• It was carved out of **southern Bihar** and was primarily created to address the socio-economic and political aspirations of the tribal population in the region. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• The **Tana Bhagat movement** was a significant chapter in India’s tribal history, showcasing the unique blend of tribal traditions and Gandhian ideals. 
• It highlights the role of tribal communities in India’s **freedom struggle**, often overlooked in mainstream narratives. 
• The movement also reflects the socio-economic challenges faced by tribal communities under colonial rule, including **land alienation, economic exploitation, and cultural suppression**. 
• Understanding such movements is crucial for appreciating the diversity of India’s freedom struggle and the contributions of various marginalized communities.

question: The Subsidiary Alliance system had which of the following conditions for the allied Indian rulers?

options.text: They were allowed to maintain their own independent armies.
They had to keep a British Resident in their court.
They were free to enter into alliances with other Indian rulers without British consent.
They were not required to pay any revenue to the British.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The Subsidiary Alliance system had which of the following conditions for the allied Indian rulers?**__.
 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
 __ 
• **Statement 1:** They were allowed to maintain their own independent armies. This statement is **incorrect** as the Subsidiary Alliance system required allied Indian rulers to disband their independent armies and instead rely on British forces for defense. 
• **Statement 2:** They had to keep a British Resident in their court. This statement is **correct**. Under the Subsidiary Alliance, the allied Indian rulers were required to maintain a British Resident at their court to oversee administrative matters and safeguard British interests. 
• **Statement 3:** They were free to enter into alliances with other Indian rulers without British consent. This statement is **incorrect**. The system explicitly prohibited allied Indian rulers from entering into diplomatic or military alliances with other rulers without British approval. 
• **Statement 4:** They were not required to pay any revenue to the British. This statement is **incorrect**. The allied rulers had to pay a subsidy or revenue to the British for the maintenance of the British troops stationed within their territories. 
• **Correct Answer:** The correct condition under the Subsidiary Alliance was that allied Indian rulers had to keep a British Resident in their court (Statement 2). 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**
 __ 
• **Subsidiary Alliance System:** 
• The Subsidiary Alliance system was introduced by **Lord Wellesley**, the Governor-General of India from **1798 to 1805**, as part of British expansionist policies in India. 
• It was designed to establish British dominance over Indian states without direct annexation, enabling the British to control the political and military affairs of allied states. 
• Allied rulers under the Subsidiary Alliance system had to accept the presence of **British troops** within their territories. 
• They were required to pay a financial subsidy to the British for maintaining these troops, which often led to financial strain on the allied states. 
• **Key Features of Subsidiary Alliance:** 
• Allied rulers had to disband their independent armies and rely on British forces for protection against external and internal threats. 
• The British Resident stationed at the ruler's court acted as a political agent and monitored the ruler's actions to ensure alignment with British policies. 
• Allied rulers were prohibited from entering into alliances or engaging in diplomatic relations with other states without British approval. 
• The system often resulted in the erosion of sovereignty and autonomy of Indian rulers, making them dependent on British support. 
• **Examples of States under Subsidiary Alliance:** 
• **Hyderabad:** The Nizam of Hyderabad was among the first rulers to accept the Subsidiary Alliance in **1798**. 
• **Mysore:** After the defeat of Tipu Sultan in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Mysore was brought under the Subsidiary Alliance in **1799**. 
• **Awadh:** The Nawab of Awadh signed the Subsidiary Alliance in **1801**, leading to significant British control over the region. 
 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**
 
• **Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance:** 
• The system led to the loss of sovereignty and independence of Indian states, turning them into British dependencies. 
• It facilitated the expansion of British influence and control over Indian territories without direct annexation. 
• The financial burden of maintaining British troops often led to economic decline and political instability in allied states. 
• Many Indian rulers resented the system, considering it an infringement on their autonomy and dignity. 
• **Historical Context:** 
• The Subsidiary Alliance system played a crucial role in the establishment of British dominance in India during the late 18th and early 19th centuries. 
• It was an essential component of British imperial policies aimed at controlling Indian territories through indirect means. 
• The system laid the foundation for subsequent British annexations and consolidation of power in India. </ul

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Point__**

Wood's Despatch:

 
• In 1854, Charles Wood prepared a Despatch on an educational system for India.
 
• It was considered the "Magna Carta of English Education in India".
 
• This document was the first comprehensive plan for the spread of education in India.
 
• Some of the provisions of Charles Wood Despatch are as follows -
 
 
• It asked the Government of India to assume responsibility for the education of the masses, thus repudiating the 'downward filtration theory', at least on paper.
 
• It systematized the hierarchy from vernacular primary schools in villages at the bottom, followed by Anglo-Vernacular High Schools and an affiliated college at the district level, and affiliating universities in the presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
 
• It recommended a system of grants-in-aid to encourage private enterprise
 
• It recommended English as the medium of instruction for higher studies and vernaculars at the school level.
 
• The Despatch recommended the establishment of universities in the three Presidency towns of Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras. The universities were to be modeled after the London University and these were to have a senate consisting of a Chancellor, a Vice-Chancellor, and fellows who were nominated by the Government.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **QRSAM:**

 
 
• On 17 November 2020 the** Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile system (QRSAM) was successfully test-fired by Defense Research and Development Organisation (DRDO).**
 
• The test was conducted at** the Integrated Test Range, Chandipur off the Odisha coast.**
 
• The Test was in continuation of a series of missile tests conducted by DRDO over the past two months.
 
• **QRSAM is a canister-based system**, which means that it is stored and operated from specially designed compartments.
 
• In the canister, the inside environment is controlled, thus along with making its transport and storage easier, the shelf life of weapons also improves significantly.
 
• The system is capable of detecting and tracking targets on the move and engaging targets with short halts.
 
• It is a **short-range surface-to-air missile (SAM) system**, primarily designed and developed by DRDO to provide a protective shield to moving armored columns of the Army from enemy aerial attacks.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• 
 
 
• The entire weapon system has been configured on a mobile and maneuverable platform and is capable of providing air defense on the move.
 
• It has been designed for **induction into the Army and has a range of 25 to 30 km.**
 
• The QRSAM weapon ensemble which functions on the move consists of a fully automated command and control system.
 
• It also consists of two radars -** Active Array Battery Surveillance**
 
• **Radar and Active Array Battery Multifunction Radar - with one launcher.**
 
• Both radars have** 360-degree coverage** with the search on move and track on move capabilities.
 
• The system is compact, uses a **single-stage solid propelled missile**, and has a mid-course inertial navigation system with a two-way data link and terminal active seeker developed indigenously by DRDO.
